0.title: The Throne of Grace: The Book of 2 Samuel
0.overview:
The message. Second Samuel is the story of the king God chose, and of the promise God made him. David rises from fugitive to king of all Israel, and then God, not David, makes the great offer: “your house and your kingdom shall be made sure forever before me. Your throne shall be established forever” (7:16). Then the king who received that promise falls into adultery and murder, and the rest of his reign is spent under its consequences, in his own family. So the book teaches two things at once: God’s promise rests on God’s faithfulness, not on the king’s goodness; and even the best of Israel’s kings could not be the king his people needed. It leaves us looking for a Son of David who will keep the throne and not stain it.

Background: the writer. Samuel was one book in the Hebrew Bible, divided in two later because of its length, so 2 Samuel continues straight on from the death of Saul. The author is not named. Jewish tradition credited Samuel with the first part and the prophets Nathan and Gad with the rest, and Chronicles names records of David’s reign kept by all three (1 Chronicles 29:29). Its final editor drew on such records, and a note about “the kings of Judah” (1 Samuel 27:6) shows that he wrote after the kingdom divided. Many scholars see Samuel as part of a longer history from Deuteronomy to Kings, edited as late as the exile. This commentary takes the book to rest on early, eyewitness sources, prophetic in outlook, put into its final shape some time after Solomon.

When and where. David began to reign at thirty and reigned forty years, seven and a half at Hebron over Judah and thirty-three at Jerusalem over all Israel (5:4–5), about 1010 to 970 BC. It was a rare moment. Egypt was weak and Assyria had not yet risen, so a small kingdom in the hills could grow strong. The book records wars with the Philistines, Moab, Ammon, Edom and the Aramean kingdoms to the north (chapters 5, 8, 10). David took Jerusalem, a Jebusite city no tribe had held, and made it the capital of a united nation and the home of the ark. An inscription found at Tel Dan in the 1990s, written little more than a century later, refers to the king of Judah as king of “the house of David”.

The kind of writing. This is narrative history, and some of the finest prose in the ancient world. The narrator seldom comments, and in the long account of David’s court (chapters 9 to 20) only three times does he say plainly what God thought: “the thing that David had done displeased the LORD” (11:27); of Solomon, “the LORD loved him” (12:24); and that the LORD had ordained the defeat of Ahithophel’s counsel (17:14). Much that he records he does not approve; we are meant to measure it against God’s law. The Hebrew text of Samuel has more copying slips than most books, especially in numbers, and modern Bibles sometimes follow the Greek translation or the Dead Sea scroll of Samuel, as their footnotes show; no teaching of the book depends on these.

How the book makes its case. First the kingdom is given [1–5]. David mourns Saul and Jonathan, waits through years of civil war, refuses to take the throne by murder, and is anointed king over all Israel (5:3). Then the kingdom is set in order under God [6–10]: the ark comes to Jerusalem, God promises David a house that will last for ever (chapter 7), the enemies are subdued, and the crippled grandson of Saul is brought to eat at the king’s table (chapter 9). At the centre comes the fall [11–12]. With his army at war, David takes Bathsheba and arranges the death of her husband Uriah, until Nathan tells him, “You are the man!” (12:7). David confesses, “I have sinned against the LORD”, and is forgiven in the same breath (12:13), but “the sword shall never depart from your house” (12:10). Chapters 13–20 show that word coming true: Amnon’s rape of Tamar, Absalom’s murder of Amnon and his rebellion, David’s flight from Jerusalem, and Absalom’s death, with Joab loyal and ruthless throughout. The last four chapters [21–24] are an appendix arranged by theme, not date, built in matching pairs around two poems: a national disaster, lists of warriors, David’s song of deliverance (which is Psalm 18), his last words, more warriors, and a second disaster. The book does not end with David’s glory but with his sin, his sacrifice, and a plague stopped above Jerusalem at a threshing floor he insists on paying for: “I will not offer burnt offerings to the LORD my God that cost me nothing” (24:24).

A man after God’s own heart? Readers are often troubled that the man God called “a man after my heart” (Acts 13:22) committed adultery and murder. Some treat David as a hero to copy, passing quickly over the dark chapters; some modern scholars read the book as royal propaganda, defending a ruthless usurper. But propaganda does not tell the story of Bathsheba and Uriah, and the book refuses to make David either a saint or a villain. Scripture’s own summary is that he “did what was right in the eyes of the LORD … all the days of his life, except in the matter of Uriah the Hittite” (1 Kings 15:5). This commentary’s view is that the phrase speaks of God’s free choice of David and of a heart turned to God, not of a sinless life. What set him apart from Saul was not that he sinned less but that, when he was confronted, he did not excuse himself; Psalm 51 records his repentance.

Where it leads: to Christ. Second Samuel leads to Christ first by promise. God told David of a son: “I will be to him a father, and he shall be to me a son” (7:14), and “I will establish the throne of his kingdom forever” (7:13). Solomon received it first, but no son of David kept the throne for ever until the angel said of Mary’s child, “the Lord God will give to him the throne of his father David, and he will reign over the house of Jacob forever, and of his kingdom there will be no end” (Luke 1:32–33). Hebrews applies 7:14 to Jesus (Hebrews 1:5), and Peter preached that the oath to set one of David’s descendants on his throne was kept when God raised Jesus (Acts 2:30–32). This commentary holds that he reigns on David’s throne now, at the Father’s right hand. It also leads by the need it exposes. David’s last words picture the righteous king who “dawns on them like the morning light” (23:4), and David himself was not that king. And it gives patterns that Jesus fills out: a crippled enemy’s grandson given a seat at the king’s table for another man’s sake (9:7); a father who cried over his rebel son, “Would I had died instead of you” (18:33), and could not, where God “did not spare his own Son but gave him up for us all” (Romans 8:32); and the threshing floor on which judgment stopped, the ground where the temple would stand.

For us. Second Samuel is honest about sin, even in the best of God’s servants, and about how long its consequences run. It warns that a fall can begin with staying home when duty lay elsewhere (11:1). But it shows that a guilty man who says, “I have sinned against the LORD” is met at once with pardon. Our hope does not rest on our own faithfulness, any more than David’s did, but on God’s promise to David, kept in Jesus Christ, “risen from the dead, the offspring of David” (2 Timothy 2:8), whose kingdom will have no end.

1.title: The Lament of the Bow
1.text: <sup>1</sup>After the death of Saul, when David had returned from striking down the Amalekites, David remained two days in Ziklag.<sup>2</sup>And on the third day, behold, a man came from Saul's camp, with his clothes torn and dirt on his head. And when he came to David, he fell to the ground and paid homage.<sup>3</sup>David said to him, "Where do you come from?" And he said to him, "I have escaped from the camp of Israel."<sup>4</sup>And David said to him, "How did it go? Tell me." "Jonathan lies slain on your high places.<sup>26</sup>I am distressed for you, my brother Jonathan; very pleasant have you been to me; your love to me was extraordinary, surpassing the love of women.<sup>27</sup>"How the mighty have fallen, and the weapons of war perished!"
1.overview:
Where we are. First Samuel ended on Mount Gilboa, with Saul and three of his sons dead (1 Samuel 31). Second Samuel opens far to the south, in the burnt town of Ziklag, where David has just rescued his people from the Amalekites and does not yet know any of it.

The message. The man God has chosen will not take the kingdom by grasping it. When a crown is laid at his feet with a boast that the messenger killed the king, David answers with grief, not gladness, and with justice, not reward. He holds the LORD’s anointed sacred on the day it costs him nothing, as he did for years when it cost him everything, and he honours the man whose throne he is about to receive.

Why it was said. Israel needed to know that David came to the throne as God’s gift, not by murder or rebellion (see the introduction). This chapter answers the suspicion before it is raised: the one man who claimed Saul’s blood died for the claim, and David taught the nation to mourn Saul, not to celebrate his fall.

How the chapter makes its case. An Amalekite arrives with Saul’s crown and a story that he killed the king himself (vv. 1–10). David and his men mourn until evening, and then David has the man executed on his own confession (vv. 11–16). Then David composes the Song of the Bow and has it taught to Judah (vv. 17–27): it honours Saul and Jonathan as Israel’s glory, without bitterness and without a word for David himself, and ends in grief for Jonathan, whose covenant love was beyond anything David had known.

Where it leads. To Christ by pattern, and by the need the chapter exposes. David would not seize the crown, and received it from God by way of grief; the Son of God “did not count equality with God a thing to be grasped” (Philippians 2:6), and was given the name above every name. At the cross the rulers did set themselves “against the Lord and against his Anointed” (Acts 4:26), and God made that death the way to the crown (Hebrews 2:9). And the refrain, “How the mighty have fallen!”, shows that Israel’s mightiest could not save it: it needed a King who would fall in death and rise again.

For us. When those who wronged us fall, Christ’s people do not gloat; we grieve, and say the true good things about them. We need not grasp at what God has promised, because our King received his throne by laying down his life. And grief need not be tidy to be godly: God kept this lament in his Word.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–10 — A Man Came from Saul's Camp
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A lying messenger expects to be rewarded for bringing David the crown. Two days after David returns to Ziklag from defeating the Amalekites, a young man arrives from Saul’s camp with torn clothes and dirt on his head, the signs of a man carrying disaster, and bows to the ground before David (vv. 1–2). He reports that Israel has fled and that Saul and Jonathan are dead (vv. 3–4). Asked how he knows, he tells a detailed story of finding Saul wounded on Mount Gilboa and killing him at the king’s own request, and he produces Saul’s crown and armlet as proof (vv. 5–10). He is an Amalekite, and his story does not match the account of Saul’s death in 1 Samuel 31.
verseByVerse.theology: The story is false, and the reader knows it: Saul fell on his own sword, and his armour-bearer saw that Saul was dead (1 Sam. 31:4-5). This man is a scavenger who stripped the royal insignia off the body and invented a part for himself.
verseByVerse.examples: And he is an Amalekite. Saul lost the kingdom for sparing that nation (1 Sam. 15), and David has come to Ziklag straight from cutting down the Amalekites who burned it (1 Sam. 30). The narrator offers no comment whatever.

verseByVerse.quote: After the death of Saul, when David had returned from striking down the Amalekites, David remained two days in Ziklag. And on the third day, behold, a man came from Saul's camp, with his clothes torn and dirt on his head. And when he came to David, he fell to the ground and paid homage. David said to him, "Where do you come from?" And he said to him, "I have escaped from the camp of Israel." And David said to him, "How did it go? Tell me." And he answered, "The people fled from the battle, and also many of the people have fallen and are dead, and Saul and his son Jonathan are also dead." Then David said to the young man who told him, "How do you know that Saul and his son Jonathan are dead?" And the young man who told him said, "By chance I happened to be on Mount Gilboa, and there was Saul leaning on his spear, and behold, the chariots and the horsemen were close upon him. And when he looked behind him, he saw me, and called to me. And I answered, 'Here I am.' And he said to me, 'Who are you?' I answered him, 'I am an Amalekite.' And he said to me, 'Stand beside me and kill me, for anguish has seized me, and yet my life still lingers.' So I stood beside him and killed him, because I was sure that he could not live after he had fallen. And I took the crown that was on his head and the armlet that was on his arm, and I have brought them here to my lord."
verseByVerse.commentary:
A stranger brings David the crown with a story that he killed Saul himself, a lie calculated to win a reward from the man he assumes will be glad to hear it.

After the death of Saul (v. 1). Two books meet in that sentence. First Samuel ended on Gilboa, with a body on a wall and the men of Jabesh-gilead walking all night to take it down. This one opens far to the south, in a burnt town, with a man who does not yet know any of it. Note where he has just been: striking down the Amalekites. Keep that in mind until verse 8.

Dirt on his head (v. 2). Torn clothes and dirt on the head were the recognised signs of a man carrying a disaster (see mourning customs), and here they are also a costume. He falls on his face, as one does before a king, not before a raiders’ captain in a burnt village: he thinks he is greeting the next king.

How did it go (vv. 3–5). He answers in the right order, worst last, and the last words are the ones that matter to his hearer. David’s next question is a lawyer’s: How do you know? He will not take the news on the strength of torn clothes; he wants to know what the man saw.

By chance (v. 6). Nobody is on a battlefield after the fighting by chance. Men go there to strip the dead.

I stood beside him and killed him (vv. 7–10). It is a good story, told with detail, and it is not true. The reader already knows what happened: Saul’s armour-bearer refused to kill him, so “Saul took his own sword and fell upon it” (1 Samuel 31:4). There was no Amalekite in that account, and no breath left in Saul to bargain with.

What probably happened. A scavenger found the king’s body after the battle, took the crown and the armlet, and walked south for three days working out what to say. He judged that a rival for the throne would pay not for the news, which anyone could bring, but for the deed. He assumed the years of being hunted had made David bitter, as such years usually do, and that a crown and a corpse were a business opportunity. He was wrong about all of it, and it kills him. David later says as much: the man “thought he was bringing good news” (4:10).

I am an Amalekite (v. 8). The writer leaves the word alone. Saul lost the kingdom over Amalek: the command he would not carry out at Gilgal, and the reason Samuel gave at Endor (1 Samuel 15:1–23; 28:18). David has just come back from killing the Amalekites who burned this town, and four hundred of them got away on camels (1 Samuel 30:17). Here is one, holding Saul’s crown and claiming to have finished the man who spared his people. The narrator sets the facts side by side and lets the careful reader do the rest.

The crown that cannot be bought. The Amalekite thought a crown could be won by striking the LORD’s anointed. At the cross men did strike the LORD’s Anointed, and God made that death the way to the crown: Jesus is “crowned with glory and honor because of the suffering of death” (Hebrews 2:9). The only blood that wins a kingdom is the King’s own.
verseByVerse.note: The Amalekite’s story contradicts 1 Samuel 31, where Saul fell on his own sword; he was probably lying to win David’s favour.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 11–16 — Your Own Mouth Has Testified Against You
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: David grieves before he judges, and then he judges by the principle he has kept for years. He and his men tear their clothes, weep and fast until evening for Saul, for Jonathan, and for the LORD’s people who have fallen (vv. 11–12). Only then does David turn to the messenger. He asks again where he comes from, and hears that he is the son of a resident foreigner, an Amalekite (v. 13). How was he not afraid to lift his hand against the LORD’s anointed (v. 14)? David has him executed, and passes sentence on the man’s own words: “I have killed the LORD’s anointed” (vv. 15–16). The man who expected a reward receives justice.
verseByVerse.theology: The order of the day matters. Hours of public grief come first, and the sentence afterwards, and the list he mourns for runs outward: Saul, Jonathan, the people of the LORD, the house of Israel.
verseByVerse.examples: He is condemned on his testimony, not his deed, and he almost certainly did not do it. And the principle enforced is the one David held through seven chapters of being hunted: nobody puts a hand on the LORD's anointed.

verseByVerse.quote: Then David took hold of his clothes and tore them, and so did all the men who were with him. And they mourned and wept and fasted until evening for Saul and for Jonathan his son and for the people of the LORD and for the house of Israel, because they had fallen by the sword. And David said to the young man who told him, "Where do you come from?" And he answered, "I am the son of a sojourner, an Amalekite." David said to him, "How is it you were not afraid to put out your hand to destroy the LORD's anointed?" Then David called one of the young men and said, "Go, execute him." And he struck him down so that he died. And David said to him, "Your blood be on your head, for your own mouth has testified against you, saying, 'I have killed the LORD's anointed.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
David mourns before he judges, and then, on his first day with power, he enforces the rule he kept when it cost him everything: no one may lift a hand against the LORD’s anointed.

Until evening (vv. 11–12). Before he says a word he tears his clothes, and his men tear theirs. The whole day goes to grief, and the list runs outward: for Saul first, the man who had hunted him for the better part of a decade; for Jonathan his son, a whole life in one clause, which will get its own verses at the end of the chapter; and for the LORD’s people, because the army is gone and the northern towns are abandoned to the Philistines.

Real grief. Is this a performance? The signs say not. There is no audience but his own men, who know exactly what Saul did to him and lost everything at Ziklag days before. And he grieves before he judges, with the Amalekite standing there the whole time.

The son of a sojourner (v. 13). A sojourner (ger) was a resident foreigner, living under Israel’s law without being of Israel, bound by it and protected by it like the native-born (Leviticus 24:22). By his own account, this man lived under that law and put his hand on the king.

Not afraid (v. 14). Anyone who has read 1 Samuel has heard this before: “The LORD forbid that I should do this thing to my lord, the LORD’s anointed” (1 Samuel 24:6); “who can put out his hand against the LORD’s anointed and be guiltless?” (1 Samuel 26:9). David held that principle for years when it cost him everything, with two chances to end it in an afternoon and his own men urging him on. Now the crown is in front of him and there is no one to answer to, and he keeps the same rule. Almost anyone can hold a principle while it costs them; the test is whether it survives the day the power arrives.

Go, execute him (v. 15). It is done at once and by somebody else, both deliberately: David will not let the sentence look like private revenge.

Your own mouth (v. 16). Read it carefully, because it shows that David knows. He does not say, in effect, that the man killed the king, but that he said he did. The sentence rests on the confession, and the act in all likelihood never happened. The man claimed, unprompted and before witnesses, to have killed the LORD’s anointed, and David treats him exactly as he has described himself. There is a hard justice in it that Scripture does not soften: he came to be paid for claiming a thing, and he was paid for it. It also settled something for the nation. No one in Israel could say afterwards that David had paid for Saul’s death or welcomed it.

A better King. David honoured the anointed king who had wronged him. Jesus prayed for the very men who lifted their hands against him: “Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do” (Luke 23:34).

Was it just to execute a man for what may have been a lie? A judge can only judge by the evidence, and here it was the man’s own boast, made freely before witnesses. If it was a lie, it was the lie he chose to tell in order to profit from a king’s death.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 17–24 — Tell It Not in Gath
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: David teaches Israel to honour the king who hunted him. He composes a lament for Saul and Jonathan and orders it taught to Judah (vv. 17–18). Its refrain, “How the mighty have fallen!”, sounds at the start (v. 19). He begs that the news be kept from the Philistine cities, where it will be celebrated (v. 20), and curses the mountain where Saul’s shield lay neglected (v. 21). He praises father and son as warriors, undivided in death (vv. 22–23), and calls the women of Israel to weep for the king who made them prosperous (v. 24). There is no bitterness in the poem, and no word for David himself.
verseByVerse.theology: A shield's leather was rubbed with oil to keep it supple and turn a blade. Saul's lies on Gilboa unattended, a king's gear left to rot in the rain, which is why the same verse asks the rain not to come.
verseByVerse.examples: In verse 24 David remembers Saul's reign for what it actually gave the nation, and he says it to the women who once sang the song that nearly got him killed.

verseByVerse.quote: And David lamented with this lamentation over Saul and Jonathan his son, and he said it should be taught to the people of Judah; behold, it is written in the Book of Jashar. He said:
verseByVerse.commentary:
David turns his grief into a poem for the whole nation and has it taught to Judah, so that Israel would remember Saul with honour.

Teach it to Judah (vv. 17–18). He does not only grieve; he has the poem taught, so that a generation’s memory of Saul will be shaped by what David felt. He is about to be made king of Judah, and the obvious course for an incoming man is to let the old regime be remembered badly without saying a word. Instead he composes a poem that honours Saul without qualification and orders it memorised.

The Book of Jashar. An older collection of Israel’s poems, cited once before (Joshua 10:13) and now lost. This poem survived because it was copied into Scripture.

Uncertain wording. The Hebrew of verse 18 reads literally “to teach the sons of Judah ‘the Bow’”. “The Bow” is probably the poem’s title, taken from Jonathan’s bow in verse 22, which is why it is often called the Song of the Bow; some take it instead as an instruction to teach Judah archery. The title reading fits best, and either way the lament itself is clear.
verseByVerse.note: The Book of Jashar was an old collection of poems, now lost.

verseByVerse.quote: "Your glory, O Israel, is slain on your high places! How the mighty have fallen! Tell it not in Gath, publish it not in the streets of Ashkelon, lest the daughters of the Philistines rejoice, lest the daughters of the uncircumcised exult.
verseByVerse.commentary:
David mourns Saul and Jonathan as Israel’s glory, and begs that the news be kept from the Philistines, who will celebrate the shame of God’s people.

How the mighty have fallen (v. 19). The poem is built around this refrain, which comes three times: here, at verse 25, and in the last verse. Saul and Jonathan lie dead on Israel’s own heights.

Tell it not in Gath (v. 20). The line has passed into the language, and most who use it have no idea it is about Saul. Here it is concrete. The runners have already gone out “to carry the good news to the house of their idols and to the people” (1 Samuel 31:9), and there will be dancing in those streets tonight. David knows what it looks like when the women of a city sing about a battle (1 Samuel 18:7), and he knows Gath from the inside (1 Samuel 27:2).

Gath … Ashkelon … the uncircumcised. Two of the five chief Philistine cities, and “the uncircumcised” names the Philistines as outsiders to God’s covenant. David grieves not only for two men but for the shame their deaths bring on the people of the LORD. Micah would later take up the line (Micah 1:10).

Uncertain wording. The word translated “glory” (v. 19) can also mean “gazelle”, the graceful animal of the hills. Either sense fits: Saul and Jonathan were Israel’s pride and beauty, struck down on the heights where gazelles run. “Glory” is the more likely meaning, but the poet may intend both.

verseByVerse.quote: "You mountains of Gilboa, let there be no dew or rain upon you, nor fields of offerings! For there the shield of the mighty was defiled, the shield of Saul, not anointed with oil.
verseByVerse.commentary:
David curses the mountain where Saul fell, and says that the king is dead through a picture of his shield left out in the weather, unoiled.

You mountains of Gilboa (v. 21). He curses the ground. This is the language of grief in a poem, not teaching about the land: the mountain is where it happened, so let nothing grow there again.

The shield of Saul, not anointed with oil. The detail that carries the grief is a piece of equipment. Leather shields were rubbed with olive oil to keep them ready for battle (compare Isaiah 21:5), and nobody is going to oil Saul’s again: good gear left out in the weather, because the man who looked after it is not coming back. And anointed is the word the whole of 1 Samuel turns on, used of Saul again and again, and what David called him seven verses ago (v. 14). Here it is, in its ordinary sense, about a shield.

Uncertain wording. “Nor fields of offerings” is difficult. It probably means fields whose harvest would supply firstfruits for the LORD’s altar: the mountain where the anointed king fell is to give nothing to God or man. Others take it more generally as “nor bountiful fields”, no harvest of any kind. Either way the sense, a wish that the place be barren, is clear.

verseByVerse.quote: "From the blood of the slain, from the fat of the mighty, the bow of Jonathan turned not back, and the sword of Saul returned not empty. "Saul and Jonathan, beloved and lovely! In life and in death they were not divided; they were swifter than eagles; they were stronger than lions.
verseByVerse.commentary:
David praises Saul and Jonathan as brave warriors who stood together to the end, choosing the largest true thing he could say rather than the most damaging.

The bow of Jonathan (v. 22). Both men are praised as soldiers, and the praise is true. Jonathan’s bow is the right thing to remember him by: the weapon he used to signal David on the day they parted (1 Samuel 20:20–22).

From the blood of the slain, from the fat of the mighty. The weapons are pictured as hungry, feeding on the enemy, as Moses’ song speaks of arrows drunk with blood (Deuteronomy 32:42). Whatever else was true of them, they fought Israel’s enemies to the end.

Not divided (v. 23). That is more generous than the bare facts. Saul hurled a spear at Jonathan for defending David, and Jonathan left the table in fierce anger (1 Samuel 20:33–34). Jonathan made a covenant with the man his father was hunting. David knew all of it; most of it was done for his sake.

The largest true thing. Yet in the end they were not divided: the son stood in his father’s line on his father’s mountain and died there with him, when he had every reason to be elsewhere. This is not dishonesty. Out of everything he could truthfully report about a dead man, David chooses the honourable part, in a poem he means the nation to memorise, about a king whose crown he is about to wear. Nearly everyone, given a grievance and an audience, tells the truth in the way that does most damage. David had more material than anybody and used none of it. That is what love that “is not irritable or resentful” (1 Corinthians 13:5) looks like at a graveside.

Swifter than eagles, stronger than lions. The language of praise for warriors (compare 2:18). The two men who now lie still are remembered in motion, swift and strong as the lion.

verseByVerse.quote: "You daughters of Israel, weep over Saul, who clothed you luxuriously in scarlet, who put ornaments of gold on your apparel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
David calls the women who once sang his praises over Saul’s to weep for Saul, and reminds them of the true good he did.

Daughters of Israel (v. 24). These are the women who sang, “Saul has struck down his thousands, and David his ten thousands” (1 Samuel 18:7), the song that put a spear in Saul’s hand and nearly cost David his life twice. Now David calls them to weep for Saul.

Scarlet and gold. What he tells them to remember is the prosperity. Scarlet and gold meant a country secure enough for ordinary women to dress well, and that was Saul’s doing: he beat the Ammonites at Jabesh and the Philistines at Michmash, and Israel had a king, an army and something in the barn. It is the true good thing, and David goes looking for it and says it out loud.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 25–27 — Your Love to Me Was Extraordinary
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The poem ends in private grief for Jonathan. The refrain returns, and the lament narrows from the nation’s loss to one name: Jonathan lies slain on the heights (v. 25). David speaks to him directly, as his brother, distressed and weighed down by the loss of a friend whose love had been extraordinary, beyond even the love of women (v. 26). This is the love of a sworn friend who kept covenant at the cost of a throne. The refrain sounds a third time and closes the poem with the weapons of war perished, Israel’s defenders lying dead on the hill (v. 27).
verseByVerse.theology: David is comparing two different kinds of love, not two amounts of the same love. Jonathan and David were sworn brothers under a covenant made three times before the LORD, and the loyalty that held it is hesed; David says he has never met its equal.
verseByVerse.examples: David can grieve a friend without needing to explain the loss; so may we.

verseByVerse.quote: "How the mighty have fallen in the midst of the battle! "Jonathan lies slain on your high places. I am distressed for you, my brother Jonathan; very pleasant have you been to me; your love to me was extraordinary, surpassing the love of women. "How the mighty have fallen, and the weapons of war perished!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The lament ends in personal grief for Jonathan, whose covenant faithfulness to David, at the cost of his own throne, was a love David had found nowhere else.

My brother Jonathan (vv. 25–26). The refrain comes back, and the poem narrows to one name. Everything before this has been public; this is not. I am distressed for you uses a word for being hemmed in and pressed: grief felt as a weight. They were brothers-in-law by a marriage Saul dissolved by force, and brothers by covenant, which was the tie that held. Very pleasant have you been to me: not “useful” or “loyal”, though he was both past reckoning. Being with him was good.

Surpassing the love of women. The line people stop at deserves a plain answer. The comparison is between two kinds of love, sworn friendship and marriage, not two amounts of one kind. What Jonathan gave David was covenant loyalty, hesed, love that keeps its promises after the reasons have gone, sworn before the LORD more than once (1 Samuel 18:3; 20:16–17, 42; 23:18).

Your love to me was extraordinary. Look at what it consisted of. The heir to the throne gave a shepherd his own robe, armour, sword, bow and belt (1 Samuel 18:4). He defended him to a king who hurled a spear at him for it. He said, “You shall be king over Israel, and I shall be next to you” (1 Samuel 23:17), giving up everything he was born to. He walked into a wilderness his father’s army was searching to strengthen a frightened man’s hand in God, and then went home and died in his father’s lost battle. David had never met anything like it, though he had a wife who loved him and saved his life by letting him down through a window (1 Samuel 19:12).

The weapons of war perished (v. 27). The last line is about equipment again, as verse 21 was, and it means more than swords: the men who were Israel’s defence are lying on a hill.

A greater love. Jonathan, the king’s son, stripped off his robe and gave up his throne for David. The Son of the King of heaven “emptied himself, by taking the form of a servant” (Philippians 2:7), and laid down not only a throne but his life: “Greater love has no one than this, that someone lay down his life for his friends” (John 15:13).

No word about himself. Read the whole poem back and look for two things that are not in it. The first is David: nine verses, and not one word about what any of this means for him, no relief, nothing about the throne he has waited years for. He is not a man who hides his feelings; the psalms are full of him saying exactly what is in him. Whatever relief he felt, this is not where he put it.

No mention of God. The second absence is stranger: no appeal, no theology of any kind, from a man who seldom gets through a psalm without speaking to God directly. Scripture keeps it exactly as it came out.

Permission to grieve. Anyone who has been made to feel that grief must be tidy or theological before it is permitted should sit with that. On the day the news came, the man after God’s own heart wrote a poem full of scarlet and eagles and an unoiled shield, with no doctrine in it and nothing about himself, and God preserved it. Sometimes the godly thing is not to explain the loss but to say plainly how good the dead were and how much it hurts. Jesus wept at a friend’s grave (John 11:35), and Christians grieve, though not “as others do who have no hope” (1 Thessalonians 4:13).

What it does not mean. Nothing in the text points the line at anything other than a man grieving the friend who kept faith with him at the cost of a kingdom. Reading it as erotic imports a meaning the passage gives no sign of; covenant friends in that world spoke of love in just these words (1 Samuel 18:1–3). And a king wrote it in the first person and had it taught to a nation, which is not what men in his position do with a secret.

1.theology:
A misreading that kills (vv. 6-16). The Amalekite's story is false, and the reader knows it from the chapter before. He calculated that a rival claimant would pay not for the news but for the deed, which shows how he expected years of being hunted to have shaped David. He was wrong, and he was judged by the account he chose to give of himself.

The principle survives the arrival of power (v. 14). How is it you were not afraid to put out your hand to destroy the LORD's anointed? puts to the Amalekite the principle David stated in the cave at Engedi (1 Sam. 24:6) and to Abishai over the sleeping king (1 Sam. 26:9). He held it while hunted, hungry and living in caves, and twice stopped his own men from breaking it. Almost anyone can keep a principle while it is costing them and feel righteous doing it; the test is the day it costs nothing and nobody would notice its absence.

Choosing which true thing to say (vv. 17-24). An incoming king could simply have let the old regime be remembered badly. Instead David writes a poem honouring Saul and has it taught to Judah, choosing out of everything he could accurately report about a dead man the part that is honourable.

Grief that is allowed to be grief (vv. 25-27). The poem says nothing about David and nothing about God, and Scripture keeps it as it came. That matters a great deal to anybody made to feel that grief must be tidy or theological before it is permitted.

A crown he would not take over a body (vv. 10, 14-16). The Amalekite brought David a crown lifted off a corpse and expected thanks for the death. David would not have the throne that way. The Son of David met the same offer on a grander scale, all the kingdoms of the world for one act of worship, and refused (Matthew 4:8-10). He did not take his throne over anyone else’s body; he came to it through his own, obedient to the point of death, and was therefore highly exalted (Philippians 2:8-9). And the grief David puts in the poem without explaining it is grief the Lord himself shared: at the grave of his friend, before he raised him, Jesus wept (John 11:35).
1.examples:
Then: A man walked three days south carrying a dead king's crown and a story he had made up on the road, expecting to be paid for claiming a murder, and was executed on the strength of his own account by the one person in Israel who had twice refused to commit it when he had the chance.

Now: Two things. The Amalekite is a study in misreading somebody: he assumed that years of persecution had made David into the kind of man who would reward the news. People will tell you what they think you are by what they think will please you. And the lament is the harder lesson. David had more accurate, damaging material about Saul than any person alive, an audience ready to hear it, and every political reason to let it out, and instead he went looking for what was genuinely good about the man and taught it to a nation. That is not pretending. It is choosing which true thing to say. Christians can afford to speak that way about those who wronged them because God has dealt that way with us: in Christ he does not keep the record of our worst, and the Spirit he gives produces a love that covers a multitude of sins.

keyVerse.quote: How is it you were not afraid to put out your hand to destroy the LORD’s anointed?
keyVerse.note: David asks the Amalekite the question he had answered for himself twice, in the cave and over the sleeping king, when the throne could have been his in a moment. Now that the crown lies before him he keeps the same rule, showing that he will receive the kingdom from God and not take it. The Son of David went further still, praying for the men who lifted their hands against him.

1.reflection:
The Amalekite misjudged David completely, assuming that years of being hunted had made him bitter and that he would pay for Saul’s death (vv. 1–10). What does David’s response reveal about his heart? How do we tend to react when someone who has wronged us falls?

David enforced the same principle on the day he gained power as he had kept when it cost him everything (v. 14; 1 Samuel 24:6). Where are you tempted to hold convictions only while they are costly, or only while they are cheap?

In his lament David chose the true and honourable things to say about Saul, though he had more grievances than anyone (vv. 22–24). What would it look like for you to speak in this way about someone who has hurt you, without pretending the wrongs never happened?

The poem mentions neither God nor David himself, and yet God kept it in Scripture. What does that teach us about grief? How does Jesus, who wept at Lazarus’ tomb and laid down his life for his friends, change the way Christians mourn?

2.title: Two Kings in Israel
2.text: <sup>1</sup>After this David inquired of the LORD, "Shall I go up into any of the cities of Judah?" And the LORD said to him, "Go up." David said, "To which shall I go up?" And he said, "To Hebron."<sup>2</sup>So David went up there, and his two wives also, Ahinoam of Jezreel and Abigail the widow of Nabal of Carmel.<sup>3</sup>And David brought up his men who were with him, everyone with his household, and they lived in the towns of Hebron.<sup>4</sup>And the men of Judah came, and there they anointed David king over the house of Judah. When they told David, "It was the men of Jabesh-gilead who buried Saul,"<sup>5</sup>David sent messengers to the men of Jabesh-gilead and said to them, "May you be blessed by the LORD, because you showed this loyalty to Saul your lord and buried him.<sup>6</sup>Now may the LORD show steadfast love and faithfulness to you. And I will do good to you because you have done this thing.<sup>7</sup>Now therefore let your hands be strong, and be valiant, for Saul your lord is dead, and the house of Judah has anointed me king over them."<sup>8</sup>But Abner the son of Ner, commander of Saul's army, took Ish-bosheth the son of Saul and brought him over to Mahanaim,<sup>9</sup>and he made him king over Gilead and the Ashurites and Jezreel and Ephraim and Benjamin and all Israel.<sup>10</sup>Ish-bosheth, Saul's son, was forty years old when he began to reign over Israel, and he reigned two years. But the house of Judah followed David.<sup>11</sup>And the time that David was king in Hebron over the house of Judah was seven years and six months.<sup>12</sup>Abner the son of Ner, and the servants of Ish-bosheth the son of Saul, went out from Mahanaim to Gibeon.<sup>13</sup>And Joab the son of Zeruiah and the servants of David went out and met them at the pool of Gibeon. And they sat down, the one on the one side of the pool, and the other on the other side of the pool.<sup>14</sup>And Abner said to Joab, "Let the young men arise and compete before us." And Joab said, "Let them arise."<sup>15</sup>Then they arose and passed over by number, twelve for Benjamin and Ish-bosheth the son of Saul, and twelve of the servants of David.<sup>16</sup>And each caught his opponent by the head and thrust his sword in his opponent's side, so they fell down together. Therefore that place was called Helkath-hazzurim, which is at Gibeon.<sup>17</sup>And the battle was very fierce that day. And Abner and the men of Israel were beaten before the servants of David.<sup>18</sup>And the three sons of Zeruiah were there, Joab, Abishai, and Asahel. Now Asahel was as swift of foot as a wild gazelle.<sup>19</sup>And Asahel pursued Abner, and as he went, he turned neither to the right hand nor to the left from following Abner.<sup>20</sup>Then Abner looked behind him and said, "Is it you, Asahel?" And he answered, "It is I."<sup>21</sup>Abner said to him, "Turn aside to your right hand or to your left, and seize one of the young men and take his spoil." But Asahel would not turn aside from following him.<sup>22</sup>And Abner said again to Asahel, "Turn aside from following me. Why should I strike you to the ground? How then could I lift up my face to your brother Joab?"<sup>23</sup>But he refused to turn aside. Therefore Abner struck him in the stomach with the butt of his spear, so that the spear came out at his back. And he fell there and died where he was. And all who came to the place where Asahel had fallen and died, stood still.<sup>24</sup>But Joab and Abishai pursued Abner. And as the sun was going down they came to the hill of Ammah, which lies before Giah on the way to the wilderness of Gibeon.<sup>25</sup>And the people of Benjamin gathered themselves together behind Abner and became one group and took their stand on the top of a hill.<sup>26</sup>Then Abner called to Joab, "Shall the sword devour forever? Do you not know that the end will be bitter? How long will it be before you tell your people to turn from the pursuit of their brothers?"<sup>27</sup>And Joab said, "As God lives, if you had not spoken, surely the men would not have given up the pursuit of their brothers until the morning."<sup>28</sup>So Joab blew the trumpet, and all the men stopped and pursued Israel no more, nor did they fight anymore.<sup>29</sup>And Abner and his men went all that night through the Arabah. They crossed the Jordan, and marching the whole morning, they came to Mahanaim.<sup>30</sup>Joab returned from the pursuit of Abner. And when he had gathered all the people together, there were missing from David's servants nineteen men besides Asahel.<sup>31</sup>But the servants of David had struck down of Benjamin 360 of Abner's men.<sup>32</sup>And they took up Asahel and buried him in the tomb of his father, which was at Bethlehem. And Joab and his men marched all night, and the day broke upon them at Hebron.
2.overview:
Where we are. Saul and Jonathan are dead, and David has mourned them and executed the man who claimed to have killed the king (chapter 1). The throne stands empty, and David has been anointed for it years before (1 Samuel 16:13). How will he come to it?

The message. The kingdom God has promised comes to the man who waits for God, not to the men who reach for it with swords. David asks the LORD before he takes a step, receives one tribe, and honours the loyalists of his old enemy. Meanwhile Abner sets up a rival king, and a contest meant to keep the war small ends in a field of corpses and a feud that will outlive the day. Human strength cannot heal a divided people; only God’s chosen king, given in God’s time, can.

Why it was said. The first readers knew the kingdom had split once and could split again (see the introduction). This chapter shows them that David did not seize the north by force, and that the long war between Israelites was the fruit of men resisting what God had said, not of David’s ambition.

How the chapter makes its case. David inquires of the LORD, goes up to Hebron, is anointed king of Judah, and sends a blessing to Jabesh-gilead for burying Saul (vv. 1–7). Abner makes Saul’s son Ish-bosheth king of the north, and at the pool of Gibeon twelve champions from each side kill one another at once, and a fierce battle follows (vv. 8–17). Asahel chases Abner and will not turn aside, and Abner kills him, against his will (vv. 18–23). Abner calls out, “Shall the sword devour forever?”, Joab stops the pursuit, and both armies march all night with nothing settled (vv. 24–32).

Where it leads. To Christ by pattern and by the need the chapter exposes. David asks before he moves, as the Son “can do nothing of his own accord, but only what he sees the Father doing” (John 5:19); and like David, Jesus is rightful King while much of his people still follow another. Abner’s cry has only one answer. Brothers killing brothers is the story of a fallen world, and the sword does devour until the Prince of Peace comes, who “himself is our peace, who has made us both one” (Ephesians 2:14).

For us. Ask God before you act, and keep asking after the first yes. Honour faithfulness wherever you find it, even among those who were on the other side. And when a quarrel has outlived its cause, be the one who calls a halt: the end of it will be bitter, and Christ has made peace at the cost of his own blood.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–7 — David Inquired of the LORD
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: David begins his reign by asking the LORD, not by seizing what is within reach. With Saul dead and the throne empty, he asks whether he should go up to Judah, and then asks which town, and is told Hebron (v. 1). He goes up with his two wives and his men and their households, and the men of Judah anoint him king over their tribe (vv. 2–4). His first recorded act as king is to bless the men of Jabesh-gilead, who risked their lives to bury Saul, and to promise them his own kindness, while telling them plainly that Judah has made him king (vv. 4–7).
verseByVerse.theology: Being told he may go is not being told where, and David will not choose the place himself and call that God’s guidance.
verseByVerse.examples: His first recorded act as king is a thank-you to the town that buried Saul. Kindness to people who loved our opponents can be both sincere and wise.

verseByVerse.quote: After this David inquired of the LORD, "Shall I go up into any of the cities of Judah?" And the LORD said to him, "Go up." David said, "To which shall I go up?" And he said, "To Hebron." So David went up there, and his two wives also, Ahinoam of Jezreel and Abigail the widow of Nabal of Carmel. And David brought up his men who were with him, everyone with his household, and they lived in the towns of Hebron. And the men of Judah came, and there they anointed David king over the house of Judah. When they told David, "It was the men of Jabesh-gilead who buried Saul," David sent messengers to the men of Jabesh-gilead and said to them, "May you be blessed by the LORD, because you showed this loyalty to Saul your lord and buried him. Now may the LORD show steadfast love and faithfulness to you. And I will do good to you because you have done this thing. Now therefore let your hands be strong, and be valiant, for Saul your lord is dead, and the house of Judah has anointed me king over them."
verseByVerse.commentary:
With nothing standing between him and the throne, David asks the LORD where to go, receives Judah’s anointing, and begins his reign by blessing the men who honoured Saul.

David inquired of the LORD (v. 1). One short sentence, and it is the whole difference between this man and the last one. Consider what he is holding as he asks: the dead king’s crown, brought by the Amalekite; Samuel’s anointing at Bethlehem; six hundred men, and the tribe of Judah waiting. Saul and his heir are dead, and there is no living person he needs permission from. He asks anyway.

To which shall I go up? Then he does something more instructive still. He gets a yes, go up, and does not run with it. He asks a second question: being told he may go is not being told where, and he will not choose the place himself and call it God’s guidance.

The last large decision. Set this beside the last large decision we watched him make: “Then David said in his heart, ‘Now I shall perish one day by the hand of Saul. There is nothing better for me than that I should escape to the land of the Philistines’” (1 Samuel 27:1). No priest, no ephod, no prophet, though all three were within reach. The difference is Ziklag: he asked for the ephod standing in the ashes of his own town (1 Samuel 30:7–8), and he has not stopped since.

To Hebron. Hebron is the right answer, and he could not have known why. It is the oldest covenant ground in the country: Abraham bought the field and the cave there, and Abraham, Isaac and Jacob are buried in it (Genesis 23; 49:31). It was a priests’ city and a city of refuge (Joshua 20:7; 21:13), at the centre of Judah. He is not told why; he is told where.

His two wives (vv. 2–3). Six hundred households move at once, and the writer names the wives. Abigail is here, who talked him out of a massacre, and Ahinoam. Michal, his first wife, is not: Saul gave her to another man, and getting her back will be David’s condition in the next chapter.

King over the house of Judah (v. 4). The second anointing, each given by a wider circle. Samuel poured the oil at Bethlehem in front of the brothers who had been passed over (1 Samuel 16:13). Now his own tribe does it publicly. Seven and a half years later the elders of all Israel will do it a third time (5:3). God keeps confirming the same thing before larger audiences, and each confirmation comes only after David has waited for it.

The men of Jabesh-gilead (vv. 4–5). David’s first recorded act as king is to thank the men who buried his enemy. They had walked all night through occupied country, taken the bodies of Saul and his sons from the wall of Beth-shan, burned them, buried the bones under a tamarisk and fasted seven days (1 Samuel 31:11–13), for a king who could no longer reward them. They did it because of a day decades before, when the Spirit of God rushed on Saul and he marched through the night to save their town (1 Samuel 11). David sees what that was and names it: loyalty.

Steadfast love and faithfulness (v. 6). The first word is hesed, love that keeps its promises when the reasons for keeping them have gone: what Jonathan asked David to show his family, and what Jabesh showed Saul. We tend to hear “love” as a feeling and “faithfulness” as a duty. In the Old Testament they belong together: hesed is love that has bound itself by a promise, and faithfulness (’emet, often “truth”) is the reliability that makes the promise worth leaning on. They are the words God used of himself when he proclaimed his name to Moses: “The LORD, the LORD, a God merciful and gracious, slow to anger, and abounding in steadfast love and faithfulness” (Exodus 34:6). So David asks God to repay Jabesh in kind, asking for what God already is. See Steadfast love in the Theological Dictionary.

Full of grace and truth. Most of our love is quietly conditional: it lasts while the other person is still worth it. God’s does not. John chose words that echo Exodus when he wrote that in Jesus the glory of God came to live among us, “full of grace and truth” (John 1:14), and at the cross that love was kept to people who had given it every reason to stop. This week, keep one promise whose reason has gone.

Saul your lord is dead (v. 7). Then, at the end, the politics, and it would be dishonest to pretend it is not there. He tells the most loyal pro-Saul town in the country that Saul is dead and Judah has crowned him, and asks them for nothing. The gratitude is real: he wrote a lament for Saul that nobody made him write. And he knows the north is watching to see whether the new king counts them as enemies, and he chooses the one gesture that answers the question before it is asked. Godly and shrewd are not opposites; they are only harder to hold together than either alone.
verseByVerse.note: David was anointed three times: privately by Samuel, then king of Judah at Hebron, then king of all Israel.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 8–17 — Let the Young Men Compete Before Us
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A rival king and a contest meant to limit the war plunge Israel into civil war. Abner, Saul’s commander, takes Saul’s son Ish-bosheth across the Jordan to Mahanaim and makes him king over the northern tribes, while Judah follows David (vv. 8–11). The two forces meet at the pool of Gibeon and sit on either side of it (vv. 12–13). Abner proposes that twelve young men from each side fight it out, but all twenty-four kill one another at the same moment, so that the place is named for the sword-edges (vv. 14–16). Nothing is settled, and a very fierce battle follows, which David’s men win (v. 17).
verseByVerse.theology: Both armies are Israelite. This is a civil war, and Abner, not Ish-bosheth, is the real power in the north.
verseByVerse.examples: Measures meant to contain a quarrel can feed it when neither side will accept a result it does not like.

verseByVerse.quote: But Abner the son of Ner, commander of Saul's army, took Ish-bosheth the son of Saul and brought him over to Mahanaim, and he made him king over Gilead and the Ashurites and Jezreel and Ephraim and Benjamin and all Israel. Ish-bosheth, Saul's son, was forty years old when he began to reign over Israel, and he reigned two years. But the house of Judah followed David. And the time that David was king in Hebron over the house of Judah was seven years and six months. Abner the son of Ner, and the servants of Ish-bosheth the son of Saul, went out from Mahanaim to Gibeon. And Joab the son of Zeruiah and the servants of David went out and met them at the pool of Gibeon. And they sat down, the one on the one side of the pool, and the other on the other side of the pool. And Abner said to Joab, "Let the young men arise and compete before us." And Joab said, "Let them arise." Then they arose and passed over by number, twelve for Benjamin and Ish-bosheth the son of Saul, and twelve of the servants of David. And each caught his opponent by the head and thrust his sword in his opponent's side, so they fell down together. Therefore that place was called Helkath-hazzurim, which is at Gibeon. And the battle was very fierce that day. And Abner and the men of Israel were beaten before the servants of David.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Abner sets up Saul’s son as a rival king, and a contest meant to keep the war small ends in twenty-four deaths and a full battle between brothers.

Abner took Ish-bosheth (vv. 8–9). Read the verbs: Abner took him, brought him over, and made him king. Ish-bosheth does nothing in that sentence, and little in the rest of the book. He speaks once, makes an accusation that destroys his own kingdom, and is murdered in his bed at noon. Abner holds the power; Saul’s son supplies the royal name. They go to Mahanaim, across the Jordan, because the heartland is not safe enough to be crowned in.

Ish-bosheth. The name means “man of shame”. Chronicles calls him Eshbaal (1 Chronicles 8:33). Scribes probably replaced baal, which could simply mean “lord”, with bosheth, “shame”, as they did in other names, to avoid the name of the Canaanite god.

Two years, seven and a half (vv. 10–11). Ish-bosheth’s reign is short and David’s Hebron years are long: David sat in Hebron for the better part of eight years as king of one tribe out of twelve, waiting, as he had waited for years already.

The pool of Gibeon (vv. 12–13). Two armies sit down on opposite sides of a water tank and look at each other. Archaeologists at Gibeon have uncovered a great rock-cut shaft with a spiral stair, probably this pool or part of the same water system. And every man on both sides is an Israelite; some fought in the same line at Michmash. Joab is David’s nephew and Abner is Saul’s kinsman (1 Samuel 14:50): this is a family quarrel with armies.

Let the young men compete (v. 14). The word is the ordinary one for play. Abner proposes a contest of champions, a fixed number from each side with the result standing for the whole, a recognised way of settling a matter without committing two armies; Goliath had proposed the same (1 Samuel 17:8–9). The intention is not bloodthirsty. Two generals who know this war cannot really be won are looking for a way to keep the cost down.

They fell down together (vv. 15–16). All twenty-four die at once, one of the more terrible moments in the book, told simply by describing the movements. Each man seizes his opposite number by the head and drives a sword into his side, and they go down in pairs. No winner, not even a fight worth describing, and Israel put a name on the ground and kept it.

Very fierce that day (v. 17). So the armies go in anyway, and a war runs for years (3:1). It is a common pattern: a measure meant to contain a conflict ignites it, because the men involved were never willing to accept a result they did not like. Abner would not have gone home if his twelve had lost; neither would Joab. “The beginning of strife is like letting out water” (Proverbs 17:14).

How do two years and seven and a half fit? Ish-bosheth was probably made king some years after Saul’s death, once Abner had regained the north from the Philistines; his two years fell within David’s seven and a half at Hebron, and the war between the houses ran through the whole period (3:1).

Uncertain wording. Two names here are not certain. Who “the Ashurites” (v. 9) were is unknown; perhaps the tribe of Asher, perhaps a group east of the Jordan near Gilead. And Helkath-hazzurim (v. 16) most likely means “field of sword-edges”, though other meanings, such as “field of flints”, have been suggested. Neither affects the story.
verseByVerse.note: Ish-bosheth means “man of shame,” probably a scribal replacement for Esh-baal (“man of Baal”). “Helkath-hazzurim” means “the field of sword-edges” (ESV note).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 18–23 — Turn Aside from Following Me
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A young man’s refusal to turn aside starts a blood feud that will run for decades. Asahel, Joab’s brother, fast as a gazelle, pursues Abner himself and will not turn to the right or the left (vv. 18–19). Abner recognises him and twice urges him to break off and take another man’s armour instead, because he does not want to kill Joab’s brother (vv. 20–22). Asahel refuses, and Abner strikes backward with the butt of his spear, which goes right through him, and he dies where he falls; everyone who comes to the place stops still (v. 23).
verseByVerse.theology: Abner is the most experienced soldier in Israel and he does not want this killing. He can see the whole feud coming.
verseByVerse.examples: A blow meant to stop a young man, driven home by his own speed, becomes the fuse for a murder at the gate in the next chapter and for Joab's own execution more than thirty years later (1 Kings 2:5-6). One death in anger can set off a chain of others for a generation.

verseByVerse.quote: And the three sons of Zeruiah were there, Joab, Abishai, and Asahel. Now Asahel was as swift of foot as a wild gazelle. And Asahel pursued Abner, and as he went, he turned neither to the right hand nor to the left from following Abner. Then Abner looked behind him and said, "Is it you, Asahel?" And he answered, "It is I." Abner said to him, "Turn aside to your right hand or to your left, and seize one of the young men and take his spoil." But Asahel would not turn aside from following him. And Abner said again to Asahel, "Turn aside from following me. Why should I strike you to the ground? How then could I lift up my face to your brother Joab?" But he refused to turn aside. Therefore Abner struck him in the stomach with the butt of his spear, so that the spear came out at his back. And he fell there and died where he was. And all who came to the place where Asahel had fallen and died, stood still.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Asahel will not stop chasing Abner, and Abner, who tried twice to spare him, kills him with a backward blow and starts a blood feud he foresaw.

The three sons of Zeruiah (v. 18). David’s nephews, who between them will run his army, win his wars and cause him more trouble than any of his enemies. Asahel is introduced by the one thing everybody knew about him: he could run.

Neither to the right hand nor to the left (v. 19). He picks the commander of the opposing army and goes after him in a straight line. The phrase is usually praise in Scripture, said of keeping God’s law (Deuteronomy 17:20; Joshua 1:7). Here it describes a young man who has fixed on a target and will not be talked out of it.

Is it you, Asahel (v. 20). Abner knows him by name. Of course he does: they are one nation, and everyone knew who the fast one was.

Turn aside (v. 21). The first warning, and note its shape: not “go home” but “take somebody else”. He offers the boy an honourable way out with plunder in his hands, so that nothing has to be explained afterwards.

Your brother Joab (v. 22). The second warning, and the reason foretells much of the book. Abner is not worried about the fight; he could kill this boy in a moment and both of them know it. He is worried about what follows. Blood between families does not stay where it falls: if he kills Asahel, Joab will come for him, whatever the circumstances. He is not begging for his life; he is warning a young man that his death will start something neither of them can stop. And Asahel keeps running.

The butt of his spear (v. 23). That detail shows what Abner intended. He does not turn and run him through with the point; he jabs backward with the butt, a blow meant to stop him. But spear butts were often shod with metal for planting in the ground, and Asahel, running flat out, ran onto it. Abner was still trying not to kill him at the moment he killed him.

All who came stood still. Men come round the shoulder of the hill, see who is lying there, and cannot go on. Everyone knows whose brother he is, and understands in the same instant what has been set in motion. In the next chapter Joab will take Abner aside in the gate of Hebron and strike him in the stomach, the same wound in the same place (3:27). Decades later, dying, David will still be naming it to Solomon: “you also know what Joab the son of Zeruiah did to me, how he dealt with the two commanders of the armies of Israel, Abner the son of Ner, and Amasa the son of Jether, whom he killed, avenging in time of peace for blood that had been shed in war” (1 Kings 2:5). Joab will die holding the horns of the altar (1 Kings 2:28–34). All of it comes out of a boy who could run fast and would not turn aside.

What it does not mean. Not turning aside is not always a virtue. Persistence is only as good as the thing it is fixed on, and Asahel’s single-mindedness was courage without wisdom. The steadfastness Scripture praises is a heart fixed on God and his commandments, not on proving ourselves against the strongest man on the field.
verseByVerse.note: Zeruiah was David’s sister: Joab, Abishai and Asahel were his nephews.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 24–32 — Shall the Sword Devour Forever?
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The man who started the fighting calls for it to stop, and the day ends with nothing decided. Joab and Abishai pursue Abner until sunset, and the Benjaminites rally on a hilltop (vv. 24–25). Abner calls down, “Shall the sword devour forever?”, reminding Joab that the end will be bitter and that they are pursuing their brothers (v. 26). Joab blows the trumpet and the pursuit stops (vv. 27–28). Abner marches all night back to Mahanaim (v. 29). David has lost nineteen men and Asahel, and Abner three hundred and sixty (vv. 30–31). Asahel is buried at Bethlehem, and Joab marches all night to Hebron (v. 32).
verseByVerse.theology: The best sentence in the chapter comes from the person most responsible for the day.
verseByVerse.examples: A victory that changes nothing is still paid for in lives.

verseByVerse.quote: But Joab and Abishai pursued Abner. And as the sun was going down they came to the hill of Ammah, which lies before Giah on the way to the wilderness of Gibeon. And the people of Benjamin gathered themselves together behind Abner and became one group and took their stand on the top of a hill. Then Abner called to Joab, "Shall the sword devour forever? Do you not know that the end will be bitter? How long will it be before you tell your people to turn from the pursuit of their brothers?" And Joab said, "As God lives, if you had not spoken, surely the men would not have given up the pursuit of their brothers until the morning." So Joab blew the trumpet, and all the men stopped and pursued Israel no more, nor did they fight anymore. And Abner and his men went all that night through the Arabah. They crossed the Jordan, and marching the whole morning, they came to Mahanaim. Joab returned from the pursuit of Abner. And when he had gathered all the people together, there were missing from David's servants nineteen men besides Asahel. But the servants of David had struck down of Benjamin 360 of Abner's men. And they took up Asahel and buried him in the tomb of his father, which was at Bethlehem. And Joab and his men marched all night, and the day broke upon them at Hebron.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The man who began the fighting calls for it to end, and both armies march away through the night with their dead, having settled nothing.

On the top of a hill (vv. 24–25). The dead man’s two brothers keep going until sundown. Abner’s Benjaminites rally on high ground, so that any attack will now cost both sides dearly.

Shall the sword devour forever (v. 26). The best thing anybody says in this chapter. The picture is of a weapon that eats, with an appetite of its own that does not stop when the reason for drawing it has gone; anyone who has watched a quarrel outlive its cause knows the image is exact.

Do you not know that the end will be bitter? He is not appealing to mercy. He is telling a professional soldier what a professional soldier already knows: this ends badly for your side too, and the taste of it lasts. And he gives the day its true description: the pursuit of their brothers. Not enemies, but brothers.

Self-interest and truth. Honesty requires the rest. Abner started this. Twenty-four young men are dead because of his suggestion, and he calls for peace from a hilltop because he is about to be overrun. All of that is true, and the sentence is still true. Right words are not always spoken by people with nothing to gain, and self-interest does not make a thing false. Abner is manoeuvring, and he is also correct, and Joab knows it.

If you had not spoken (v. 27). Joab’s answer is colder than it looks. He does not disagree. He says that if Abner had not spoken, the pursuit would have gone on until morning: I would not have stopped; you stopped me. It is a complaint or a confession, probably both. And there is not a word in it about Asahel, from a man who will settle that account in the next chapter with a blade.

Joab blew the trumpet (v. 28). He stops at once. Whatever else is true of Joab, and much is, he does not lose control of himself or his troops.

Nineteen men besides Asahel (vv. 29–31). The writer counts both sides. Three hundred and eighty Israelites dead in one day by a water tank, and one name among them, because that is the one that will cost more than all the rest. David’s side won convincingly, eighteen to one, and it changed nothing; the war would go on a long time (3:1).

The tomb of his father (v. 32). The chapter ends with two night marches in opposite directions. Abner crosses the Jordan in the dark. Joab carries his brother to Bethlehem, buries him in their father’s tomb, and walks through the night to Hebron, and the day breaks on him as he arrives.

What it costs. Both armies spend the same night walking away from a battle that decided nothing, and the writer offers no comment. The kingdom is coming to David; this is what it costs while it comes, and most of the cost is paid by people who never chose either side.

Will the sword devour forever? Not forever. Brothers fighting brothers is the story of a fallen world, from Cain onward, and no general’s truce can end it, because “your passions are at war within you” (James 4:1). The answer to Abner’s question is the Son of David, the Prince of Peace, of whose “government and of peace there will be no end, on the throne of David” (Isaiah 9:7), who made peace by his blood and breaks down “the dividing wall of hostility” (Ephesians 2:14). “Blessed are the peacemakers” (Matthew 5:9): those who belong to him can be the ones who blow the trumpet and call a quarrel to a halt.

2.theology:
He asks, and then he asks again (v. 1). His claim to the throne was beyond dispute and the moment had plainly come, and he still put it to God; and having been told go up, he would not treat that as an answer to where. He is told where to go but not why, and Hebron turns out to be the oldest covenant ground in the country. What changed this man was Ziklag, where he called for the ephod standing in the ashes.

Each confirmation after the waiting (v. 4). Samuel's oil among his brothers, his own tribe now, and in time the elders of all Israel (5:3): God keeps confirming the same word in front of larger audiences, and each confirmation arrives only after the waiting.

Godly and shrewd together (vv. 5-7). The thank-you to Jabesh-gilead is real gratitude and also a careful word to the watching north, and the text is comfortable with both.

Peace-keeping that starts a war (vv. 14-17). A contest meant to keep a war small settles nothing, because neither general would have accepted a losing result. And Abner, who did not want to kill Asahel, kills him all the same, and that one death runs forward through the rest of David's life (see the note on v. 23).

A king recognised by one tribe (vv. 4, 8-11). David is the anointed king, crowned in Hebron, and for seven and a half years most of Israel follows someone else. His kingdom grows not by his seizing it but because God swore it, and his first act toward the doubtful north is a message of kindness, not a sword. That is the New Testament’s picture of the Son of David now. He is already crowned, yet at present, we do not yet see everything in subjection to him. But we see him... crowned with glory and honor (Hebrews 2:8-9), and he reigns until he has put all his enemies under his feet (1 Corinthians 15:25). Meanwhile he gathers rebels by a gracious word, as David wrote to Jabesh.

The right words from a man with something to gain (v. 26). Abner is calling for peace because he is about to be overrun, and the sentence is still true: the sword does devour, it is bitter in the end, and they are brothers. Self-interest does not automatically make a thing false.
2.examples:
Then: Two Israelite armies sat down on opposite sides of a rock-cut water tank and agreed to settle the matter with twelve men a side, and every one of the twenty-four caught his opposite number by the head and put a sword in his ribs at the same instant, so that nothing at all was decided. They named the ground the Field of Sword-Edges and then fought the battle anyway.

Now: Verse 1 is the practical lesson: David got a clear yes and still would not assume it answered the next question. Most bad decisions made by people who genuinely want to obey are made in exactly that gap, a real leading about whether quietly extended to cover where, when and how. God has not left his people to guess: he gives his word, and the Spirit who leads us through it, and he answers those who keep asking, as he answered a man who had not asked for sixteen months. Abner's line is the other lesson: a quarrel does not stop when its cause has been dealt with, because the sword has an appetite of its own. Somebody usually has to call across the valley and say so, and it is very often the person least entitled to. Christians can be that voice because the Son of David has already made peace for us at his own cost.

keyVerse.quote: Shall the sword devour forever? Do you not know that the end will be bitter? How long will it be before you tell your people to turn from the pursuit of their brothers?
keyVerse.note: Abner speaks for the whole chapter: a war between brothers that no contest or victory could settle, with a hunger of its own. The words are true even from the man who began the fighting, and they expose a need no general could meet. Only the Son of David, the Prince of Peace, finally answers the question.

2.reflection:
David had every human reason to take the throne at once, yet he asked the LORD, and then asked again which town (v. 1). Why do we so often take God’s first “yes” and run with it? What would it look like for you to seek his guidance in the next step, not only the general direction?

David’s first act as king was to honour the men who had been loyal to Saul (vv. 4–7). Why does faithfulness deserve honour even when it was shown to the other side? Whose faithfulness have you been slow to recognise?

Asahel “turned neither to the right hand nor to the left” (v. 19), and it cost him his life and set off a feud that lasted decades. When is persistence a virtue and when is it folly? How can we tell the difference?

Abner’s question, “Shall the sword devour forever?” (v. 26), is true even though he started the fight. Is there a quarrel in your family, church or work that has outlived its cause? How does the peace Christ made by his cross help you be the one who calls a halt?

3.title: Abner's Defection and Joab's Revenge
3.text: <sup>1</sup>There was a long war between the house of Saul and the house of David. And David grew stronger and stronger, while the house of Saul became weaker and weaker.<sup>2</sup>And sons were born to David at Hebron: his firstborn was Amnon, of Ahinoam of Jezreel;<sup>3</sup>and his second, Chileab, of Abigail the widow of Nabal of Carmel; and the third, Absalom the son of Maacah the daughter of Talmai king of Geshur;<sup>4</sup>and the fourth, Adonijah the son of Haggith; and the fifth, Shephatiah the son of Abital;<sup>5</sup>and the sixth, Ithream, of Eglah, David's wife. These were born to David in Hebron.<sup>6</sup>While there was war between the house of Saul and the house of David, Abner was making himself strong in the house of Saul.<sup>7</sup>Now Saul had a concubine whose name was Rizpah, the daughter of Aiah. And Ish-bosheth said to Abner, "Why have you gone in to my father's concubine?"<sup>8</sup>Then Abner was very angry over the words of Ish-bosheth and said, "Am I a dog's head of Judah? To this day I keep showing steadfast love to the house of Saul your father, to his brothers, and to his friends, and have not given you into the hand of David. And yet you charge me today with a fault concerning a woman.<sup>9</sup>God do so to Abner and more also, if I do not accomplish for David what the LORD has sworn to him,<sup>10</sup>to transfer the kingdom from the house of Saul and set up the throne of David over Israel and over Judah, from Dan to Beersheba."<sup>11</sup>And Ish-bosheth could not answer Abner another word, because he feared him.<sup>12</sup>And Abner sent messengers to David on his behalf, saying, "To whom does the land belong? Make your covenant with me, and behold, my hand shall be with you to bring over all Israel to you."<sup>13</sup>And he said, "Good; I will make a covenant with you. But one thing I require of you; that is, you shall not see my face unless you first bring Michal, Saul's daughter, when you come to see my face."<sup>14</sup>Then David sent messengers to Ish-bosheth, Saul's son, saying, "Give me my wife Michal, for whom I paid the bridal price of a hundred foreskins of the Philistines."<sup>15</sup>And Ish-bosheth sent and took her from her husband Paltiel the son of Laish.<sup>16</sup>But her husband went with her, weeping after her all the way to Bahurim. Then Abner said to him, "Go, return." And he returned.<sup>17</sup>And Abner conferred with the elders of Israel, saying, "For some time past you have been seeking David as king over you.<sup>18</sup>Now then bring it about, for the LORD has promised David, saying, 'By the hand of my servant David I will save my people Israel from the hand of the Philistines, and from the hand of all their enemies.'"<sup>19</sup>Abner also spoke to Benjamin. And then Abner went to tell David at Hebron all that Israel and the whole house of Benjamin thought good to do.<sup>20</sup>When Abner came with twenty men to David at Hebron, David made a feast for Abner and the men who were with him.<sup>21</sup>And Abner said to David, "I will arise and go and will gather all Israel to my lord the king, that they may make a covenant with you, and that you may reign over all that your heart desires." So David sent Abner away, and he went in peace.<sup>22</sup>Just then the servants of David arrived with Joab from a raid, bringing much spoil with them. But Abner was not with David at Hebron, for he had sent him away, and he had gone in peace.<sup>23</sup>When Joab and all the army that was with him came, it was told Joab, "Abner the son of Ner came to the king, and he has let him go, and he has gone in peace."<sup>24</sup>Then Joab went to the king and said, "What have you done? Behold, Abner came to you. Why is it that you have sent him away, so that he is gone?<sup>25</sup>You know that Abner the son of Ner came to deceive you and to know your going out and your coming in, and to know all that you are doing."<sup>26</sup>When Joab came out from David's presence, he sent messengers after Abner, and they brought him back from the cistern of Sirah.
