But David did not know about it.<sup>27</sup>And when Abner returned to Hebron, Joab took him aside into the midst of the gate to speak with him privately, and there he struck him in the stomach, so that he died, for the blood of Asahel his brother.<sup>28</sup>Afterward, when David heard of it, he said, "I and my kingdom are forever guiltless before the LORD for the blood of Abner the son of Ner.<sup>29</sup>May it fall upon the head of Joab and upon all his father's house, and may the house of Joab never be without one who has a discharge or who is leprous or who holds a spindle or who falls by the sword or who lacks bread!"<sup>30</sup>So Joab and Abishai his brother killed Abner, because he had put their brother Asahel to death in the battle at Gibeon.<sup>31</sup>Then David said to Joab and to all the people who were with him, "Tear your clothes and put on sackcloth and mourn before Abner." And King David followed the bier.<sup>32</sup>They buried Abner at Hebron. And the king lifted up his voice and wept at the grave of Abner, and all the people wept.<sup>33</sup>And the king lamented for Abner, saying, "Should Abner die as a fool dies?<sup>34</sup>Your hands were not bound; your feet were not fettered; as one falls before the wicked you have fallen." And all the people wept again over him.<sup>35</sup>Then all the people came to persuade David to eat bread while it was yet day. But David swore, saying, "God do so to me and more also, if I taste bread or anything else till the sun goes down!"<sup>36</sup>And all the people took notice of it, and it pleased them, as everything that the king did pleased all the people.<sup>37</sup>So all the people and all Israel understood that day that it had not been the king's will to put to death Abner the son of Ner.<sup>38</sup>And the king said to his servants, "Do you not know that a prince and a great man has fallen this day in Israel?<sup>39</sup>And I was gentle today, though anointed king. These men, the sons of Zeruiah, are more severe than I. The LORD repay the evildoer according to his wickedness!"
3.overview:
Where we are. David reigns over Judah at Hebron, and Abner rules the north through Saul’s son Ish-bosheth. The battle at Gibeon settled nothing, and Joab now owes Abner a brother’s blood (chapter 2).

The message. What God has sworn, God brings about, and he does it through proud, angry and violent men who neither deserve nor intend to serve him. The kingdom passes to David because the LORD swore it, not because anyone in the chapter is good; and the chapter is honest that David himself, God’s chosen king, is too weak to bring the justice his people need.

Why it was said. Israel’s first readers needed to know that David had no hand in the murder of Saul’s commander, a charge his enemies could easily make (see the introduction). The narrator gives the evidence, and he also refuses to hide what the union of the kingdom cost, or the weakness of the king.

How the chapter makes its case. The long war turns David’s way, and a list of his sons by six wives quietly plants the sorrows to come (vv. 1–5). Ish-bosheth accuses Abner over Saul’s concubine, and Abner in fury swears to do what “the LORD has sworn” to David (vv. 6–11). He opens talks; David demands Michal back, and she is taken from her weeping husband; Abner wins over the elders and is feasted at Hebron and sent away in peace (vv. 12–21). Joab, back from a raid, lures Abner into the gate and kills him for Asahel’s blood, without David’s knowledge (vv. 22–30). David curses Joab, mourns Abner publicly, and confesses that the sons of Zeruiah are too hard for him (vv. 31–39).

Where it leads. To Christ by promise and by the need it exposes. Abner quotes God’s word that “by the hand of my servant David I will save my people” (v. 18), and Zechariah sang its fulfilment: God “has raised up a horn of salvation for us in the house of his servant David … that we should be saved from our enemies” (Luke 1:69–71). But David cannot even judge the murderer in his own house. Israel needed a King who would “judge the poor” with righteousness (Isaiah 11:4), who is neither too weak to do justice nor too hard to show mercy, and who bears the blood guilt of his people himself.

For us. God’s purposes do not wait for good motives, so we need not despair when the people around us, or we ourselves, are mixed. Do not leave undone the hard duty that is yours on the day it is yours. And take comfort that the King we serve is never too weak to put things right, and never too hard to forgive.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–11 — What the LORD Has Sworn to Him
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God’s sworn purpose advances through a long war, a crowded household and a quarrel over a woman. The war between the two houses drags on, but David grows steadily stronger and Saul’s house weaker (v. 1). Six sons are born to David at Hebron by six different wives, a list that includes Amnon, Absalom and Adonijah and plants much of the sorrow to come (vv. 2–5). Abner has become the real power in the north, and when Ish-bosheth accuses him of taking Saul’s concubine, Abner in fury swears to give David the whole kingdom, as the LORD had sworn (vv. 6–10). Ish-bosheth is too afraid to answer him a word (v. 11).
verseByVerse.theology: The list of sons looks like a routine record, but these sons bring trouble for the rest of the book.
verseByVerse.examples: Abner's change of side in verse 9 comes from wounded pride, not from repentance, and God's purpose moves forward through it all the same.

verseByVerse.quote: There was a long war between the house of Saul and the house of David. And David grew stronger and stronger, while the house of Saul became weaker and weaker.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Through years of war between Israelites, God’s word comes true at the pace of ordinary events: David grows stronger and Saul’s house weaker.

There was a long war. One verse covers years, and does two things at once. It tells us this went on a long time: not a season of skirmishing but a war between two halves of the same nation, with the pool of Gibeon somewhere near its beginning.

David grew stronger and stronger. And it gives away the ending in the flattest possible way: stronger and stronger, weaker and weaker. There is no drama in the sentence, and that is the point. What God said would happen is happening, at the pace of ordinary events, while people fight about it.

The house of Saul and the house of David. The war is a quarrel between two royal houses, and the word “house” runs through the next four chapters until God takes it up himself and promises David a house of a different kind (see the note on 7:10–11). Which house stands is settled not finally by battles but by what God has said.

verseByVerse.quote: And sons were born to David at Hebron: his firstborn was Amnon, of Ahinoam of Jezreel; and his second, Chileab, of Abigail the widow of Nabal of Carmel; and the third, Absalom the son of Maacah the daughter of Talmai king of Geshur; and the fourth, Adonijah the son of Haggith; and the fifth, Shephatiah the son of Abital; and the sixth, Ithream, of Eglah, David's wife. These were born to David in Hebron.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A list of six sons by six wives, set quietly into a war report, plants the sorrows that will tear David’s house apart.

Sons were born to David at Hebron. Six sons by six mothers, dropped into the war report like an administrative note, and three of the names fill much of the rest of the book. Amnon, the firstborn, will rape his half-sister Tamar and be murdered at a sheep-shearing feast (chapter 13). Absalom will do the murdering, flee to his grandfather, come back, steal the hearts of Israel at the city gate, drive his father out of Jerusalem barefoot, lie with his father’s concubines in public, and die hanging in an oak (chapters 13–18). Adonijah will try to take the throne as David lies dying, and be executed by Solomon (1 Kings 1–2).

What the law said. Every one by a different woman. The law had warned Israel’s king in one sentence: “he shall not acquire many wives for himself, lest his heart turn away” (Deuteronomy 17:17). The rule is not only about desire. A household of rival wives and rival sons splits into factions, and when it is the royal household, the factions fight for the throne.

The daughter of Talmai king of Geshur. Absalom’s mother was a foreign princess, so the marriage was a treaty. When Absalom kills his brother, he runs to Geshur, to his grandfather, and stays three years (13:37–38). The alliance David made to secure a border produced the son who nearly took his throne, and the hiding place he escaped to. The narrator says none of this. He sets a list of names between a war summary and a palace quarrel, and lets it sit.

Chileab, of Abigail. Not every name goes on to a story. Abigail, the wise woman who kept David from bloodshed (1 Samuel 25), bore him Chileab, called Daniel in Chronicles (1 Chronicles 3:1), and he is never heard of again; he probably died young. Shephatiah and Ithream are names only.

The true Bridegroom. David gathered wives, and his house divided. The Son of David has one bride, the church, and he did not take her for advantage but “loved the church and gave himself up for her” (Ephesians 5:25).

Did God approve David’s many wives? No. God’s design is one man and one woman (Genesis 2:24), and the law told Israel’s king not to multiply wives (Deuteronomy 17:17). Scripture records David’s polygamy without approving it, and the following chapters show its fruit: rape, murder and rebellion among his sons.

verseByVerse.quote: While there was war between the house of Saul and the house of David, Abner was making himself strong in the house of Saul. Now Saul had a concubine whose name was Rizpah, the daughter of Aiah. And Ish-bosheth said to Abner, "Why have you gone in to my father's concubine?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Abner has become the real power in the north, and Ish-bosheth’s accusation over Saul’s concubine is really a quarrel about the throne.

Abner was making himself strong in the house of Saul (v. 6). The verse says what the quarrel is really about before it starts. As the war wore on, the real power in the north passed to Abner, and Ish-bosheth knew it.

Rizpah, the daughter of Aiah (v. 7). She is named because she matters. Years later she will keep watch over the bodies of her two sons, executed for Saul’s bloodguilt, from harvest until the rain, until David hears of it and gives Saul’s family an honourable burial (21:8–14).

Why have you gone in to my father’s concubine? The accusation looks domestic, but it is about the throne. In that world, taking a dead king’s women was a claim on his throne, and everybody understood it: the recognised public way of saying “the succession is mine”. Absalom will do it deliberately, on a roof, before the whole city, on Ahithophel’s advice, precisely because it is unmistakable (16:21–22). So Ish-bosheth is accusing his general of moving on the crown, and he may well be right.

Ish-bosheth’s one decision. He is also finished the moment he says it. Abner is the army, the government and the reason Ish-bosheth is king at all. Insulting him is the only independent decision this man makes in the whole book, and it destroys him.
verseByVerse.note: The same claim lies behind Absalom on the palace roof (16:21-22) and behind Adonijah's request for Abishag, which cost him his life (1 Kings 2:13-25).

verseByVerse.quote: Then Abner was very angry over the words of Ish-bosheth and said, "Am I a dog's head of Judah? To this day I keep showing steadfast love to the house of Saul your father, to his brothers, and to his friends, and have not given you into the hand of David. And yet you charge me today with a fault concerning a woman. God do so to Abner and more also, if I do not accomplish for David what the LORD has sworn to him, to transfer the kingdom from the house of Saul and set up the throne of David over Israel and over Judah, from Dan to Beersheba." And Ish-bosheth could not answer Abner another word, because he feared him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Stung by the insult, Abner swears to hand the kingdom to David, admitting that he had known all along that the LORD had sworn it.

Abner was very angry (v. 8). He does not deny it. His answer is a list of services rendered and a complaint about ingratitude: after everything I have done for your father’s house, you raise this?

I keep showing steadfast love. He uses the great covenant word, hesed, for his loyalty to Saul’s house. But it is loyalty that keeps accounts, and it ends the moment it is insulted.

God do so to Abner and more also (v. 9). The solemn oath of Israel, calling down on oneself God’s judgment, and worse, if the promise is not kept (compare Ruth 1:17; 1 Samuel 3:17). Abner swears by the God whose sworn word he has been resisting for years, and stakes his life on accomplishing it.

What the LORD has sworn to him. This is the key sentence of the chapter. Abner has known all along that God swore it. He can quote it, geography and all, from Dan to Beersheba, the whole country from top to bottom (v. 10).

What Abner did with it. Now count what he has done with that knowledge. He served a king God had rejected. He took Saul’s surviving son across the Jordan and crowned him. He ran a civil war for years against the man God had sworn to enthrone. Twenty-four young men died at the pool of Gibeon because of a proposal he made, and Asahel died on the end of his spear. He did all of it knowingly.

What changes his mind. Not conviction, not repentance, not the word of God he has just quoted, but being spoken to disrespectfully about a woman. This is more common than a dramatic change of heart. Few people who resist what they know to be right are won by an argument. They are moved when the arrangement they were defending finally insults them; then they discover they had known all along, and say so loudly, as though the knowledge were new.

God at work through it. God’s purpose goes forward anyway. He is using a furious general with wounded pride and no change of heart whatever, and the kingdom moves a step closer to the man Abner has fought for years. God’s promises never depend on the goodness of the people he uses to keep them.

He could not answer Abner another word (v. 11). Because he feared him. That is the measure of this king: at the one moment that mattered, he had nothing to say.

Uncertain wording. “Am I a dog’s head of Judah?” is a rare expression. A dog was a byword for something worthless (compare 1 Samuel 24:14), so the general sense is clear: “Am I some worthless traitor in Judah’s pay?” But exactly what a “dog’s head” meant, and how “of Judah” fits, is uncertain. The insult and its sneer at Judah are plain either way.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The kingdom is negotiated, and the cost falls on people nobody consults. Abner offers David a covenant and the whole of Israel (v. 12). David agrees, on one condition: Michal, Saul’s daughter and David’s first wife, must be returned to him, and he sends to Ish-bosheth for her, citing the price he paid for her (vv. 13–14). She is taken from her husband Paltiel, who follows weeping until Abner sends him home (vv. 15–16). Abner reminds the elders of Israel that they have long wanted David and that the LORD promised to save Israel by David’s hand, and he speaks to Benjamin too (vv. 17–19). David feasts Abner at Hebron and sends him away in peace (vv. 20–21).
verseByVerse.theology: David's demand for Michal is both politics and a husband's claim, and the cost of it falls on two people who are never consulted.
verseByVerse.examples: Abner's diplomacy with the elders is skilful, and the narrator's triple in peace makes sure we remember the safe conduct he was given.

verseByVerse.quote: And Abner sent messengers to David on his behalf, saying, "To whom does the land belong? Make your covenant with me, and behold, my hand shall be with you to bring over all Israel to you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Abner offers David the whole kingdom by covenant, coming as a power broker, not a penitent.

To whom does the land belong? He means: we both know the answer, and we both know I am the only man who can deliver it.

Make your covenant with me. Abner proposes a treaty, a binding agreement sworn before God, and offers what only he can give: “my hand shall be with you to bring over all Israel to you.” He has quoted God’s oath to David (v. 9), but he negotiates as though the kingdom were his to hand over, and he means to have a place in the new order when it comes.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said, "Good; I will make a covenant with you. But one thing I require of you; that is, you shall not see my face unless you first bring Michal, Saul's daughter, when you come to see my face." Then David sent messengers to Ish-bosheth, Saul's son, saying, "Give me my wife Michal, for whom I paid the bridal price of a hundred foreskins of the Philistines." And Ish-bosheth sent and took her from her husband Paltiel the son of Laish. But her husband went with her, weeping after her all the way to Bahurim. Then Abner said to him, "Go, return." And he returned.
verseByVerse.commentary:
David’s one condition is the return of Michal, his lawful wife, and the price of the bargain is paid by her weeping husband and by Michal herself, whom no one asks.

One thing I require of you (v. 13). David sets one condition, and it is a woman: Michal, Saul’s younger daughter, who loved David. The narrator said so outright (1 Samuel 18:20), a thing he says of no other woman in either book of Samuel. She warned David the night the assassins came, let him down through a window, put an idol in his bed with goats’ hair at its head to buy him time, and lied to her father’s face about it (1 Samuel 19:11–17). Then Saul gave her to another man while David was in the wilderness, as though the marriage had never happened (1 Samuel 25:44).

Why does David want her back? Both reasons are real, and the text will not sort them out. She is Saul’s daughter, and a king of Judah married to Saul’s daughter has a claim the northern tribes can recognise; that is politics, and it is why he raises it in a negotiation about the kingdom and not before. And she was his wife, taken from him by force by a man who was trying to kill him, and he never accepted it. That is not nothing.

I paid the bridal price (v. 14). David also sends to Ish-bosheth himself, so that the return is lawful, and cites the price. It was Saul’s idea, meant to get David killed: a hundred Philistines was expected to be the end of him (1 Samuel 18:25). He brought two hundred (1 Samuel 18:27; the Greek Old Testament there reads a hundred, and David here names the price that was asked). He is reminding Saul’s house that he paid what Saul asked, twice over, and that the marriage was lawful.

Weeping after her all the way to Bahurim (vv. 15–16). The hardest thing in the chapter. Paltiel gets no dialogue, no protest. He walks behind the party, crying, all the way to Bahurim, until a general who has killed men with a spear says two words to him, Go, return, and he turns round and goes home. He had been married to her for years. Nobody consulted him and nobody compensated him. There is no suggestion he did anything wrong: he was given a wife by his king, he loved her, and now two governments have agreed on something and he is walking back to Gallim alone.

Nobody asks Michal. Ish-bosheth took her from her husband, Abner delivered her, David received her, and she does not speak in this chapter or the next. The last time she spoke she was lying to her father to save David’s life. The next time, three chapters on, she will despise him from a window, and the writer will tell us she had no child to the day of her death (6:16–23). Something happened to that woman between the window she let David down from and the window she despised him from, and this chapter is a large part of it.

The God who sees. It would be easy, and wrong, to hurry past this. The narrator does not accuse David here, but he seldom accuses anybody, and he has made sure we watch a man weep all the way to Bahurim. Anyone who has been treated as a piece in other people’s bargains, handed on without being asked, should know that Scripture records this without approving it. The God of Israel is the God who sees the one nobody consulted (Genesis 16:13), and the Son of David gave himself for his bride rather than taking her for advantage (Ephesians 5:25).

Did taking her back break the law? Deuteronomy 24:1–4 forbids taking back a wife after she has been divorced and has married another. But David had not divorced Michal; Saul took her and gave her to Paltiel against the law (1 Samuel 25:44). David reclaimed his own wife. That answers the legal question; it does not answer the human one.

verseByVerse.quote: And Abner conferred with the elders of Israel, saying, "For some time past you have been seeking David as king over you. Now then bring it about, for the LORD has promised David, saying, 'By the hand of my servant David I will save my people Israel from the hand of the Philistines, and from the hand of all their enemies.'" Abner also spoke to Benjamin. And then Abner went to tell David at Hebron all that Israel and the whole house of Benjamin thought good to do.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Abner wins over the elders of Israel by reminding them of what they already wanted and of what the LORD had promised: to save Israel by David’s hand.

Abner conferred with the elders of Israel (v. 17). The tribal elders were the men whose word carried a region. Abner wins them by telling them what they already wanted: For some time past you have been seeking David as king over you. So the northern enthusiasm for David was there all along, and Abner was the man holding it back. Now he presents himself as the one making it possible.

The LORD has promised David (v. 18). Again he quotes God, and again he knows what God has said, and always did. No such word is recorded earlier, so Abner is probably summing up what was known of God’s choice of David. But the words echo what God said of Saul on the day he was chosen: “He shall save my people from the hand of the Philistines” (1 Samuel 9:16). The work Saul was anointed to do and never finished is now David’s, and the elders are told that the LORD himself has made the change.

A promise kept in a greater Son. David did save Israel from the Philistines (5:17–25; 8:1). But the promise reached further. When John the Baptist was born, his father Zechariah sang that God “has raised up a horn of salvation for us in the house of his servant David … that we should be saved from our enemies and from the hand of all who hate us” (Luke 1:69–71). The enemies Jesus defeats are the ones no army can reach: sin, death and the devil.

Abner also spoke to Benjamin (v. 19). Benjamin gets a separate conversation, because it is Saul’s own tribe and has the most to lose.

verseByVerse.quote: When Abner came with twenty men to David at Hebron, David made a feast for Abner and the men who were with him. And Abner said to David, "I will arise and go and will gather all Israel to my lord the king, that they may make a covenant with you, and that you may reign over all that your heart desires." So David sent Abner away, and he went in peace.
verseByVerse.commentary:
David seals the agreement with a feast and sends Abner away in peace, under the king’s protection.

David made a feast for Abner (v. 20). In that world a shared meal sealed an agreement and put the guest under the host’s protection (compare Genesis 26:30; 31:54). Abner’s promise in return is generous: to gather all Israel that you may reign over all that your heart desires (v. 21). The covenant is all but done, and the feast makes what happens next a breach of the king’s table as well as his word.

And he went in peace. The phrase comes three times in three verses (vv. 21–23), the writer’s way of pressing it home. Abner came under safe conduct, ate at the king’s table, and left with the king’s word on him. Everything about to happen violates that.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 22–30 — In the Midst of the Gate
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Joab murders Abner for his brother’s blood, and David declares himself innocent. Joab returns from a raid to find that Abner has come and gone in peace, rebukes the king, and claims Abner came to spy (vv. 22–25). Without David’s knowledge he sends for Abner, takes him aside in the gate of Hebron as if to speak privately, and stabs him in the stomach, for the blood of Asahel (vv. 26–27). When David hears, he declares that he and his kingdom are guiltless before the LORD and calls down a lasting curse on Joab’s house (vv. 28–29). The narrator states the true motive: revenge for Asahel, killed in battle (v. 30).
verseByVerse.theology: Joab's murder is planned down to its place and manner, and the narrator's quiet line that David did not know about it is the hinge of the whole affair.
verseByVerse.examples: David's first concern is to clear himself and his kingdom of the blood before the LORD; his second is a curse; and there is no third.

verseByVerse.quote: Just then the servants of David arrived with Joab from a raid, bringing much spoil with them. But Abner was not with David at Hebron, for he had sent him away, and he had gone in peace. When Joab and all the army that was with him came, it was told Joab, "Abner the son of Ner came to the king, and he has let him go, and he has gone in peace." Then Joab went to the king and said, "What have you done? Behold, Abner came to you. Why is it that you have sent him away, so that he is gone? You know that Abner the son of Ner came to deceive you and to know your going out and your coming in, and to know all that you are doing." When Joab came out from David's presence, he sent messengers after Abner, and they brought him back from the cistern of Sirah. But David did not know about it. And when Abner returned to Hebron, Joab took him aside into the midst of the gate to speak with him privately, and there he struck him in the stomach, so that he died, for the blood of Asahel his brother. Afterward, when David heard of it, he said, "I and my kingdom are forever guiltless before the LORD for the blood of Abner the son of Ner. May it fall upon the head of Joab and upon all his father's house, and may the house of Joab never be without one who has a discharge or who is leprous or who holds a spindle or who falls by the sword or who lacks bread!" So Joab and Abishai his brother killed Abner, because he had put their brother Asahel to death in the battle at Gibeon.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Joab, driven by revenge for his brother and fear for his own position, lures Abner back and murders him in the gate of Hebron; David had no part in it, declares himself innocent, and curses Joab, but does nothing more.

What have you done? (vv. 22–24). Joab has been away, which is why there was a deal at all. When he returns he rebukes the king to his face, in the king’s own house, and nothing happens to him.

Came to deceive you (v. 25). The charge is that Abner was a spy. Nothing in the chapter supports it, and Joab offers no evidence. It is the excuse that lay to hand. The real reason is a body in a tomb at Bethlehem: Abner killed Asahel at Gibeon, and Joab buried his brother, walked all night to Hebron, and has been waiting ever since. There is a second motive too, and it would be naive to leave it out. If Abner delivers the northern tribes, he becomes the most important man in the kingdom after the king, which is Joab’s place now. The spy story covers a blood feud, and the feud runs alongside a rank he does not intend to lose.

But David did not know about it (v. 26). The writer puts that in deliberately, and it is the hinge of the whole affair. Everything that follows is done in the king’s name, with the king’s messengers, from the king’s town, without the king’s knowledge. Abner turns back from the cistern of Sirah because he has no reason not to: he has eaten at David’s table, and a summons from Hebron means the king wants another word.

Four outrages (v. 27). The verse holds four separate outrages, stated without raising the voice. The first is the place: Hebron, one of the six cities God set apart as cities of refuge (Joshua 20:7), where a man who had killed someone “without intent” could be safe from the avenger of blood, the dead man’s nearest kinsman, until a proper hearing (Numbers 35:11–12). And Abner’s killing of Asahel was a clear case: he warned the boy twice, offered him another target, said he did not want to face Joab, and struck backward with the butt of his spear. If any death in Scripture was manslaughter rather than murder, it is that one. The city that existed to protect exactly this man is where he is killed for exactly this death.

Into the midst of the gate. The second is the spot. The city gate was the courthouse, where elders sat, property changed hands and witnesses stood; Boaz settled the redemption of Ruth in a gate with ten elders watching. It was the most public and legally protected ground in the town. The third is the method: he is killed by the offer of a private word, the gesture of trust used as the weapon. Abner has to lean in for it to work. The fourth is the wound: in the stomach, where Abner’s spear went into Asahel (2:23). It is a debt repaid in kind. Joab is not a hot-tempered man. He waited, chose the ground, and matched the wound.

I and my kingdom are forever guiltless (v. 28). David’s first concern is guilt resting on the whole kingdom. In Israel, shed blood defiled the land and lay on the community until it was answered (Numbers 35:33), and a killing by the king’s commander, in the king’s city, through the king’s messengers, would ordinarily lie on the king. David declares before God that it does not.

May it fall upon the head of Joab (v. 29). Then he curses him, comprehensively and permanently, and does nothing else. The curse runs through what that world most dreaded: a discharge or leprosy, which made a man unclean and shut him out of worship (Leviticus 13; 15); weakness; death by the sword; and hunger. That gap between the curse and any action is the point of the chapter’s last verse.

Because he had put their brother Asahel to death (v. 30). The narrator’s verdict sets Joab’s excuse aside: the reason was not spying but Asahel. And in the battle matters. This was a death in war, and Joab avenged it in peacetime, the very thing David will still be naming on his deathbed (1 Kings 2:5). Solomon will put it plainly: Joab killed “two men more righteous and better than himself” (1 Kings 2:32).

The King who is never compromised. David’s innocence had to be argued, because his commander did his killing for him. Jesus’ innocence needed no press office: even the judge who condemned him said, “I find no guilt in this man” (Luke 23:4). And where Joab shed blood to settle a score, Jesus shed his own blood to settle ours.

Isn’t this just royal spin? A suspicious modern reader will say that a line like David did not know about it is exactly what a court historian would write. Some scholars read these chapters as just that, a defence of David against the charge that he profited from three convenient deaths, and the suspicion is fair: every regime has its press office. But a press office does not keep what this writer keeps. It does not make us watch Paltiel weep all the way to Bahurim, list six wives taken against the law, record the king admitting he is too weak to judge his own nephews, or, a few chapters on, tell the whole story of Bathsheba. Timothy Keller often pointed out that the Gospels are full of details nobody inventing a flattering story would have chosen, and Samuel is the same. The hero of this book is not David but the God who keeps his oath through people who need forgiving. That is good news for those of us who run press offices of our own, trimming the record until we come out innocent. For those in Christ there is “no condemnation” (Romans 8:1), and so nothing left to spin.

Uncertain wording. The phrase “who holds a spindle” (v. 29) is uncertain. It probably means a man fit only for women’s work, spinning, rather than for war; some read it instead as one who leans on a crutch, a cripple. Either way it is a curse of weakness on a house of fighting men.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 31–39 — The Sons of Zeruiah Are More Severe Than I
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: David honours his enemy in death, and confesses that he is too weak to bring justice. He commands Joab and all the people to tear their clothes, put on sackcloth and mourn for Abner, and he follows the bier himself (v. 31). He weeps aloud at the grave and sings a lament that Abner should have died like a fool, not as a prisoner but at the hands of the wicked (vv. 32–34). He refuses food until sunset, and all the people see that the king had no part in the killing (vv. 35–37). Then he tells his servants that a prince and a great man has fallen, admits that the sons of Zeruiah are too hard for him, and leaves their punishment to the LORD (vv. 38–39).
verseByVerse.theology: David's public mourning is real grief and shrewd statecraft at once, and the narrator does not make us choose between them.
verseByVerse.examples: Verse 39 is David naming his own weakness in public, and it is the truest thing he says all chapter.

verseByVerse.quote: Then David said to Joab and to all the people who were with him, "Tear your clothes and put on sackcloth and mourn before Abner." And King David followed the bier. They buried Abner at Hebron. And the king lifted up his voice and wept at the grave of Abner, and all the people wept.
verseByVerse.commentary:
David makes the murderer mourn his victim and walks behind the bier himself, honouring the enemy general as a great man of Israel.

Tear your clothes and put on sackcloth (v. 31). David makes the murderer walk in the funeral. Joab must tear his clothes, put on sackcloth (see mourning customs) and mourn in public for the man he has just killed, before the whole town. It is not justice, and David knows it is not. It is the only thing he can make him do.

King David followed the bier. Then the king walks behind the coffin. Think who is in that procession: David following the bier of the general who fought him for years, crowned a rival, ran the war against him, and killed David’s own nephew. He grieves for the commander of the opposing army, publicly, at the head of his people.

They buried Abner at Hebron (v. 32). Abner was a Benjaminite, from Saul’s country to the north, yet he is buried in David’s own city in the king’s presence, an honour and a public statement: David claims him as a great man of Israel, not a fallen enemy. When Ish-bosheth’s head is brought to Hebron in the next chapter, it is buried in Abner’s tomb (4:12).

Weeping for an enemy. David wept at the grave of the man who had made war on him. The Son of David wept over the city that would reject him (Luke 19:41), and died for his enemies: “while we were enemies we were reconciled to God by the death of his Son” (Romans 5:10).

verseByVerse.quote: And the king lamented for Abner, saying, "Should Abner die as a fool dies? Your hands were not bound; your feet were not fettered; as one falls before the wicked you have fallen." And all the people wept again over him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
David’s lament says that Abner did not deserve to die as he did: not in battle, nor as a condemned prisoner, but murdered by the wicked.

The king lamented for Abner (v. 33). A second lament, the second poem in three chapters that David has composed for a man on the other side.

Should Abner die as a fool dies? The word for “fool” is nabal, the name of the churlish man of 1 Samuel 25 (25:25), and in the Old Testament it describes a man who brings ruin on himself by his own folly and godlessness. David’s question means: did Abner deserve to die like that, through some reckless act of his own? The protest is not that he died but how. A soldier of his rank should fall in the line with a weapon in his hand, an honour his whole world recognised.

Your hands were not bound; your feet were not fettered (v. 34). He was not a prisoner, taken, tried, condemned and led out. He was a free man walking into a gate under safe conduct to hear what the king wanted.

As one falls before the wicked you have fallen. That is the verdict: the folly and the guilt were somebody else’s, and the word wicked is aimed at a man standing in the crowd in sackcloth. And all the people wept again over him: the lament did what it was meant to do.

verseByVerse.quote: Then all the people came to persuade David to eat bread while it was yet day. But David swore, saying, "God do so to me and more also, if I taste bread or anything else till the sun goes down!" And all the people took notice of it, and it pleased them, as everything that the king did pleased all the people. So all the people and all Israel understood that day that it had not been the king's will to put to death Abner the son of Ner.
verseByVerse.commentary:
David fasts until sunset, and his grief convinces the whole nation that Abner’s murder was not his will.

If I taste bread or anything else (v. 35). Fasting until evening was the custom of mourning, as David and his men had fasted for Saul and Jonathan (1:12). The people urge him to eat, perhaps from concern, perhaps as the custom of the mourners’ meal, and he swears before them all that he will not. His grief will not be ended by courtesy. As everything that the king did pleased all the people (v. 36): David has the people’s trust, which is exactly what Joab’s murder put at risk.

It had not been the king’s will (v. 37). This verse says what the day was for, and it is politics as well as grief, because the text says so. Abner has just persuaded the northern tribes to come over, and before he reaches home he is dead in David’s city, killed by David’s commander, recalled by messengers from David’s house. Every man in the north is asking one question, and if the answer is “the king had him killed”, the union is finished before it starts and the war goes on for another decade. So David makes it impossible to believe: he curses Joab publicly, walks behind the coffin, weeps at the grave before witnesses, composes a lament, and swears not to eat.

The grief is real. None of that makes it false. The man who wrote a lament for Saul with nothing in it for himself wrote this one too. He can mean every word and know exactly what it will accomplish at the same time, which is what it is to be a public man with a real heart. The easy course was open: say nothing, accept the convenient death of the one man who might have rivalled Joab, and let people think what they liked. Plenty of kings would have. It would have cost him the north.

verseByVerse.quote: And the king said to his servants, "Do you not know that a prince and a great man has fallen this day in Israel? And I was gentle today, though anointed king. These men, the sons of Zeruiah, are more severe than I. The LORD repay the evildoer according to his wickedness!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
David honours Abner as a prince of Israel, then admits that he is too weak to punish his own nephews and leaves it to the LORD, an honest confession of a failure the rest of the book will make him pay for.

A prince and a great man (v. 38). Said of an enemy general, to his own staff, on the record. David has a habit by now, and it should be named: he says the true good thing about people who have cost him a great deal. Saul got scarlet and gold and eagles; Abner gets a prince and a great man. Neither had earned it from him personally.

I was gentle today, though anointed king (v. 39). The most honest sentence he speaks all day, and not a compliment to himself. He is saying: I am the anointed king, a murder was committed under my nose by my own commander, and I have done nothing about it but make him wear sackcloth.

These men, the sons of Zeruiah, are more severe than I. His own nephews. Joab and Abishai are harder men than he is, they hold the army’s loyalty, and he needs them.

The LORD repay the evildoer according to his wickedness! It sounds like the cave at Engedi: “May the LORD judge between me and you” (1 Samuel 24:12). But it is not the same situation at all. There he was a fugitive with no power, and handing the case to God was faith. Here he is the king, the law is his to administer (compare Romans 13:4), and handing the case to God is a way of not doing his job. Scripture lets that stand without comment, and the rest of the book shows what it cost.

What it cost. Joab, unpunished, will run David’s army for most of the reign. He will murder Amasa in the same way: a friendly greeting, a hand on the beard, a blade in the stomach (20:9–10). He will kill Absalom with three javelins while the young man hangs helpless in a tree, against an order the whole army heard (18:5, 14). He will speak to David as no subject should speak to a king, and get away with it, because he knows too much and holds too much. And on his deathbed David will hand the unfinished business to a young man with the strength to do what he never did: “Act therefore according to your wisdom, but do not let his gray head go down to Sheol in peace” (1 Kings 2:6). More than thirty years is a long time to carry a thing you should have dealt with on the day.

The King who is not too weak. David named his own weakness accurately, in public, and lived with it for the rest of his reign. His people needed a King who would “judge the poor” with righteousness and “strike the earth with the rod of his mouth” (Isaiah 11:4), and who would also be gentle with the bruised reed (Matthew 12:20). Jesus is both: never too weak to do justice, never too hard to show mercy, and at the cross he did both at once.

What it does not mean. Leaving vengeance to God (Romans 12:19) is right for the private person who has been wronged. It is not an excuse for those who hold authority, whether parents, elders or rulers, to leave undone the justice that is theirs to do. Where someone is in danger, whether from abuse or violence, those responsible must act, and must call the police where the law requires it; prayer is not a substitute for protecting the vulnerable.

Uncertain wording. The word translated “gentle” (v. 39) means soft or tender, and can mean weak or inexperienced. It is not certain whether David means that he is too soft to act, or that his kingship is still young and insecure beside his hardened nephews. Both may be in view; either way he admits he is not strong enough to do what justice requires.

3.theology:
God keeps his oath through people who are not keeping theirs. Hardly anything in this chapter is done from a pure motive. Abner changes sides because he has been insulted, David asks for Michal for reasons of state as well as love, and Joab kills for a brother and for his own position. Yet the LORD's sworn word to David (v. 9) moves forward through all of it. That excuses none of them. It is the reason a reader can trust God's purpose even when the people carrying it forward are compromised, and it is a comfort to anyone who knows their own motives are mixed.

The roots of the later sorrows are already in the ground. Two things in this chapter grow into the rest of the book: a divided household, built against the law's warning to the king (Deut. 17:17), and a commander David would not judge. The narrator comments on neither. He lets the reader watch them grow.

Grief and politics need not be rivals. David's mourning for Abner was meant to be seen, and it was also sincere. A leader can know exactly what his public grief will accomplish and still grieve truly. What the chapter faults is not the funeral but the justice that never followed it.

The king Israel still needed (v. 39). David can name the evil and cannot judge it; he is too weak for his own commanders. The prophets therefore look for a son of David who will with righteousness judge the poor and strike the wicked with the breath of his lips (Isaiah 11:4), a king neither cruel like Joab nor helpless like David. Jesus is that king. When his own disciples wanted fire from heaven on a village that refused him, he turned and rebuked them (Luke 9:54-55), and when Peter drew a sword, he told him to put it away (Matthew 26:52). He restrains the sons of violence, and one day he will judge every hidden murder in the gate with perfect justice.
3.examples:
Then: A general who had spent years fighting a war he knew God had already decided changed sides because his king insulted him, won over the northern elders, ate at his new king's table, and was stabbed before he got home, inside a city of refuge, by a man who had asked for a quiet word.

Now: Two things, pulling in different directions. Abner is the warning: it is possible to know the promise of God, say it accurately, and act on it only when the wrong side stops rewarding you. David is the other: he could name exactly what Joab was and still not act, because acting would cost something today. Naming a problem is not the same as addressing it, and that gap lasted thirty years. None of us is cured of either fault by resolve. The God who kept his oath to David through all of it is the one who forgives our long delays when we confess them, and his Spirit gives the courage to deal with the thing on the day rather than leave it to the next generation.

keyVerse.quote: By the hand of my servant David I will save my people Israel from the hand of the Philistines, and from the hand of all their enemies.
keyVerse.note: Abner quotes God’s promise to win over the elders, and the chapter shows it coming true through men who neither deserve nor intend to serve it. Yet David could not even bring justice in his own house. The promise looked beyond him to the Son of David, through whom God has “raised up a horn of salvation for us” (Luke 1:69).

3.reflection:
Abner had known all along “what the LORD has sworn” to David (v. 9), yet fought against it for years, and changed sides only when his pride was wounded. Are there truths you know God has spoken that you resist until circumstances force your hand? What would it mean to yield to them now?

Michal and Paltiel are treated as pieces in a political bargain, and no one asks them (vv. 13–16). Where are people treated this way today, in families, churches or workplaces? How does knowing that God sees the one nobody consulted change how we treat them?

David’s grief for Abner was both sincere and politically wise (vv. 31–37). Is it possible to act with real feeling and with shrewd awareness at the same time? Where do you find it hard to hold the two together?

David admitted he was too weak to deal with Joab and left it to the LORD (v. 39), and the problem lasted his whole reign. What hard duty might you be leaving undone while calling it trust? How does Jesus, the King who is neither too weak nor too hard, give you both courage and gentleness?

4.title: Ish-bosheth Murdered
4.text: <sup>1</sup>When Ish-bosheth, Saul's son, heard that Abner had died at Hebron, his courage failed, and all Israel was dismayed.<sup>2</sup>Now Saul's son had two men who were captains of raiding bands; the name of the one was Baanah, and the name of the other Rechab, sons of Rimmon a man of Benjamin from Beeroth (for Beeroth also is counted part of Benjamin;<sup>3</sup>the Beerothites fled to Gittaim and have been sojourners there to this day).<sup>4</sup>Jonathan, the son of Saul, had a son who was crippled in his feet. He was five years old when the news about Saul and Jonathan came from Jezreel, and his nurse took him up and fled, and as she fled in her haste, he fell and became lame. And his name was Mephibosheth.<sup>5</sup>Now the sons of Rimmon the Beerothite, Rechab and Baanah, set out, and about the heat of the day they came to the house of Ish-bosheth as he was taking his noonday rest.<sup>6</sup>And they came into the midst of the house as if to get wheat, and they stabbed him in the stomach. Then Rechab and Baanah his brother escaped.<sup>7</sup>When they came into the house, as he lay on his bed in his bedroom, they struck him and put him to death and beheaded him. They took his head and went by the way of the Arabah all night,<sup>8</sup>and brought the head of Ish-bosheth to David at Hebron. And they said to the king, "Here is the head of Ish-bosheth, the son of Saul, your enemy, who sought your life. The LORD has avenged my lord the king this day on Saul and on his offspring."<sup>9</sup>But David answered Rechab and Baanah his brother, the sons of Rimmon the Beerothite, "As the LORD lives, who has redeemed my life out of every adversity,<sup>10</sup>when one told me, 'Behold, Saul is dead,' and thought he was bringing good news, I seized him and killed him at Ziklag, which was the reward I gave him for his news.<sup>11</sup>How much more, when wicked men have killed a righteous man in his own house on his bed, shall I not now require his blood at your hand and destroy you from the earth?"<sup>12</sup>And David commanded his young men, and they killed them and cut off their hands and feet and hanged them beside the pool at Hebron. But they took the head of Ish-bosheth and buried it in the tomb of Abner at Hebron.
4.overview:
Where we are. The long war between the houses of Saul and David is ending. Abner, who made Ish-bosheth king, has gone over to David and been murdered by Joab in the gate of Hebron (3:27). The northern throne is left with a frightened man on it and no one to hold it up.

The message. God’s king will not receive God’s kingdom through murder, even murder that claims God’s name. Two officers kill their sleeping king and bring his head to David as the LORD’s work. David answers that the LORD who has rescued him from every trouble has never needed a knife like theirs, and does justice on the killers. The kingdom is God’s gift, and will be received God’s way.

Why it was said. The first readers needed to know that David came to the throne innocent of the blood of Saul’s house, a charge that was still being thrown at him years later (16:7–8; see the introduction). This chapter closes the case: the last king of Saul’s line died at the hands of his own men, and David executed them for it.

How the chapter makes its case. Ish-bosheth’s hands go slack at the news of Abner’s death, and two captains from his own tribe are introduced; then the narrator stops to mention Jonathan’s lame son, the last of Saul’s heirs, hidden and harmless (vv. 1–4). The captains walk into the king’s house at the midday rest, kill him in his bed and carry his head through the night to Hebron, crediting the LORD (vv. 5–8). David swears by the LORD who has redeemed his life, calls the dead man righteous, executes the murderers and buries the head in Abner’s tomb (vv. 9–12).

Where it leads. To Christ by pattern, and by the character of God revealed in him. David would not take the throne over a rival’s body; the Son of David refused the kingdoms of the world on Satan’s terms (Matthew 4:8–10), told Peter to put away his sword, and received the throne by giving his own life, not taking another’s (John 10:18). And the price behind David’s word “redeemed” was paid by Christ, who came “to give his life as a ransom for many” (Mark 10:45). The lame boy in verse 4 is waiting for the day when a king will seat him at his table (chapter 9).

For us. Being sure where God is taking history never licenses us to do wrong to help him get there. The God who has redeemed us has already carried us through every trouble and paid for us at the cross, so we do not need to secure our future by pushing someone else out of the way.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The house of Saul is collapsing, and the narrator shows it from three sides. Ish-bosheth’s nerve fails at the news of Abner’s death, and the whole northern kingdom shares his dismay, because its strength had been one man (v. 1). Two captains of raiding bands are introduced with care: Benjaminites, from Saul’s own tribe, from a town with a troubled past (vv. 2–3). Then, with no explanation, comes a lame five-year-old who fell on the day of Gilboa. Mephibosheth is the last of Saul’s line left alive and the least able to defend himself, and the story will come back for him in chapter 9 (v. 4).
verseByVerse.theology: With Abner gone, the son of Saul is no longer really a king; he is a man waiting in a house for whatever comes.
verseByVerse.examples: Verse 4 looks like a digression, but it is placed here to prepare for chapter 9.

verseByVerse.quote: When Ish-bosheth, Saul's son, heard that Abner had died at Hebron, his courage failed, and all Israel was dismayed. Now Saul's son had two men who were captains of raiding bands; the name of the one was Baanah, and the name of the other Rechab, sons of Rimmon a man of Benjamin from Beeroth (for Beeroth also is counted part of Benjamin; the Beerothites fled to Gittaim and have been sojourners there to this day). Jonathan, the son of Saul, had a son who was crippled in his feet. He was five years old when the news about Saul and Jonathan came from Jezreel, and his nurse took him up and fled, and as she fled in her haste, he fell and became lame. And his name was Mephibosheth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When Abner dies, Ish-bosheth’s kingdom dies with him; and in the middle of its collapse the narrator sets down a lame child, the last of Saul’s line, whom the story will not forget.

His courage failed (v. 1). The Hebrew is more physical than the English: his hands went slack. It is the exact image for a man whose support has been taken away. Nothing has happened to him personally; the news is about someone else in another town. But Abner was never just his general. Chapter 2 said it in the verbs: Abner took him, brought him over and made him king (2:8–9). Now he has nothing to hold on to, and he cannot hold anything. And all Israel was dismayed: the whole northern kingdom had been leaning on the same man.

Sons of Rimmon a man of Benjamin (vv. 2–3). The writer takes trouble over where the two captains come from. They are Benjaminites, of Saul’s own tribe, and captains of raiding bands in Ish-bosheth’s army, trusted men with troops of their own. The king they are about to kill is their tribesman and their employer. The aside about Beeroth hints at an old grievance: something drove its people out of their town, and they were still living displaced when this was written. Whatever it was, these two had a history, and their loyalty to the house of Saul may never have been what it looked like.

Jonathan, the son of Saul, had a son (v. 4). The verse has nothing to do with the story it sits in. In the middle of an assassination the narrator stops to tell us about a child who fell years ago, because it will matter later. The scene takes one sentence. A five-year-old in a royal household; a runner from Jezreel with the news of Gilboa: the king is dead, his sons are dead, the army is destroyed, the Philistines are coming. The palace empties. A nurse picks up the boy and runs, because in that world a new dynasty often began by killing the old king’s grandsons. And she drops him. Something broke that never set, and he is crippled in both feet for the rest of his life. That was the day it happened: the day he lost his father, his grandfather, his uncles and a kingdom.

One left of Saul’s house. In a story where the house of Saul is being removed piece by piece (Abner dead in a gate, Ish-bosheth about to die in his bed), there is one left, and he is a lame boy nobody has mentioned, hidden east of the Jordan (9:4). The writer says nothing more of him for five chapters. Then a king who has won everything will ask, “Is there still anyone left of the house of Saul, that I may show him kindness for Jonathan’s sake?” (9:1), and the answer will be this child, grown up and afraid, saying, “What is your servant, that you should show regard for a dead dog such as I?” (9:8). Verse 4 is here so that when that day comes we already know what it cost to be him.

The grace that is coming. In a chapter about men who think the way to please a king is to bring him a dead rival, the narrator plants a living one: the heir most worth removing, and the least able to resist. The king’s answer to him will be a seat at his table, for another man’s sake. That is the shape of the gospel, in which helpless enemies are sought out and brought to the King’s table for the sake of his Son (Romans 5:10; Luke 14:21).

Uncertain wording. Beeroth (“wells”) was one of the four Gibeonite towns that made a treaty with Joshua (Joshua 9:17), later counted to Benjamin (Joshua 18:25). Why its people fled to Gittaim, and when, is not known. Some suggest Saul drove them out when he tried to wipe out the Gibeonites (21:1–2), which would give the brothers a motive against his house; but Rechab and Baanah are themselves called Benjaminites, and the text does not say. The aside shows only that the writer knew of a displacement his readers would recognise.
verseByVerse.note: Mephibosheth is another form of Merib-baal (1 Chr 8:34); like Ish-bosheth, the name probably swaps “shame” (bosheth) for “Baal.”

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 5–8 — Behold, the Head of Ish-bosheth
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Two trusted officers murder their king and present it to David as the LORD’s vengeance. Rechab and Baanah walk into Ish-bosheth’s house in the heat of the day, as though collecting wheat, and kill him on his bed during his midday rest (vv. 5–7). They behead him and carry the head all night down the Jordan valley to Hebron (vv. 7–8). Their speech lays every label on the dead man (“your enemy, who sought your life”) and puts God at the front of the deed (“The LORD has avenged”). They are right about what God is doing and wrong to think he needed them.
verseByVerse.theology: He dies as he reigned, passively, killed in his sleep by men he trusted.
verseByVerse.examples: This is the second time in this book someone has brought David a dead rival and expected payment, and this time the claim comes dressed in theology.

verseByVerse.quote: Now the sons of Rimmon the Beerothite, Rechab and Baanah, set out, and about the heat of the day they came to the house of Ish-bosheth as he was taking his noonday rest. And they came into the midst of the house as if to get wheat, and they stabbed him in the stomach. Then Rechab and Baanah his brother escaped. When they came into the house, as he lay on his bed in his bedroom, they struck him and put him to death and beheaded him. They took his head and went by the way of the Arabah all night, and brought the head of Ish-bosheth to David at Hebron. And they said to the king, "Here is the head of Ish-bosheth, the son of Saul, your enemy, who sought your life. The LORD has avenged my lord the king this day on Saul and on his offspring."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Two of Ish-bosheth’s own officers murder him in his bed and bring his head to David, dressing their crime in the language of God’s justice.

His noonday rest (v. 5). Everything is small and domestic, and it is about to become murder: the heat of the day, the rest after the midday meal that everyone took in that climate, a house rather than a fortress. No guard is mentioned, no court: two of his own officers walk in during the quiet hour. As if to get wheat (v. 6): they come on ordinary business, the sort of errand that would bring officers to the king’s stores, and nobody looks twice.

They stabbed him in the stomach (v. 6). It is the third such wound in three chapters. Abner killed Asahel that way (2:23); Joab killed Abner that way (3:27). The writer notes it each time, tying the three deaths together as one chain of bloodshed.

As he lay on his bed in his bedroom (v. 7). Verse 7 goes back over the killing to add the detail that makes it worse. He never woke. There was no confrontation and no last word. The last king of Saul’s house dies asleep and is beheaded where he lies, by men who had sworn to serve him. Then they walk all night by the way of the Arabah, the Jordan valley, carrying a head. Ish-bosheth reigned from Mahanaim, east of the Jordan (2:8), so their road ran down the valley and up into the hill country of Judah.

The LORD has avenged my lord the king (v. 8). It is the Amalekite’s journey again (1:2–10), and a more polished version of his speech. They do not claim the credit; they put God at the front of the sentence and stand behind him. They load the victim with labels: the son of Saul, your enemy, who sought your life. It is not even accurate. Saul sought David’s life; Ish-bosheth was a frightened figurehead who never did David any harm.

Right about God, wrong about themselves. They are not wrong about what God is doing. He is removing the house of Saul: Samuel said so at Gilgal and at Endor (1 Samuel 15:28; 28:17), and Abner quoted the LORD’s oath himself (3:9–10). Their error is to take a true belief about God’s purpose and appoint themselves to carry it out. Knowing what God intends does not make anyone its instrument, and no amount of being right about the direction of history authorises the thing you do next. God had said the kingdom would pass to David; he had said nothing at all to Rechab and Baanah. David’s men reasoned the same way in the cave (1 Samuel 24:4), Abishai standing over Saul with a spear (1 Samuel 26:8), and Saul himself at Keilah (1 Samuel 23:7). The reasoning was sound, the circumstance real, the conclusion catastrophic. David talked the first two out of it. These two asked nobody.

Building the future on someone else’s body. Rechab and Baanah reasoned the way serious people always have when they are sure where history is going: one death now, for a better kingdom later. The last century worked that sum on a vast scale and filled its graves with the people who stood in the way of the future. Most of us do it more quietly: the colleague edged out, the friend dropped, the truth bent a little, because the cause or the career is good and somebody has to pay. The chapter’s answer is not that God has no plan, but that his plan does not need our knives.

One death, freely given. The high priest did the same sum about Jesus: “it is better for you that one man should die for the people, not that the whole nation should perish” (John 11:50). God did build the future on one death, but not one taken from a victim. The Son gave it: “No one takes it from me, but I lay it down of my own accord” (John 10:18). A kingdom founded on a death freely given has no use for anyone else’s.

Textual note. Verses 6–7 tell the killing twice, and the ancient Greek translation reads verse 6 differently: the doorkeeper of the house had been cleaning wheat, grew drowsy and fell asleep, and so the brothers slipped in (the ESV footnote gives this reading). Either way the meaning is the same: the king’s house was unguarded, and he was killed asleep by men he trusted. The repetition in the Hebrew may simply be the narrator returning to the moment to add the bedroom.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 9–12 — Who Has Redeemed My Life out of Every Adversity
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: David refuses the gift and condemns the givers, because the LORD has never needed murder to keep him. He swears by the God “who has redeemed my life out of every adversity” (v. 9), recalls the Amalekite who brought Saul’s crown and received death for a reward (v. 10), and argues from lesser to greater: these men have killed an innocent man in his own house on his bed (v. 11). The killers are executed and their bodies displayed at the pool of Hebron, and Ish-bosheth’s head is buried in Abner’s tomb (v. 12). The principle of chapters 1 to 4 is now complete: no one will be rewarded for killing David’s rivals.
verseByVerse.theology: David's opening oath carries the theology of the first four chapters of this book: God is the one who rescues him.
verseByVerse.examples: Justice and generosity come together here: the killers are judged, and the rival is given the honour he is owed.

verseByVerse.quote: But David answered Rechab and Baanah his brother, the sons of Rimmon the Beerothite, "As the LORD lives, who has redeemed my life out of every adversity, when one told me, 'Behold, Saul is dead,' and thought he was bringing good news, I seized him and killed him at Ziklag, which was the reward I gave him for his news. How much more, when wicked men have killed a righteous man in his own house on his bed, shall I not now require his blood at your hand and destroy you from the earth?" And David commanded his young men, and they killed them and cut off their hands and feet and hanged them beside the pool at Hebron. But they took the head of Ish-bosheth and buried it in the tomb of Abner at Hebron.
verseByVerse.commentary:
David swears by the God who has rescued him from every trouble without a murderer’s help, and he answers the killers of his rival with justice, not reward.

As the LORD lives (v. 9). David begins with an oath, and the clause he chooses to describe God answers their whole speech: who has redeemed my life out of every adversity. Every: not most, not the big ones. And he states it as settled history, not a hope. He has the evidence: a lion and a bear at the sheepfold, a giant in the Valley of Elah, three spears from a king, a window in the night, three thousand chosen men hunting him in the wilderness, twice, a whole army put into a deep sleep from the LORD so that he could walk through it, a Philistine gate he escaped by letting spittle run down his beard, Ziklag burning and every captive recovered. Not one of those was arranged by a volunteer with a knife. So the sentence answers Rechab and Baanah before he has said a word about them: you tell me God has avenged me; I know what God does, he has been doing it since I was a boy, and he has never once required this.

What it means to be redeemed. To us “redeem” is a word for vouchers and second chances. In Israel it was a word about a price. The verb (padah) was used for buying back a firstborn son, a slave, or a life that had been forfeited: someone paid, and someone went free. So David means more than that God got him out of tight corners. God has claimed his life as his own and paid whatever it took to keep it. David never saw the price; we have. “Truly no man can ransom another, or give to God the price of his life” (Psalm 49:7), and so the Son of David came “to give his life as a ransom for many” (Mark 10:45). You were ransomed, Peter says, “not with perishable things such as silver or gold, but with the precious blood of Christ” (1 Peter 1:18–19). That is why David could refuse a shortcut through somebody else’s blood: a redeemed life does not have to secure itself. Before you push for the thing you are sure you must have, write down, as David did, the times God has already brought you through, and end the list at the cross. See Redemption in the Theological Dictionary.

Thought he was bringing good news (v. 10). The Amalekite is the exact precedent, and these six words are the whole misjudgment of both episodes. Men in these chapters keep looking at David and concluding that a dead rival would please him, reading him by what would have pleased themselves. The reward I gave him for his news is grim on purpose: he came for payment, and he was paid.

How much more (v. 11). The argument runs from the lesser case to the greater. First, David calls Ish-bosheth a righteous man: his rival, crowned against him, in whose name a long war was fought. In the legal sense the word means innocent, in the right in the matter at hand, and Ish-bosheth was. He never sought David’s life or fought a battle; a general put him on a throne and two captains took him off it, and in between he said one rash sentence about a concubine (3:7). David gives him the word he is owed. Second, in his own house on his bed: the Amalekite claimed to have killed a dying man on a battlefield at his own request; this is a sleeping man killed in his bedroom by his own officers, and the sentence is heavier. Third, require his blood at your hand, the language of Genesis 9:5–6: shed blood has a claim on the one who shed it. David is not taking revenge for himself; as king he is carrying out a duty that has fallen to him.

Hanged them beside the pool at Hebron (v. 12). The execution is brutal and deliberately public. The hands did it and the feet carried it to Hebron, and both are cut off and displayed beside the town’s water supply, where every household comes. This is the third time in four chapters David has had to make the point, and no one in Israel can now miss it: there will be no reward in this kingdom for killing the king’s enemies.

Buried it in the tomb of Abner. The chapter ends with a kindness. The rival king’s head receives an honourable burial, in the tomb of the general who made him king and fought David for years, buried at Hebron because David walked behind his coffin (3:31–32). The two men who led the war against him now lie in one grave in David’s own city, at his order (see burial customs).

Chapters 1 to 4 together. Stand back, because these chapters are one argument and this is where it closes. Three times a man has killed a rival of David’s: the Amalekite with Saul’s crown, Rechab and Baanah with a head in a bag, and between them Joab, who murdered Abner in a gate and was cursed and made to walk in the funeral, but not executed, because he was David’s nephew and ran the army (3:39). Two were dealt with; one was not, and that exception is the crack that runs through the rest of the book. But the principle is established, the same one David kept in the cave and the camp when he had nothing: the kingdom of God is not built by killing the people standing in front of it. He waited years for a throne he had been anointed to, and he would not receive it over a dead body.

The long way to the throne. A greater Son of David was offered the kingdoms of the world by a shortcut and would not take them either (Matthew 4:8–10), and he said to a man with a sword in a garden: “Put your sword back into its place. For all who take the sword will perish by the sword” (Matthew 26:52). He had every right to the throne of the universe, and he went to a cross to receive it, the long way, on his Father’s timing.

Was David right to do this? The death sentence itself is what the law required for deliberate murder, with no ransom allowed (Genesis 9:6; Numbers 35:31). Cutting off hands and feet and displaying the bodies was the custom of that age, and the narrator records it without commending it; the law itself forbade leaving a hanged body exposed beyond the day (Deuteronomy 21:22–23). Scripture shows a king of that world doing justice in that world’s way, and does not hand Christians a pattern for punishment. Paul takes that same law about a body hung on a tree and applies it to the Son of David, who became a curse for us (Galatians 3:13), and that is where Christian thinking about justice now begins.

4.theology:
Right doctrine, self-appointed execution (v. 8). The murderers' mistake is a religious one, and the chapter takes it seriously. God was removing the house of Saul; everyone knew it. But knowing what God has purposed does not make anyone the instrument of it, and the murder of a sleeping man is no less a murder for being on the winning side of history. The stomach wound, the third in three chapters, ties this killing to the two before it: whatever reasons are given, it is one chain of bloodshed.

A king who will not take his throne over a dead body. David's oath by the God who has redeemed my life out of every adversity (v. 9) answers the murderers before he speaks of them, and his treatment of Ish-bosheth as a righteous man gives an enemy the justice he is owed. The one exception, Joab, will cost David dearly. But the principle stands: the kingdom of God does not get built by killing the people standing in front of it.

And a greater Son of David. Offered the kingdoms of the world on a shortcut, he refused them, and told a man with a sword in a garden to put it away (Matt. 26:52). He had every right to the throne of the universe and went to a cross to get it, on his Father's timing, and he reigns now by the gospel, not the sword.
4.examples:
Then: Two officers killed their own king in his sleep, carried his head all night to Hebron, and laid it before the man they were sure would reward them, who had them executed and buried the head honourably in the tomb of the general who had fought him.

Now: The useful thing here is their error, because it is a religious error and not a crude one. They had the doctrine right, and moved from "this is what God is doing" to "therefore I may do it". Being correct about where history is going does not mean God has sent you to bring it about. And they never asked anybody: not God, not a prophet, not a friend who might have said no. A conclusion you are unwilling to test is usually the one that most needs testing. David could wait because he had learned that the LORD redeems his own; the same Lord, who has already rescued us in Christ, gives his Spirit and his people so that we need not seize by our own hand what he has promised to give.

keyVerse.quote: As the LORD lives, who has redeemed my life out of every adversity
keyVerse.note: Before David says a word about the murderers, he answers their claim with the God he knows. The LORD has rescued him from every danger without any man’s knife, so he will not take the throne over a sleeping man’s body. The ransom David could only glimpse was paid in full by the Son of David, which is why his people need not secure their own future at someone else’s expense.

4.reflection:
Rechab and Baanah were right that God was removing Saul’s house, and wrong to make themselves the means (vv. 5–8). Where are Christians tempted to reason, “God wants this outcome, so whatever gets us there is justified”?

David answered them by recalling that the LORD had “redeemed my life out of every adversity” (v. 9). Try listing the times God has brought you through. How does remembering them, and the cross above all, free you from having to secure your own future?

David called his rival “a righteous man” and gave him an honourable burial (vv. 11–12). What would it look like for you to be fair, even generous, in speaking about someone who has stood against you?

In the middle of all this violence the narrator mentions a lame boy who will one day be brought to the king’s table (v. 4; 9:1–13). What does that tell you about how God sees the helpless and forgotten, and about how Christ has treated you?

5.title: King of All Israel
5.text: <sup>1</sup>Then all the tribes of Israel came to David at Hebron and said, "Behold, we are your bone and flesh.<sup>2</sup>In times past, when Saul was king over us, it was you who led out and brought in Israel. And the LORD said to you, 'You shall be shepherd of my people Israel, and you shall be prince over Israel.'"<sup>3</sup>So all the elders of Israel came to the king at Hebron, and King David made a covenant with them at Hebron before the LORD, and they anointed David king over Israel.<sup>4</sup>David was thirty years old when he began to reign, and he reigned forty years.<sup>5</sup>At Hebron he reigned over Judah seven years and six months, and at Jerusalem he reigned over all Israel and Judah thirty-three years.<sup>6</sup>And the king and his men went to Jerusalem against the Jebusites, the inhabitants of the land, who said to David, "You will not come in here, but the blind and the lame will ward you off"—thinking, "David cannot come in here."<sup>7</sup>Nevertheless, David took the stronghold of Zion, that is, the city of David.<sup>8</sup>And David said on that day, "Whoever would strike the Jebusites, let him get up the water shaft to attack 'the lame and the blind,' who are hated by David's soul." Therefore it is said, "The blind and the lame shall not come into the house."<sup>9</sup>And David lived in the stronghold and called it the city of David. And David built the city all around from the Millo inward.<sup>10</sup>And David became greater and greater, for the LORD, the God of hosts, was with him.<sup>11</sup>And Hiram king of Tyre sent messengers to David, and cedar trees, also carpenters and masons who built David a house.<sup>12</sup>And David knew that the LORD had established him king over Israel, and that he had exalted his kingdom for the sake of his people Israel.<sup>13</sup>And David took more concubines and wives from Jerusalem, after he came from Hebron, and more sons and daughters were born to David.<sup>14</sup>And these are the names of those who were born to him in Jerusalem: Shammua, Shobab, Nathan, Solomon,<sup>15</sup>Ibhar, Elishua, Nepheg, Japhia,<sup>16</sup>Elishama, Eliada, and Eliphelet.<sup>17</sup>When the Philistines heard that David had been anointed king over Israel, all the Philistines went up to search for David. But David heard of it and went down to the stronghold.<sup>18</sup>Now the Philistines had come and spread out in the Valley of Rephaim.<sup>19</sup>And David inquired of the LORD, "Shall I go up against the Philistines? Will you give them into my hand?" And the LORD said to David, "Go up, for I will certainly give the Philistines into your hand."<sup>20</sup>And David came to Baal-perazim, and David defeated them there. And he said, "The LORD has broken through my enemies before me like a breaking flood." Therefore the name of that place is called Baal-perazim.<sup>21</sup>And the Philistines left their idols there, and David and his men carried them away.<sup>22</sup>And the Philistines came up yet again and spread out in the Valley of Rephaim.<sup>23</sup>And when David inquired of the LORD, he said, "You shall not go up; go around to their rear, and come against them opposite the balsam trees.<sup>24</sup>And when you hear the sound of marching in the tops of the balsam trees, then rouse yourself, for then the LORD has gone out before you to strike down the army of the Philistines."<sup>25</sup>And David did as the LORD commanded him, and struck down the Philistines from Geba to Gezer.
5.overview:
Where we are. Abner and Ish-bosheth are dead, and David has refused to profit from either murder (chapters 3–4). The northern tribes have no king and no general, and the moment the story has been moving towards since 1 Samuel 16 has come.

The message. God keeps his word to his king, in his own time and for his people’s sake. The promise made to a shepherd boy is fulfilled: David is anointed king over all Israel, takes Jerusalem and defeats the Philistines. But the chapter insists on why: the LORD exalted his kingdom “for the sake of his people Israel” (v. 12). The throne is a trust, not a prize, and the king is strong only as long as he keeps asking the LORD what to do.

Why it was said. Israel needed to know that David’s kingship rested on the word of the LORD and a covenant made before him, not on force; and later readers, living under David’s sons, needed to see what a king in Israel was for (see the introduction).

How the chapter makes its case. The tribes come to Hebron with three arguments, kinship, David’s record and the LORD’s word that he would shepherd Israel, and David makes a covenant with them before the LORD and is anointed (vv. 1–5). He takes the Jebusite stronghold of Zion, a city that belongs to no tribe, and the LORD makes him great; and David knows why (vv. 6–12). Then, with no comment, he takes more wives, and among the sons born in Jerusalem are Solomon and Nathan (vv. 13–16). Finally the Philistines come up twice to the Valley of Rephaim, and twice David asks the LORD, and receives two different answers (vv. 17–25).
