Where it leads. To Christ by promise and by pattern. The tribes’ words, “You shall be shepherd of my people Israel” (v. 2), become God’s promise of “one shepherd, my servant David” (Ezekiel 34:23), and Jesus says, “I am the good shepherd” (John 10:11). His is the one kingship in which the king exists wholly for his people, laying down his life for the sheep. In Zion, the city David took, the Son of David would die and rise. The chapter also exposes a need: verse 13 shows the king who knew what the throne was for already beginning to take for himself.

For us. Any authority we hold, in a home, a church or a workplace, is given for the sake of others and is held under God. God’s promises are worth waiting for, even when the waiting is long. And yesterday’s guidance is no substitute for asking him again today.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–5 — Your Bone and Your Flesh
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: All Israel at last accepts the king God chose, and the kingdom is founded on a covenant before the LORD. The tribes come to Hebron and give three reasons: we are your own kin; you led us even under Saul; and the LORD said you would shepherd his people (vv. 1–2). The elders make a covenant with David before the LORD, so that the king is bound by terms as the people are, and only then is he anointed (v. 3). The figures that follow (vv. 4–5) show both the long wait, since David was a boy when Samuel anointed him and is thirty now, and the shape of the reign to come.
verseByVerse.theology: The elders argue from kinship, from record and from the word of God, and the last of these should have settled the matter years before.
verseByVerse.examples: This is David's third anointing, and the long road between the first and this one is part of what the chapter wants us to notice.

verseByVerse.quote: Then all the tribes of Israel came to David at Hebron and said, "Behold, we are your bone and flesh. In times past, when Saul was king over us, it was you who led out and brought in Israel. And the LORD said to you, 'You shall be shepherd of my people Israel, and you shall be prince over Israel.'" So all the elders of Israel came to the king at Hebron, and King David made a covenant with them at Hebron before the LORD, and they anointed David king over Israel. David was thirty years old when he began to reign, and he reigned forty years. At Hebron he reigned over Judah seven years and six months, and at Jerusalem he reigned over all Israel and Judah thirty-three years.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The tribes of Israel come to David at last, owning him as their kinsman, their proven leader and the shepherd God appointed, and he becomes king of all Israel by a covenant made before the LORD. The promise made to a shepherd boy many years before is kept.

All the tribes of Israel came to David (v. 1). They come to him. After seven and a half years of war, a delegation walks into Hebron and settles it with a speech of three arguments.

We are your bone and flesh. The first is kinship. It is the language Adam used when he first saw the woman, “bone of my bones and flesh of my flesh” (Genesis 2:23), now applied to a nation and its king: whatever the last seven years looked like, you are one of us. The King we need is our kinsman too: since we share in flesh and blood, the Son of God “himself likewise partook of the same things” (Hebrews 2:14).

It was you who led out (v. 2). The second argument is his record, and they are honest about the awkward part of it. When Saul was king over us, they say, naming the man they served, it was you who led out and brought in Israel.

The LORD said to you. The third is the word of God, and it decides the matter. The elders could quote God’s promise about David, and Abner had reminded them of it: “For some time past you have been seeking David as king over you” (3:17). They had known it for years, fought a war anyway, and obeyed God’s word only when it became politically convenient.

You shall be shepherd of my people Israel. It is what David was when Samuel sent for him, and it is what God calls the office. A king in Israel looks after sheep that belong to God, not to him. A shepherd lived out with the flock, found it grass and water, went after the strays, and stood between the sheep and whatever came to kill them; David had done it against a lion and a bear (1 Samuel 17:34–35). And the flock was not his: he answered to the owner for every animal. Most of us, given any authority at all, quietly turn that round, and the people under us become the means of getting what we want. David himself will do it in chapter 11.

The good shepherd. God never accepted that reversal. When Israel’s shepherds fed themselves and not the flock, he promised, long after David was dead, “I will set up over them one shepherd, my servant David” (Ezekiel 34:23). Jesus said who that was: “I am the good shepherd. The good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep” (John 10:11). Other kings spend their sheep to save themselves; this one spent himself to save his sheep. So if you lead anyone, a team, a class, a family, ask this week not what they owe you but what they need from you, and remember whose sheep they are (1 Peter 5:2–4).

King David made a covenant with them (v. 3). He does not simply accept the crown. He makes a covenant with the elders, before the LORD, and then they anoint him. That is not what a king with unlimited power does. There are terms, sworn in God’s presence, and the king is bound by them as much as the people. Israel’s king was always meant to sit under the law, not over it: he was to write out a copy of it for himself and read it all the days of his life (Deuteronomy 17:18–19).

David was thirty years old (v. 4). Do the arithmetic, because it is the whole story of the last twenty chapters. When Samuel poured oil on the head of Jesse’s youngest son at Bethlehem, he was a boy, young enough that nobody thought to call him in from the sheep; perhaps fifteen. So something like fifteen years passed between the anointing and the throne, and we know what was in them: a giant, a harp, three spears, a window in the night, a massacre of priests, two caves, three thousand chosen men twice, sixteen months in a Philistine town, a burnt village, and seven and a half years as king of one tribe out of twelve. God said it and took fifteen years to do it, and explained the delay to nobody.

Why does God take so long? Fifteen years is a long time to hold a promise with nothing to show for it. Next-day delivery has trained us to read delay as refusal. But David’s years were not wasted. In the caves and the wilderness he learned to ask before he acted, to spare a man he could have killed, and to hold power as a trust (v. 12). The waiting was the school, not the gap between lessons. Luke records the same age for David’s greater Son: “Jesus, when he began his ministry, was about thirty years of age” (Luke 3:23). He waited through years in Nazareth that nobody wrote down, and was sent “when the fullness of time had come” (Galatians 4:4), not a day before. Even now he is seated at God’s right hand, “waiting from that time until his enemies should be made a footstool for his feet” (Hebrews 10:13). If the King can wait on his Father’s timing, so can his people.

He reigned forty years (vv. 4–5). The writer divides the reign before it starts: seven and a half years over Judah alone, then thirty-three over the whole nation (see regnal years).
verseByVerse.note: The same figures are given at David's death (1 Kings 2:11; 1 Chron. 29:27).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God makes David great, and David understands that the greatness is for Israel’s sake. His first campaign takes Jerusalem, a fortress the Jebusites thought could be held by the blind and the lame, and which no tribe had ever kept (vv. 6–8). It becomes the city of David, a capital that belongs to no tribe and can hold twelve together (v. 9). David grows greater because the LORD of hosts is with him, and a foreign king sends cedar and craftsmen to build him a house (vv. 10–11). The key sentence closes the section: David knew the LORD had established him, and had exalted his kingdom for the sake of his people (v. 12).
verseByVerse.theology: Jerusalem is chosen as much for what it is not as for what it is. It is no tribe's city, and for twelve tribes that have just been fighting each other, that is worth more than its walls.
verseByVerse.examples: Verse 12 tells us what David understood about his own throne, and the very next verse puts that understanding to the test.

verseByVerse.quote: And the king and his men went to Jerusalem against the Jebusites, the inhabitants of the land, who said to David, "You will not come in here, but the blind and the lame will ward you off"—thinking, "David cannot come in here." Nevertheless, David took the stronghold of Zion, that is, the city of David. And David said on that day, "Whoever would strike the Jebusites, let him get up the water shaft to attack 'the lame and the blind,' who are hated by David's soul." Therefore it is said, "The blind and the lame shall not come into the house." And David lived in the stronghold and called it the city of David. And David built the city all around from the Millo inward. And David became greater and greater, for the LORD, the God of hosts, was with him. And Hiram king of Tyre sent messengers to David, and cedar trees, also carpenters and masons who built David a house. And David knew that the LORD had established him king over Israel, and that he had exalted his kingdom for the sake of his people Israel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
David takes Jerusalem, the fortress no tribe had ever held, and makes it the capital of a united nation; and he knows that the LORD has made him great, and that he has done it for the sake of his people.

The Jebusites, the inhabitants of the land (v. 6). Jerusalem is not yet an Israelite city. Judah once stormed and burned it (Judges 1:8), but Israel never kept it: “the people of Benjamin did not drive out the Jebusites who lived in Jerusalem, so the Jebusites have lived with the people of Benjamin in Jerusalem to this day” (Judges 1:21). It had sat there unconquered through the judges and the whole reign of Saul, and everyone had learned to live around it.

The blind and the lame will ward you off. The Jebusites are confident enough to be funny about it: even our blind and lame could hold this place against you. They had grounds. The city sat on a spur with steep ravines on three sides and a spring below, and it had held out for generations.

David took the stronghold of Zion (v. 7). The capture takes one sentence, and the narrator does not say how it was done. Verse 8 hints that David’s men climbed in by the water shaft. The city’s water came from the Gihon spring, outside the walls at the foot of the slope, and a shaft cut through the rock let the defenders reach it without going out. David sends men up the one route the walls do not cover.

Who are hated by David’s soul (v. 8). The rest of verse 8 is harsh, and the writer records the saying without endorsing it. David turned the Jebusites’ taunt back on them, and the saying about “the house” became a proverb about the Jebusites, not a law barring disabled people from God’s presence: Jesus healed the blind and the lame in the temple (Matthew 21:14). And hold on to it for four chapters: the man David goes looking for in chapter 9, and seats at his own table for the rest of his life, “was lame in both his feet” (9:13).

Why Jerusalem (v. 9). The choice is one of the shrewdest in the Old Testament. The city sits on the border of Judah and Benjamin, and though Joshua’s allotment gave it to Benjamin (Joshua 18:28), no tribe had ever held it. A capital in Judah, David’s tribe, would have looked like the south annexing the country; one in Benjamin, Saul’s tribe, would have been unbearable. A foreign city taken by David’s own men belongs to no tribal inheritance, which is why it is called the city of David. He has just spent seven and a half years watching a nation tear itself in half along tribal lines, and a capital that belongs to nobody is the one thing that can hold twelve tribes together. Here the Son of David would one day die and rise, and from here the gospel would go out to the nations (Luke 24:47).

For the LORD, the God of hosts, was with him (v. 10). The writer makes sure the credit goes to the right place: David grew great because the LORD was with him.

Hiram king of Tyre (v. 11). Tyre was the great Phoenician port up the coast, and cedar was its export, the timber everyone wanted and only Lebanon had. Unasked, Hiram sends timber and craftsmen, an investment in a neighbour suddenly worth having as a friend. Hiram was still reigning well into Solomon’s time (1 Kings 5:1; 9:10–11), so many think the writer has placed this notice here because it fits the subject, not because it happened at this point. Keep that cedar in mind: two chapters later David tells Nathan, “I dwell in a house of cedar, but the ark of God dwells in a tent” (7:2), and the gift becomes the occasion of the greatest promise in the Old Testament.

The LORD had established him king (v. 12). This is the key sentence of the chapter, and David knows two things. First, that God did this: not the elders, not the covenant at Hebron, not the water shaft, not Hiram’s cedar. Second, and harder and rarer, that it was for the sake of his people Israel. The kingdom is not a reward for fifteen patient years or compensation for the caves. It was not given to David for David; it was given to Israel, and David is the means by which they receive it. He is the shepherd the elders named in verse 2, and the sheep are the point of the job.

Authority for others’ sake. That principle lies under every position of authority in Scripture, and it is exactly what fails in chapter 11, when a king who should be at war stays home and uses the kingdom for himself. Everything good in this reign flows from verse 12, and everything catastrophic from forgetting it.

Uncertain wording. Verses 6 and 8 are among the hardest Hebrew in the book, and the ancient translations differ. The taunt about “the blind and the lame” may be simple mockery (our weakest could stop you), or refer to men posted on the walls as an insult; some suggest a ritual curse, with disabled figures set up as a warning of what would befall attackers. The word translated water shaft (tsinnor) occurs elsewhere only in Psalm 42:7 (“waterfalls”), and others take it as a grappling hook or a weapon; tunnels reaching the Gihon spring have been excavated on the hill, but which, if any, David’s men climbed is still debated. The Millo (v. 9), “the filling”, was probably the stone terracing that held up buildings on the steep slope. What is certain is the tone of the taunt, contempt, and the outcome: the city fell.
verseByVerse.note: The Chronicler's account adds that Joab was the first man up and so became commander (1 Chron. 11:6).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 13–16 — And David Took More Concubines and Wives
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Immediately after the finest thing said of David, the narrator records that he took more wives and concubines. There is no comment, but the placing is the comment. The law had told Israel’s king not to multiply wives, “lest his heart turn away” (Deuteronomy 17:17), and the rest of the book shows what follows from a palace of rival mothers and half-brothers (vv. 13–14). The list of eleven sons born in Jerusalem looks like an aside (vv. 14–16), but it holds two names of great consequence: Solomon, who will inherit the throne and build the temple, and Nathan, through whom Luke traces the line of Jesus.
verseByVerse.theology: The narrator sets David's best insight and his taking of more wives side by side, and leaves the reader to draw the line between them.
verseByVerse.examples: This list adds eleven sons to the six born at Hebron, and two of the new names, Solomon and Nathan, matter far beyond this chapter.

verseByVerse.quote: And David took more concubines and wives from Jerusalem, after he came from Hebron, and more sons and daughters were born to David. And these are the names of those who were born to him in Jerusalem: Shammua, Shobab, Nathan, Solomon, Ibhar, Elishua, Nepheg, Japhia, Elishama, Eliada, and Eliphelet.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Straight after the finest thing said of David, the narrator records, without comment, that he took more wives and concubines; and among the sons born in Jerusalem are the two through whom the line of the Messiah will run.

David took more concubines and wives (v. 13). Read it immediately after verse 12, as the writer intends. The previous sentence was the finest thing said about David in the book: he understood that God had exalted his kingdom for the sake of the people. The next is that he took more women. There is no transition, no comment, no rebuke. Israel’s narrators often do their most serious work this way: they set two facts side by side and trust the reader to see the connection. And keep the verb in mind: David took.

The law for kings. Israel’s king had been given three prohibitions in one short passage: not to multiply horses, not to multiply silver and gold, and, in the middle, “he shall not acquire many wives for himself, lest his heart turn away” (Deuteronomy 17:17). The reason is not mainly appetite: many wives would draw his heart from the LORD.

Faction. Two things follow from a household like this, and both arrive in this book. The first is faction. Six sons by six mothers were born at Hebron (3:2–5), and eleven more are listed here. Boys who grow up as rivals with rival mothers and rival claims make a palace into a civil war waiting for a trigger. Amnon rapes his half-sister Tamar; Absalom kills Amnon; Adonijah makes his move while his father is dying. Each crime is made possible by the arrangement recorded in this verse.

The habit. The second is the habit itself. A man who has spent years taking women in marriage whenever he wanted them, as kings of that time did, has practised something. Late one spring afternoon he will look down from a roof at a woman bathing, send to find out who she is, send messengers, and take her (11:2–4). The same verb again.

The names of those who were born to him (v. 14). Eleven names, and two of them matter enormously. Solomon will build the temple David wants to build and inherit the throne and the promise. Nathan, not the prophet but another son, is hardly mentioned again, except in one place of great consequence: Luke traces the genealogy of Jesus back to David not through Solomon but through this Nathan (Luke 3:31), while Matthew traces the royal line through Solomon (Matthew 1:6). So a list dropped in as an aside, in a paragraph the narrator declines to comment on, holds the names the Messiah’s line runs through. God weaves his promise even through a household David should never have built.

Did God approve David’s many wives? No. God’s design is one man and one woman (Genesis 2:24), and the law told Israel’s king not to acquire many wives for himself (Deuteronomy 17:17). Scripture records David’s polygamy without approving it, and the following chapters show its fruit: rape, murder and rebellion among his sons.
verseByVerse.note: Nathan was the son through whom Luke traces Jesus’ line; Solomon the one through whom Matthew does.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The united kingdom is attacked at once, and David wins because he asks the LORD every time. The Philistines, content with a divided Israel, come up to destroy its new king, and David goes down to the stronghold (vv. 17–18). He asks whether to go up and is told yes; the LORD breaks through the enemy like a flood, and the Philistines leave their idols on the field (vv. 19–21). When they return to the same valley, David does not assume the old answer still stands. He asks again and is told to circle behind them and wait for the sound of the LORD marching in the treetops, and the Philistines are driven out of the hill country (vv. 22–25).
verseByVerse.theology: The second battle is recorded because the enemy, the valley and the king are the same, and God's answer is not.
verseByVerse.examples: David waits for the sign he is given rather than the moment he judges right, and the victory is the LORD's before it is his.

verseByVerse.quote: When the Philistines heard that David had been anointed king over Israel, all the Philistines went up to search for David. But David heard of it and went down to the stronghold. Now the Philistines had come and spread out in the Valley of Rephaim.
verseByVerse.commentary:
As soon as Israel is united under David, the Philistines come up to destroy him, and he goes down to the stronghold.

All the Philistines went up to search for David (v. 17). They had been content with a divided country, and with David as their vassal at Ziklag. A single kingdom under the man who killed Goliath threatens their very existence, and they come to end it before it starts. The Valley of Rephaim runs south-west from Jerusalem towards the Philistine plain, so they were probably striking at the heart of the new kingdom and trying to cut David off from Judah.

David heard of it and went down to the stronghold. One goes up to Zion, so “went down to the stronghold” probably means a fortress in the lower country, very likely the cave of Adullam, called “the stronghold” in a later story set at the same time, with the Philistines camped in the same valley (23:13–14; 1 Samuel 22:1–4). The new king does not wait in his capital to be besieged. He goes back to the place where God kept him as a fugitive.
verseByVerse.note: The Chronicler tells both battles in 1 Chronicles 14:8-17.

verseByVerse.quote: And David inquired of the LORD, "Shall I go up against the Philistines? Will you give them into my hand?" And the LORD said to David, "Go up, for I will certainly give the Philistines into your hand." And David came to Baal-perazim, and David defeated them there. And he said, "The LORD has broken through my enemies before me like a breaking flood." Therefore the name of that place is called Baal-perazim. And the Philistines left their idols there, and David and his men carried them away.
verseByVerse.commentary:
David asks the LORD before he moves, and the LORD breaks through the Philistines like a flood, so that they flee and leave their gods behind.

David inquired of the LORD (v. 19). By now this is the established rhythm of the man, and the writer records it every time because it is the difference between David’s good years and everything else. He asked before going to Hebron (2:1). He asked twice at Keilah (1 Samuel 23:2, 4) and again when Saul came (23:10–12). He asked at Ziklag with his town in ashes (1 Samuel 30:8). He asks here the two questions he always asks: shall I go, and will you give them into my hand?

Like a breaking flood (v. 20). He names the ground Baal-perazim, “lord of breaking through”, after what God did. The picture is of a dry riverbed in a sudden storm, or a dam giving way: a wall of water that goes through whatever is in front of it. That is what happened to the Philistine line, and David says so and puts it on the map. Baal means lord or master, and here it is used of the LORD, before the name of the Canaanite god made Israel avoid it. Isaiah remembers this day: “the LORD will rise up as on Mount Perazim” (Isaiah 28:21). But he gives it a fearful turn. The God who broke through Israel’s enemies will break through Israel itself if she will not listen, and he calls it his “strange” work.

The Philistines left their idols there (v. 21). Any Israelite would have caught the reversal. Two generations earlier the Philistines beat Israel at Aphek and carried the ark of God into the temple of Dagon at Ashdod, and Dagon was found face down before it, and the next morning with his head and hands broken off (1 Samuel 5:1–5). Now the Philistines flee, and the gods they carried into battle are picked up off the ground by the men who beat them. The Chronicler adds that David had them burned (1 Chronicles 14:12), as the law required (Deuteronomy 7:5, 25). Gods that have to be carried, and can be abandoned and captured, cannot save. The God of Israel goes out before his people (v. 24).

verseByVerse.quote: And the Philistines came up yet again and spread out in the Valley of Rephaim. And when David inquired of the LORD, he said, "You shall not go up; go around to their rear, and come against them opposite the balsam trees.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When the same enemy returns to the same valley, David does not assume that the last answer still stands; he asks again, and God gives a different plan.

The Philistines came up yet again (v. 22). That is why the chapter tells two battles instead of one. Consider how easy it would have been not to ask. David had a word from God about this exact enemy, in this exact valley, given only recently, and it could not have been clearer: “Go up, for I will certainly give the Philistines into your hand” (v. 19). He obeyed it, it worked, and he named a place after it. Any reasonable man would treat that as covering the rematch.

You shall not go up (v. 23). He would have been wrong. This time the answer is: go round behind them. Different approach, different direction, different plan. Why God changes the instruction is not stated; perhaps the Philistines were braced for the frontal attack that had beaten them before. What the passage establishes is the principle: a word God gave last time is not a standing order for this time.

In everyday life. Believers get this wrong constantly and in good faith. God blessed a thing once, so it becomes the method; it can be sincere and grateful and still a way of never asking again, because the answer is already on file. David had every excuse to run on the previous instruction, and he asked. We do not receive answers as David did, through the priest’s ephod (1 Samuel 23:9–12), but we have the Scriptures and a Father who invites us to ask for wisdom (James 1:5).

verseByVerse.quote: And when you hear the sound of marching in the tops of the balsam trees, then rouse yourself, for then the LORD has gone out before you to strike down the army of the Philistines." And David did as the LORD commanded him, and struck down the Philistines from Geba to Gezer.
verseByVerse.commentary:
David is to wait until he hears the LORD marching out ahead of him, and then follow; he obeys, and the Philistines are driven out of the hill country.

The sound of marching in the tops of the balsam trees (v. 24). The signal is not a scouting report or David’s own sense of the moment. He is to wait behind an enemy army until he hears something moving in the treetops, and then go. Picture that waiting: the men in position, every soldier’s instinct saying go, and the order is to stand still until you hear leaves move.

Then the LORD has gone out before you. The whole chapter in one clause. The sound is not the wind giving David his cue; it is the noise of God going out ahead of him. The LORD strikes the Philistine army, and David’s men follow him into it. The battle is the LORD’s, and he goes first. So the Son of David went ahead of us into the last battle, against sin and death, and won it alone; his people follow where he has already gone (Hebrews 2:14–15; 6:20).

David did as the LORD commanded him (v. 25). He does exactly what he was told, and the Philistine power in the hill country is broken from one end to the other. This is the man at his best. Hold the picture clearly, because six chapters later there is a spring afternoon when he does not ask anybody anything.

From Geba to Gezer. Gezer stood where the hill country meets the coastal plain, on the road to Philistia. The Philistines are not only beaten but driven down out of the hills to their own plain. Chronicles reads “from Gibeon to Gezer” (1 Chronicles 14:16), and either way the line runs from the heart of Benjamin to the edge of Philistine land. The enemy who had ruled these hills since Saul’s last battle is gone from them.

Uncertain wording. The trees (baka) are not certainly identified. “Balsam” is a guess shared by many translations; others suggest the mastic tree, a kind of poplar or the mulberry, and the word may be linked to a verb for weeping, perhaps from a tree that drips sap. What matters is clear: a stand of trees whose leaves would rustle audibly, and a sound that David was to take as the LORD on the march.

5.theology:
A throne under the law. David makes a covenant with the elders before he is anointed (v. 3), and that matters. Israel's king was never meant to rule above God's law; he was to write out a copy of it and read it all his life (Deut. 17:18-19), and the terms sworn at Hebron bound him as much as the people.

The shepherd who became our bone and flesh. Kinship and shepherding, two of the elders' claims, are the very things the prophets later promise in a coming king whom they call David: I will set up over them one shepherd, my servant David (Ezekiel 34:23), spoken centuries after David died. Jesus takes that office as his own, I am the good shepherd (John 10:11), and Hebrews says he became our bone and flesh in the plainest sense: since the children share in flesh and blood, he himself shared the same (Hebrews 2:14). Israel came to Hebron and told David he was one of them. In Christ the King came to us first and made himself one of us. And the stronghold David took becomes, in Hebrews, the picture of the city every believer has already come to: Mount Zion and... the city of the living God (Hebrews 12:22).

Authority is held for others. Verse 12 states the principle under every authority in Scripture: the king is the means by which Israel receives the kingdom, not its owner. Everything good in this reign flows from remembering it, and everything catastrophic from forgetting it, as chapter 11 will show. Verse 13, set down at once without a word of comment, is the first sign that David will not always remember it.

Asking again. The two battles in the Valley of Rephaim show that God's guidance is a living relationship and not a file of past answers. David is at his best here because he asked when he thought he already knew. And the Philistine gods left lying on the field show whose battle it was. Two generations before, the Philistines had carried the ark off to Dagon's house (1 Sam. 5:1-5); now their own gods are carried off.
5.examples:
Then: A king who had just been given a clear word from God about how to beat a particular army in a particular valley met the same army in the same valley again, asked again, and was told to do something completely different, and to wait behind them until he heard a noise in the treetops.

Now: Verse 23 is uncomfortable, because the mistake it guards against is made by grateful people. A prayer answered, a method God plainly blessed, and it quietly becomes standing policy, so that the asking stops. Keep asking; the Lord who goes out before his people has not stopped speaking through his word and by his Spirit. Verse 12 is uncomfortable too: every position anybody holds, at work, at church, at home, is held for the sake of others. We hold them badly, and chapter 11 shows what forgetting it costs; but the true Son of David served perfectly where David failed, and in him the failures we confess are forgiven.

keyVerse.quote: And David knew that the LORD had established him king over Israel, and that he had exalted his kingdom for the sake of his people Israel.
keyVerse.note: This is the hinge of the chapter. David knows that the throne came from God, not from the elders or his own skill, and that it was given for the people’s good, not his own. Everything good in his reign flows from remembering this, and everything catastrophic from forgetting it; only Jesus, the good shepherd, has held his kingship wholly for his people’s sake.

5.reflection:
The elders could quote God’s promise about David (v. 2; 3:17), yet they fought against him for years. Are there things you know God has said that you are still resisting because obeying them is inconvenient?

David waited perhaps fifteen years between his anointing and the throne (v. 4). What did those years teach him? What might God be teaching you in a time of waiting, and how does Jesus’ own patience with his Father’s timing help?

Verse 12 says God exalted David’s kingdom “for the sake of his people Israel”, and verse 13 shows David beginning to take for himself. Where has God given you some influence or authority, and how can you use it for the good of others rather than for yourself?

David asked the LORD again before the second battle, though he had a clear answer the first time (vv. 22–23). In what areas of life are you running on “the answer already on file” instead of seeking God afresh through his Word and prayer?

6.title: The Ark Comes to Jerusalem
6.text: <sup>1</sup>David again gathered all the chosen men of Israel, thirty thousand.<sup>2</sup>And David arose and went with all the people who were with him from Baale-judah to bring up from there the ark of God, which is called by the name of the LORD of hosts who sits enthroned on the cherubim.<sup>3</sup>And they carried the ark of God on a new cart and brought it out of the house of Abinadab, which was on the hill. And Uzzah and Ahio, the sons of Abinadab, were driving the new cart,<sup>4</sup>with the ark of God, and Ahio went before the ark.<sup>5</sup>And David and all the house of Israel were celebrating before the LORD, with songs and lyres and harps and tambourines and castanets and cymbals.<sup>6</sup>And when they came to the threshing floor of Nacon, Uzzah put out his hand to the ark of God and took hold of it, for the oxen stumbled.<sup>7</sup>And the anger of the LORD was kindled against Uzzah, and God struck him down there because of his error, and he died there beside the ark of God.<sup>8</sup>And David was angry because the LORD had broken out against Uzzah. And that place is called Perez-uzzah to this day.<sup>9</sup>And David was afraid of the LORD that day, and he said, "How can the ark of the LORD come to me?"<sup>10</sup>So David was not willing to take the ark of the LORD into the city of David. But David took it aside to the house of Obed-edom the Gittite.<sup>11</sup>And the ark of the LORD remained in the house of Obed-edom the Gittite three months, and the LORD blessed Obed-edom and all his household.<sup>12</sup>And it was told King David, "The LORD has blessed the household of Obed-edom and all that belongs to him, because of the ark of God." So David went and brought up the ark of God from the house of Obed-edom to the city of David with rejoicing.<sup>13</sup>And when those who bore the ark of the LORD had gone six steps, he sacrificed an ox and a fattened animal.<sup>14</sup>And David danced before the LORD with all his might. And David was wearing a linen ephod.<sup>15</sup>So David and all the house of Israel brought up the ark of the LORD with shouting and with the sound of the horn.<sup>16</sup>As the ark of the LORD came into the city of David, Michal the daughter of Saul looked out of the window and saw King David leaping and dancing before the LORD, and she despised him in her heart.<sup>17</sup>And they brought in the ark of the LORD and set it in its place, inside the tent that David had pitched for it. And David offered burnt offerings and peace offerings before the LORD.<sup>18</sup>And when David had finished offering the burnt offerings and the peace offerings, he blessed the people in the name of the LORD of hosts<sup>19</sup>and distributed among all the people, the whole multitude of Israel, both men and women, a cake of bread, a portion of meat, and a cake of raisins to each one. Then all the people departed, each to his house.<sup>20</sup>And David returned to bless his household. But Michal the daughter of Saul came out to meet David and said, "How the king of Israel honored himself today, uncovering himself today before the eyes of his servants' female servants, as one of the vulgar fellows shamelessly uncovers himself!"<sup>21</sup>And David said to Michal, "It was before the LORD, who chose me above your father and above all his house, to appoint me as prince over Israel, the people of the LORD—and I will celebrate before the LORD.<sup>22</sup>I will make myself yet more contemptible than this, and I will be abased in your eyes. But by the female servants of whom you have spoken, by them I shall be held in honor."<sup>23</sup>And Michal the daughter of Saul had no child to the day of her death.
6.overview:
Where we are. David is king over all Israel, Jerusalem is his capital, and the Philistines have twice been driven back (chapter 5). Now he brings the ark of God, neglected in a private house for a generation, into the city.

The message. The holy God truly comes to live among his people, but on his terms, not ours. The presence that strikes down a man who handles it carelessly fills an obedient household with blessing, and the king who has learned to fear God dances before him with all his might. God is the King enthroned on the cherubim, and to be near him is both the most dangerous and the most joyful thing in the world.

Why it was said. Israel needed to know that the God of Sinai had come to Jerusalem with David’s throne beneath his, not as a trophy of David’s (see the introduction), and every later worshipper needed both halves of this day, the fear and the joy.

How the chapter makes its case. David sets the ark on a new cart, as the Philistines had done, though God’s law said it must be carried by the Levites (vv. 1–5). The oxen stumble, Uzzah takes hold of the ark, and God strikes him dead; David, angry and then afraid, leaves it with Obed-edom the Gittite, whose household the LORD blesses (vv. 6–11). Three months later the ark is carried up as the law commanded, with sacrifice; the king dances in a linen ephod, blesses the people and feeds every one of them (vv. 12–19). Michal mocks him, David answers that it was before the LORD, and the chapter ends with her childlessness (vv. 20–23).

Where it leads. The chapter’s question is David’s own: “How can the ark of the LORD come to me?” (v. 9). Christ answers it, by pattern and by the need the chapter exposes. The ark was God’s throne among his people, its lid the mercy seat where blood was sprinkled; in Jesus the Word became flesh and dwelt among us (John 1:14), and God put him forward “as a propitiation by his blood” (Romans 3:25), so that sinners may come near and live. And the king in priestly linen who blesses the people and gladly makes himself contemptible before the LORD is a small picture of the Son of David who is priest and king for ever, and who “emptied himself, by taking the form of a servant” (Philippians 2:7).

For us. Sincerity is not obedience: which of your well-meant ways of serving God have you never checked against what he has said? But do not let Uzzah keep you at a distance. Through the blood of Jesus the holy God has made himself approachable: come with reverence, and with all your might.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–5 — They Carried It on a New Cart
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: David is right to want God’s presence at the centre of the nation, and wrong in how he goes about it. He gathers thirty thousand chosen men to bring up the ark, called by the name of the LORD of hosts who sits enthroned on the cherubim, from the hill town where it has lain for a generation (vv. 1–2). They set it on a new cart, a careful choice and a Philistine one, though the law said the ark must be carried on poles by the Levites and never touched (vv. 3–4). The whole nation celebrates with every instrument it has (v. 5). The joy is real, and the method is about to be exposed.
verseByVerse.theology: The impulse is entirely right. After decades in a private house at Kiriath-jearim (1 Sam. 7:2), David wants the presence of God at the centre of the nation's life, and the whole nation shares his joy.
verseByVerse.examples: The trouble lies in one ordinary-sounding phrase, a new cart, and in what the law had said about how this ark was to travel (Ex. 25:14-15; Num. 7:9; 4:15).

verseByVerse.quote: David again gathered all the chosen men of Israel, thirty thousand. And David arose and went with all the people who were with him from Baale-judah to bring up from there the ark of God, which is called by the name of the LORD of hosts who sits enthroned on the cherubim. And they carried the ark of God on a new cart and brought it out of the house of Abinadab, which was on the hill. And Uzzah and Ahio, the sons of Abinadab, were driving the new cart, with the ark of God, and Ahio went before the ark. And David and all the house of Israel were celebrating before the LORD, with songs and lyres and harps and tambourines and castanets and cymbals.
verseByVerse.commentary:
David rightly wants the throne of God at the centre of the nation, but he moves it the way the Philistines did, not the way God had commanded. The joy is genuine and the intention good; the method is borrowed from people who never had God’s instructions, while Israel had them in writing.

All the chosen men of Israel, thirty thousand. Not a delegation but a national mobilisation: a people just reunited after years of civil war, marching together behind the throne of God.

Who sits enthroned on the cherubim. The ark’s full title is given because we must remember what this object is. It is not a relic or a mere symbol. God had said precisely where he would meet Israel: “There I will meet with you, and from above the mercy seat, from between the two cherubim that are on the ark of the testimony, I will speak with you” (Exodus 25:22). The lid was a throne with the invisible King seated on it, and the chest beneath held the tablets of the covenant.

Where the ark has been. The Philistines captured it at Aphek; it threw down their god Dagon and afflicted them with tumours for seven months, until they sent it back on a cart of their own making (1 Samuel 5–6). At Beth-shemesh men looked into it and died, and the people of Kiriath-jearim took it to the house of Abinadab on the hill: “From the day that the ark was lodged at Kiriath-jearim, a long time passed, some twenty years” (1 Samuel 7:2). Baale-judah (v. 2) is the same town under another name (Joshua 15:9; 1 Chronicles 13:6), some miles west of Jerusalem.

The house of Abinadab. There it stayed, in a private house, through the whole reign of Saul, who never sent for it. He asked for it once, in a panic during a battle, and changed his mind before it arrived (1 Samuel 14:18–19; the Hebrew there reads ark and the Greek Old Testament ephod, and many think the Greek is right). So David’s plan is the first genuinely good idea anyone has had about the ark in a generation. He is not building a shrine to himself; he wants the presence of God at the heart of the new capital, and he wants the nation to see it come.

On a new cart. The phrase the chapter turns on sounds like transport arrangements. New shows care: not an old farm wagon but one built for the purpose, unused and clean. Somebody wanted to do this properly. And a cart is exactly how the Philistines had done it. Wanting the ark out of their country, they were told by their priests, “Now then, take and prepare a new cart and two milk cows on which there has never come a yoke” (1 Samuel 6:7). They were pagans with no law and no priesthood of the LORD, improvising a way to be rid of something dangerous, and God bore with their ignorance. Israel had the book.

What the law said. The instructions were neither obscure nor buried. Rings were cast on the ark’s four feet and poles put through them: “The poles shall remain in the rings of the ark; they shall not be taken from it” (Exodus 25:15). The ark was always ready to be lifted and never needed to be touched. Who lifted it was specified too. When wagons were given to the Levite clans, the sons of Kohath received none, “because they were charged with the service of the holy things that had to be carried on the shoulder” (Numbers 7:9): the one clan whose work was the ark was the one clan given no carts. And the warning was explicit: “they must not touch the holy things, lest they die” (Numbers 4:15). Every one of those sentences could be read. There were priests and Levites in the land and thirty thousand men present, and nobody said anything.

Celebrating before the LORD. The joy is real, and the writer lists the instruments so that we feel it. There is nothing cynical anywhere in this procession, which is what makes the next verse so hard. A good motive, even a joyful one, does not turn a borrowed method into an obedient one.

Uncertain wording. Some of the instruments in verse 5 are hard to identify. The word translated castanets occurs only here in the Old Testament and probably means some kind of rattle shaken in the hand; the others are known in general terms, but not their exact form.

Textual note. In the traditional Hebrew text, verse 5 says they were celebrating with all kinds of instruments of cypress wood. The ESV, with the Greek Old Testament and the parallel in 1 Chronicles 13:8, reads with songs; Chronicles has “with all their might, with song”. The meaning of the verse is not affected.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 6–11 — God Struck Him Down There
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God’s holiness is not safe to handle, and it is also full of blessing. When the oxen stumble, Uzzah takes hold of the ark and God strikes him down beside it (vv. 6–7). The fault lay in the whole procession’s disregard of God’s word, and Uzzah’s hand is where it came into the open. David is angry, then afraid, and asks the question the chapter turns on: how can the ark of the LORD come to me? (vv. 8–9). He leaves it with Obed-edom the Gittite, and for three months the ark that killed a man brings blessing on a whole household (vv. 10–11).
verseByVerse.theology: Uzzah's death is a hard verse, and the commentary below takes the objection to it seriously before it answers, beginning with David's own later verdict on what went wrong.
verseByVerse.examples: David's anger is recorded without softening, and so is the fear that follows it. Then the same ark that killed a man brings blessing to a house whose master is called a man of Gath.

verseByVerse.quote: And when they came to the threshing floor of Nacon, Uzzah put out his hand to the ark of God and took hold of it, for the oxen stumbled. And the anger of the LORD was kindled against Uzzah, and God struck him down there because of his error, and he died there beside the ark of God. And David was angry because the LORD had broken out against Uzzah. And that place is called Perez-uzzah to this day. And David was afraid of the LORD that day, and he said, "How can the ark of the LORD come to me?" So David was not willing to take the ark of the LORD into the city of David. But David took it aside to the house of Obed-edom the Gittite. And the ark of the LORD remained in the house of Obed-edom the Gittite three months, and the LORD blessed Obed-edom and all his household.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When Uzzah takes hold of the ark, God strikes him dead: the whole procession had disregarded God’s word, and Uzzah’s hand is where it came into the open. David’s anger turns to fear, the ark is left with a man of Gath, and the presence that killed a careless Israelite blesses that household for three months.

For the oxen stumbled. At the threshing floor of Nacon the cart lurches and the ark tips, and a man walking beside the wheel does what anyone would do in the half second available: he puts out his hand to steady it.

God struck him down there. Anyone reading this for the first time stops here, and should. Almost everyone’s reaction is that it is not fair. He was helping. He did not steal anything or mock anything; he reacted, and died for reacting. That deserves an answer rather than a lecture, and the text gives four.

The cart, not the hand. First, the sin was the cart. Uzzah’s hand was the point at which an offence shared by all thirty thousand came into the open: the procession had been breaking an explicit law from the moment it left the hill. The poles existed so that no one would ever have to touch the ark; take them away and put it on a wagon, and sooner or later an ox stumbles and somebody has to. This is not a modern reading imposed on the text. It is David’s own verdict three months later: “Because you did not carry it the first time, the LORD our God broke out against us, because we did not seek him according to the rule” (1 Chronicles 15:13). Us, not Uzzah: the king says the fault was the nation’s and his own.

A son of Abinadab. Second, who Uzzah was. The ark had stood in his father’s house for decades, and he had quite possibly lived his whole life with the throne of God in the family property, walking past it every day. That is not stated as an accusation and should not be read as one, but it is the likeliest explanation of the reflex, and it names the most ordinary danger in the world: the thing you live closest to is the thing you stop seeing.

As if God needed help. Third, what the instinct assumed: that God’s throne was in danger from a pothole and a man’s hand was the remedy; that holy things are fragile and human hands are safe. It is exactly backwards, and it is the reflex of every religious person who has tried to protect God’s reputation by means God never authorised. This ark had thrown the god of Ashdod face down in his own temple, with head and hands broken off on the threshold (1 Samuel 5:4). It did not need steadying.

The anger of the LORD was kindled. Fourth, the thing that will not be argued away, and should not be: this is a hard verse, and it is meant to be. Israel had seen men die at Beth-shemesh for looking into this same box (1 Samuel 6:19; the traditional Hebrew text there reads fifty thousand and seventy men, and most modern translations think the larger figure entered in copying), and had learned nothing in all the years since. The sense of unfairness most readers feel should be examined rather than suppressed, because of what it measures. It does not show that God is harsh. It shows how small a thing we take holiness to be: we assume, without ever having decided it, that God’s presence is basically safe, and that a good motive is a sufficient answer to a plain command.

Because of his error. Uzzah was almost certainly sincere, but sincerity was not the question. He stood beside the place where the God who made the world had said he would sit, on a cart copied from the Philistines, in a nation that had his instructions in writing. None of this makes it comfortable, and it would be dishonest to pretend it does. The narrator comforts no one: the man died there beside the ark of God, and the story moves on to the king.

Does God still strike people down for a mistake in worship? The answer runs through Christ. The ark’s lid was the mercy seat, where once a year blood was sprinkled so that a holy God could live among sinners, and Paul uses the Greek Old Testament’s word for that lid of Christ himself, “whom God put forward as a propitiation by his blood” (Romans 3:25), the sacrifice that turns away God’s just anger. The holiness that broke out at Nacon is the holiness that fell on the Son at the cross, so that those who trust him “have confidence to enter the holy places by the blood of Jesus” (Hebrews 10:19). Uzzah’s death shows what coming near costs without that blood. It does not mean that a believer who stumbles in worship today is in danger of being struck down. Yet Hebrews, having set the terrors of Sinai beside the joyful assembly of Mount Zion, still calls us to worship “with reverence and awe, for our God is a consuming fire” (Hebrews 12:28–29). He is not a fragile God to be steadied, nor a tame one to be handled, but a holy God who has made himself approachable at his own cost.

David was angry. Scripture records it without apology, and the word is strong: in Hebrew it is the verb used of the LORD’s burning anger one verse earlier. David had organised the greatest day of his reign out of what he was sure was pure devotion, and God had killed a man in the middle of it. He even puts his grievance on the map: Perez-uzzah, “the breaking out against Uzzah”, the word with which he had named Baal-perazim in joy one chapter earlier (5:20).

Anger brought to God. God does not strike him for the anger, and he is not rebuked for it here or anywhere. Scripture is not squeamish about people being angry with God: Job is, Jeremiah is, Habakkuk is, and the psalms are full of it, several of them David’s. Anger brought into God’s presence is still a way of dealing with him; it is not the same as walking away.

How can the ark of the LORD come to me? The anger becomes fear, and the fear asks the right question, the one the men of Beth-shemesh asked: “Who is able to stand before the LORD, this holy God?” (1 Samuel 6:20). The difference is what each did next. Beth-shemesh passed the ark on to somebody else. David also sends it away, but he spends three months finding out how it should be done, and comes back.

Obed-edom the Gittite. A man of Gath: Goliath’s city, the Philistine city where David had twice taken refuge. The writer gives him that label and leaves it without comment. (Chronicles names an Obed-edom among the Levites who served the ark, 1 Chronicles 15:18, 24; 26:4–5. Some think he is this man, a Levite from the Levitical town of Gath-rimmon, Joshua 21:24; others think he was a man of Gath settled in Israel. Samuel does not settle it.)

The LORD blessed Obed-edom. Without this half of the story the first half would give a false picture of God. The same ark, in the same country and the same season, killed an Israelite at a threshing floor and blessed a Gittite’s household for three months. The difference was not in the ark. The presence of God is neither a hazard to be managed nor a convenience to be used. It is God, and God is not tame: the nearness that destroyed a careless man filled a house with blessing until people began to talk about it. That is what gets David moving again. He hears that the thing he is frightened of has been making a family prosper, and he goes back for it.

Uncertain wording. The word translated error (v. 7) occurs only here in the Old Testament, and its exact sense is uncertain; it is usually taken to mean irreverence or negligence, and the parallel in 1 Chronicles 13:10 says simply “because he put out his hand to the ark”. The place name is also uncertain: Chronicles calls it the threshing floor of Chidon (1 Chronicles 13:9). Either way the meaning is clear: God struck him because he laid hands on what God had said must not be touched.
verseByVerse.note: The Chronicler tells this first attempt in 1 Chronicles 13, and the second in 1 Chronicles 15.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 12–19 — Dancing Before the LORD with All His Might
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: When God is approached his way, his presence brings a joy that overflows to everyone. Hearing that the ark has blessed Obed-edom’s house, David brings it up again, and this time it is carried as the law commanded, with sacrifice after the first six steps (vv. 12–13). The king lays aside his royal robes, puts on a linen ephod and dances before the LORD with all his might, while the nation shouts and the horn sounds (vv. 14–15). Michal watches from a window and despises him (v. 16). The ark is set in its tent, offerings are made, and David blesses the people in the LORD’s name and gives food to every man and woman in the crowd (vv. 17–19).
verseByVerse.theology: This time the Levites carry the ark on their shoulders, exactly as Moses commanded, and the procession is punctuated by blood, because the first attempt taught them what it costs to come near.
verseByVerse.examples: The king lays aside what marks him as king, puts on the linen of a worshipper, and ends the day by feeding every person in the crowd.

verseByVerse.quote: And it was told King David, "The LORD has blessed the household of Obed-edom and all that belongs to him, because of the ark of God." So David went and brought up the ark of God from the house of Obed-edom to the city of David with rejoicing. And when those who bore the ark of the LORD had gone six steps, he sacrificed an ox and a fattened animal.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Hearing that the ark has brought blessing, David brings it up again, and this time it is carried as God commanded and the way is marked with sacrifice. Three months of fear end with news about the blessing on somebody else’s house.

It was told King David. The report shows him that the problem was never the ark. God had not withdrawn his presence from Israel; Israel had handled it wrongly. So he goes back, and this time he does it right.

Those who bore the ark of the LORD. One phrase has changed, and it makes all the difference. There is no cart and there are no oxen: men are carrying the ark, as the law said. Chronicles fills in the three months. David declared that “no one but the Levites may carry the ark of God, for the LORD had chosen them to carry the ark of the LORD and to minister to him forever” (1 Chronicles 15:2), and admitted that the first failure was the nation’s and his own (15:13). So “the Levites carried the ark of God on their shoulders with the poles, as Moses had commanded according to the word of the LORD” (15:15).

Repentance that reads the instructions. He went and found out what God had said. That is what repentance looks like when it is real and not only a feeling: angry, then afraid, and then doing what God had actually commanded instead.

He sacrificed an ox and a fattened animal. After six steps, sacrifice. Whatever was done along the rest of the route, the point of that first offering is unmistakable. The last time this ark moved, a man died; before it goes further than six paces, blood is shed. They have learned what it costs to come near, and they will not take another step as though it were safe. The way into God’s presence has always been marked by blood, and it is the blood of Christ that marks it now (Hebrews 9:22–24).

verseByVerse.quote: And David danced before the LORD with all his might. And David was wearing a linen ephod. So David and all the house of Israel brought up the ark of the LORD with shouting and with the sound of the horn.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The king lays aside his royal dignity and dances before the LORD with all his might, dressed as a worshipper, while the nation greets its true King with shouting and the horn.

With all his might. Chronicles uses the phrase of the whole nation’s celebration on the first attempt (1 Chronicles 13:8); here it describes one man. This is not dignified swaying but leaping and whirling (v. 16), a king spending himself before God.

A linen ephod. Not the high priest’s ephod but the simple linen garment of those who served at the sanctuary, which the boy Samuel wore at Shiloh (1 Samuel 2:18). It is not a royal robe. David has taken off the clothes that say king and put on the clothes that say worshipper, and he dances before his whole capital dressed as a servant of the sanctuary. That deliberate act is what his wife is about to call an indecency, and what he is about to defend.

With shouting and with the sound of the horn. The horn is the shofar, the ram’s horn blown when a king was proclaimed (1 Kings 1:39) and at Israel’s great feasts, and the shout is a people’s acclaim of its king. The King they greet is not David. Psalm 47 sings of the same sound: “God has gone up with a shout, the LORD with the sound of a trumpet” (Psalm 47:5). Many have heard this procession behind Psalm 24 as well, where the gates are told to lift up their heads, “that the King of glory may come in” (Psalm 24:7).

A king in priestly linen. Was a king allowed to wear it, or to offer sacrifices (vv. 13, 17)? The text does not blame him, and the offerings were very likely made through the priests, as a king is said to do what he orders done (compare 1 Kings 8:62–64). But the picture is striking. In Jerusalem, which most identify with Melchizedek’s Salem, a son of Judah in priestly linen blesses the people in the LORD’s name and feeds them. David himself later wrote of one who would be “a priest forever after the order of Melchizedek” (Psalm 110:4), and Hebrews says that King-Priest is Jesus (Hebrews 7). David wore the linen for a day; his Son holds both offices for ever.

What it does not mean. David’s “uncovering” (v. 20) means that he laid aside his royal robes for a simple linen ephod; Michal’s word makes the worst of it. And it was God who judged Michal’s contempt, not David’s joy: exuberant gladness before God has a place among his people.

Where Christians differ: should dance have a place in the church’s gathered worship? Many churches, holding that worship may include whatever Scripture does not forbid, take David’s dance as a warrant for it. Others note that this was a festal procession through the streets, not the gathered assembly at worship, and that the New Testament, which calls for all things to be done “decently and in order” (1 Corinthians 14:40), gives no rule for dancing in public worship and never names it among the parts of Christian worship. This commentary’s view: Scripture governs the elements of the church’s worship, so liturgical dance is an addition to what God has given. But David’s joy is no embarrassment to be explained away: wholehearted gladness before God, in song and in all of life, belongs to his people.

verseByVerse.quote: As the ark of the LORD came into the city of David, Michal the daughter of Saul looked out of the window and saw King David leaping and dancing before the LORD, and she despised him in her heart.
verseByVerse.commentary:
While all Israel rejoices in the street, Saul’s daughter watches alone from a window and despises the king in her heart.

Looked out of the window. Everything in the sentence is set up as a contrast. All Israel is outside with the horn and the shouting; Michal is inside, behind a window, alone, looking down. Once before she had stood at a window for David, letting him down through it to escape her father’s men (1 Samuel 19:12).

Michal the daughter of Saul. Not the wife of David. The writer uses this title three times before the chapter ends, identifying her in every line by the house that lost.

She despised him in her heart. It is the verb used of Goliath, who looked at the young David and “disdained him” (1 Samuel 17:42). Michal sees only a king making a fool of himself, not what he is doing it for, and her contempt stays in her heart until he comes home (see the note on vv. 20–23).

verseByVerse.quote: And they brought in the ark of the LORD and set it in its place, inside the tent that David had pitched for it. And David offered burnt offerings and peace offerings before the LORD. And when David had finished offering the burnt offerings and the peace offerings, he blessed the people in the name of the LORD of hosts and distributed among all the people, the whole multitude of Israel, both men and women, a cake of bread, a portion of meat, and a cake of raisins to each one. Then all the people departed, each to his house.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The ark is set in its place, and the king offers sacrifices, blesses the people in the LORD’s name and gives food to every one of them, so that the whole nation feasts in God’s presence.

Inside the tent that David had pitched for it. A tent, not a temple, and that is the subject of the next chapter, which begins with David noticing it (7:2). It is a new tent, too: the tabernacle Moses made seems to have stood at Gibeon in these years, where Chronicles places it with its altar (1 Chronicles 16:39; 21:29), so through David’s reign the ark and the old tabernacle were in different places. Psalm 132 remembers this day: David would not rest until he found “a dwelling place for the Mighty One of Jacob”, and the people sang, “Arise, O LORD, and go to your resting place, you and the ark of your might” (Psalm 132:5, 8).

Burnt offerings and peace offerings. Burnt offerings were given wholly to God; peace offerings were shared and eaten, so the meat here is the meat of the sacrifice, and the whole nation sits down to a meal in God’s presence.

He blessed the people in the name of the LORD of hosts. This is the name under which the ark was introduced at the start, “the LORD of hosts who sits enthroned on the cherubim” (v. 2). The king speaks God’s blessing over the people, as Solomon will at the dedication of the temple (1 Kings 8:14, 55).

Both men and women. Every person, not only officials, fighting men or heads of households, receives bread, meat and a raisin cake. The last thing the king does on the greatest day of his reign is hand out food to the crowd, in a linen ephod, having danced in front of them. It is a small picture of the King who blessed and broke bread for a hungry crowd on a hillside (Mark 6:41–42), and who will gather his people to a feast in the presence of God (Revelation 19:9).

Then all the people departed, each to his house. David too goes home to bless his own household (v. 20), where the day will end very differently.

Uncertain wording. A portion of meat translates a word found only here and in the parallel (1 Chronicles 16:3), and its meaning is not certain: ancient translators understood a piece of meat, while some scholars think it was a cake of dates. A cake of raisins is fairly certain, a pressed cake of dried grapes. Either way, each person went home with a generous festal portion.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 20–23 — I Will Make Myself Yet More Contemptible
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Worship that is truly before the LORD cares more for his approval than for anyone’s idea of dignity. David comes home to bless his household, and Michal meets him with contempt: the king has made a shameless display of himself before servant girls (v. 20). David answers that it was before the LORD, who chose him over her father, and that he will make himself more contemptible still, for the very servant girls she mentions will honour him (vv. 21–22). The happiest day of his reign closes with a bleak sentence: Michal, still called the daughter of Saul, had no child to the day of her death (v. 23).
verseByVerse.theology: Michal is wrong about what the dancing was, and she has also been badly wronged, handed between men and never asked anything. The commentary below holds both together.
verseByVerse.examples: David's answer is true and it is not kind. Above your father is aimed at the wound, and he knows it. And the last verse states a fact and gives no reason for it: the text does not say whether this was God's judgment, David's withdrawal, or simple childlessness, and it is not honest to decide.

verseByVerse.quote: And David returned to bless his household. But Michal the daughter of Saul came out to meet David and said, "How the king of Israel honored himself today, uncovering himself today before the eyes of his servants' female servants, as one of the vulgar fellows shamelessly uncovers himself!" And David said to Michal, "It was before the LORD, who chose me above your father and above all his house, to appoint me as prince over Israel, the people of the LORD—and I will celebrate before the LORD. I will make myself yet more contemptible than this, and I will be abased in your eyes. But by the female servants of whom you have spoken, by them I shall be held in honor." And Michal the daughter of Saul had no child to the day of her death.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Michal despises the king for humbling himself, and David answers that it was before the LORD and that he will gladly be humbled further; the chapter ends with Michal childless, and the last hope of uniting Saul’s house with David’s is gone. She is wrong about the dancing, and she has also been badly wronged, and both are true at once.

How the king of Israel honored himself today. The sarcasm is expert: the title is used to show how far he fell short of it. Her complaint is specific. He uncovered himself in front of the servant girls and behaved like one of the vulgar fellows, men with no sense of shame. She is not entirely wrong about the facts: a king leaping in a short linen garment in a crowd is not keeping the distance kings keep. She is right that he looked like any ordinary man, and wrong about what it meant, because standing before God as an ordinary worshipper was the point.

Michal’s side. Before David answers, she is owed a hearing, which the chapter does not give her and a reader should. Michal loved David. The narrator says so outright (1 Samuel 18:20, and again at 18:28), and says it of no other woman in Samuel, and perhaps of no other woman in all Old Testament narrative. When her father sent men to kill him in the night, she let him down through a window, put an idol in the bed with goats’ hair at its head to buy him hours, and lied to Saul’s face, so that Saul said to her, “Why have you deceived me thus?” (1 Samuel 19:11–17). She saved his life, and he fled, and he did not come back for her.

Taken from Paltiel. Her father then gave her to Paltiel the son of Laish, and she lived as his wife for years, long enough for him to love her: he followed weeping as far as Bahurim when she was taken away, and turned back only when Abner told him to (3:15–16). She was taken because David made her return a condition of his agreement with Abner, at the moment when a wife from Saul’s house would help him with the northern tribes: not in the years at Hebron with six wives, but when it was useful. Nobody in that transaction asked her a single question. So she stands at a window in a city she did not choose, watching a man she once risked her life for dance before the God who took her father’s kingdom and gave it to him. Her contempt is genuinely wrong, and she has genuinely been wronged, and both are true at the same moment.

It was before the LORD. The first clause is the answer, and it cannot be answered. Everything she said assumed an audience of servant girls. David says the audience was God: what she watched from her window was not a performance for anybody in the street.

Above your father and above all his house. This is aimed to hurt, and it should not be smoothed over. He could have defended the dancing without mentioning Saul at all, and he puts his hand on the wound. This is not the David of chapter 1, who lamented the same father with nothing in it for himself; it is a man in his own doorway, sneered at by his wife, hitting back with the one fact that hurts.

I will make myself yet more contemptible than this. This is the great sentence of the chapter. He does not deny that he looked ridiculous; he agrees, and offers to go further. He does not humble himself before God reluctantly, and if it costs him her good opinion, he is content to pay it. There is a Son of David who went immeasurably further, who “emptied himself, by taking the form of a servant” and humbled himself to a criminal’s death (Philippians 2:7–8). David’s humbling is small beside that, but the man in the linen ephod points the same way, and he humbled himself on purpose.

By them I shall be held in honor. The last line is sharp, shrewd and perhaps not gracious: the servant girls she is so concerned about will think more of him, not less. Ordinary people understand this, he is saying, and she does not.

Who is the audience? Michal’s window is a very modern place to stand. We are watched more than any generation before us, and we have learned to watch ourselves: to check how we look, curate what is seen, and keep an ironic distance from anything that might make us look foolish. Søren Kierkegaard argued that in worship we usually get the roles the wrong way round. We think the preacher is the performer and we are the audience, judging him; in fact, he said, the worshippers are the performers, the preacher only the prompter, and God is the audience. That is David’s answer exactly. The one who knows that God is watching, and watching with favour, is free to look ridiculous. That freedom comes from the Son of David who went much further than a dance, to a cross where he was stripped and stared at, and who “for the joy that was set before him endured the cross, despising the shame” (Hebrews 12:2). Because he bore the contempt, those who belong to him can come away from the window.

Had no child to the day of her death. The chapter ends with a fact and no explanation. Readers reach for one at once, and two are on offer: either God closed her womb in judgment for despising the ark’s homecoming, or David never went near her again. The text says neither. It says she had no child, and stops, and this commentary does not choose.

No heir of both houses. What the sentence certainly does is close a door on a dynasty. A son of David by Saul’s daughter would have united the two houses in one person and been the obvious heir. There is no such child. The union of the two houses ends in a childless woman at a window, and the throne passes wholly to David’s line, and in time to a son of Bathsheba.

Why the chapter ends here. She is called the daughter of Saul one last time, the third time in eight verses: the writer’s verdict and her epitaph in one phrase. Whatever she was at that first window, she died as her father’s daughter. It is a bleak ending to the happiest day of David’s reign, and the writer puts it there on purpose. The ark is in Jerusalem, the nation has eaten in God’s presence, the king has danced himself breathless, and inside the house there is a marriage that is finished, and a woman nobody ever asked.

6.theology:
Sincerity is not enough, and it is not nothing. Everything about the first procession was right except the method (v. 3). The cart was built with care, and it copied pagans who had no instructions, while Israel had them in writing. Uzzah's reflex, reaching out as though God's throne needed a human hand to keep it from the dirt, is the reflex of every religious person who has tried to protect God's reputation by means God never authorised. And familiarity made it easy: he had very likely grown up with the ark in the house.

The holiness that kills and the holiness that blesses are one. The sense of unfairness most readers feel at verse 7 measures how small a thing we take holiness to be. The same ark killed a careless Israelite and blessed a Gittite's house; the presence of God is neither a hazard to be managed nor a convenience to be used. The answer to the fear it raises runs through the mercy seat and the blood of Christ, discussed at verse 7.

Repentance that reads the instructions. David is furious with God and is not rebuked for it; anger brought to God is still a way of turning to him, not of walking away. Where Beth-shemesh passed the ark on, David spent three months finding out how it was supposed to be done, and came back (vv. 8-15).

Humbled before God. David's reply to Michal has three parts. It was before the LORD cannot be answered. Above your father is cruel. Yet more contemptible is great: he is willing to be humbled further before God, and in that he points toward the Son of David who emptied himself, by taking the form of a servant (Phil. 2:7-8). Verse 23 gives no reason for her childlessness, and this commentary does not choose one.
6.examples:
Then: A nation moved the throne of God on a brand-new cart, copying a method invented by pagans who had never read the instructions; when an ox stumbled and a man reached out to steady it, he died on the spot, and the king went home angry with God.

Now: Uzzah’s death raises the question whether sincerity is enough, and the answer is that it is not: good intentions did not turn a Philistine method into an obedient one. The question worth asking is which of your own well-meant arrangements has never been checked against what God said. And David's three months show the way back: furious, then frightened, then he found out what the rule actually was and did that, which is what repentance looks like when it is more than a feeling. We can come back like that because the holy God has opened the way himself, through the blood of his Son, and the Spirit he gives teaches us to worship him with reverence and joy. David came back, did it the right way, and danced.

keyVerse.quote: How can the ark of the LORD come to me?
keyVerse.note: This is the question the whole chapter raises and answers. Uzzah’s death shows that the holy God cannot be handled on our terms; Obed-edom’s blessing and the second procession show that he gladly comes to those who approach him his way, by sacrifice. The final answer is Christ, the Word who dwelt among us and the true mercy seat, through whose blood the holy God comes near to sinners and they live.

6.reflection:
The first procession was joyful, sincere and carefully planned, yet it ignored what God had said about carrying the ark (vv. 3–7). Where might good intentions, in your own life or your church, have taken the place of asking what God has actually said?

Most readers feel that Uzzah’s death was unfair. What does that reaction reveal about how we think of God’s holiness? How does the cross of Christ both confirm the warning and open the way to God (Hebrews 10:19; 12:28–29)?

David was angry with God, then afraid, and then went and found out how the ark should be carried (vv. 8–13). What does this teach about bringing honest feelings to God, and about what real repentance looks like?

Michal watched from a window and despised what she saw; David said, “It was before the LORD” (vv. 16, 21). What keeps you at the window when it comes to wholehearted worship, and how does Christ, who despised the shame of the cross, set you free?

7.title: The Throne Forever
7.text: <sup>1</sup>Now when the king lived in his house and the LORD had given him rest from all his surrounding enemies,<sup>2</sup>the king said to Nathan the prophet, "See now, I dwell in a house of cedar, but the ark of God dwells in a tent."<sup>3</sup>And Nathan said to the king, "Go, do all that is in your heart, for the LORD is with you."<sup>4</sup>But that same night the word of the LORD came to Nathan,<sup>5</sup>"Go and tell my servant David, 'Thus says the LORD: Would you build me a house to dwell in?<sup>6</sup>I have not lived in a house since the day I brought up the people of Israel from Egypt to this day, but I have been moving about in a tent for my dwelling.<sup>7</sup>In all places where I have moved with all the people of Israel, did I speak a word with any of the judges of Israel, whom I commanded to shepherd my people Israel, saying, "Why have you not built me a house of cedar?"'<sup>8</sup>Now, therefore, thus you shall say to my servant David, 'Thus says the LORD of hosts, I took you from the pasture, from following the sheep, that you should be prince over my people Israel.<sup>9</sup>And I have been with you wherever you went and have cut off all your enemies from before you. And I will make for you a great name, like the name of the great ones of the earth.<sup>10</sup>And I will appoint a place for my people Israel and will plant them, so that they may dwell in their own place and be disturbed no more. And violent men shall afflict them no more, as formerly,<sup>11</sup>from the time that I appointed judges over my people Israel. And I will give you rest from all your enemies.
