Moreover, the LORD declares to you that the LORD will make you a house.<sup>12</sup>When your days are fulfilled and you lie down with your fathers, I will raise up your offspring after you, who shall come from your body, and I will establish his kingdom.<sup>13</sup>He shall build a house for my name, and I will establish the throne of his kingdom forever.<sup>14</sup>I will be to him a father, and he shall be to me a son. When he commits iniquity, I will discipline him with the rod of men, with the stripes of the sons of men,<sup>15</sup>but my steadfast love will not depart from him, as I took it from Saul, whom I put away from before you.<sup>16</sup>And your house and your kingdom shall be made sure forever before me. Your throne shall be established forever.'"<sup>17</sup>In accordance with all these words, and in accordance with all this vision, Nathan spoke to David.<sup>18</sup>Then King David went in and sat before the LORD and said, "Who am I, O Lord GOD, and what is my house, that you have brought me thus far?<sup>19</sup>And yet this was a small thing in your eyes, O Lord GOD. You have spoken also of your servant's house for a great while to come, and this is instruction for mankind, O Lord GOD!<sup>20</sup>And what more can David say to you? For you know your servant, O Lord GOD!<sup>21</sup>Because of your promise, and according to your own heart, you have brought about all this greatness, to make your servant know it.<sup>22</sup>Therefore you are great, O Lord GOD. For there is none like you, and there is no God besides you, according to all that we have heard with our ears.<sup>23</sup>And who is like your people Israel, the one nation on earth whom God went to redeem to be his people, making himself a name and doing for them great and awesome things by driving out before your people, whom you redeemed for yourself from Egypt, a nation and its gods?<sup>24</sup>And you established for yourself your people Israel to be your people forever. And you, O LORD, became their God.<sup>25</sup>And now, O LORD God, confirm forever the word that you have spoken concerning your servant and concerning his house, and do as you have spoken.<sup>26</sup>And your name will be magnified forever, saying, 'The LORD of hosts is God over Israel,' and the house of your servant David will be established before you.<sup>27</sup>For you, O LORD of hosts, the God of Israel, have made this revelation to your servant, saying, 'I will build you a house.' Therefore your servant has found courage to pray this prayer to you.<sup>28</sup>And now, O Lord GOD, you are God, and your words are true, and you have promised this good thing to your servant.<sup>29</sup>Now therefore may it please you to bless the house of your servant, so that it may continue forever before you. For you, O Lord GOD, have spoken, and with your blessing shall the house of your servant be blessed forever."
7.overview:
Where we are. David is king of all Israel, his palace is built of Hiram’s cedar (5:11), and in chapter 6 the ark was brought up to Jerusalem with dancing. This chapter, the summit of the book, opens in a rare moment of rest.

The message. No one can put God in his debt. David offers to build the LORD a house, and the LORD answers that he will build David a house: a family line, with a son whose throne will be established for ever, who will be disciplined when he sins but never cast off as Saul was. It all rests on God’s word and God’s heart, and the right response is David’s: wonder, praise, and prayer that asks God to do as he has spoken.

Why it was said. Israel lived under David’s sons, many of them failures, and later watched the line of kings go into exile (see the introduction). They needed to know that the promise rested not on the kings’ goodness but on God’s faithfulness, and so did not die when the kings failed.

How the chapter makes its case. David wants to build for the ark, and Nathan approves; that night God corrects him: he has moved with his people in a tent since Egypt and never asked for a house (vv. 1–7). God recounts what he has done for David and promises his people a secure place (vv. 8–11). Then the promise: David’s son will build God’s house and God will be his father, disciplining his sins but never withdrawing his steadfast love, and David’s throne will be made sure for ever (vv. 11–17). David sits before the LORD, asks who he is to be brought so far, and praises the God who redeemed Israel (vv. 18–24). Only then does he ask, and he asks for exactly what God has promised (vv. 25–29).

Where it leads. To Christ by direct promise, one of the clearest in the Old Testament. Solomon built the temple, but his throne did not last for ever. Gabriel told Mary that her son would receive “the throne of his father David” and reign for ever (Luke 1:32–33); Hebrews applies verse 14 to Jesus (Hebrews 1:5); Peter preached that the oath was kept when God raised him (Acts 2:30–31). The sinless Son bore the stripes promised to David’s sinful sons, and he builds the house that will never fall, his people.

For us. Like David, we come offering God something and find ourselves receiving everything. Our place in God’s family rests on his promise, kept in Christ, not on our record, so his discipline is the treatment of sons, never a sign of rejection. And we may pray with confidence for whatever he has promised, because his words are true.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–7 — Would You Build Me a House to Dwell In?
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A good man’s good idea is not the same as a word from God. At rest from his enemies and living in cedar, David is troubled that the ark of God still dwells in a tent, and Nathan the prophet tells him to go ahead (vv. 1–3). That same night the LORD corrects Nathan. He asks whether David would build him a house, reminds him that ever since the exodus he has chosen to move about with his people in a tent, and points out that he never once asked any of Israel’s leaders for a house of cedar (vv. 4–7). The idea came from love, but it did not come from God.
verseByVerse.theology: Nathan's first answer and God's correction stand in consecutive verses, so that no reader can miss the difference between a good man's judgment and the word of the LORD.
verseByVerse.examples: God has never asked for a house. He has been moving with his people since Egypt, in a tent, by choice.

verseByVerse.quote: Now when the king lived in his house and the LORD had given him rest from all his surrounding enemies, the king said to Nathan the prophet, "See now, I dwell in a house of cedar, but the ark of God dwells in a tent." And Nathan said to the king, "Go, do all that is in your heart, for the LORD is with you." But that same night the word of the LORD came to Nathan, "Go and tell my servant David, 'Thus says the LORD: Would you build me a house to dwell in? I have not lived in a house since the day I brought up the people of Israel from Egypt to this day, but I have been moving about in a tent for my dwelling. In all places where I have moved with all the people of Israel, did I speak a word with any of the judges of Israel, whom I commanded to shepherd my people Israel, saying, "Why have you not built me a house of cedar?"'
verseByVerse.commentary:
At rest in his cedar palace, David wants to build a house for the ark; Nathan tells him to go ahead, but that night God corrects him: in all Israel’s history he has never asked anyone for a house. The chapter that holds the greatest promise in the book begins with a good man’s good idea, and with God gently turning it down.

The LORD had given him rest from all his surrounding enemies (v. 1). The Philistines are broken, the civil war is over, the tribes are united, the capital is taken and the ark is home. For the first time in David’s life nothing is trying to kill him. The law had tied rest and a house for God together: when the LORD gave Israel “rest from all your enemies around”, then would come “the place that the LORD your God will choose, to make his name dwell there” (Deuteronomy 12:10–11). So rest naturally turns David’s mind to a house for God. (The wars of chapter 8 are told after this, so the writer has probably arranged these chapters by subject, as he seems to have done with Hiram, and God’s promise in verse 11 still speaks of rest to come.)

I dwell in a house of cedar, but the ark of God dwells in a tent (v. 2). The cedar is Hiram’s, sent from Tyre with the craftsmen who built the palace (5:11), the finest building material in the ancient Near East. David sits in it while the throne of God stands under canvas in the same city. He proposes nothing and asks no permission; he sets the two facts side by side, and Nathan understands him perfectly. This is the man at his best: when the pressure comes off, his first thought is that God’s honour is lagging behind his own comfort.

Go, do all that is in your heart, for the LORD is with you (v. 3). Nathan is a genuine prophet, not a court flatterer: five chapters from now he will walk in on this same king and say, “You are the man!” (12:7). But here he answers at once, and the answer is his own opinion. Look how good it is. The proposal is godly, the motive pure, the man the LORD’s anointed at the height of his obedience in a season of plain blessing, and Nathan adds the clincher, the LORD is with you. All of it is true, and the conclusion is wrong.

But that same night the word of the LORD came to Nathan (v. 4). God corrects him before morning, which is a kindness to both men. The text sets a good man’s counsel and the word of the LORD in consecutive verses so that no reader can miss the difference, and the difference is not the godliness of the counsellor. A prophet speaking his own mind is a wise man speaking his own mind, and no more. Nathan’s willingness to come back and reverse himself before the king is worth its own sentence: verse 17 says he told David all these words, including the correction of what he himself had said the day before.

Would you build me a house to dwell in? (v. 5). The question is not a rebuke. Nothing that follows says David was wrong to want this, and a great deal says God is pleased with him. But it turns the proposal over. Notice the order of the words: you, build, me. Is David to provide for God, when all his life God has provided for him?

I have been moving about in a tent for my dwelling (v. 6). This is God’s own account of four hundred years, and it is startling. He is not saying he was homeless or badly served, but that this was the arrangement he chose. The tabernacle was made to be taken down, carried and put up again, because the people it belonged to were going somewhere and God meant to go with them: through the wilderness, into the land, through the disorder of the judges. A house is a good thing, but it stays in one place.

Why have you not built me a house of cedar? (v. 7). He never asked. Four centuries of leaders, Othniel, Deborah, Gideon, Jephthah, Samson, Samuel, and not one was told that God wanted a permanent building, or reproached for not providing one. The idea is David’s, and God points out, without heat, that it did not come from him.

God pitched his tent among us. The God who chose a tent did the same again, more deeply. “The Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1:14), and the word John uses for dwelt means “pitched his tent”. In Jesus, God came to live among his people as one of them, on the road with them; and Jesus is the true temple, the place where God meets sinners: “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up” (John 2:19).

Counsel and the word of God. This is one of the most useful passages in Scripture on guidance. The LORD is with you is no guarantee that a particular plan is his. A proposal can be sincerely devout, strategically sound and endorsed by a genuinely spiritual person, and still not be what God wants; the check on all of it is not the quality of the advisers but whether God has actually spoken. It is possible to want something for God that he has not asked for, out of real love, and to be wrong. The test of a plan is not how much devotion went into it.

What rest means. We think of rest as a break between bouts of work, earned by the work and spent getting ready for more. In Scripture rest is first something God gives: being settled and safe in the place he has given, with nothing left to fight for. Timothy Keller often pointed out that when Deuteronomy gives the reason for the Sabbath, it points back to Egypt (Deuteronomy 5:15): rest is the mark of a free people, and someone who can never stop is still a slave, to the work, to other people’s opinion or to the need to prove himself. David’s rest did not last. Hebrews says that if Joshua had really brought Israel into it, “God would not have spoken of another day later on” (Hebrews 4:8). The real rest is a person: “Come to me, all who labor and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest” (Matthew 11:28). Christ has done the work that settles our standing with God, so we no longer work to be accepted but because we are. Keep the Lord’s Day this week as a real stop, and treat the stopping as an act of faith: the world, and your reputation, are in better hands than yours.

Why could David not build the temple? This chapter does not say. The reason comes later, twice, in David’s own mouth: “the word of the LORD came to me, saying, ‘You have shed much blood and have waged great wars. You shall not build a house to my name, because you have shed so much blood before me on the earth’” (1 Chronicles 22:8; see 28:3). The man who secured the land by war is not the man to build the house of peace. His son Solomon will, and Solomon’s name means peace.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 8–17 — The LORD Will Make You a House
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: David offered to build God a house; God promises to build David one, and it will stand for ever. The LORD recounts what he has done for David since the sheepfold, and promises him a great name and his people a secure place (vv. 8–11). Then comes the heart of the chapter: the LORD will make David a house, a line of descendants. His son will build the house for God’s name, and God will be his father; when he sins he will be disciplined, but God’s steadfast love will never be taken from him as it was from Saul, and his throne will be established for ever (vv. 11–16). Nathan delivers every word (v. 17).
verseByVerse.theology: Count the pronouns in verses 8-11. David offered to do something for God, and the reply is a list of what God has done and will do for him.
verseByVerse.examples: Verse 15 is where this kingship parts company with Saul's: David's sons will be disciplined when they sin, but they will not be cast off.

verseByVerse.quote: Now, therefore, thus you shall say to my servant David, 'Thus says the LORD of hosts, I took you from the pasture, from following the sheep, that you should be prince over my people Israel. And I have been with you wherever you went and have cut off all your enemies from before you. And I will make for you a great name, like the name of the great ones of the earth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God answers David’s offer to do something for him by recounting what God has done for David, and promising more: a great name. David came to give; the reply is a list in which God is the one acting in nearly every line.

I took you from the pasture, from following the sheep (v. 8). The answer begins with David’s biography, and its first three words sum it up: I took you. That is where the messenger found him on the day Samuel came to Bethlehem: the youngest son, not even called in, out with the flock because somebody had to be, while seven older brothers were looked over (1 Samuel 16:10–11). God reminds a man in a cedar palace where he was standing when all this began, and does it just before making him one of the largest promises in the Old Testament.

My servant David … prince over my people Israel. God gives David the title of honour he gave Moses (Numbers 12:7; Joshua 1:2), and calls him prince (nagid), the word for a leader appointed by God, not a king who rules in his own right. And the people are still my people: like any shepherd, David looks after a flock that belongs to its owner.

I have been with you wherever you went and have cut off all your enemies (v. 9). Goliath, Saul’s long pursuit and the Philistines in the Valley of Rephaim (5:17–25) all lie behind this clause. What David survived, God did. Count how often God says “I” in verses 8 to 11, because that is the point.

And I will make for you a great name. The phrase has a history. At Babel men said, “let us make a name for ourselves”, and were scattered (Genesis 11:4). To Abram God said, “I will bless you and make your name great”, and the whole covenant followed (Genesis 12:2). A great name is something people grasp at and God gives, and the grasping never succeeds. The name promised here reaches its height in David’s Son, to whom God gave “the name that is above every name” (Philippians 2:9).
verseByVerse.note: Psalms 89 and 132 sing this covenant back to God, and 1 Chronicles 17 gives a parallel account of the chapter.

verseByVerse.quote: And I will appoint a place for my people Israel and will plant them, so that they may dwell in their own place and be disturbed no more. And violent men shall afflict them no more, as formerly, from the time that I appointed judges over my people Israel. And I will give you rest from all your enemies. Moreover, the LORD declares to you that the LORD will make you a house.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Before he speaks of David’s family, God promises his people a secure place; then he turns David’s offer upside down: David will not build the LORD a house, the LORD will make David a house.

And I will appoint a place for my people Israel (v. 10). God speaks of the people before the king, an order that keeps recurring. The kingdom was exalted “for the sake of his people Israel” (5:12); David is prince over my people Israel (v. 8); and here the promise of security is Israel’s before it is the king’s. The dynasty exists for the nation, not the nation for the dynasty.

And will plant them. Israel is pictured as a tree set in its own soil, as in the song by the sea: “You will bring them in and plant them on your own mountain” (Exodus 15:17). As formerly, from the time that I appointed judges recalls the book of Judges, where Israel was raided and oppressed again and again. I will give you rest repeats the word of verse 1: the rest David enjoys is God’s gift, and God promises to keep giving it.

The LORD will make you a house (v. 11). This is the turning point of the chapter, and it turns on one word used twice. The Hebrew bayit does the same double duty as the English house: it means a building, and it means a family line, the house of Saul or the house of David, as the writer has been using it for six chapters. David said, I will build you a bayit, and meant a temple. God says, I will make you a bayit, and means a dynasty.

Out-given. That exchange sums up the whole chapter. A man offers God a building and is told he will be given a family that does not end. He came to give and is comprehensively out-given, which is what happens to anyone who sets out to do something for God. “Who has given a gift to him that he might be repaid?” (Romans 11:35). And the greatest gift folded into this promise is still to come: the Son of David himself, given for us.

verseByVerse.quote: When your days are fulfilled and you lie down with your fathers, I will raise up your offspring after you, who shall come from your body, and I will establish his kingdom. He shall build a house for my name, and I will establish the throne of his kingdom forever.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God promises David a son who will succeed him, build the house for God’s name and have his throne established for ever: words that come true first in Solomon and reach far beyond him.

When your days are fulfilled and you lie down with your fathers (v. 12). The promise begins with David’s death. It is not about how long he will live but about what will outlast him.

I will raise up your offspring after you. Now the promise works on two levels at once, both real and neither to be dropped. The first is Solomon. He comes from David’s body, he builds the house, and Kings records its completion in just these terms (1 Kings 8:20). Everything in verses 12 to 15 refers first and plainly to the son who succeeds him.

He shall build a house for my name (v. 13). The temple is God’s house only as the place where he puts his name, where he makes himself known and may be called on (Deuteronomy 12:5, 11; 1 Kings 8:27–29). David’s wish is not refused for ever, only postponed to his son (1 Chronicles 22:8–10).

I will establish the throne of his kingdom forever. Then comes a word that fits no mortal king. Forever occurs three times in these verses (vv. 13, 16), and it is not the language of an ordinary succession. Solomon’s temple was burned and his line lost the throne; the promise outlived both. It reaches the Son of David who said, “I will build my church” (Matthew 16:18), a house of living people that no army can burn, for “we are his house” (Hebrews 3:6).

verseByVerse.quote: I will be to him a father, and he shall be to me a son. When he commits iniquity, I will discipline him with the rod of men, with the stripes of the sons of men, but my steadfast love will not depart from him, as I took it from Saul, whom I put away from before you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God will be a father to David’s son: when the son sins he will be disciplined, but God’s steadfast love will never be taken from him as it was from Saul. The two halves of verse 14 pull in different directions, and the New Testament keeps both.

I will be to him a father, and he shall be to me a son (v. 14). This is adoption language, the formula by which Israel’s king is declared God’s own son. Psalm 2 uses it: “You are my Son; today I have begotten you” (Psalm 2:7). And the writer to the Hebrews opens his proof that Christ is greater than the angels with two quotations, the second of them this verse: “to which of the angels did God ever say … ‘I will be to him a father, and he shall be to me a son’?” (Hebrews 1:5).

When he commits iniquity, I will discipline him with the rod of men. David’s line will sin. Solomon will go after other gods in his old age, and many of the kings after him will be idolaters and fools. The discipline is promised in advance and it is not gentle: the stripes of the sons of men. David will feel its first stroke in chapter 12, in his own household, and it will run through the rest of his life.

But my steadfast love will not depart from him (v. 15). Steadfast love is hesed, the loyal love that keeps covenant, and here it is God’s. Saul is named as the contrast. Saul sinned and the kingdom was taken; the Spirit departed; God would not answer him by dreams or Urim (the priest’s sacred lots) or prophets; and he died on a mountain, told the day before that he would. That is what removal looks like. David’s sons will be disciplined, but the love does not go. This is why the promise differs in kind from anything before it: it rests not on the son’s faithfulness but on God’s.

Near and far fulfilment. The second half of verse 14 cannot be said of Christ, who committed no iniquity (Hebrews 4:15; 1 Peter 2:22). The honest course is to keep both halves and explain neither away, because the New Testament does exactly that. Much Old Testament prophecy works like this: the words come true first in someone close at hand, and then reach a greater fulfilment in Christ. The near fulfilment is Solomon and the kings after him, sinners who were disciplined, sometimes disastrously, but never removed. The far one reaches past them all to a son of David whose throne really is for ever. Gabriel says of the child of Mary, “the Lord God will give to him the throne of his father David, and he will reign over the house of Jacob forever, and of his kingdom there will be no end” (Luke 1:32–33). Peter preaches at Pentecost that David, “knowing that God had sworn with an oath to him that he would set one of his descendants on his throne”, foresaw the resurrection (Acts 2:30–31). And in the Bible’s last chapter Jesus says, “I am the root and the descendant of David” (Revelation 22:16).

The rod fell on the sinless Son. Many Christians have seen a further mercy in the rod and the stripes. The punishment promised to David’s sinful sons fell at last on the one Son who had no sin, and “with his wounds we are healed” (Isaiah 53:5; 1 Peter 2:24). That is how God’s love can stay with sinners while their sin is still dealt with.

To his people too. Paul widens the words of verse 14 to the whole church: “I will be a father to you, and you shall be sons and daughters to me” (2 Corinthians 6:18). What was sworn to David’s son belongs, in Christ, to everyone joined to that Son.

Discipline, not removal. That is the difference between a relationship that lasts only while conditions are met and one that rests on God’s promise. Discipline is what happens to sons; removal is what happened to Saul. Any Christian who has wondered whether some failure has finally put them outside God’s love is standing in front of this verse, and the New Testament makes exactly this argument: “the Lord disciplines the one he loves … It is for discipline that you have to endure. God is treating you as sons” (Hebrews 12:6–7).

verseByVerse.quote: And your house and your kingdom shall be made sure forever before me. Your throne shall be established forever.'" In accordance with all these words, and in accordance with all this vision, Nathan spoke to David.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God seals the promise: David’s house, kingdom and throne are made sure for ever; and Nathan delivers every word, including the ones that overturn his own advice.

And your house and your kingdom shall be made sure forever before me (v. 16). Verse 16 makes three things sure, house, kingdom and throne, and says forever twice. Made sure translates a word from the same root as amen: firm, reliable, to be trusted. Isaiah calls this promise God’s “steadfast, sure love for David” (Isaiah 55:3), and Paul applies those words to the resurrection of Jesus (Acts 13:34): the throne is sure because its King will never die again.

Nathan spoke to David (v. 17). Nathan delivers the whole of it: the part that reverses what he said the day before, and the sentence telling the king he will not be building anything. He does not soften it, delay it or shape it into something easier to receive. That is what a prophet is for, and it is why this man can be trusted five chapters later when he walks in with a story about a lamb.

How Jewish readers take it. Jewish readers take Nathan’s oracle as the charter of the house of David, first fulfilled in Solomon, and as the root of the hope that God will restore David’s throne under an anointed king; daily Jewish prayer still asks God to establish the throne of David. The father and son language is read as God’s adoption of the king, not as a claim that he is divine. Here the two readings share a great deal. This commentary holds that the promise of a throne for ever is met only in Jesus, raised from the dead and enthroned as David’s son (Luke 1:32–33; Acts 2:30–31).

Where Christians differ. Is the eternal throne fulfilled now, or in a future earthly kingdom? Dispensationalists, and premillennial Christians more widely, look for Christ to reign from Jerusalem for a thousand years after his return, and see that reign as a fulfilment of this promise. They too confess Jesus as David’s Son and King, and faithful believers differ here.

This commentary’s view. Peter says that God swore to seat a descendant of David on his throne and kept the oath by raising Christ to his right hand (Acts 2:30–36). The line of kings seemed to end at the exile, but the promise did not: it rests on the Son of David who reigns now and for ever (Luke 1:32–33). This commentary takes the amillennial view because Peter places David’s throne in Christ’s present reign at the Father’s right hand.

Textual note. “Before me” in verse 16 follows the Greek Old Testament; the Hebrew reads “before you”.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 18–24 — Who Am I, O Lord GOD?
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Grace received produces wonder before it produces requests. David goes in and sits before the LORD, and asks who he is, and what his family is, that God has brought him so far and spoken of his house for generations to come (vv. 18–20). He traces everything to God’s promise and God’s own heart, and his thanks becomes praise: there is none like the LORD (vv. 21–22). Then, instead of dwelling on his own dynasty, he turns to Israel, the one nation God went to redeem from Egypt and made his own for ever (vv. 23–24).
verseByVerse.theology: David's posture says as much as his words: this is a man overwhelmed by grace, not a petitioner arriving with a list.
verseByVerse.examples: The prayer never asks for anything until verse 25. Its whole first half is about who God is and what God has done, and when David finally moves off himself he moves not to his dynasty but to the nation: who is like your people Israel.

verseByVerse.quote: Then King David went in and sat before the LORD and said, "Who am I, O Lord GOD, and what is my house, that you have brought me thus far? And yet this was a small thing in your eyes, O Lord GOD. You have spoken also of your servant's house for a great while to come, and this is instruction for mankind, O Lord GOD! And what more can David say to you? For you know your servant, O Lord GOD! Because of your promise, and according to your own heart, you have brought about all this greatness, to make your servant know it. Therefore you are great, O Lord GOD. For there is none like you, and there is no God besides you, according to all that we have heard with our ears. And who is like your people Israel, the one nation on earth whom God went to redeem to be his people, making himself a name and doing for them great and awesome things by driving out before your people, whom you redeemed for yourself from Egypt, a nation and its gods? And you established for yourself your people Israel to be your people forever. And you, O LORD, became their God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Overwhelmed by the promise, David sits before the LORD and at first asks for nothing: he marvels that God has brought him so far, traces it all to God’s promise and God’s own heart, and praises the God who has no equal and who redeemed a people for himself.

Then King David went in and sat before the LORD (v. 18). He goes into the tent he pitched for the ark and sits down. Commentators have long remarked on the posture. Israelites stood to pray, or knelt, or lay face down: Solomon knelt at the dedication of the temple, Ezra fell on his knees, Daniel knelt three times a day. Sitting is the posture neither of petition nor of ceremony. It is what a man does when he has been handed something he cannot stand up under. He will not ask for a single thing until verse 25; he has come simply to be in the presence of what has just been said to him.

Who am I, O Lord GOD? This is not a set phrase, and it is not false modesty. He has just been told his family will hold a throne for ever, and the honest response from the youngest son of a Bethlehem farmer is who am I? The last time anyone described him at length it was as a boy with a sling in a valley, and before that as the one out with the sheep.

And what is my house? The same word again, in a third sense: not a palace and not a dynasty but simply his family, which is nobody in particular. Jesse’s people were farmers in a small town, and Jesse’s grandmother Ruth had walked in from Moab with nothing.

And this is instruction for mankind (v. 19). Whatever the exact sense of this hard phrase (see below), the astonishment underneath it is plain. Either David is saying that this promise reaches beyond his family to the whole human race, or that nobody has ever dealt with anyone like this. Either way he has grasped that something has happened out of all proportion to the occasion.

What more can David say to you? For you know your servant (v. 20). He gives up trying to respond adequately, and the reason he gives is the best there is. There is no point telling God what this means to him, because God already knows him, better than he knows himself, as chapters 11 and 12 will show with terrible thoroughness.

Because of your promise, and according to your own heart (v. 21). Two reasons for everything that has happened, and neither is anything in David. The second is the deeper: God did this because of what he is like, not because of anything found in David and not because of any need in himself. The reason for the covenant lies in God’s own character, the only place any covenant in Scripture is ever grounded.

Therefore you are great, O Lord GOD (v. 22). The prayer turns into praise, and the subject changes from what David has been given to who gave it. Note the word therefore. He does not begin with God’s greatness as a formality; he arrives at it, out of what has just been done for him.

And who is like your people Israel? (v. 23). Just promised an eternal throne for his own family, he turns not to his dynasty but to the exodus and the nation, and uses of Israel the very form of words he has just used of God: there is none like you, and no nation like this one. The reason lies wholly in God’s action: the one nation on earth whom God went to redeem. God went: he came down to Egypt and brought them out. And he did it making himself a name. In verse 9 God makes David’s name great; here he makes his own known. The exodus was as much about who God is as about who Israel is.

And you, O LORD, became their God (v. 24). This echoes the oldest summary of the covenant: “you shall be my people, and I will be your God” (Jeremiah 30:22; compare Exodus 6:7). The man with the newest and largest promise in Israel’s history reaches back to the oldest one and puts his own dynasty inside it. What he has been given is not a new arrangement running alongside what God did in the exodus; it is the same covenant promise, carried forward.

The God who went to redeem. The God who went down to Egypt went further still. “When the fullness of time had come, God sent forth his Son, born of woman, born under the law, to redeem those who were under the law, so that we might receive adoption as sons” (Galatians 4:4–5). The promise David is marvelling at, I will be to him a father, reaches us through that redemption.

Where does a self come from? Who am I? is one of the great questions of our time, and the usual modern answer is to look inside and then make yourself: choose your values, shape your story, become who you really are. It sounds like freedom and it is exhausting, for a self-made self has to be kept up by its maker and is only as secure as its last performance. David asks the question and does not look inward at all. He looks at what God has said, and rests on the fact that God knows him. In a Nazi prison in 1944 Dietrich Bonhoeffer wrote a poem with the same title. Others saw a calm, cheerful man; inside he felt restless and afraid, and could not tell which was really he. He ended by handing the question to God: whoever I am, you know me, and I am yours. A self comes not from what we make of ourselves but from whose we are. In Christ the answer is spoken over us before we have done anything: “See what kind of love the Father has given to us, that we should be called children of God; and so we are” (1 John 3:1).

Uncertain wording. The last clause of verse 19 is among the harder Hebrew in the book. Literally it is something like and this is the law of the man (torat ha’adam). Some read it as a statement: this is the charter, or instruction, for humanity, meaning that what God has promised David is his way of dealing with the whole human race, not merely one family’s succession. Others read it as a question, as older English versions did (is this the manner of man?): do human beings deal with one another like this? The parallel in Chronicles reads differently again, “and have shown me future generations” (1 Chronicles 17:17). The grammar does not decide, and the readings are not far apart in effect. Verse 23 is also compressed: it shifts from them to your people in mid-sentence, and a nation and its gods is an unusual phrase, where Chronicles has the smoother “driving out nations before your people” (1 Chronicles 17:21). The sense is clear either way: God drove out nations and their gods to make room for the people he had redeemed.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 25–29 — Do as You Have Spoken
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The boldest prayer asks God to do what he has said. Only now does David ask for anything, and he asks for nothing new: confirm the word you have spoken, and do as you have spoken (v. 25). He wants God’s name magnified first, and his own house established as its consequence (v. 26). His courage to pray comes from God’s revelation, not from himself (v. 27), and it rests on three facts: you are God, your words are true, and you have promised this good thing. So he asks for the blessing God has already pledged (vv. 28–29).
verseByVerse.theology: He prays the promise back. Each request in this half of the prayer hands God's own words back to him with do as you have spoken attached, taking him at his word in his hearing.
verseByVerse.examples: Verse 27 says where the courage came from: not from David, who would never have dared ask for a dynasty, but from what God had said first.

verseByVerse.quote: And now, O LORD God, confirm forever the word that you have spoken concerning your servant and concerning his house, and do as you have spoken. And your name will be magnified forever, saying, 'The LORD of hosts is God over Israel,' and the house of your servant David will be established before you. For you, O LORD of hosts, the God of Israel, have made this revelation to your servant, saying, 'I will build you a house.' Therefore your servant has found courage to pray this prayer to you. And now, O Lord GOD, you are God, and your words are true, and you have promised this good thing to your servant. Now therefore may it please you to bless the house of your servant, so that it may continue forever before you. For you, O Lord GOD, have spoken, and with your blessing shall the house of your servant be blessed forever."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Only now does David ask, and he asks for nothing new: he takes God’s promise, hands it back, and asks God to do what he has said, for the glory of God’s name.

Confirm forever the word … and do as you have spoken (v. 25). The first request in the prayer arrives seven verses in. He proposes nothing and tells God of no need; he takes the promise God has just made and asks God to do it. This is praying the promise, and it is the pattern of many of the great prayers in Scripture. Abraham does it over Sodom, holding God to his own justice. Moses does it after the golden calf, pleading God’s oath to Abraham (Exodus 32:13). Daniel does it with Jeremiah’s seventy years open before him (Daniel 9:2). And Jesus taught his disciples to pray your kingdom come, asking God for the very thing he has announced he will do. There is nothing presumptuous in it. God is not being reminded; he is being taken at his word in his own hearing, which is the sincerest thing anyone can do with a promise.

And your name will be magnified forever (v. 26). Look at the order. God’s name comes first and David’s house second, and the second follows from the first. He asks for the dynasty because a lasting house of David will be a lasting witness that the LORD of hosts is God over Israel. Whether he could keep that order under pressure is another question, and chapter 11 is the answer; but here he has it right, and it is the same order as 5:12.

Therefore your servant has found courage to pray this prayer to you (v. 27). Literally, he found his heart. He would never have dared. Asking God to set your family on a throne for ever is not something a man thinks up for himself; David can ask only because God said it first. Take away verse 11 and verse 27 is presumption; with verse 11 it is obedience.

What may I ask for? Most Christians have felt that question without putting it into words. Here is one answer: you may ask for what God has said he will do. The size of the request is not the issue; what matters is whether he has promised it.

You are God, and your words are true (v. 28). Three statements ground everything he has said: you are God; your words are true; you have promised this good thing. Take any one away and the prayer collapses. Together they are the whole basis of confidence: the one who spoke is God, what he says is true, and this particular thing has actually been said. Paul adds the last word: “all the promises of God find their Yes in him” (2 Corinthians 1:20). In Christ every promise is kept, and through him we say our Amen.

With your blessing shall the house of your servant be blessed forever (v. 29). He ends where the whole conversation began, on the word house, which by now has travelled a long way. He came in wanting to build one. He goes out having been given one, and asking that it may stand.

The hinge of the Old Testament. Step back from the chapter, because a great deal hangs on it, and everything after it in Israel’s story is read against this promise. The prophets appeal to it as the monarchy collapses: Isaiah’s child who will sit “on the throne of David and over his kingdom … from this time forth and forevermore” (Isaiah 9:7); Jeremiah’s “righteous Branch” raised up for David as the dynasty goes into exile (Jeremiah 23:5). And when the line of kings runs out, the promise does not. For centuries no son of David sits on any throne anywhere, and then an angel stands before a girl in a village and announces it again (Luke 1:32–33). God took some fifteen years to give David a crown, and explained nothing; he took a thousand to keep this word, and it held the whole way.

More than you dared to ask. David wanted to build God a house and was told no. What he received instead was a son who would build the house, and a Son whose house would never fall. It is the discovery every believer eventually makes: the thing you wanted to give God turns out to be the occasion on which he gives you something you would never have dared to ask for.

7.theology:
Good counsel is not the word of God. Nathan's first answer (v. 3) was devout, wise and wrong, and God corrected it before morning. The difference between counsel and revelation is not the godliness of the counsellor but whether God has spoken, and Nathan's readiness to come back and reverse himself in front of the king (v. 17) is part of what made him trustworthy. It is possible to want something for God that he has not asked for, out of real love, and still be wrong.

God out-gives those who offer to give. David offered a building and was promised a house of another kind. In verses 8-11 God is the subject of nearly every verb, and the reason given for it all is your promise and your own heart (v. 21), not anything found in David. A great name is a thing men grasp at, as at Babel (Gen. 11:4), and a thing God gives, as to Abram (Gen. 12:2).

A promise that keeps travelling. The promise applies first to Solomon and the kings after him, sinners who were disciplined but never removed as Saul was, and then reaches past all of them to the Son whose throne truly is for ever. The prophets appealed to it as the monarchy collapsed (Isa. 9:7; Jer. 23:5), and it outlasted the line of kings itself.

Prayer that rests on a promise. David's prayer dwells first on who God is and what he has done, and only then asks, and asks only for what God has said: do as you have spoken. With verse 11 behind it, that is not presumption but obedience.
7.examples:
Then: A king in a cedar palace decided the tent God lived in was not good enough, was told that God had never asked for a building, and in the same breath was promised a throne for his family that would not end. Then he went in and sat down in front of a tent and asked for nothing for seven verses.

Now: Two things, and the first is uncomfortable because it concerns good advice. A proposal can be devout, sound, blessed by every visible circumstance and endorsed by someone genuinely spiritual, and still not be what God has asked for. The second is verse 27. Most people pray timidly because they are not sure what they are entitled to ask for. David asked for a dynasty forever because God had said it first. Find what he has actually promised, and ask for it plainly: do as you have spoken. The promise does not rest on how well we pray or serve; it rests on the Son of David who kept faith where David's sons failed, and whose Father is now ours.

keyVerse.quote: And your house and your kingdom shall be made sure forever before me. Your throne shall be established forever.
keyVerse.note: This is the promise the rest of the Bible keeps returning to. House, kingdom and throne are made sure for ever, and they rest not on the faithfulness of David’s sons but on the word of God. Gabriel’s announcement to Mary (Luke 1:32–33) and Peter’s sermon at Pentecost (Acts 2:30–31) both declare it kept in Jesus.

7.reflection:
David’s plan was devout, Nathan approved it, and it was still not what God wanted (vv. 1–7). How can we tell the difference between good advice and what God has actually said? Has a godly plan of yours ever been redirected?

David offered God a house and was promised a house he could never have built (v. 11). Where are you tempted to think you can put God in your debt, and what does it mean that he always out-gives us, above all in his Son?

Verses 14–15 promise discipline but never removal. How could these verses, with Hebrews 12:6–7, help a Christian who fears that some failure has put them outside God’s love?

David prays, “do as you have spoken” (v. 25), and finds courage because God spoke first (v. 27). Which promises of God could you pray back to him this week for yourself, your family or your church?

8.title: David's Victories
8.text: <sup>1</sup>After this David defeated the Philistines and subdued them, and David took Metheg-ammah out of the hand of the Philistines.<sup>2</sup>And he defeated Moab and he measured them with a line, making them lie down on the ground. Two lines he measured to be put to death, and one full line to be spared. And the Moabites became servants to David and brought tribute.<sup>3</sup>David also defeated Hadadezer the son of Rehob, king of Zobah, as he went to restore his power at the river Euphrates.<sup>4</sup>And David took from him 1,700 horsemen, and 20,000 foot soldiers. And David hamstrung all the chariot horses but left enough for 100 chariots.<sup>5</sup>And when the Syrians of Damascus came to help Hadadezer king of Zobah, David struck down 22,000 men of the Syrians.<sup>6</sup>Then David put garrisons in Aram of Damascus, and the Syrians became servants to David and brought tribute. And the LORD gave victory to David wherever he went.<sup>7</sup>And David took the shields of gold that were carried by the servants of Hadadezer and brought them to Jerusalem.<sup>8</sup>And from Betah and from Berothai, cities of Hadadezer, King David took very much bronze.<sup>9</sup>When Toi king of Hamath heard that David had defeated the whole army of Hadadezer,<sup>10</sup>Toi sent his son Joram to King David, to ask about his health and to bless him because he had fought against Hadadezer and defeated him, for Hadadezer had often been at war with Toi. And Joram brought with him articles of silver, of gold, and of bronze.<sup>11</sup>These also King David dedicated to the LORD, together with the silver and gold that he dedicated from all the nations he subdued,<sup>12</sup>from Edom, Moab, the Ammonites, the Philistines, Amalek, and from the spoil of Hadadezer the son of Rehob, king of Zobah.<sup>13</sup>And David made a name for himself when he returned from striking down 18,000 Edomites in the Valley of Salt.<sup>14</sup>Then he put garrisons in Edom; throughout all Edom he put garrisons, and all the Edomites became David's servants. And the LORD gave victory to David wherever he went.<sup>15</sup>So David reigned over all Israel. And David administered justice and equity to all his people.<sup>16</sup>Joab the son of Zeruiah was over the army, and Jehoshaphat the son of Ahilud was recorder,<sup>17</sup>and Zadok the son of Ahitub and Ahimelech the son of Abiathar were priests, and Seraiah was secretary,<sup>18</sup>and Benaiah the son of Jehoiada was over the Cherethites and the Pelethites, and David's sons were priests.
8.overview:
Where we are. In chapter 7 God told David that he had cut off his enemies and would give him “rest from all your enemies” (7:9, 11). Chapter 8 shows that promise kept, compressing perhaps twenty years of campaigns into eighteen verses, probably arranged by subject rather than date. The next chapter turns from the battlefield to the king’s table.

The message. God keeps his word through ordinary history, and the victories are his: “the LORD gave victory to David wherever he went” (vv. 6, 14). The right use of what God gives is to give it back, and David dedicates all his plunder to the LORD and governs his people with justice and equity. Yet the same report records a cruelty in Moab without a word of approval, a reminder that even this king, at his best, is not the King his people finally need.

Why it was said. Later Israel needed to see that the promise to David was not mere words: God gave the rest he had spoken of, and the treasure of these wars went into the temple (see the introduction). The chapter also showed every later king what a throne is for.

How the chapter makes its case. First the campaigns: west against the Philistines, east against Moab, with the measuring of prisoners, and north against Hadadezer of Zobah and Damascus, where David hamstrings the captured chariot horses in obedience to the law about kings; the section ends with the refrain that the LORD gave the victory (vv. 1–8). Then the spoil: a friendly king’s gifts and the plunder of every nation are dedicated to the LORD, and Edom falls, with the refrain again (vv. 9–14). Last, the reign at home: justice and equity for all, and the officials of the new state (vv. 15–18).

Where it leads. To Christ by pattern and by the need it exposes. A son of David ruling the nations with justice and righteousness is what the psalms and prophets longed for (Psalm 72; Isaiah 9:7; Jeremiah 23:5), and David gives a first taste of it. But his kingdom was won by the sword, in Moab by the cord, and his justice did not last. Jesus reigns over the nations with justice that never lapses, and he wins them not by taking tribute but by giving his own blood (Revelation 5:9).

For us. Whatever victories we have are God’s gifts, to be given back to him. The things we lean on instead of God, our chariots, are worth giving up for the sake of trusting him. And any authority we hold is for justice, to all, especially those who cannot demand it.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–8 — The LORD Gave Victory to David Wherever He Went
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God keeps his word to cut off David’s enemies, and the writer makes sure we know who won. David subdues the Philistines to the west (v. 1) and Moab to the east, where he puts two-thirds of the prisoners to death by a measuring line, a cruelty the text records without approval (v. 2). In the north he defeats Hadadezer of Zobah and the Syrians of Damascus who come to his aid, and hamstrings the captured chariot horses in costly obedience to the law about kings (vv. 3–6). Gold shields and bronze come to Jerusalem (vv. 7–8). Over it all stands the refrain: the LORD gave victory to David wherever he went (v. 6).
verseByVerse.theology: The Moab measurement is savage, and the text supplies no reason for it. It is all the harder to read because of David's own family ties to Moab, which the commentary below sets out.
verseByVerse.examples: The hamstrung horses are the opposite case: an act of obedience to the law about kings, and a costly one, which his son Solomon would not repeat.

verseByVerse.quote: After this David defeated the Philistines and subdued them, and David took Metheg-ammah out of the hand of the Philistines. And he defeated Moab and he measured them with a line, making them lie down on the ground. Two lines he measured to be put to death, and one full line to be spared. And the Moabites became servants to David and brought tribute. David also defeated Hadadezer the son of Rehob, king of Zobah, as he went to restore his power at the river Euphrates. And David took from him 1,700 horsemen, and 20,000 foot soldiers. And David hamstrung all the chariot horses but left enough for 100 chariots. And when the Syrians of Damascus came to help Hadadezer king of Zobah, David struck down 22,000 men of the Syrians. Then David put garrisons in Aram of Damascus, and the Syrians became servants to David and brought tribute. And the LORD gave victory to David wherever he went. And David took the shields of gold that were carried by the servants of Hadadezer and brought them to Jerusalem. And from Betah and from Berothai, cities of Hadadezer, King David took very much bronze.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God keeps his promise to give David rest from his enemies: the Philistines, Moab and the Aramean kingdoms of the north all fall, and the writer insists that the victories were the LORD’s. His report sets one of the ugliest acts in the book beside one of the costliest acts of obedience.

After this David defeated the Philistines (v. 1). After the summit of chapter 7, this is the same man doing his job, and the two chapters belong together. God promised to cut off all your enemies from before you and give Israel a place where they would be disturbed no more (7:9–10). Chapter 8 is that happening: the promise kept in the ordinary events of a reign. Chronicles says David took “Gath and its villages” (1 Chronicles 18:1), so he probably took control of the leading Philistine city (on Metheg-ammah, see below).

And he measured them with a line (v. 2). This is one of the ugliest verses in the book, and it will not be softened here. Moabite prisoners are made to lie in a row on the ground, and a cord is stretched along them. Two cord-lengths of men are killed and one cord-length is spared, and who lives depends on where a man happens to be lying. The text offers no justification: no provocation, no atrocity avenged, no command of God, no comment. It states what happened and moves to the next campaign. (The Chronicler records Moab’s defeat and tribute but leaves out the measuring line, 1 Chronicles 18:2.)

The irony of Moab. Two things should be named. The first is the irony. When David was a fugitive with a price on his head, it was to Moab that he sent his parents for safety: “Please let my father and my mother stay with you, till I know what God will do for me” (1 Samuel 22:3). And he had family reasons for choosing it: his great-grandmother was Ruth, who came out of Moab to Bethlehem and would not go back. There is Moabite blood in the man measuring the cord. Some suppose that the Moabites had killed his parents. It is possible, but the text does not say so, and inventing a reason the writer withheld serves nobody.

The narrator’s silence. The second is what the silence means. This narrator said nothing when David wiped out villages to protect a lie at Ziklag, or when Joab murdered Abner, or when David took more wives. He records, and when he says nothing he is not approving: he expects the reader to judge.

Hadadezer the son of Rehob, king of Zobah (v. 3). Zobah was an Aramean (Syrian) kingdom north of Damascus, the strongest power between Israel and the Euphrates, and Damascus sent troops to prop it up (v. 5). Its defeat carried David’s rule far beyond Israel’s tribal borders, toward the frontier God had named to Abraham: “from the river of Egypt to the great river, the river Euphrates” (Genesis 15:18).

And David hamstrung all the chariot horses (v. 4). Then comes an act of obedience that costs him a great deal. He has captured the finest chariot force in the region, the heavy armour of the ancient world, which Israel had never had and had feared since the judges; any other king would have taken it into his own army. David has the horses hamstrung: the tendon is cut, the animal can never pull a chariot again, and a fortune in military power is destroyed on the field. It is what Joshua had been told to do at the waters of Merom: “You shall hamstring their horses and burn their chariots with fire” (Joshua 11:6).

The law about horses. Why? Because of a sentence in the law about kings, in the same short passage that warned about wives: “Only he must not acquire many horses for himself or cause the people to return to Egypt in order to acquire many horses” (Deuteronomy 17:16). The reason is trust. A chariot corps is what a nation leans on instead of God: “Some trust in chariots and some in horses, but we trust in the name of the LORD our God” (Psalm 20:7), very likely David’s own line. So he obeys a command that costs him a strategic advantage, on the day he wins it.

Solomon’s horses. Set that beside his son. “Solomon also had 40,000 stalls of horses for his chariots, and 12,000 horsemen” (1 Kings 4:26), and he imported horses from Egypt, the second thing the law forbade in the same breath. The father cut the tendons; the son built the stables. (Chronicles gives four thousand stalls, 2 Chronicles 9:25, and many think the larger figure is a copying slip.) And it is the same law, one verse further on, that David is breaking in his own household by taking wives. Nobody keeps the whole of it.

And the LORD gave victory to David wherever he went (v. 6). This sentence returns in verse 14, so that everything between is enclosed by it. The tactics and the soldiering were real, and the men who fell were killed by other men, but the writer will not allow the account to be read as a list of David’s achievements. It matches the answers David kept receiving when he inquired of the LORD before battle (5:19): the king who asked before every battle is now told, by the historian, whose the victories were.

The shields of gold … very much bronze (vv. 7–8). The plunder comes to Jerusalem, and Chronicles adds what became of the bronze: “With it Solomon made the bronze sea and the pillars and the vessels of bronze” (1 Chronicles 18:8). The spoils of David’s wars went into the house he was not allowed to build (see the note on vv. 9–14).

A greater Son of David. David’s kingdom grew by the sword, and in Moab by the cord. His greater Son said, “My kingdom is not of this world”, so that his servants do not fight for it (John 18:36), and he gathers the nations by giving his own blood, not by taking their tribute (Revelation 5:9). Ruth the Moabite stands in his family line (Matthew 1:5), and in his kingdom Moabites, Edomites and Arameans are welcomed as brothers, not measured on the ground.

The chariots we keep in the stable. Few of us own horses, but we all keep chariots: whatever we lean on so as not to lean on God, the savings, the qualifications, the backup plan behind the backup plan. None of them is wrong in itself, and the law did not forbid Israel a single horse. What it forbade was many: the piling up that quietly becomes trust. The wise modern rule is to keep every option open and every advantage in reserve, and by that rule David’s knife looks like madness. But chariots have their own cost. A life built on control has to stay in control, and the stable is never quite big enough. The surprise of Scripture is that God’s power reaches its height in a refusal of force. Jesus told Peter he could ask his Father for “more than twelve legions of angels” (Matthew 26:53), and did not ask. “He was crucified in weakness, but lives by the power of God” (2 Corinthians 13:4). People who know they are held by that power can afford to let a few chariots go.

Uncertain wording. Metheg-ammah (v. 1) is not known as a place and may not be a name at all; it could mean something like the bridle of the mother city, that is, control of the chief Philistine town, which would fit Chronicles’ “Gath and its villages”. In verse 3, to restore his power is literally to return his hand. “Hand” can mean power or a monument (Chronicles has “to set up his monument”, 1 Chronicles 18:3), and the Hebrew does not make plain whether “he” is Hadadezer reasserting his hold on the Euphrates or David extending his own.

Textual note. Why do the numbers sometimes differ from the parallel account? Numbers in Hebrew manuscripts were easily miscopied, since they were often written with letters or abbreviations, and parallel accounts sometimes count different things, such as chariots and charioteers, or a total and a part. Here the Greek Old Testament reads 1,000 chariots and 7,000 horsemen in verse 4, as Chronicles does (1 Chronicles 18:4), which suggests words dropped out of the Hebrew in copying. None of this touches what the passage teaches. This commentary holds, with the historic confessions, that Scripture as God gave it is true in all it says; most differences of this kind are explained by copying, though not every one can now be settled with certainty.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 9–14 — These Also King David Dedicated to the LORD
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: What God gives, David gives back. Toi king of Hamath, glad to see his old enemy Hadadezer beaten, sends his son with gifts of silver, gold and bronze (vv. 9–10). David dedicates them all to the LORD, with the silver and gold of every nation he has subdued: treasure that would one day go into the temple he was not allowed to build (vv. 11–12). Edom falls in the Valley of Salt and becomes David’s servant, as God had said of Esau long before, and the refrain sounds again: the LORD gave victory to David wherever he went (vv. 13–14).
verseByVerse.theology: Everything goes to the LORD: the tribute of a friendly king and the plunder of every defeated nation.
verseByVerse.examples: The Chronicler makes plain what this treasure was for, and why it is the most moving thing in the chapter (1 Chron. 22:14; 29:2-5).

verseByVerse.quote: When Toi king of Hamath heard that David had defeated the whole army of Hadadezer, Toi sent his son Joram to King David, to ask about his health and to bless him because he had fought against Hadadezer and defeated him, for Hadadezer had often been at war with Toi. And Joram brought with him articles of silver, of gold, and of bronze. These also King David dedicated to the LORD, together with the silver and gold that he dedicated from all the nations he subdued, from Edom, Moab, the Ammonites, the Philistines, Amalek, and from the spoil of Hadadezer the son of Rehob, king of Zobah. And David made a name for himself when he returned from striking down 18,000 Edomites in the Valley of Salt. Then he put garrisons in Edom; throughout all Edom he put garrisons, and all the Edomites became David's servants. And the LORD gave victory to David wherever he went.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The gifts of a friendly king and the spoil of every conquered nation all go to the LORD; and Edom, Esau’s country, becomes David’s servant, as God had said centuries before.

Toi sent his son Joram to King David (vv. 9–10). A king David has never met sends his son with congratulations, and the reason is practical: David has just destroyed the man who had been fighting Toi for years. Hamath lies far to the north, beyond Damascus, and the whole region is adjusting to David’s new power.

These also King David dedicated to the LORD (v. 11). The heart of the chapter is a single verb: dedicated. Not banked, not shared out, not spent on the palace, as every other king in the region would have done, but set apart for the LORD. And it is not a share but all of it: the gifts of a friendly king in the north, the plunder of every nation he has defeated, and the spoil of Hadadezer’s kingdom.

Why the giving is so moving. Put this beside the previous chapter. David asked to build God a house and was told no, and the reason, given elsewhere in his own words, was blood: “You have shed much blood and have waged great wars. You shall not build a house to my name” (1 Chronicles 22:8). So for the rest of his reign he wins wars and gives the proceeds to the project he is forbidden to work on. The Chronicler says this is where the temple’s funding came from. David tells Solomon that he has laid up, with great pains, “100,000 talents of gold, a million talents of silver, and bronze and iron beyond weighing” (1 Chronicles 22:14; see talent), and at the end of his life he gives his own fortune as well, “because of my devotion to the house of my God” (1 Chronicles 29:2–5). He never saw a stone of it laid. The foundations went in after he was dead.

When God says no. Anyone told no about the thing they most wanted to do for God can learn here. David did not sulk, lose interest, or decide that if he could not build it, it was not his concern. He funded it for years and handed his son the materials and a set of plans (1 Chronicles 28:11–12). Wanting the work done matters more than being the one who does it, and that is a harder test than the refusal was. He could give like that because he knew that all he had won, the LORD had given (v. 14): “all things come from you, and of your own have we given you” (1 Chronicles 29:14).

And David made a name for himself (v. 13). The name returns, and should be read alongside 7:9, where God said, I will make for you a great name. The name David made is the one God gave him.

All the Edomites became David’s servants (v. 14). Edom deserves a note, because a promise made centuries earlier is being kept in it. Edom is Esau’s country, and what was said to Rebekah before the twins were born was “the older shall serve the younger” (Genesis 25:23). Isaac said the same to Jacob, and Balaam foresaw a star out of Jacob by whom “Edom shall be dispossessed” (Numbers 24:17–18). It takes the better part of a thousand years and a battle in the Valley of Salt, and here it is. That is how God’s promises work in this book: God says a thing, and then history does it, slowly, by ordinary means, long after everyone who heard the promise is dead.

And the LORD gave victory to David wherever he went. The sentence of verse 6 returns to close the list. The last word on all the campaigns is not David’s skill but God’s gift.

Who defeated Edom? David, his commander Abishai (1 Chronicles 18:12) and Joab (the title of Psalm 60) are all credited with the Edomite victory, as a king is credited with his generals’ battles. The 12,000 of the psalm’s title may count one part of the campaign.

Textual note. The traditional Hebrew text of verse 13 reads Syrians, and the KJV follows it; in Hebrew the two names differ by one easily confused letter, and the ESV follows the Greek and Chronicles in reading Edomites (1 Chronicles 18:12).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 15–18 — Justice and Equity to All His People
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A kingdom is measured by its justice, not its size. After eighteen verses of conquest, one sentence sums up David’s rule at home: he reigned over all Israel and administered justice and equity to all his people, which is what a shepherd-king is for (v. 15). Then come the officers of the new state: Joab over the army, a recorder and a secretary, two priests, Benaiah over the foreign bodyguard, and David’s sons in some office close to the king (vv. 16–18). Nearly every name carries a history, and the list is not entirely reassuring.
verseByVerse.theology: One sentence covers the domestic government, and it is the right one: justice and equity to all his people, which is what a shepherd-king is for.
verseByVerse.examples: The cabinet list is brief, but nearly every name in it carries a history, and its last clause is a genuine puzzle.

verseByVerse.quote: So David reigned over all Israel. And David administered justice and equity to all his people. Joab the son of Zeruiah was over the army, and Jehoshaphat the son of Ahilud was recorder, and Zadok the son of Ahitub and Ahimelech the son of Abiathar were priests, and Seraiah was secretary, and Benaiah the son of Jehoiada was over the Cherethites and the Pelethites, and David's sons were priests.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The summary of David’s reign is not the size of his empire but the way he governed, with justice and equity for all his people; and the list of his officials quietly prepares for troubles to come.

So David reigned over all Israel (v. 15). Eighteen verses of conquest, and one sentence about how he governed; and the measure of the reign is not the garrisons or the treasury but justice and equity to all his people.

Justice and equity. The two words are the standard Old Testament pair for good government: mishpat, judgment given rightly in actual cases, and tsedaqah, righteousness, doing right by people, particularly people who cannot enforce their own claims. Together they are what a king exists for. To all his people, not only to those with influence: that phrase is the test, which is why the courts of the ancient world were judged by how they treated widows, foreigners and the poor, the people nobody was forced to treat fairly. This is the principle of 5:12, the kingdom exalted for the sake of his people Israel, now seen in practice. David is the shepherd the elders named at Hebron, and this is what shepherding a nation looks like on an ordinary day: hearing cases.

The King the psalms longed for. Israel prayed for exactly this in its kings, “Give the king your justice, O God” (Psalm 72:1), and seldom received it for long. The prophets fastened the hope to a coming son of David who would “execute justice and righteousness in the land” (Jeremiah 23:5). David’s justice in verse 15 was a first instalment, and it did not last. Jesus is the King whose justice never lapses and reaches all his people, the needy and those who have no helper (Psalm 72:12–14); and he does more than judge rightly, for at his own cost he makes the unrighteous righteous (2 Corinthians 5:21).

Turned against him. Hold on to verse 15, because it will be used against him. Seven chapters from now his son Absalom will rise early every morning, stand beside the way of the city gate, and stop every man coming with a lawsuit: “See, your claims are good and right, but there is no man designated by the king to hear you”, and then, “Oh that I were judge in the land! Then every man with a dispute or cause might come to me, and I would give him justice” (15:3–4). That rebellion is built on the claim that verse 15 is no longer true, and it works: “So Absalom stole the hearts of the men of Israel” (15:6). Was the claim fair? The text leaves it open, and the honest answer is probably that a kingdom this size had outgrown one man hearing cases, and David had not noticed. What is certain is that a son found the one place his father was no longer paying attention, and stood in it every morning for four years.

Joab the son of Zeruiah was over the army (v. 16). Joab is still there. Five chapters ago he murdered the commander of the opposing army inside a city of refuge and was cursed for it in public. Here he heads the list, running the army, and he will still be running it years from now when he kills the king’s son against a direct order. The writer does not remark on it. He simply puts the name at the top, as he will again at 20:23, and lets the reader remember what David said: “These men, the sons of Zeruiah, are more severe than I” (3:39).

Jehoshaphat … was recorder … Seraiah was secretary (vv. 16–17). The kingdom now has the offices of a state: a recorder, probably the royal herald who kept records and made the king’s decisions known, and a secretary, the royal scribe who handled the king’s correspondence.

Zadok the son of Ahitub and Ahimelech the son of Abiathar were priests (v. 17). Two priests, and the second name carries a history. Abiathar was the priest’s son who escaped from Nob with the ephod (the priestly garment used to inquire of God) when Doeg the Edomite killed eighty-five priests on Saul’s order, and ran to David in the wilderness (1 Samuel 22:20–23). David said to him then, “Stay with me; do not be afraid … With me you shall be in safekeeping.” A generation later his family is in the king’s cabinet. Elsewhere Abiathar is the son of Ahimelech (1 Samuel 22:20), so either Abiathar named his own son after his father, or the names were reversed in copying. Zadok’s line would hold the priesthood from Solomon’s day (1 Kings 2:35).

Benaiah the son of Jehoiada was over the Cherethites and the Pelethites (v. 18). Benaiah commands the royal bodyguard, and the Cherethites and Pelethites are foreign troops: most probably Cretan and Philistine mercenaries, men David may have come to know during his sixteen months at Ziklag. A foreign guard is a shrewd choice in a country just out of civil war. Benaiah himself is one of the mighty men, and the writer will come back to him: he struck down two ariels of Moab (the meaning of the word is uncertain), a lion in a pit on a snowy day, and an Egyptian giant with the Egyptian’s own spear (23:20–21). He ends up commanding Solomon’s army after executing Joab.

And David’s sons were priests. The last clause is a genuine puzzle, and it is better to admit it (see below).

Uncertain wording. David’s sons were priests uses the ordinary word for priest (kohen). But David’s sons were not Levites, and the priesthood was closed to anyone outside Aaron’s line. The word may be used here in a wider sense, for royal ministers or advisers; the Chronicler, listing the same officials, writes that “David’s sons were the chief officials in the service of the king” (1 Chronicles 18:17), which is probably the meaning. Saying the term is uncertain is better than inventing a certainty about it.

8.theology:
The victories are the LORD's. The sentence repeated in verses 6 and 14 stands on either side of the list of victories, so that the list cannot be read as a list of David's achievements. The tactics and the soldiering were real, but the king who asked before every battle is told by the historian whose the victories were. Even the old word to Rebekah, the older shall serve the younger (Gen. 25:23), is kept here in a valley in Edom, slowly and by ordinary means.

Obedience is partial, and grace still works. David obeys the law about horses at real cost, trusting the LORD rather than chariots (Ps. 20:7), and in the same years breaks the law about wives at home. Moab's prisoners are measured with a cord and the narrator says nothing; silence here is not approval. Then a man who has been refused gives everything he has won to the house he may not build, and the giving is the finest thing in the chapter.

The king the psalms kept asking for. Justice and righteousness are what Israel prayed for in its kings (Psalm 72:1-2) and seldom received for long, and the prophets fastened the pair to a coming son of David: a throne upheld with justice and with righteousness from this time forth and forevermore (Isaiah 9:7), a Branch who shall execute justice and righteousness in the land (Jeremiah 23:5). David's justice in verse 15 was a first instalment of that, and it did not last. The empire it governed was won with the sword and, in Moab, measured with a cord. The King who fulfils it said his kingdom is not of this world, so his servants do not fight for it (John 18:36), and he gathers the nations not by tribute taken but by his own blood given (Revelation 5:9).
8.examples:
Then: A king captured the best chariot force in the region and had almost every horse hamstrung where it stood, destroying on the day he won it the advantage every kingdom around him was built on, because of one sentence about what a king must not acquire.

Now: The dedicated plunder is the thing to remember. David was told he could not build the temple, and spent the rest of his working life funding it. Being refused the work you wanted is not the same as being released from caring whether it gets done, and the temptation after a no is to lose interest and call it acceptance. He could give like that because everything he had won, the LORD had given; and the same Lord gives his Spirit to make our giving glad rather than grudging. And verse 15 says what all authority is for, and the telling word is all: justice for everyone, not only for those who matter.

keyVerse.quote: And the LORD gave victory to David wherever he went.
keyVerse.note: This sentence comes twice (vv. 6, 14) and frames the whole record of David’s wars, so that it cannot be read as a list of his achievements. It is God keeping his promise of 7:9 through ordinary battles. The final victory of the Son of David is God’s gift too, won not by the sword but by the cross.

8.reflection:
The writer says twice that “the LORD gave victory to David wherever he went” (vv. 6, 14). Where are you tempted to take the credit for what God has given you, and how might you give it back to him?

David hamstrung the chariot horses in obedience to God’s law, at real cost (v. 4). What “chariots” do you lean on instead of God, and what might it look like to let some of them go?

The writer records the killing of the Moabite prisoners (v. 2) without approving it. How should we read the parts of the Bible that report what God’s people did wrong? What does the contrast with Jesus, who conquers by giving his own blood, teach us?

David could not build the temple, so he gave his plunder to it (vv. 11–12), and he ruled with “justice and equity to all his people” (v. 15). How do you respond when God says no to something you wanted to do for him? And who, in your sphere, most needs you to do justice?

9.title: Mephibosheth: Grace at the King's Table
9.text: <sup>1</sup>And David said, "Is there still anyone left of the house of Saul, that I may show him kindness for Jonathan's sake?"<sup>2</sup>Now there was a servant of the house of Saul whose name was Ziba, and they called him to David. And the king said to him, "Are you Ziba?" And he said, "I am your servant."<sup>3</sup>And the king said, "Is there not still someone of the house of Saul, that I may show the kindness of God to him?" Ziba said to the king, "There is still a son of Jonathan; he is crippled in his feet."<sup>4</sup>The king said to him, "Where is he?" And Ziba said to the king, "He is in the house of Machir the son of Ammiel, at Lo-debar."<sup>5</sup>Then King David sent and brought him from the house of Machir the son of Ammiel, at Lo-debar.<sup>6</sup>And Mephibosheth the son of Jonathan, son of Saul, came to David and fell on his face and paid homage. And David said, "Mephibosheth!" And he answered, "Behold, I am your servant."<sup>7</sup>And David said to him, "Do not fear, for I will show you kindness for the sake of your father Jonathan, and I will restore to you all the land of Saul your father, and you shall eat at my table always."<sup>8</sup>And he paid homage and said, "What is your servant, that you should show regard for a dead dog such as I?"<sup>9</sup>Then the king called Ziba, Saul's servant, and said to him, "All that belonged to Saul and to all his house I have given to your master's grandson.<sup>10</sup>And you and your sons and your servants shall till the land for him and shall bring in the produce, that your master's grandson may have bread to eat. But Mephibosheth your master's grandson shall always eat at my table."
