Now Ziba had fifteen sons and twenty servants.<sup>11</sup>Then Ziba said to the king, "According to all that my lord the king commands his servant, so will your servant do." So Mephibosheth ate at David's table, like one of the king's sons.<sup>12</sup>And Mephibosheth had a young son, whose name was Mica. And all who lived in Ziba's house became Mephibosheth's servants.<sup>13</sup>So Mephibosheth lived in Jerusalem, for he ate always at the king's table. Now he was lame in both his feet.
9.overview:
Where we are. The kingdom is secure: the wars of chapter 8 are won and David rules with justice for all his people. Now, with nothing to gain, the king asks whether anyone is left of the family that hunted him. The chapter also opens the long account of David’s court and family that runs on into 1 Kings 2.

The message. The kindness of God’s king is the kindness of God himself: steadfast love that keeps its promises, seeks out the helpless, gives everything for another’s sake, and seats an enemy’s heir at the king’s table as a son. Mephibosheth brings nothing but fear and the confession that he is a dead dog. He receives everything because of Jonathan. And he is still lame: grace gives him a place before it gives him healing.

Why it was said. Some in Israel accused David of destroying Saul’s house to take the throne (16:7–8). The first thing told of the secure king is that he went looking for Saul’s family to do it good, keeping his covenant with Jonathan (1 Samuel 20:14–17; see the introduction).

How the chapter makes its case. David asks for anyone left of Saul’s house to whom he can show kindness for Jonathan’s sake; Saul’s servant Ziba tells him of Jonathan’s lame son at Lo-debar, and David sends for him (vv. 1–5). Mephibosheth falls on his face; the king says his name, tells him not to fear, restores Saul’s land and gives him a place at the royal table, and Mephibosheth calls himself a dead dog (vv. 6–8). Ziba’s household is set to farm the estate, Mephibosheth eats like one of the king’s sons, Jonathan’s line goes on, and the last word is that he was lame in both his feet (vv. 9–13).

Where it leads. To Christ by pattern, and by the character of God shown in both kings. The story is not an allegory, but its shape is the gospel’s: the king takes the first step, the helpless are sent for, everything is given for the sake of another and his covenant, and the unworthy are seated at the table as sons. God forgives us “in Christ” (Ephesians 4:32); the Son of David came “to seek and to save the lost” (Luke 19:10), and his servants are sent to bring in “the poor and crippled and blind and lame” (Luke 14:21).

For us. We come to God with no claim on him and are received for Jesus’ sake, not ours, as children at his table. His grace does not yet mend everything that is wrong with us, but our place does not depend on it. And those who have been welcomed like this keep their promises and open their own tables to the overlooked.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–5 — Is There Still Anyone Left?
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The king’s kindness begins with the king. Unasked, with his kingdom secure, David looks for anyone left of Saul’s house to whom he can show kindness for Jonathan’s sake, keeping a promise made years before that no one could have enforced (v. 1). Saul’s old servant Ziba is found, and David raises the standard: he wants to show the kindness of God (vv. 2–3). Ziba tells him of a son of Jonathan, crippled in his feet, living in another man’s house at Lo-debar across the Jordan (vv. 3–4). David sends and brings him (v. 5).
verseByVerse.theology: David initiates all of this, and the word he uses twice is hesed, the covenant love that keeps going after the reason for keeping it has gone. The second time he calls it the kindness of God, which is the standard he is measuring by.
verseByVerse.examples: He is keeping a promise made to Jonathan (1 Sam. 20:14-15), and Jonathan had named the exact moment it would be tested.

verseByVerse.quote: And David said, "Is there still anyone left of the house of Saul, that I may show him kindness for Jonathan's sake?" Now there was a servant of the house of Saul whose name was Ziba, and they called him to David. And the king said to him, "Are you Ziba?" And he said, "I am your servant." And the king said, "Is there not still someone of the house of Saul, that I may show the kindness of God to him?" Ziba said to the king, "There is still a son of Jonathan; he is crippled in his feet." The king said to him, "Where is he?" And Ziba said to the king, "He is in the house of Machir the son of Ammiel, at Lo-debar." Then King David sent and brought him from the house of Machir the son of Ammiel, at Lo-debar.
verseByVerse.commentary:
With his kingdom secure, David goes looking for someone of Saul’s family to whom he can show kindness for Jonathan’s sake, and finds Jonathan’s lame son living out of sight across the Jordan. The kindness is the king’s own idea, and he calls it the kindness of God.

Is there still anyone left of the house of Saul (v. 1)? Nobody asked him. There is no petition, no delegation, no political pressure. The wars of chapter 8 are won and the treasury is full, and one day the king asks whether anybody is left from the family that tried to kill him for a decade.

That I may show him kindness for Jonathan’s sake. The question has a reason attached. Years before, in a field outside Gibeah, Jonathan had said: “If I am still alive, show me the steadfast love of the LORD, that I may not die; and do not cut off your steadfast love from my house forever, when the LORD cuts off every one of the enemies of David from the face of the earth” (1 Samuel 20:14–15). Read what he asked for. Protection while he lived is almost an afterthought. What he asks is kindness to his descendants at the very moment David will have no reason on earth to give it: when every one of David’s enemies is cut off. Jonathan knew what he was asking. When a new dynasty was secure, it removed the old one; that was simply what happened, in every kingdom around them, and Jonathan was the crown prince of the house being replaced. He was asking David to break the rule.

A promise no one could enforce. Now, years later, with Jonathan dead on a mountain and the house of Saul finished, David raises the subject himself. The promise was made to a man long dead, about a person David has never met, in a conversation with no witnesses and no legal force, when David was a fugitive with nothing. There is not one outside reason to remember it. He remembers it. Psalm 15 describes the one who may dwell on God’s holy hill as a man “who swears to his own hurt and does not change” (Psalm 15:4). For a believer that means keeping the promises nobody would hold us to: the word given to a friend who has since died, the commitment made when we were in need and no longer are, the care promised to someone’s children. We can keep such promises because God keeps his to us, long after we have stopped deserving it.

A servant of the house of Saul whose name was Ziba (v. 2). They have to find a former servant of Saul’s household to answer the question, which shows how completely that house has vanished. Remember Ziba: he comes back twice, and both times he seems to be seeking his own advantage (16:1–4; 19:24–30).

That I may show the kindness of God to him (v. 3). The king asks again and raises the standard as he does. Not ordinary generosity, or a ruler’s show of goodwill, but the kindness God shows, which in the Old Testament means kindness to people who have no claim on it, faithfully kept when nothing compels it. The word is hesed, the steadfast love God has just promised will never depart from David’s son (7:15). David has received it, and now he passes it on.

He is crippled in his feet. Ziba’s answer is oddly put. Asked whether anyone is left, he says there is a son of Jonathan, and at once volunteers the disability, though nobody asked. It may be an honest attempt to help: you should know he cannot walk. It may be something less generous: this one is not worth troubling about, no threat and no use. The text does not say. But the writer records that the first fact anyone offers David about this man is what is wrong with him. How he came to be lame was told earlier, in one terrible sentence. When the news came from Gilboa that Saul and Jonathan were dead, the household panicked: “his nurse took him up and fled, and as she fled in her haste, he fell and became lame. And his name was Mephibosheth” (4:4). He was five years old. Somebody dropped him while running for their lives, and he never walked again.

In the house of Machir the son of Ammiel, at Lo-debar (v. 4). Lo-debar lies across the Jordan, in Gilead, well away from anywhere that matters. The name is often explained as “no pasture” or “no thing”, and much has been preached on it, but the text makes nothing of it; it is a real village with a real man living in it. Notice, though, where the grandson of a king of Israel has been living for years: in somebody else’s house, on the far side of the river. Notice too his host. Machir appears once more in this book, in the last place you would expect: when David flees from Absalom, broken and hungry, Machir of Lo-debar is one of three men who bring him food at Mahanaim (17:27–29). The man who sheltered Saul’s grandson feeds David in his worst hour.

Then King David sent and brought him (v. 5). David sends. Mephibosheth does not come and ask, and the whole chapter depends on it. He has been keeping his head down across the river for years, expecting nothing, asking for nothing, and almost certainly hoping the king had never heard of him. Then the king’s men arrive at Machir’s door with an order to bring him to Jerusalem. Everything in this chapter is begun by the king.

Why the writer tells it here. Chapter 8 closed with a summary of David’s reign; chapter 9 opens the long account of his court and family that runs on into 1 Kings 2, and it brings on stage Mephibosheth and Ziba, who will matter again when Absalom rebels. It also answers a charge some in Israel made, that David had destroyed Saul’s house to take its throne (16:7–8). The first thing told of the secure king is that he went looking for Saul’s family in order to do it good.

The King who comes looking. This is how God deals with sinners. We do not find our way to him; he sends for us. “The Son of Man came to seek and to save the lost” (Luke 19:10), and “while we were enemies we were reconciled to God by the death of his Son” (Romans 5:10).
verseByVerse.note: Chronicles calls him Merib-baal (1 Chron. 8:34; 9:40).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 6–8 — A Dead Dog Such as I
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The man who expected death is given a place at the king’s table. Mephibosheth, Saul’s grandson and a possible rival for the throne, falls on his face before David. The king calls him by name, tells him not to fear, and gives him three gifts: kindness for the sake of his father Jonathan, all Saul’s land restored, and a seat at the king’s table always (vv. 6–7). Mephibosheth can only ask why the king should regard a dead dog like him, the very words David once used of himself when Saul hunted him (v. 8).
verseByVerse.theology: He is Saul's grandson, a rival claimant with a better hereditary title than the man on the throne, summoned from the far side of the Jordan. There was one normal outcome to a journey like that.
verseByVerse.examples: A dead dog is not a phrase Mephibosheth invented, and where it came from is one of the quiet wonders of the chapter.

verseByVerse.quote: And Mephibosheth the son of Jonathan, son of Saul, came to David and fell on his face and paid homage. And David said, "Mephibosheth!" And he answered, "Behold, I am your servant." And David said to him, "Do not fear, for I will show you kindness for the sake of your father Jonathan, and I will restore to you all the land of Saul your father, and you shall eat at my table always." And he paid homage and said, "What is your servant, that you should show regard for a dead dog such as I?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Saul’s grandson arrives on his face, expecting death; the king calls him by name, tells him not to fear, and gives him his grandfather’s land and a permanent place at the royal table, all for his father Jonathan’s sake.

And Mephibosheth the son of Jonathan, son of Saul, came to David and fell on his face (v. 6). See this arrival from his side of the room. The writer gives his full pedigree, and that is the whole problem. He is not a private citizen but the direct male descendant of the previous king, in the eyes of anyone who cared about hereditary right the rightful heir to the throne of the king he is being carried in to see. He is here because the king’s men came for him. He is on the floor, on his face, and getting up again will not be easy for him. He has grown up hearing one version of David: the man who broke his grandfather, took the kingdom and fought a long war against his uncle’s regime. Whatever else he expects from this interview, he does not expect to survive it.

And David said, “Mephibosheth!” The king says his name. Not son of Saul, the kind of label the writer pinned on Michal three times in chapter 6; not a title or a charge, but his name.

Do not fear (v. 7). Which tells you how afraid he was. Then come three things, each larger than the last.

For I will show you kindness for the sake of your father Jonathan. The first is the reason. Not for anything Mephibosheth is or has done or might be useful for. He receives all of this on account of somebody else, and he is told so to his face at the start, before anything is given.

And I will restore to you all the land of Saul your father. The second is the land. (Father here means grandfather, as often in Hebrew.) All Saul’s estate, which had presumably passed to the crown as a defeated dynasty’s property did, is restored. That is a fortune, and it is also a statement: the house of Saul is not to be treated as forfeit.

And you shall eat at my table always. The third is the table, and it costs David most and matters most. Not a pension paid to a man in a distant village, not permission to live quietly, but a permanent seat in the king’s own household, at the king’s own meals, every day for the rest of his life. Hold that against a saying this same book gave four chapters ago. When David took Jerusalem, the Jebusites jeered that the blind and the lame could hold it against him, and out of that day came the proverb, “The blind and the lame shall not come into the house” (5:8). Now, into the house, to the king’s own table, comes a man lame in both feet, and he stays there.

What is your servant, that you should show regard for a dead dog such as I? (v. 8). This is the sentence everyone remembers, and the phrase in it has a history. Dogs in that world were not pets but scavengers on the edge of a village, and a dead one was refuse; it is about as low as a person can put himself. But those words have been spoken before in this story, and they were spoken by David. Outside the cave at Engedi, holding a corner of Saul’s robe, he shouted to the king who was hunting him: “After whom has the king of Israel come out? After whom do you pursue? After a dead dog! After a flea!” (1 Samuel 24:14). David said it of himself, to Saul. Now Saul’s grandson says it of himself, to David. The wheel has come full circle, and if anyone in Israel understood how it felt to speak that sentence, it was the man being spoken to.

For another’s sake. This is the shape of the gospel. Sinners come before God with no claim of their own and are told, before anything is given, why they are received: for the sake of another. Paul tells believers to forgive “as God in Christ forgave you” (Ephesians 4:32), and says to those who were once far off that they “have been brought near by the blood of Christ” (Ephesians 2:13). Many come to God as Mephibosheth came to David, face down and sure the interview can only end badly, and the King’s first word to them is the same: do not fear.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 9–13 — He Ate Always at the King's Table
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Grace gives a lasting place as a son before it gives healing. David sets Ziba, with his fifteen sons and twenty servants, to farm Saul’s estate for Mephibosheth, while Mephibosheth himself eats at the king’s table (vv. 9–10). Ziba agrees, and the writer adds that Mephibosheth ate there like one of the king’s sons, and that his young son Mica carried Jonathan’s line on (vv. 11–12). The chapter ends with the table and the truth together: he lived in Jerusalem and always ate at the king’s table, and he was lame in both his feet (v. 13).
verseByVerse.theology: The king's generosity is not a pension paid at a distance but a place in the household, and the writer says it four times in seven verses.
verseByVerse.examples: The writer ends on the disability rather than the honour, and the commentary below explains why that is the most hopeful thing he could have done.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the king called Ziba, Saul's servant, and said to him, "All that belonged to Saul and to all his house I have given to your master's grandson. And you and your sons and your servants shall till the land for him and shall bring in the produce, that your master's grandson may have bread to eat. But Mephibosheth your master's grandson shall always eat at my table." Now Ziba had fifteen sons and twenty servants. Then Ziba said to the king, "According to all that my lord the king commands his servant, so will your servant do." So Mephibosheth ate at David's table, like one of the king's sons. And Mephibosheth had a young son, whose name was Mica. And all who lived in Ziba's house became Mephibosheth's servants. So Mephibosheth lived in Jerusalem, for he ate always at the king's table. Now he was lame in both his feet.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Ziba’s whole household is set to farm Saul’s land for Mephibosheth, and Mephibosheth eats at the king’s table like one of his sons for the rest of his life; but the chapter ends by saying he was still lame in both feet.

Then the king called Ziba, Saul’s servant (v. 9). Ziba came in as a free agent, the servant of a household that no longer existed, and leaves as a steward with a master again. Note the phrase David uses of Mephibosheth three times: your master’s grandson. Ziba is reminded whose man he is.

Now Ziba had fifteen sons and twenty servants (v. 10). The arrangement is complete and generous. Ziba is no poor man: fifteen sons and twenty servants is a considerable operation, and the whole of it is now put to work farming Saul’s estate for a man who cannot walk out to inspect it. That is a great deal to ask of Ziba, and the writer plants the detail on purpose. When David flees from Absalom, Ziba meets him on the road with two hundred loaves and a story: Mephibosheth has stayed in Jerusalem hoping to get the kingdom back. David believes him on the spot and gives him the entire estate (16:1–4). When David returns, Mephibosheth comes to meet him with his feet unwashed and his beard untrimmed since the day the king left, and says Ziba deceived him (19:24–30). David never settles it. He divides the land between them, and Mephibosheth says, “Oh, let him take it all, since my lord the king has come safely home” (19:30).

So Mephibosheth ate at David’s table, like one of the king’s sons (v. 11). The phrase is the writer’s own, not David’s. Amnon and Absalom, Adonijah and Solomon sat at that table, and so did the grandson of the man who threw spears at their father. He is not a pensioner and not a hostage. He is family.

And Mephibosheth had a young son, whose name was Mica (v. 12). The line of Jonathan continues, and the Chronicler follows it down for generations (1 Chronicles 8:34–40), so Jonathan’s request was answered further than he could have known. He asked for kindness to his house, and his house went on.

Now he was lame in both his feet (v. 13). Four times in this chapter the writer says that Mephibosheth ate at the king’s table, and then he ends on something else. The last clause is deliberate, and it should not be tidied into something more triumphant. Nothing here is healed. Mephibosheth is fed, restored, honoured and given a permanent place among the king’s sons, and he is still carried to the table. He will be lame at every meal for the rest of his life. The chapter that could have ended on like one of the king’s sons ends on the disability instead.

Not an allegory, but a likeness. This story follows the pattern of the gospel, and it would be strange not to say so, provided it is said carefully. It is not an allegory, a story in which every detail stands for something else, and forcing it does it no favours. What is genuinely there is this. A man who could not come is sent for. He is found far from the king, expecting judgment, and receives the opposite. He is given everything on account of somebody else’s covenant, and told so plainly at the start. He is seated at the king’s table not as a guest but as a son. And he brings nothing to it but the admission that he is a dead dog. Every one of those is in the text, and the likeness is no accident: this is how God has always dealt with people, and the Old Testament keeps showing it.

The table of the Son of David. The Son of David told of a great banquet where the servant is sent out to “bring in the poor and crippled and blind and lame” (Luke 14:21), and he ate with the people his world kept outside the house. His table is spread now, and its fullness is still to come: “Blessed are those who are invited to the marriage supper of the Lamb” (Revelation 19:9). This is not a hidden code in the chapter. It is the same God with the same heart, doing fully in Christ what David did in part in a palace.

Who tells you who you are? Every culture answers that question, and ours answers it in two ways that look like opposites. The older answer is achievement: you are what you make of yourself, so a man who has made nothing is a dead dog. The newer answer turns the wound into the name: you are what was done to you, and the first fact about Mephibosheth, as Ziba offered it, is that he is lame. Both put the weight of a whole self on something that cannot bear it. Achievement can be lost in an afternoon, and a self built on an injury has to keep the injury open to stay itself. The chapter gives a third answer, the one the Bible gives everywhere: Mephibosheth is who the king says he is. He did nothing to earn the name, and his lameness, though real at every meal, is no longer the whole truth about him. That is what the gospel does with an identity. It neither flatters it nor erases it, but speaks over it a word from outside: “you are no longer a slave, but a son” (Galatians 4:7).

Carried to the table. Which brings us back to the last clause. Being brought to the table does not undo what happened to him when he was five years old. He eats as a son and he arrives carried, and both are true for the rest of his life. Any Christian who has wondered why grace has not fixed the thing that is actually wrong with them (the illness, the memory, the temperament, the damage somebody else did in a moment of panic) is looking at the right verse. The table is real and the lameness is real, and the writer put them in the same sentence on purpose. Seeking help, from a wise biblical counsellor or a doctor, is no failure of faith; but some things are not mended in this life, and Scripture never pretends the meantime is comfortable. Yet the healing does come. The Son of David made the lame walk as a sign of what his kingdom brings (Matthew 11:5), and on the day he raises his people, “then shall the lame man leap like a deer” (Isaiah 35:6).

9.theology:
Kindness that keeps a promise no one could enforce. David's hesed, his loyal covenant love, is kept to a dead man, about a person he had never met, when nobody would have known if it lapsed (v. 1). He calls it the kindness of God (v. 3) because that is what God's kindness is: given to people with no claim on it, and faithfully kept when nothing compels it.

Grace takes the first step. Mephibosheth does not come and ask; he is sent for from across the river (v. 5). The king says his name, tells him not to fear, and gives the reason before the gift, for the sake of your father Jonathan, so that he knows from the start that none of it is on his own account. The proverb that the lame shall not come into the house (5:8) is undone at the king's own table, and Jonathan's line goes on for generations (1 Chron. 8:34-40), further than he could have known to ask.

Received as a son, and still carried. Mephibosheth contributes nothing but the confession that he is a dead dog, the very words the hunted David once used of himself (1 Sam. 24:14). He is seated as one of the king's sons, and nothing in the chapter heals him. The grace is real and the lameness is real, and the writer will not let either cancel the other. Ziba, who will return twice seeking his own advantage (16:1-4; 19:24-30), is a reminder that even good arrangements are lived out among people with mixed motives.
9.examples:
Then: A king sent across the Jordan for the surviving heir of the dynasty he had replaced, gave him back his grandfather's entire estate, and sat him at the royal table with the princes for the rest of his life, because of a promise made in a field to that man's father years before.

Now: Two things. The first is about promises. Nothing enforced this one, and no one alive would have known if David had let it lapse. Most promises that get broken are broken exactly there, allowed to lapse once the reason for them is gone; that is precisely where hesed is tested. We keep faith like that badly, but we have been kept by a God who never lets his word to us lapse, and his Spirit makes us people who keep ours. The second is the last clause. Mephibosheth eats as a son and is still carried to the table. The seat does not depend on his legs being healed, and they are not healed.

keyVerse.quote: Do not fear, for I will show you kindness for the sake of your father Jonathan, and I will restore to you all the land of Saul your father, and you shall eat at my table always.
keyVerse.note: Here the chapter turns from fear to welcome. Every gift is given “for the sake of your father Jonathan”, on account of a covenant Mephibosheth had no part in making, and the greatest gift is a place at the king’s table for life. It is the shape of the gospel: sinners received for the sake of another, and welcomed to the King’s table.

9.reflection:
David kept a promise to Jonathan that no one could have enforced (v. 1; 1 Samuel 20:14–15). Are there promises you have made that you are tempted to let lapse because nobody would notice?

Mephibosheth did not come asking; he was sent for (v. 5), and everything he received was “for the sake of your father Jonathan” (v. 7). How does this picture the way God has dealt with you in Christ?

Mephibosheth called himself “a dead dog” and was given a seat “like one of the king’s sons” (vv. 8, 11). Where do you tend to find your sense of who you are: in what you have achieved, in what has been done to you, or in what the King says over you?

The chapter ends, “Now he was lame in both his feet” (v. 13). How does it help to know that God gives us a place at his table before he heals everything that is wrong with us? Who could you welcome to your own table?

10.title: War with Ammon and Aram
10.text: <sup>1</sup>After this the king of the Ammonites died, and Hanun his son reigned in his place.<sup>2</sup>And David said, "I will deal loyally with Hanun the son of Nahash, as his father dealt loyally with me." So David sent by his servants to console him concerning his father. And David's servants came into the land of the Ammonites.<sup>3</sup>But the princes of the Ammonites said to Hanun their lord, "Do you think, because David has sent comforters to you, that he is honoring your father? Has not David sent his servants to you to search the city and to spy it out and to overthrow it?"<sup>4</sup>So Hanun took David's servants and shaved off half the beard of each and cut off their garments in the middle, at their hips, and sent them away.<sup>5</sup>When it was told David, he sent to meet them, for the men were greatly ashamed. And the king said, "Remain at Jericho until your beards have grown and then return."<sup>6</sup>When the Ammonites saw that they had become a stench to David, the Ammonites sent and hired the Syrians of Beth-rehob, and the Syrians of Zobah, 20,000 foot soldiers, and the king of Maacah with 1,000 men, and the men of Tob, 12,000 men.<sup>7</sup>And when David heard of it, he sent Joab and all the host of the mighty men.<sup>8</sup>And the Ammonites came out and drew up in battle array at the entrance of the gate, and the Syrians of Zobah and of Rehob and the men of Tob and Maacah were by themselves in the open country.<sup>9</sup>When Joab saw that the battle was set against him both in front and in the rear, he chose some of the best men of Israel and arrayed them against the Syrians.<sup>10</sup>The rest of his men he put in the charge of Abishai his brother, and he arrayed them against the Ammonites.<sup>11</sup>And he said, "If the Syrians are too strong for me, then you shall help me, but if the Ammonites are too strong for you, then I will come and help you.<sup>12</sup>Be of good courage, and let us be courageous for our people, and for the cities of our God, and may the LORD do what seems good to him."<sup>13</sup>So Joab and the people who were with him drew near to battle against the Syrians, and they fled before him.<sup>14</sup>And when the Ammonites saw that the Syrians fled, they likewise fled before Abishai and entered the city. Then Joab returned from fighting against the Ammonites and came to Jerusalem.<sup>15</sup>But when the Syrians saw that they had been defeated by Israel, they gathered themselves together.<sup>16</sup>And Hadadezer sent and brought out the Syrians who were beyond the Euphrates. They came to Helam, with Shobach the commander of the army of Hadadezer at their head.<sup>17</sup>And when it was told David, he gathered all Israel together and crossed the Jordan and came to Helam. The Syrians arrayed themselves against David and fought with him.<sup>18</sup>And the Syrians fled before Israel, and David killed of the Syrians the men of 700 chariots, and 40,000 horsemen, and wounded Shobach the commander of their army, so that he died there.<sup>19</sup>And when all the kings who were servants of Hadadezer saw that they had been defeated by Israel, they made peace with Israel and became subject to them. So the Syrians were afraid to save the Ammonites anymore.
10.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 9 ended with Saul’s crippled grandson eating at the king’s table for Jonathan’s sake. Chapter 10 opens with the same word, hesed, loyal kindness, offered to the son of a dead Ammonite king, and ends with the war that keeps the army at Rabbah in chapter 11.

The message. Kindness from the king can be refused, and refusing it is ruinous. Hanun’s counsellors read David’s comfort as a trick, shame his envoys, and buy a war that Ammon and all its allies cannot win, because the LORD is doing what he promised: cutting off David’s enemies before him (7:9). In the middle of it Joab speaks a sentence worth keeping: fight for God’s people with everything you have, and leave the outcome with the LORD.

Why it was said. Israel needed to see the promise of chapter 7 at work in real wars (see the introduction). And the writer is setting the scene for chapter 11: he shows David at his best, fighting his own war in person, so that “But David remained at Jerusalem” (11:1) will land as the accusation it is.

How the chapter makes its case. David’s comforters are called spies and sent home half-shaven, and David spares them the walk home in shame (vv. 1–5). Ammon hires thirty-three thousand Syrians; Joab, caught between two armies, divides his force, pledges mutual help and commits the result to the LORD, and both enemies run (vv. 6–14). When Hadadezer brings up the Syrians from beyond the Euphrates, David himself crosses the Jordan and destroys them, and Ammon is left alone behind the walls of Rabbah (vv. 15–19).

Where it leads. The chapter leads to Christ by promise, by pattern and by the character of God. By promise, because these victories are God keeping his word to David, and the Son of David “must reign until he has put all his enemies under his feet” (1 Corinthians 15:25). By pattern, because a king’s kindness answered with contempt for his messengers is the story Jesus told of his Father’s vineyard (Mark 12:1–8). And by character, because the deepest suspicion of all, that God cannot be trusted, is answered by a deed: “God shows his love for us in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us” (Romans 5:8).

For us. Suspicion that is never switched off leaves us clever, alone and at war; ask, wait and watch before you treat a kindness as a trick, and above all do not treat God’s kindness so. And in your own battles, Joab’s pattern holds: do the work as well as it can be done, and then leave what seems good to God with God.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–5 — As His Father Dealt Loyally with Me
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Loyal kindness offered can be thrown back in the giver’s face. David remembers a kindness from Nahash and sends envoys to comfort his son Hanun on his father’s death (vv. 1–2). Hanun’s princes, with no evidence, call the comforters spies, and Hanun shaves off half of each man’s beard, cuts their robes off at the hips and sends them home to be seen (vv. 3–4). The insult is aimed at David. His first concern is for the men: he sends to meet them and lets them wait at Jericho until they can show their faces again (v. 5).
verseByVerse.theology: Two chapters running, David initiates hesed on account of somebody who is dead, and this time the dead man is a foreign king. When and how Nahash showed him kindness the text never says.
verseByVerse.examples: The insult is aimed past the envoys at the king who sent them. A leader insulted through his people is tempted to make their shame his own grievance and display it; David makes their shame his first care and hides it.

verseByVerse.quote: After this the king of the Ammonites died, and Hanun his son reigned in his place. And David said, "I will deal loyally with Hanun the son of Nahash, as his father dealt loyally with me." So David sent by his servants to console him concerning his father. And David's servants came into the land of the Ammonites. But the princes of the Ammonites said to Hanun their lord, "Do you think, because David has sent comforters to you, that he is honoring your father? Has not David sent his servants to you to search the city and to spy it out and to overthrow it?" So Hanun took David's servants and shaved off half the beard of each and cut off their garments in the middle, at their hips, and sent them away. When it was told David, he sent to meet them, for the men were greatly ashamed. And the king said, "Remain at Jericho until your beards have grown and then return."
verseByVerse.commentary:
David offers the son of a dead Ammonite king the loyal kindness he owed the father, and Hanun’s counsellors, on no evidence, turn it into a public insult. The chapter that ends in war begins with a visit of condolence.

I will deal loyally with Hanun. It is the word that drove chapter 9: hesed, loyalty that outlasts the reason for it. There David showed it to Jonathan’s son; here he extends it to a foreigner.

Who Nahash was. Nahash the Ammonite is no stranger to this story. He besieged Jabesh-gilead at the start of Saul’s reign and offered a treaty on condition that he gouge out every right eye in the place, and thus bring disgrace on all Israel (1 Samuel 11:2). That threat brought the Spirit on Saul and made him king in fact as well as in name. Ammon lay east of the Jordan on the edge of the desert, with its capital at Rabbah, modern Amman; the Ammonites traced their descent to Lot (Genesis 19:38), and Israel had been told not to take their land (Deuteronomy 2:19).

As his father dealt loyally with me. At some point this man showed David kindness. The text never says when or how; perhaps during the fugitive years, when Ammon would gladly have helped any enemy of Saul. It is better to leave it unexplained than to invent something. What we are told is that David remembered it and meant to repay it to the man’s son.

The princes of the Ammonites. The counsellors talk Hanun out of it in a sentence. A delegation of condolence has arrived, exactly as such delegations do; the princes have no information, only a theory that sounds shrewd and the flattering assumption that they are too clever to be taken in. Their fear was not absurd: David had spent two chapters subduing Moab, Zobah, Damascus and Edom, and a young, untested king might well be nervous. The trouble is what they do with the suspicion. They do not investigate it, watch the envoys or politely hasten their departure; they act on it as a certainty. It is the opposite of the love that “believes all things” (1 Corinthians 13:7). A believer who suspects a motive can ask, wait or watch, but should not punish a suspicion as if it were a proven fact.

The age of suspicion. Hanun’s princes would feel at home today. The philosopher Paul Ricoeur called Marx, Nietzsche and Freud the masters of suspicion, because each taught the modern mind to look beneath what people say for the interest it hides: class, power, desire. There is real wisdom in that, and Scripture got there first, since it knows the heart is deceitful (Jeremiah 17:9). But a suspicion that is never switched off becomes a kind of blindness. If every kindness is a move in a game, no kindness can ever reach you, and you are left alone, clever and unreachable, behind your own walls. That is where Hanun ends this chapter, and it costs him dearly.

The deepest suspicion. The oldest suspicion of all is the one the serpent planted, that God himself is holding out on us (see the note on Genesis 3:1–7). Arguments alone do not cure it. A deed does: “God shows his love for us in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us” (Romans 5:8). It is very hard to find a hidden angle in a man who dies for his enemies.

Shaved off half the beard. The insult is planned, not done in a moment of temper. A beard was a man’s dignity in that world, and shaving the whole of it was a sign of mourning that could be borne; half a beard makes every face a joke that cannot be explained. The robes cut off at the hips left the men exposed on a public road all the way home. In one respect it is worse than a beating: it is designed to be seen, carried home and displayed to the man who sent them. Hanun’s real target is not the envoys. He is using them to insult David in public.

Remain at Jericho. David’s response is the best thing in the chapter. He does not march the men into Jerusalem so that the nation can see the outrage and be roused by it, which is precisely what a king who wanted a war would do. He sends word to the first town on their road and tells them to stay there until they can face people again. For the men were greatly ashamed: that is the narrator’s whole explanation. The king’s first thought is their humiliation, and his first act is to spare them the rest of it. How a man treats people who have been made ridiculous in his service is a real test, and it is not usually recorded.

A greater King and our shame. David could only hide his servants until their shame grew out. The Son of David went further: he “endured the cross, despising the shame” (Hebrews 12:2), stripped and mocked on a public road outside the city, so that those who belong to him need never be put to shame (Romans 10:11).
verseByVerse.note: The law's rule about trimming the beard is in Leviticus 19:27; shaving the whole beard was a sign of mourning (Isa. 15:2; Jer. 48:37).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 6–14 — Let Us Be Courageous for Our People
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Faithful courage does all it can and leaves the outcome with God. Knowing they have made themselves a stench to David, the Ammonites hire thirty-three thousand Syrians, and Joab finds one army drawn up before the city gate and another behind him in the open country (vv. 6–9). He takes the best men against the Syrians, gives the rest to Abishai against the Ammonites, and agrees that whichever is losing will be helped (vv. 9–11). Then he speaks the chapter’s great sentence: be courageous for our people and the cities of our God, and may the LORD do what seems good to him (v. 12). The Syrians flee, the Ammonites run inside their walls, and Joab goes home (vv. 13–14).
verseByVerse.theology: Joab is a professional and this is professional work: a two-front trap answered by splitting the force, keeping the elite for the harder enemy, and arranging mutual reinforcement before either engages.
verseByVerse.examples: Joab's sentence can be borrowed as a prayer by anyone who knows how far their own life falls short of their words. A true prayer does not become false because the one praying it has not yet lived up to it.

verseByVerse.quote: When the Ammonites saw that they had become a stench to David, the Ammonites sent and hired the Syrians of Beth-rehob, and the Syrians of Zobah, 20,000 foot soldiers, and the king of Maacah with 1,000 men, and the men of Tob, 12,000 men. And when David heard of it, he sent Joab and all the host of the mighty men. And the Ammonites came out and drew up in battle array at the entrance of the gate, and the Syrians of Zobah and of Rehob and the men of Tob and Maacah were by themselves in the open country. When Joab saw that the battle was set against him both in front and in the rear, he chose some of the best men of Israel and arrayed them against the Syrians. The rest of his men he put in the charge of Abishai his brother, and he arrayed them against the Ammonites. And he said, "If the Syrians are too strong for me, then you shall help me, but if the Ammonites are too strong for you, then I will come and help you. Be of good courage, and let us be courageous for our people, and for the cities of our God, and may the LORD do what seems good to him." So Joab and the people who were with him drew near to battle against the Syrians, and they fled before him. And when the Ammonites saw that the Syrians fled, they likewise fled before Abishai and entered the city. Then Joab returned from fighting against the Ammonites and came to Jerusalem.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Caught between two armies, Joab divides his force, pledges mutual help and commits the outcome to the LORD, and the hired Syrians and the Ammonites both run. The best sentence in the chapter comes from the most troubling man in it.

A stench to David. Hanun knows what he has done, and buys an army: thirty-three thousand hired troops from four sources, an enormous outlay. The main supplier is the Syrians of Zobah, whose king Hadadezer David defeated two chapters ago (8:3–8), so this is the northern coalition getting a second attempt, paid for by Ammon.

Both in front and in the rear. The Ammonites are drawn up before their own city gate, and the hired Syrians are in the open country behind Joab: the classic trap, an enemy on each side able to close on him at a signal.

He chose some of the best men of Israel. He splits the army, which takes nerve, and the allocation shows that he knows his trade. He takes the picked men himself against the Syrians, the professionals, in the harder fight on open ground; Abishai gets the rest and the Ammonites, who are defending a gate and can retreat through it. Then, before either force engages, the agreement: whichever of us is losing, the other comes. It is a plan for the situation actually in front of them, and it removes from both commanders the temptation to look after their own front and let the other manage. Neither can win alone.

Be of good courage. Then comes Joab’s sentence, and it is a good deal better than Joab. It has two halves, and the balance between them is what makes it worth having. The first half is duty: let us be courageous for our people, and for the cities of our God. He names what they are fighting for, and it is not the king, plunder or their own reputations. It is God’s people and God’s land.

May the LORD do what seems good to him. The second half is submission. He does not promise victory or claim that the LORD will certainly give the enemy into their hand. He has done everything a competent general can do, and then he hands the result over without a guarantee. That is the right pattern for anybody’s work, and it is hard to keep: do the thing as well as it can be done, fight as if it depends on you, and then leave the outcome with God, knowing that what seems good to him may not be what seems good to you.

The sentence fulfilled. Only one man has ever lived that sentence without a crack in it. In Gethsemane the Son of David faced the hardest battle there has ever been, held nothing back, and prayed, “not my will, but yours, be done” (Luke 22:42). Joab’s words were true; in Christ they were also kept.

Who is speaking. They come from the mouth of a murderer. This is the man who called Abner aside in the gate of Hebron as though to speak privately and stabbed him in the stomach, in a city of refuge (a town where the law promised safety), in peacetime, and was cursed for it in public by his own king (3:27–29). He will kill Absalom against a direct royal order, kill Amasa the way he killed Abner, and die holding the horns of the altar (1 Kings 2:28–34).

Left unreconciled. The writer does not explain how a man can speak like this and behave like that, or suggest the words are hypocrisy; he puts the speech in the record and moves on. It is a fair warning about how little a true sentence proves about the person saying it, and equally a reminder that a true sentence is still true. Joab was right about the people, about the cities of God and about leaving the outcome with the LORD, and he was a murderer. Both are true of the same man.

They fled before him. The hired men break first, as hired men do, and the Ammonites go back inside their walls the moment they see it. Joab does not besiege the city: he has beaten the field army, and he goes home. The war is not over. Rabbah is still standing, and somebody will have to come back for it next spring.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 15–19 — Afraid to Save the Ammonites Anymore
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The LORD gives David victory over every enemy who rises against him, as he promised. Beaten once, the Syrians regroup, and Hadadezer brings up troops from beyond the Euphrates under his commander Shobach (vv. 15–16). This time David himself gathers all Israel, crosses the Jordan and destroys them at Helam; Shobach dies on the field (vv. 17–18). Hadadezer’s vassal kings make peace and become subject to Israel, and the Syrians will not help Ammon again (v. 19). Ammon is now alone, and Rabbah is still standing: the stage is set for the spring of chapter 11.
verseByVerse.theology: David goes out himself here, and wins. Remember it when the next chapter opens with him doing the opposite.
verseByVerse.examples: The vassal kings make peace, and one enemy is left behind its walls. Unfinished business often sets the scene for temptation: the next chapter's sin happens in the gap between a war begun and a war finished.

verseByVerse.quote: But when the Syrians saw that they had been defeated by Israel, they gathered themselves together. And Hadadezer sent and brought out the Syrians who were beyond the Euphrates. They came to Helam, with Shobach the commander of the army of Hadadezer at their head. And when it was told David, he gathered all Israel together and crossed the Jordan and came to Helam. The Syrians arrayed themselves against David and fought with him. And the Syrians fled before Israel, and David killed of the Syrians the men of 700 chariots, and 40,000 horsemen, and wounded Shobach the commander of their army, so that he died there. And when all the kings who were servants of Hadadezer saw that they had been defeated by Israel, they made peace with Israel and became subject to them. So the Syrians were afraid to save the Ammonites anymore.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When the whole Aramean world comes against Israel, David himself takes the field and destroys it, and Ammon is left without allies behind the walls of Rabbah. The LORD is cutting off David’s enemies before him, as he promised (7:9).

Beyond the Euphrates. This has stopped being about Ammon. Hadadezer calls up troops from the far side of the Euphrates, which means the whole Aramean world is being mobilised, and his commander-in-chief takes the field in person. What began as a diplomatic insult in a small kingdom has become a war for control of the north.

He gathered all Israel together. David goes himself. Mark that sentence, because a few verses later the writer will say the opposite of him in words that shape the rest of the book. Here, when the enemy is a serious army under a serious commander, the king gathers all Israel, crosses the river and stands in the line. The Syrian army is destroyed and its commander killed on the field.

The Syrians were afraid. The coalition collapses, and the last clause is the one that matters for what comes next: the Syrians were afraid to save the Ammonites anymore. The hired army is gone, the great power behind it has been beaten twice and has decided this is no longer its quarrel, and the men who shaved the beards of David’s envoys are sitting inside Rabbah with nobody coming. The city has not been taken.

Looking ahead to chapter 11. Campaigning stopped for the winter, and in the spring the army went back under Joab to besiege Rabbah. Then come the words on which the whole book turns: But David remained at Jerusalem (11:1). This chapter is why that sentence is an accusation. There is a war on, it is his war, it began when his own envoys were humiliated, he fought the northern half of it in person and won, and the army is now in the field finishing it without him.

The King whose enemies are made his footstool. These victories are God’s promise to David at work, and they look beyond him. The LORD says to David’s Lord, “Sit at my right hand, until I make your enemies your footstool” (Psalm 110:1), and the risen Christ “must reign until he has put all his enemies under his feet” (1 Corinthians 15:25). David won his battles and then, as the next chapter shows, lost the battle with himself. The Son of David wins both.

Why do the numbers differ from the parallel account? Here 2 Samuel has 700 chariots and 40,000 horsemen (v. 18), where Chronicles has 7,000 chariots and 40,000 foot soldiers (1 Chronicles 19:18). Numbers in Hebrew manuscripts were easily miscopied, since they were often written with letters or abbreviations, and parallel accounts sometimes count different things, such as chariots and charioteers, or a total and a part. Neither touches what the passage teaches. This commentary holds, with the historic confessions, that Scripture as God gave it is true in all it says; not every such difference can now be explained with certainty.

Uncertain wording. Helam (vv. 16–17) is mentioned only here, and its site is not known for certain. It lay east of the Jordan, probably in the north, towards the Aramean lands; the meaning of the passage does not depend on finding it.
verseByVerse.note: “The Euphrates” is “the River” in Hebrew (ESV note).

10.theology:
Two chapters running, faith kept with the dead (v. 2). Jonathan in chapter 9, Nahash here, and the same word both times: hesed, loyalty that outlasts the reason for it. This time the beneficiary is a foreign dynasty, and the man being repaid is best known in Scripture for a threatened atrocity (1 Sam. 11:2). The writer does not explain the debt, and inventing one is not a service; what he shows is that David paid it.

How suspicion works (v. 3). The princes' theory was not absurd: a young, untested king had some reason to be nervous of David. The fault is not in having the thought. It is in acting on it as a certainty, rather than watching, testing, or simply hastening the envoys home. Suspicion that is never checked feels like shrewdness from the inside, and it flatters the people who hold it: they are too clever to be taken in. That is why it so rarely gets checked, and why it can start a war over a condolence visit.

An insult meant to be seen, and a king who would not use it (vv. 4-5). Hanun shamed the envoys in order to insult David, and the insult was meant to be carried home and displayed. David could have displayed it himself to rouse the nation, which is what a king who wanted a war would do. His first thought was for the men instead, and the narrator gives the reason in a single clause: for the men were greatly ashamed. A king who will protect people made ridiculous in his service, when their humiliation would be useful to him, is showing the kind of rule this book has been looking for since Saul.

Joab's speech, and Joab (v. 12). Duty done for the people and the cities of God, and the result left with the LORD without a guarantee: that is the right pattern for anybody's work. It comes from a man who murdered Abner and will murder Amasa, and the writer never reconciles the two. A true sentence proves little about the person saying it, and it is still true. Both halves are worth remembering when good words come from someone whose life does not match them, including when that someone is ourselves.

Kindness taken for a threat. A king sent comfort to a grieving house and was suspected of spying, and his envoys were shamed and sent away. Jesus told a parable with the same pattern about himself: a king sends servants to call people to his son's feast, and they treat them shamefully (Matthew 22:2-6). The Son of David came with comfort to a grieving world and met the same suspicion, the council fearing that if they let him go on, the Romans would come and take away their place (John 11:48). And Joab's fine sentence about leaving the outcome with the LORD came from a man whose life contradicted it. The same prayer in Gethsemane, not as I will, but as you will (Matthew 26:39), came from the one man whose whole life matched his words; and because he kept it for us, our own half-kept prayers of surrender are not the end of us.

Why this chapter exists (vv. 17-19). When the enemy is a serious army, the king crosses the Jordan and stands in the line. By the end of the chapter the coalition is broken and Ammon is alone, but Rabbah has not been taken. That unfinished war is the setting of 11:1, and it is why but David remained at Jerusalem is an accusation rather than a detail: it is his war, begun over his own envoys, and the army is finishing it without him.
10.examples:
Then: A king's counsellors decided, on no evidence whatever, that a delegation of condolence was a reconnaissance party, and their king shamed the envoys and turned them out to walk home. The war it started ran for two campaigning seasons and cost the lives of an entire allied army and its commander.

Now: Two things. The princes of Ammon show what a plausible suspicion costs when it is acted on as a certainty. Their theory was not absurd; they simply never checked it, and by the time anybody could have, there was no way back. And Joab's line is the one to carry into ordinary work: do the thing as well as it can be done, for the people it is actually for, and then leave the result with God, on the honest understanding that what seems good to him may not be what seems good to you. We can do that because he is already our God, as he was Israel's, and his Spirit gives the courage the work needs.

keyVerse.quote: Be of good courage, and let us be courageous for our people, and for the cities of our God, and may the LORD do what seems good to him.
keyVerse.note: In the middle of a war that began with a refused kindness, this sentence holds together full human effort and full trust in God. It names what is worth fighting for, God’s people and God’s cities, and then hands the outcome to the LORD without demanding a guarantee. Its perfect form is in the mouth of the Son of David in Gethsemane: “not my will, but yours, be done” (Luke 22:42).

10.reflection:
David offered kindness to Hanun, and Hanun’s counsellors talked him into reading it as a trick (vv. 2–3). When have you treated someone’s kindness with suspicion, or had yours misread? How can we be wise about motives without becoming people no kindness can reach?

David would not let his envoys walk home in their shame, but told them to wait at Jericho until their beards had grown (v. 5). What does this teach about how to treat people who have been humiliated, especially in our service? How does Christ, who bore shame for us, change the way we handle shame?

Joab’s words in verse 12 join hard work with trust: “let us be courageous … and may the LORD do what seems good to him.” In which part of your life do you tend to neglect the first half, and in which the second?

These words came from a man who murdered Abner and would murder again. What does that teach about judging truth by the person who speaks it, and about the gap between saying true things and living them?

11.title: The Great Fall
11.text: <sup>1</sup>In the spring of the year, the time when kings go out to battle, David sent Joab, and his servants with him, and all Israel. And they ravaged the Ammonites and besieged Rabbah. But David remained at Jerusalem.<sup>2</sup>It happened, late one afternoon, when David arose from his couch and was walking on the roof of the king's house, that he saw from the roof a woman bathing; and the woman was very beautiful.<sup>3</sup>And David sent and inquired about the woman. And one said, "Is not this Bathsheba, the daughter of Eliam, the wife of Uriah the Hittite?"<sup>4</sup>So David sent messengers and took her, and she came to him, and he lay with her. (Now she had been purifying herself from her uncleanness.) Then she returned to her house.<sup>5</sup>And the woman conceived, and she sent and told David, "I am pregnant."<sup>6</sup>So David sent word to Joab, "Send me Uriah the Hittite." And Joab sent Uriah to David.<sup>7</sup>When Uriah came to him, David asked how Joab was doing and how the people were doing and how the war was going.<sup>8</sup>Then David said to Uriah, "Go down to your house and wash your feet." And Uriah went out of the king's house, and there followed him a present from the king.<sup>9</sup>But Uriah slept at the door of the king's house with all the servants of his lord, and did not go down to his house.<sup>10</sup>When they told David, "Uriah did not go down to his house," David said to Uriah, "Have you not come from a journey? Why did you not go down to your house?"<sup>11</sup>Uriah said to David, "The ark and Israel and Judah dwell in booths, and my lord Joab and the servants of my lord are camping in the open field. Shall I then go to my house, to eat and to drink and to lie with my wife? As you live, and as your soul lives, I will not do this thing."<sup>12</sup>Then David said to Uriah, "Remain here today also, and tomorrow I will send you back." So Uriah remained in Jerusalem that day and the next.<sup>13</sup>And David invited him, and he ate in his presence and drank, so that he made him drunk. And in the evening he went out to lie on his couch with the servants of his lord, but he did not go down to his house.<sup>14</sup>In the morning David wrote a letter to Joab and sent it by the hand of Uriah.<sup>15</sup>In the letter he wrote, "Set Uriah in the forefront of the hardest fighting, and then draw back from him, that he may be struck down, and die."<sup>16</sup>And as Joab was besieging the city, he assigned Uriah to the place where he knew there were valiant men.<sup>17</sup>And the men of the city came out and fought with Joab, and some of the servants of David among the people fell. Uriah the Hittite also died.<sup>18</sup>Then Joab sent and told David all the news about the fighting.<sup>19</sup>And he instructed the messenger, "When you have finished telling all the news about the fighting to the king,<sup>20</sup>then, if the king's anger rises, and if he says to you, 'Why did you go so near the city to fight? Did you not know that they would shoot from the wall?<sup>21</sup>Who killed Abimelech the son of Jerubbesheth? Did not a woman cast an upper millstone on him from the wall, so that he died at Thebez? Why did you go so near the wall?' then you shall say, 'Your servant Uriah the Hittite is dead also.'"<sup>22</sup>So the messenger went and came and told David all that Joab had sent him to tell.<sup>23</sup>The messenger said to David, "The men gained an advantage over us and came out against us in the field, but we drove them back to the entrance of the gate.<sup>24</sup>Then the archers shot at your servants from the wall. Some of the king's servants are dead, and your servant Uriah the Hittite is dead also."<sup>25</sup>David said to the messenger, "Thus shall you say to Joab, 'Do not let this matter displease you, for the sword devours now one and now another. Strengthen your attack against the city and overthrow it.' And encourage him."<sup>26</sup>When the wife of Uriah heard that Uriah her husband was dead, she lamented over her husband.<sup>27</sup>And when the mourning was over, David sent and brought her to his house, and she became his wife and bore him a son. But the thing that David had done displeased the LORD.
11.overview:
Where we are. The Ammonite war of chapter 10 enters its second spring, and the army goes back to besiege Rabbah. David has been promised a house for ever (chapter 7) and given victory on every side (chapters 8 and 10). He is at the height of God’s blessing, and he stays at home.

The message. The best of Israel’s kings, with everything God could give him, takes the one thing that was not his, and kills to hide it. Sin grows from idleness to adultery, to deceit, to murder, every step managed so that nobody sees. Nobody in Jerusalem does; the LORD does, and calls it evil (v. 27).

Why it was said. Royal records praised their kings; Israel’s history sets David’s worst deed at the centre of his reign, to teach that the promise rested on God’s faithfulness, and that David could not be the king it was looking for (see the introduction).

How the chapter makes its case. David sees a woman bathing, is told she is Uriah’s wife, and sends for her anyway; she conceives (vv. 1–5). He calls Uriah home to make the child seem his, but the loyal Hittite will not sleep in his own house while the ark and the army are in the field, even when drunk (vv. 6–13). So Uriah carries his own death warrant back to Joab, who sets him where the fighting is hardest, and other men die with him (vv. 14–21). David shrugs, marries the widow, and the narrator, silent for twenty-six verses, gives the LORD’s verdict in one clause (vv. 22–27).

Where it leads. The chapter leads to Christ chiefly by the need it exposes. The king God had promised to bless is the man who sacrifices a faithful servant to save himself, and Israel is left needing a king who will not do this. Jesus is that King, and he does the very opposite: where David sent the righteous man to die to cover his own sin, “Christ also suffered once for sins, the righteous for the unrighteous, that he might bring us to God” (1 Peter 3:18). Where David took, the Son “did not count equality with God a thing to be grasped” (Philippians 2:6). And grace runs even through this wreckage: Matthew writes it into the family tree of the Messiah, “David was the father of Solomon by the wife of Uriah” (Matthew 1:6).

For us. No one is beyond this fall, least of all the person sure he is; it began with an idle afternoon. Stop covering your sin, and come to the God who covers it by the blood of Christ: “Blessed is the one whose transgression is forgiven, whose sin is covered” (Psalm 32:1).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–5 — But David Remained at Jerusalem
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The fall begins not with a crisis but with a king at ease where he should not have been. In the spring the army besieges Rabbah, but David stays in Jerusalem (v. 1). From his roof he sees a woman bathing, and when he asks about her he is told her name, her father’s name and her husband’s name, every one of them a reason to stop (vv. 2–3). He sends, takes and lies with her: the verbs are all his, and the power is all on one side (v. 4). Then she sends him three words that end the secret: “I am pregnant” (v. 5).
verseByVerse.theology: Sin rarely needs a plan to begin; it needs an empty afternoon and a heart that has stopped asking. The man who enquired of the LORD before his battles (5:19, 23) is not recorded asking God anything in this chapter.
verseByVerse.examples: Notice how easily ordinary authority does the work. David does not argue or persuade; he sends, and people go. Anyone with power over others, in a home, a workplace or a church, should notice how little effort it takes to make other people serve our wishes, and how rarely anyone says no.

verseByVerse.quote: In the spring of the year, the time when kings go out to battle, David sent Joab, and his servants with him, and all Israel. And they ravaged the Ammonites and besieged Rabbah. But David remained at Jerusalem. It happened, late one afternoon, when David arose from his couch and was walking on the roof of the king's house, that he saw from the roof a woman bathing; and the woman was very beautiful. And David sent and inquired about the woman. And one said, "Is not this Bathsheba, the daughter of Eliam, the wife of Uriah the Hittite?" So David sent messengers and took her, and she came to him, and he lay with her. (Now she had been purifying herself from her uncleanness.) Then she returned to her house. And the woman conceived, and she sent and told David, "I am pregnant."
verseByVerse.commentary:
With the army at war, David stays at home, sees a woman bathing, is told exactly who she is, and takes her anyway. The turning point is not the glance from the roof but the moment after he hears her name and her husband’s name, when he could still have stopped.

The time when kings go out to battle. Campaigning stopped over the winter, when the roads were mud and there was nothing in the fields to live on; in the spring armies moved. The phrase is not sarcasm but a calendar note, which becomes an accusation because of what follows.

His own war. This is not some optional foreign adventure. It is the second season of the Ammonite war, which began when Hanun shamed David’s own envoys (10:1–5). Rabbah is unfinished business, and the coalition propping up the Ammonites has already quit. David fought the hard half of that war in person: when the Syrians brought up an army from beyond the Euphrates, “he gathered all Israel together and crossed the Jordan” (10:17). He knows how to do this and has just done it.

But David remained at Jerusalem. The whole army is in the field; Uriah is in the field; Joab is in the field. The man who has asked God before every battle since he came out of a cave is at home with nothing to do. Nothing in the verse says that a king may never delegate; kings did. What the verse does is put him in the one place where the next verse can happen, at the one time of year when everyone is away, with no responsibility on him for the first time in his adult life.

Late one afternoon. He is perhaps around fifty, and he has won everything. The writer, who has spent chapters showing us a man who asks God about everything, now shows us a man with an afternoon free. He gets up from a rest and walks on his roof.

He saw from the roof a woman bathing. The palace was the highest building in a small city on a steep ridge, and the houses below were packed close; from that roof you could see into many courtyards. Nothing in the text suggests that she was doing anything improper. The bathing was most likely the purification the law required after her monthly period, a detail the writer supplies in verse 4 to show that the child cannot be her husband’s. The seeing is not the sin, and it should be said plainly, because much preaching has made this chapter about a glance. What happens next is the sin.

David sent and inquired about the woman. The answer he gets is not just a name but a warning, put as a question, is not this…?, which is how a servant tells a king something he does not want to say. Every part of it should have stopped him. She has a name, Bathsheba: she is a person, and people in this city know her. She is the daughter of Eliam, and an Eliam is one of the thirty, David’s own elite, named as the son of Ahithophel the Gilonite (23:34). If he is the same man, as many think, Bathsheba was the granddaughter of David’s greatest counsellor, which would explain why, years later, Ahithophel goes over to Absalom without hesitation (15:12, 31) and gives such ferocious advice. And she is the wife of Uriah the Hittite, whose name is the last on that same list of the king’s mighty men (23:39), the writer’s own quiet memorial. At this moment he is sleeping in a field outside Rabbah on David’s orders.

He knew. David asked a question and was told, in one sentence, that the woman was somebody’s daughter and somebody’s wife, and both men were his. He went ahead. That is where the chapter turns: not on the roof, but in the half minute after the servant answered, when he had every fact he needed and could still have stopped. Knowing the facts did not stop him; temptation is seldom overcome by information alone.

David sent messengers and took her. The verbs are all David’s: he sent, he took, he lay. She came and she returned, the only two things said of her, and both are responses to being summoned. Took has appeared before, in a sentence the narrator laid down without comment: “David took more concubines and wives from Jerusalem” (5:13). Behind it stands the law for Israel’s king: “he shall not acquire many wives for himself, lest his heart turn away” (Deuteronomy 17:17). A man who has spent twenty years taking wives whenever he wanted them has practised something, and here it is.

The King who did not grasp. Set beside this the King David was meant to foreshadow. David had everything and took the one thing that was not his. The Son of David had everything, and “did not count equality with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself” (Philippians 2:6–7). Where David sent for another man’s wife, Christ gave himself for a bride who had nothing to give him (Ephesians 5:25).

Bathsheba’s part. Commentators have gone both ways for centuries, and the text supports neither confidently. Some have made her a temptress who bathed where she could be seen, which the passage does not support at all: she is washing in her own courtyard, and the man looking is on the roof of the tallest building in the city. Others have written her a full inner life of terror or of complicity. The narrator never tells us her mind, and filling the silence in either direction is invention. What the text does establish is the situation: the wife of a serving soldier, in a small city, summoned by the king of Israel through his messengers to the palace. There is no version of that scene in which she is a free party to a negotiation. Whatever she felt, the power in that room was entirely on one side, and Scripture’s own verdict, given by Nathan in the next chapter, places the guilt on one person and pictures her as a lamb that was taken.

I am pregnant. Two words in Hebrew, and they end the private phase. She sends, the one action she starts in the chapter, and the message is unanswerable. The note in verse 4 has already told the reader what David is about to work out: the child cannot be Uriah’s, because Uriah has been at Rabbah, and the whole city will be able to count. Everything from here is a cover-up, and it gets worse at every step.

Was this rape or adultery? The king sent for her, and a subject could hardly refuse a king. The text puts the whole guilt on David (12:9), and Nathan’s parable makes her the lamb, not the thief. It was an abuse of power, whatever she felt she could do, and Scripture never blames Bathsheba.

What if something like this has happened to you? If you have been used by someone with power over you, at work, in a church or in a family, the first thing this chapter says is that the guilt was his. You are the lamb in Nathan’s story, not the thief. The second is in verse 27: everyone saw what the powerful man arranged for them to see, and the LORD saw what was actually done, and called it evil. Nothing done to you was hidden from him. If you are still in danger, seek safety at once and tell someone who can act, including the police where a crime has been committed; no leader’s position puts him beyond the law or beyond God’s judgment. And God did not leave Bathsheba where this chapter leaves her. She became the mother of a king, and Matthew names her in the line of Jesus (Matthew 1:6): the Saviour came through the wound, not around it.

Textual note. In verse 1 the written Hebrew has messengers, a word one letter away from kings; the scribes’ own margin, the Greek Old Testament and Chronicles (1 Chronicles 20:1) read kings, as the ESV does.
verseByVerse.note: Rabbah, the Ammonite capital, is modern Amman in Jordan.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 6–13 — Shall I Then Go to My House?
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A foreign soldier’s integrity shows up the king of Israel. David recalls Uriah from the siege, asks politely about the war and sends him home with a gift, so that the child will pass as his (vv. 6–8). Uriah sleeps at the palace door instead (v. 9). Asked why, he answers that while the ark, the army and his commander are in the field, he will not go home to eat, drink and lie with his wife, and he swears it by the king’s own life (vv. 10–11). David keeps him another day and makes him drunk, but even drunk Uriah will not go down to his house (vv. 12–13).
verseByVerse.theology: A Hittite mercenary will not sleep under his own roof while the ark of God is in a field shelter. The king of Israel, who danced that ark into the city, is sleeping in a palace and has just taken this man's wife.
verseByVerse.examples: Some people are no different when their guard is down. Uriah drunk is more faithful than David sober. That is the integrity worth praying for: not a performance kept up while someone is watching, but a character that holds when no one is checking.

verseByVerse.quote: So David sent word to Joab, "Send me Uriah the Hittite." And Joab sent Uriah to David. When Uriah came to him, David asked how Joab was doing and how the people were doing and how the war was going. Then David said to Uriah, "Go down to your house and wash your feet." And Uriah went out of the king's house, and there followed him a present from the king. But Uriah slept at the door of the king's house with all the servants of his lord, and did not go down to his house. When they told David, "Uriah did not go down to his house," David said to Uriah, "Have you not come from a journey? Why did you not go down to your house?" Uriah said to David, "The ark and Israel and Judah dwell in booths, and my lord Joab and the servants of my lord are camping in the open field. Shall I then go to my house, to eat and to drink and to lie with my wife? As you live, and as your soul lives, I will not do this thing." Then David said to Uriah, "Remain here today also, and tomorrow I will send you back." So Uriah remained in Jerusalem that day and the next. And David invited him, and he ate in his presence and drank, so that he made him drunk. And in the evening he went out to lie on his couch with the servants of his lord, but he did not go down to his house.
verseByVerse.commentary:
David brings Uriah home to make the child seem his, and the loyal Hittite, who will not take a comfort his comrades and the ark cannot have, defeats every scheme without knowing it. The foreigner’s integrity is the mirror in which the king’s corruption shows.

Send me Uriah the Hittite. The first plan is the obvious one, and if it had worked nobody would ever have known. Bring the husband home for a night; the dates will be close enough, the child will be taken as his, and the whole thing disappears. To do it David has to pull a named officer out of an active siege, which Joab will certainly have noticed.

How the war was going. Then the small talk (v. 7), and it is repulsive. How is Joab, how are the men, how is the war: the right questions for a king to ask a soldier just in from the front, and every one a delay while the man waits to be told why he has been summoned. David asks after the welfare of the army while planning to deceive one of its officers.

Go down to your house and wash your feet. An ordinary phrase for going home and resting (compare washing feet after a journey), with a plain enough implication. Then a present is sent after him, most likely food from the palace for a homecoming meal. The king is setting up the evening. But Uriah sleeps on the doorstep with the palace servants, and the plan has failed; David does not yet know why, and neither does the reader, until Uriah is asked.

The ark and Israel and Judah dwell in booths. Uriah’s answer (v. 11) is the moral centre of the chapter, and it is spoken by a foreigner. He begins with the ark, not the army or his own comfort: while the ark of God is in a shelter, he will not sleep under his own roof. That is the ark David danced into this city in a linen ephod (6:14); the Hittite is more careful of it than the man who brought it home. Then his commander and his comrades: my lord Joab and the servants of my lord are camping in the open field. He will not take a comfort they cannot have.

As you live, and as your soul lives. He swears it by the life of the king standing in front of him trying to arrange exactly that, which is the cruellest irony in the passage.

Uriah and David. The writer has set the two men side by side and means it to be seen. Uriah is a Hittite, from a people Israel was told to drive out, serving in Israel’s army under a name usually taken to mean “the LORD is my light”; he will not sleep in his own bed because the ark of God is in a tent. David is the anointed king of Israel, who danced before the ark; he has slept in a palace, taken this man’s wife, and is now trying to get him home so that the dates will fit. Neither knows what the other knows. Uriah is being honourable in front of a king who is counting days, and every honourable thing he says makes his own death more certain.

The King who shares the field. A good king belongs with his men in the field, and David has left them there. Uriah’s refusal to take a comfort his comrades lacked is a small picture of a better King, who did not stay in the palace of heaven while his people suffered, but came and shared our hardship to the end, “made like his brothers in every respect” (Hebrews 2:17).

An open question. Did Uriah suspect? Some have thought so: the palace was small, servants talk, and his refusal is very firm. It is possible, but the text gives no answer. What it gives is a soldier’s principle stated and kept under pressure, and that is enough.

He made him drunk. Read it as what it is: the king of Israel at table with a loyal officer, filling his cup all evening to lower his guard enough to send him home to a wife the king has already slept with.
