And it does not work. Drunk, at the end of a long evening, Uriah goes out and lies down with the servants. The wine has loosened him, but it has not touched his loyalty. David has now tried decency, hospitality and alcohol, and the man will not be moved. There is one thing left, and he does it in the morning.

Uncertain wording. It is not certain where the ark was. Uriah may mean that it had gone out with the army to Rabbah, as it sometimes went to war (1 Samuel 4:3–4), or the tent David pitched for it in Jerusalem (6:17). Some also take the word for booths as the place name Succoth, a town east of the Jordan that could have served as the army’s base. Either way his point is the same: while God’s ark and God’s people are without proper shelter, he will not take his ease.
verseByVerse.note: The Hittites were counted among the peoples of Canaan (Gen. 10:15; 23:3). Uriah was not the only one in David's service: Ahimelech the Hittite was with him in the wilderness (1 Sam. 26:6).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 14–21 — Set Uriah in the Forefront
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: When the cover-up fails, David turns to murder, and drags others into it. He writes Joab a letter ordering Uriah’s death and sends it by Uriah’s own hand, trusting the man’s loyalty not to open it (vv. 14–15). Joab carries it out his own way, assigning Uriah where the defenders are strongest, so that other soldiers die with him and the death looks like the ordinary cost of a siege (vv. 16–17). Then he coaches the messenger: if the king is angry about the losses, say that Uriah is dead too (vv. 18–21). From this morning Joab holds David’s secret.
verseByVerse.theology: Sin that is hidden needs more sin to keep it hidden. In one morning David moves from covering a pregnancy to disposing of a witness, and the only thing that witness has done is behave well.
verseByVerse.examples: Count the people the cover-up has now drawn in: the servant who answered, the messengers, Bathsheba, Uriah, Joab, the soldiers at the wall and the runner with the report. One man's secret has become the business of an army.

verseByVerse.quote: In the morning David wrote a letter to Joab and sent it by the hand of Uriah. In the letter he wrote, "Set Uriah in the forefront of the hardest fighting, and then draw back from him, that he may be struck down, and die."
verseByVerse.commentary:
When the cover-up fails, David writes the order for Uriah’s death and makes Uriah carry it. The writer records no pause between the failed scheme and the murder.

In the morning. The letter is written the morning after Uriah, even when drunk, would not go down to his house (v. 13). Two attempts to hide the pregnancy have failed because of one man’s integrity.

Sent it by the hand of Uriah. He writes the order for the man’s death in his own hand and gives it to the man to carry. Uriah walks all the way back to Rabbah carrying his own execution and delivers it to his commanding officer himself. He is chosen as courier for the same reason he is being killed: he is the one man in the kingdom certain not to open it. David is using the man’s loyalty to kill him.

Draw back from him. The instruction is precise, and it is murder of a kind that leaves no body to explain and no blood on anyone’s hands. Note what David is willing to spend. A deliberate withdrawal from a man in contact with the enemy would be seen by every soldier in the line, and would need Joab to give an order that would be remembered. David does not care. Nor does he seem to consider that it will cost other men their lives, which it does.

verseByVerse.quote: And as Joab was besieging the city, he assigned Uriah to the place where he knew there were valiant men. And the men of the city came out and fought with Joab, and some of the servants of David among the people fell. Uriah the Hittite also died.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Joab carries out the order his own way, sending an assault against the strongest part of the wall, so that Uriah dies among other men and the murder looks like the ordinary cost of a siege.

As Joab was besieging the city. Rabbah, the Ammonite capital (modern Amman), stood on a strong hill, and the siege had gone on since the spring (v. 1). An attack close under the wall was the most dangerous work in such a war, because the defenders could shoot and throw down on the men below, which is exactly the objection Joab expects the king to raise (v. 20).

Where he knew there were valiant men. Joab does not stage a withdrawal. He puts Uriah where he knows the defenders are strongest and sends the whole assault in against the wall. He is a professional, and he can see what David in Jerusalem has not thought about: a visible abandonment of one named officer would be talked about in the army for twenty years and would eventually reach somebody who asked why. A costly assault on a fortified wall is a normal military disaster, and one dead officer in a casualty list is invisible. Joab’s method is safer, and it kills more people.

Some of the servants of David among the people fell. Other men die. The writer does not say how many or name them. Their families were told they fell in an assault on Rabbah, and that was true, and it was not the reason. Then, as though an afterthought: Uriah the Hittite also died, the only part of the operation David cared about.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Joab sent and told David all the news about the fighting. And he instructed the messenger, "When you have finished telling all the news about the fighting to the king, then, if the king's anger rises, and if he says to you, 'Why did you go so near the city to fight? Did you not know that they would shoot from the wall? Who killed Abimelech the son of Jerubbesheth? Did not a woman cast an upper millstone on him from the wall, so that he died at Thebez? Why did you go so near the wall?' then you shall say, 'Your servant Uriah the Hittite is dead also.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Joab coaches the messenger to end his report with Uriah’s name, knowing that one name will silence the king’s anger, and from this day he holds David’s secret.

He instructed the messenger. This is the most chilling piece of stage management in the book, and it is entirely Joab’s. He briefs the messenger on the king’s likely reaction, anticipates the exact rebuke, including the example David will reach for, and gives him the sentence that will make the anger stop.

Who killed Abimelech the son of Jerubbesheth? Jerubbesheth is Jerubbaal, the other name of Gideon (Judges 7:1); scribes often replaced baal with bosheth, “shame”, as in the name Ish-bosheth. Abimelech, Gideon’s son, went up to the door of the tower at Thebez to burn it, and a woman dropped an upper millstone on his head (Judges 9:50–54). Every officer knew the story as the standard lesson about going too near a wall. Some have seen a grim irony in the choice: a man brought down at a wall because of a woman.

Your servant Uriah the Hittite is dead also. Joab has understood the letter completely. He knows that the casualties mean nothing to the king and that one name will settle everything, and he arranges for a junior messenger to say it aloud in the throne room without knowing what he is saying.

What Joab now holds. In the same breath he establishes something. He has the letter. He has done the thing. And he has shown himself that the king will accept a report of needless dead soldiers as long as the right man is among them. From this morning, Joab owns David. Everything he does for the rest of the reign rests on it. He kills Absalom against a direct, public royal order and suffers nothing; he murders Amasa in the road as he murdered Abner and suffers nothing; he speaks to the king with a contempt no other subject would survive. And David, dying, has to ask Solomon to do what he never could (1 Kings 2:5–6). A man who has helped you do something you cannot admit is not your servant afterwards.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 22–27 — The Sword Devours Now One and Now Another
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The cover-up succeeds before every eye but one. The messenger delivers his report, Uriah’s name included (vv. 22–24), and David answers with a proverb about the chances of war, telling Joab not to be troubled by a death he himself arranged (v. 25). Bathsheba mourns her husband; when the mourning is over David brings her into his house and she bears him a son (vv. 26–27). From the outside it all looks decent. Then the narrator, who has passed no judgment for twenty-six verses, gives the LORD’s: the thing David had done was evil in his sight (v. 27).
verseByVerse.theology: David uses a proverb about the chances of war to describe a death he arranged in writing. Familiar moral language can be put to work to quiet a conscience, and the more familiar the saying, the better it works.
verseByVerse.examples: The chapter's last clause is a comfort as well as a warning: nothing done in secret escapes the eyes of the LORD, and that includes every wrong done to people like Uriah and Bathsheba that no court ever heard.

verseByVerse.quote: So the messenger went and came and told David all that Joab had sent him to tell. The messenger said to David, "The men gained an advantage over us and came out against us in the field, but we drove them back to the entrance of the gate. Then the archers shot at your servants from the wall. Some of the king's servants are dead, and your servant Uriah the Hittite is dead also." David said to the messenger, "Thus shall you say to Joab, 'Do not let this matter displease you, for the sword devours now one and now another. Strengthen your attack against the city and overthrow it.' And encourage him." When the wife of Uriah heard that Uriah her husband was dead, she lamented over her husband. And when the mourning was over, David sent and brought her to his house, and she became his wife and bore him a son. But the thing that David had done displeased the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
David brushes off the deaths with a proverb, marries the widow, and seems to have closed the matter, but the LORD saw what he had done and judged it evil. The narrator’s silence ends in one clause, and it is God’s verdict.

The sword devours now one and now another. The messenger delivers the whole report at once and never finds out whether the king would have been angry. Then comes the coldest sentence David ever speaks. On any other day it would be a decent thing for a commander to say to a commander who has taken losses: war is like that; do not blame yourself. From this man, on this morning, it is obscene. He knows exactly whom the sword devoured and why, because he wrote the instruction. He is telling the executioner not to feel bad about the execution, using a proverb about the chances of war for a death he arranged in writing. And the last words of the message: encourage him.

An echo of Abner. The phrase will come back. Abner once shouted across a valley at this same Joab, “Shall the sword devour forever? Do you not know that the end will be bitter?” (2:26). The sword does not stop, it is bitter in the end, and Nathan is about to tell David that it will never leave his house.

The wife of Uriah. She is not named here. The writer called her Bathsheba once, in the servant’s warning (v. 3); here she is the wife of Uriah, and Matthew does the same at the head of the Gospels: “David was the father of Solomon by the wife of Uriah” (Matthew 1:6). In both places it is deliberate. She is identified by the man who was killed, in the sentence that records her mourning him. That is all we are told of what this did to her: a time of mourning for a husband who would not come home to her while the ark was in a field.

David sent and brought her to his house. Sent is the verb that has driven the whole chapter: he sent Joab, sent to ask about the woman, sent for her, sent for Uriah, sent the letter, and sends now. From the outside it is a decent act. A king marries the widow of an officer killed at the siege, quickly, before anybody counts months. The child arrives inside a marriage, the dates are covered, and the business is closed.

But the thing that David had done displeased the LORD. Twenty-six verses, and the narrator has not said a word of judgment. He has reported a walk on a roof, a question, a summons, a pregnancy, a failed plan, a letter, a battle, a casualty list, a piece of coaching, a shrug and a wedding, without comment, letting the reader watch it happen and feel the sickness of it. Then he gives the verdict in one clause and stops. The Hebrew is stronger than the English: the thing was evil in the eyes of the LORD.

In the eyes of the LORD. Everything in the chapter has been about eyes. David saw a woman from a roof, and then arranged matters so that nobody else would see what had happened. The dates were made to look right, the marriage decent, the death like the ordinary toll of a siege. It worked: every person in Jerusalem who mattered saw exactly what David wanted them to see. One did not.

A year of silence. There is no punishment in this verse, no lightning, no visible consequence. A year of silence is coming, while the child is born, the household settles and the siege goes on, and Psalm 32 is probably David’s own record of that year from the inside: “when I kept silent, my bones wasted away through my groaning all day long. For day and night your hand was heavy upon me” (Psalm 32:3–4).

The exhausting work of being seen. David spent this chapter managing appearances, and few chapters in Scripture feel more modern. We curate a self for others to look at, edit out what does not fit, and keep the back rooms out of sight. It is tiring, because an image must be kept up every day, and lonely, because no one can love the person behind it if no one is allowed to see him. David’s cover-up worked on everyone in Jerusalem, and it was slowly crushing him. Notice the word he later chose for his release: “Blessed is the one whose transgression is forgiven, whose sin is covered” (Psalm 32:1). He had tried to cover it himself, with a marriage, a letter and a casualty list, and it would not stay covered. What finally covered it was God, once David stopped covering: “I acknowledged my sin to you, and I did not cover my iniquity” (Psalm 32:5). The gospel offers what image management never can: to be seen completely by the only eyes that finally matter, and covered by him, in Christ, so that there is nothing left to hide.

How could the man after God’s own heart do this? That phrase (1 Samuel 13:14) describes God’s choice of him, not a promise that he would never fall, and this chapter is Scripture’s own refusal to make a saint out of a sinner. What marks David out is not that he did not sin but what he does when he is confronted, and the mercy he finds (12:13; Psalm 51).

Why Israel was told this. Royal records in the ancient world praised their kings; this one sets the worst thing David did in the middle of his reign, soon after God promised him a house for ever (7:16). The promise rested on God’s faithfulness, not David’s, and David himself could not be the king it was looking for. The later prophets who long for a righteous son of David (Isaiah 11:1–5; Jeremiah 23:5) are longing for one who would never do what is done in this chapter, and who would bear the sins of those who have. And then a man walks into the room with a story about a lamb.

11.theology:
Why verse 1 is an accusation. Kings delegated; but this is his own unfinished war, and staying home leaves him idle at the one season when everyone else is away.

The point of no return is verse 3, not verse 4. A name, a father who is one of the thirty (23:34), and a husband who is another (23:39): David was told all of it and went ahead. Knowing the facts did not stop him; temptation is seldom overcome by information alone.

What can and cannot be said about Bathsheba. The narrator never reports her mind, and filling that silence in either direction is invention. What the text establishes is the situation, a serving soldier's wife summoned by the king, and Scripture's own verdict comes next chapter, in a parable where the lamb is not blamed.

A foreigner at the moral centre (v. 11). The Hittite is more careful of the ark than the king who danced it into the city, and every honourable sentence he speaks makes his death more certain.

An accomplice is a master (vv. 14-21). The cover-up needed Joab, and Joab now holds the letter. A man who has helped you do what you cannot admit is not your servant afterwards, and the rest of David's reign shows it.

A soldier's life spent to save a king. Uriah carries the letter, takes the front of the line, and dies so that David's sin can stay hidden. The gospel is this chapter turned inside out. Jesus said the rulers of the nations lord it over them, but the Son of Man came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many (Mark 10:45). The Son of David did not take what belonged to another; he gave up what was his own. He did not send the innocent to die for a guilty king; he is the innocent King who died for guilty subjects, David among them. And the sin this chapter hides so carefully he bore in the open, before the whole city, on a hill outside its walls.

One clause, at the very end (v. 27). The whole chapter has been about eyes: David saw a woman from a roof, and then arranged matters so that nobody would see what followed. Everyone in Jerusalem saw what he meant them to see. The LORD saw what was done, and there is no lightning in the verse, only a year of silence and then a man who walks in with a story about a lamb.
11.examples:
Then: A king wrote out the order for a man's death in his own hand and gave it to that man to carry to the general who would carry it out, choosing him as the courier for the same reason he was killing him: he was the one officer in the kingdom certain not to open it.

Now: Two things. The first is where the chapter actually turns: not the roof but verse 3, the half minute after the servant answered, when David had every fact he needed and sent anyway. Almost nobody walks into a disaster without being told first; the warning comes and is overruled, and after that one step leads to the next. The second is Joab. The cover-up required an accomplice, and from the moment he had one, David was never free of him again. And where we have already gone past the warning, the next chapter shows the way back: not a better cover, but confession, and a mercy that does not wait for us to have stopped in time.

keyVerse.quote: But the thing that David had done displeased the LORD.
keyVerse.note: For twenty-six verses the narrator reports without comment while David arranges what everyone will see, and then in one clause he gives the only verdict that matters. Everything in the chapter is about eyes, and the LORD’s eyes saw what was done. That is both the terror of the chapter and its hope, for the God who sees is the God who will send Nathan, and through David’s greater Son will cover the sin David could not hide.

11.reflection:
The chapter begins, “But David remained at Jerusalem” (v. 1). How can ease, success or idleness make us more open to temptation than hardship does? Where are you most exposed?

David was told plainly who Bathsheba was, and went ahead (vv. 3–4). Why is knowing the facts so rarely enough to stop us? What does this show about the heart, and about our need for more than information?

Uriah, a foreigner, would not take a comfort his comrades could not have, and the king plotted to break his integrity (vv. 11–13). What does Uriah’s faithfulness expose in David, and in us? How is Christ the King who shares his people’s hardship instead of using them?

David managed appearances so well that no one in Jerusalem saw the truth, but “the thing that David had done displeased the LORD” (v. 27). Where are you tempted to manage how things look rather than deal with what is true? What does Psalm 32 promise to the one who stops covering his sin?

12.title: You Are the Man
12.text: <sup>1</sup>And the LORD sent Nathan to David. He came to him and said to him, "There were two men in a certain city, the one rich and the other poor.<sup>2</sup>The rich man had very many flocks and herds,<sup>3</sup>but the poor man had nothing but one little ewe lamb, which he had bought. And he brought it up, and it grew up with him and with his children. It used to eat of his morsel and drink from his cup and lie in his arms, and it was like a daughter to him.<sup>4</sup>Now there came a traveler to the rich man, and he was unwilling to take one of his own flock or herd to prepare for the guest who had come to him, but he took the poor man's lamb and prepared it for the man who had come to him."<sup>5</sup>Then David's anger was greatly kindled against the man, and he said to Nathan, "As the LORD lives, the man who has done this deserves to die,<sup>6</sup>and he shall restore the lamb fourfold, because he did this thing, and because he had no pity."<sup>7</sup>Nathan said to David, "You are the man! Thus says the LORD, the God of Israel, 'I anointed you king over Israel, and I delivered you out of the hand of Saul.<sup>8</sup>And I gave you your master's house and your master's wives into your arms and gave you the house of Israel and of Judah. And if this were too little, I would add to you as much more.<sup>9</sup>Why have you despised the word of the LORD, to do what is evil in his sight? You have struck down Uriah the Hittite with the sword and have taken his wife to be your wife and have killed him with the sword of the Ammonites.<sup>10</sup>Now therefore the sword shall never depart from your house, because you have despised me and have taken the wife of Uriah the Hittite to be your wife.'<sup>11</sup>Thus says the LORD, 'Behold, I will raise up evil against you out of your own house. And I will take your wives before your eyes and give them to your neighbor, and he shall lie with your wives in the sight of this sun.<sup>12</sup>For you did it secretly, but I will do this thing before all Israel and before the sun.'"<sup>13</sup>David said to Nathan, "I have sinned against the LORD." And Nathan said to David, "The LORD also has put away your sin; you shall not die.<sup>14</sup>Nevertheless, because by this deed you have utterly scorned the LORD, the child who is born to you shall die."<sup>15</sup>Then Nathan went to his house. And the LORD afflicted the child that Uriah's wife bore to David, and he became sick.<sup>16</sup>David therefore sought God on behalf of the child. And David fasted and went in and lay all night on the ground.<sup>17</sup>And the elders of his house stood beside him, to raise him from the ground, but he would not, nor did he eat food with them.<sup>18</sup>On the seventh day the child died. And the servants of David were afraid to tell him that the child was dead, for they said, "Behold, while the child was yet alive, we spoke to him, and he did not listen to us. How then can we say to him the child is dead? He may do himself some harm."<sup>19</sup>But when David saw that his servants were whispering together, David understood that the child was dead. And David said to his servants, "Is the child dead?" They said, "He is dead."<sup>20</sup>Then David arose from the earth and washed and anointed himself and changed his clothes. And he went into the house of the LORD and worshiped. He then went to his own house. And when he asked, they set food before him, and he ate.<sup>21</sup>Then his servants said to him, "What is this thing that you have done? You fasted and wept for the child while he was alive; but when the child died, you arose and ate food."<sup>22</sup>He said, "While the child was still alive, I fasted and wept, for I said, 'Who knows whether the LORD will be gracious to me, that the child may live?'<sup>23</sup>But now he is dead. Why should I fast? Can I bring him back again? I shall go to him, but he will not return to me."<sup>24</sup>Then David comforted his wife, Bathsheba, and went in to her and lay with her, and she bore a son, and he called his name Solomon. And the LORD loved him<sup>25</sup>and sent a message by Nathan the prophet. So he called his name Jedidiah, because of the LORD.<sup>26</sup>Now Joab fought against Rabbah of the Ammonites and took the royal city.<sup>27</sup>And Joab sent messengers to David and said, "I have fought against Rabbah; moreover, I have taken the city of waters.<sup>28</sup>Now then gather the rest of the people together and encamp against the city and take it, lest I take the city and it be called by my name."<sup>29</sup>So David gathered all the people together and went to Rabbah and fought against it and took it.<sup>30</sup>And he took the crown of their king from his head. The weight of it was a talent of gold, and in it was a precious stone, and it was placed on David's head. And he brought out the spoil of the city, a very great amount.<sup>31</sup>And he brought out the people who were in it and set them to labor with saws and iron picks and iron axes and made them toil at the brick kilns. And thus he did to all the cities of the Ammonites. Then David and all the people returned to Jerusalem.
12.overview:
Where we are. About a year has passed since chapter 11 ended with the LORD’s verdict. The child has been born, the marriage looks respectable, the siege of Rabbah goes on, and nobody in Jerusalem has said a word. David has got away with it.

The message. God will not leave his servant hidden in his sin. He sends his word to expose it, and when David says, “I have sinned against the LORD”, he is forgiven in the same breath. Yet the child dies and the sword will never leave his house: pardon and consequence both stand. And over the wreckage God speaks love, naming a new son “beloved”.

Why it was said. Israel needed to see how God deals with a king under his covenant: sin is neither overlooked nor allowed to cancel the promise of chapter 7, and David is disciplined but not cast off as Saul was (see the introduction). Every later reader needed to see true repentance too; Psalm 51 is its fuller voice.

How the chapter makes its case. Nathan brings a case about a stolen lamb, and David sentences the thief to death (vv. 1–6). “You are the man!” God’s gifts are recited, the murder is named as David’s own, and the sword is announced for his house (vv. 7–12). David confesses, is forgiven, and is told the child will die (vv. 13–15). He pleads for seven days, then rises and worships: “I shall go to him” (vv. 16–23). The LORD loves Solomon and names him Jedidiah (vv. 24–25), and Rabbah falls (vv. 26–31).

Where it leads. The chapter leads to Christ by the need it exposes and by the promise it keeps. By his own verdict and God’s law David deserved to die, and no sacrifice covered what he had done, yet he is told, “you shall not die” (v. 13). Paul explains how a holy God can say it (Romans 4:6–8): he put Christ forward as a propitiation, “so that he might be just and the justifier of the one who has faith in Jesus” (Romans 3:26). David’s pardon was real the moment Nathan spoke it, and it was paid for centuries later outside the walls of the same city. And the son called Jedidiah, through whom the promise runs, points to the Son of whom the Father said, “This is my beloved Son” (Matthew 3:17).

For us. Outrage at other people’s sins is easy; hearing “you are the man” is not, and only those who know God forgives can afford to hear it. Confess without excuses, believe that your sin is put away the moment you do, and do not mistake lasting consequences for lasting condemnation. In grief, carry your tears to the God who is gracious.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–6 — There Were Two Men in a Certain City
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God’s word catches the king by turning his own sense of justice on himself. After a year of silence the LORD sends Nathan, who does not accuse but brings a case (v. 1). A rich man with huge flocks, wanting to feed a traveller, spared his own animals and took the poor man’s one ewe lamb, which had grown up with his children like a daughter (vv. 1–4). David, doing his duty as judge, burns with anger and swears by the LORD that the man deserves to die and must repay fourfold, because he had no pity (vv. 5–6). He has pronounced sentence before he knows who the defendant is.
verseByVerse.theology: A conscience that has been silent for a year can still be reached, but not head-on. God's messenger comes round the side, through the king's own sense of justice, and lets David's verdict do what an accusation could not.
verseByVerse.examples: David's anger is right; it is simply aimed at the wrong man. Indignation at other people's sins is easy to feel, and it can sit comfortably beside the same sin unconfessed in ourselves (compare Romans 2:1).

verseByVerse.quote: And the LORD sent Nathan to David. He came to him and said to him, "There were two men in a certain city, the one rich and the other poor. The rich man had very many flocks and herds, but the poor man had nothing but one little ewe lamb, which he had bought. And he brought it up, and it grew up with him and with his children. It used to eat of his morsel and drink from his cup and lie in his arms, and it was like a daughter to him. Now there came a traveler to the rich man, and he was unwilling to take one of his own flock or herd to prepare for the guest who had come to him, but he took the poor man's lamb and prepared it for the man who had come to him." Then David's anger was greatly kindled against the man, and he said to Nathan, "As the LORD lives, the man who has done this deserves to die, and he shall restore the lamb fourfold, because he did this thing, and because he had no pity."
verseByVerse.commentary:
After a year of silence God sends Nathan with a case about a stolen lamb, and David, judging it rightly, condemns the man to death before he knows the man is himself. The parable works because it takes David’s own sense of justice and turns it round.

The year between. The child of 11:27 has been born, so at least nine months have passed, and probably more. Nothing happened in that year. The marriage held, the household ran, the siege of Rabbah continued, and no one in Jerusalem said anything. David got away with it completely. Psalm 32 very probably reports that year from within: “when I kept silent, my bones wasted away through my groaning all day long. For day and night your hand was heavy upon me; my strength was dried up as by the heat of summer” (Psalm 32:3–4).

The LORD sent Nathan to David. Not the court, not a rival, not a rumour. It is the same prophet who brought the covenant promise in chapter 7; the man who told David his house would stand for ever now comes to tell him what is going to happen to it.

One little ewe lamb. Nathan does not accuse; he brings a case. Every detail of the lamb (v. 3) adds to the picture, down to it was like a daughter to him. The Hebrew for daughter is bat, and the woman’s name is Bath-sheba; the echo may be deliberate, and even if not, the picture is exact. The lamb stands for Uriah’s wife, not a possession but a member of the family, loved.

Now there came a traveler. The occasion is trivial, and that is the point. No famine, no desperation, no debt: a visitor arrives and a meal must be made, and the rich man will not spend one animal out of many, so he takes the only animal a poor man owns. He needed so little and destroyed so much: that is the whole case.

David’s anger was greatly kindled. The trap closes because David does his job. Nathan has brought him a legal matter, which is exactly what the king of Israel was for: “David administered justice and equity to all his people” (8:15). A man with no standing has been robbed and has no redress, the case has come up to the king, and David hears it, gets angry and gives judgment. That is why the parable works. It is not a moral tale he happens to identify with; it is a verdict he pronounces in office, under oath (as the LORD lives), before he knows who the defendant is.

He shall restore the lamb fourfold. Nobody has died in the story; a sheep was taken. Yet the king’s instant sentence is death. Then the restitution, straight out of the law: “If a man steals an ox or a sheep, and kills it or sells it, he shall repay five oxen for an ox, and four sheep for a sheep” (Exodus 22:1). David sets the figure himself. Many readers have seen that number paid in the rest of the story: four of his sons die, the child in this chapter; Amnon, murdered by his brother at a sheepshearing; Absalom, killed in an oak against David’s order; and Adonijah, executed by Solomon. The man who set the figure was their father.

Because he had no pity. The last clause of his own verdict is the sharpest thing in the chapter. Not because he broke the law, but because there was nothing in him that stopped.

The verdict that is easy to give. David’s fury at the rich man is the most natural thing in the chapter, and the most revealing. It is always easier to be outraged at a wrong done by someone else than to see the same wrong in the mirror, and a culture that brings every scandal in the world to every phone has made that easier than ever. Outrage feels like righteousness: it costs nothing, puts us on the right side, and can quietly do the work a conscience should be doing. Jesus named the pattern: the speck in a brother’s eye and the log in our own (Matthew 7:3). Nathan does not tell David his anger is wrong; the rich man deserved every word of it. He simply turns it round. That is the hardest move in the moral life, and only the gospel makes it bearable. If you are the man were the last word, no one could afford to hear it, and we would all keep our outrage pointed outward. But the God who says it to David says in the same conversation, you shall not die, and people who know that can afford to look in the mirror.
verseByVerse.note: “In his arms” is literally “in his bosom” (ESV note).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God names David’s sin, forgives it the moment it is confessed, and still lets its consequences run. “You are the man!” Nathan sets out the LORD’s gifts and his offer of more (vv. 7–8), then the charge: David despised God’s word, struck down Uriah with the sword of the Ammonites and took his wife (v. 9). So the sword will never leave his house, and what he did in secret will be done to him before the sun (vv. 10–12). David says, “I have sinned against the LORD”, and Nathan answers at once that the LORD has put away his sin and he shall not die; but the child will die (vv. 13–14). Nathan goes home, and the LORD strikes the child (v. 15).
verseByVerse.theology: The charge is built from gifts, not laws. Before it is anything else, David's sin is a refusal to trust the Giver for what he wanted.
verseByVerse.examples: Distance does not dilute guilt. Whatever we arrange for other people to do on our behalf, God counts as our own act.

verseByVerse.quote: Nathan said to David, "You are the man! Thus says the LORD, the God of Israel, 'I anointed you king over Israel, and I delivered you out of the hand of Saul. And I gave you your master's house and your master's wives into your arms and gave you the house of Israel and of Judah. And if this were too little, I would add to you as much more.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Nathan names the king as the man in the story, and God’s charge begins not with laws broken but with gifts given, and with more that was freely on offer.

You are the man! Two words in Hebrew: Attah ha-ish. No preamble, no softening, no appeal to the king’s better nature. The judge has passed sentence, and the prophet identifies the defendant. Consider what Nathan is risking. He stands alone before a man who within the last year arranged the death of one of his own mighty men, and several other soldiers, to conceal a pregnancy, and got away with it. Nathan knows this, because God has just told him, and he says it anyway.

Thus says the LORD, the God of Israel. From here Nathan stops speaking for himself and speaks in the formula of the prophets, as the LORD’s messenger. What follows is not a courtier’s opinion a king might brush aside; it is God’s own verdict, and David, who has despised God’s word (v. 9), is now under it.

I anointed you king over Israel. The indictment is not a list of laws but a list of gifts. I anointed you: at Bethlehem, when he was the youngest son, out with the sheep. I delivered you out of the hand of Saul: from the spears, through the window, in the caves. I gave you your master’s house, and Israel, and Judah. Every clause begins with God as the giver, as chapter 7 did.

If this were too little, I would add to you as much more. This line is worse than any accusation. There was more available. If the man had needed something, or wanted something, or found himself in middle age with an empty afternoon and an appetite he could not manage, he could have asked. The giver was generous and had never once refused him. He did not ask; he took. That is the kind of sin this was: not a starving man stealing bread, but a man with everything, never refused anything, helping himself to the one thing not on offer, from a household that had nothing else.

Why take what you do not even need? We usually explain wrongdoing by need: poverty, pressure, a hard childhood, a system that pushed. Sometimes that is just, but this chapter will not let it be the whole story. Augustine, in his Confessions, puzzled over a night in his youth when he and his friends stole pears from a neighbour’s tree. He had better pears at home, and they threw most of them to the pigs; what he loved, he concluded, was the stealing itself. David had a palace full of everything, and he took the one lamb. The modern mind is reluctant to believe in a heart like that, because then the cure cannot be more resources or a better environment; it has to be a new heart. And notice what God sets against the grasping: not a lecture on contentment but a reminder of a giver. The gospel makes the offer larger still: “He who did not spare his own Son but gave him up for us all, how will he not also with him graciously give us all things?” (Romans 8:32). People who believe that can stop taking.

Did God approve polygamy by giving David Saul’s wives? In that world a new king took over the old king’s household; God is saying that he had given David everything Saul had. It describes what God allowed in his providence, not what he commanded; the law still warned the king against many wives (Deuteronomy 17:17).
verseByVerse.note: Chronicles, which follows this war closely (1 Chron. 20:1-3), leaves out the whole Bathsheba episode.

verseByVerse.quote: Why have you despised the word of the LORD, to do what is evil in his sight? You have struck down Uriah the Hittite with the sword and have taken his wife to be your wife and have killed him with the sword of the Ammonites.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God names the root of both crimes, contempt for his word, and calls Uriah’s killing David’s own act, though an Ammonite weapon did it.

Why have you despised the word of the LORD? The charge begins with what lies under both crimes. David did not forget a rule; he treated what God had said as not worth regarding. In verse 10 the same verb takes God himself as its object: you have despised me. To despise the LORD’s word is to despise the LORD, because his word is how he makes himself known to his people. The adultery and the murder are what that contempt looked like in action.

You have struck down Uriah the Hittite with the sword. David never touched him. He was in Jerusalem. An Ammonite archer on a wall at Rabbah killed Uriah, in an assault ordered by Joab, and David’s only part was a sentence in a letter. God says: you struck him down. And so that nobody can miss it: you have killed him with the sword of the Ammonites. The instrument is named, the arrangement is named, and the killer is named, and it is not the archer and it is not Joab.

No hiding place. Every layer David built into the operation, the distance, the deniability, the enemy’s weapon in a lawful siege, is simply set aside. It kept the truth from his neighbours for a year. It hid nothing from God.

verseByVerse.quote: Now therefore the sword shall never depart from your house, because you have despised me and have taken the wife of Uriah the Hittite to be your wife.' Thus says the LORD, 'Behold, I will raise up evil against you out of your own house. And I will take your wives before your eyes and give them to your neighbor, and he shall lie with your wives in the sight of this sun. For you did it secretly, but I will do this thing before all Israel and before the sun.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Because David used the sword and took a wife in secret, the sword will stay in his family and his own wives will be taken in public. The judgment fits the sin exactly.

The sword shall never depart from your house. He used a sword to solve a problem, and the sword is going to live in his family: Amnon killed at a feast, Absalom run through in a tree, Adonijah executed, and a rebellion in between that costs twenty thousand men in one day (18:7). The correspondence is exact, as the judgments in this book generally are. He took a wife in secret; wives will be taken from him in public. He worked in the dark from a roof; this will happen before the sun. And it does, on that same roof, when Absalom pitches a tent on it in front of the whole city (16:22), on the advice of Ahithophel, who may well have been Bathsheba’s grandfather.

Out of your own house. That is the hardest clause in the sentence. The judgment is not an invasion or a plague; it is his own sons.

Is God the author of Absalom’s evil? God foretold the judgment and gave David over to it, but Absalom chose his own sin and was guilty of it (16:22). God rules even the wicked deeds of men without being the author of their sin (Acts 2:23).

verseByVerse.quote: David said to Nathan, "I have sinned against the LORD." And Nathan said to David, "The LORD also has put away your sin; you shall not die. Nevertheless, because by this deed you have utterly scorned the LORD, the child who is born to you shall die."
verseByVerse.commentary:
David confesses without excuse, and is forgiven in the same breath; yet the consequence still comes, and the child will die. Forgiveness removes the sin, not every result of it.

I have sinned against the LORD. Two words in Hebrew, and that is the whole of it. No excuse, no explanation of the pressures, no mention of Bathsheba or Joab or the difficulty of the situation, no attempt to distinguish what he did from what the man in the story did, no request for time. And the direction is right: against the LORD. He has wronged Uriah beyond repair, and Bathsheba, and the men who died at the wall, but he names first the one against whom the offence is finally committed.

The psalm of confession. Psalm 51 is headed as David’s, when Nathan the prophet went to him, after he had gone in to Bathsheba, and it says the same at greater length: “Against you, you only, have I sinned and done what is evil in your sight” (Psalm 51:4). The whole psalm belongs here: “Have mercy on me, O God, according to your steadfast love … blot out my transgressions … Create in me a clean heart, O God, and renew a right spirit within me. Cast me not away from your presence, and take not your Holy Spirit from me” (Psalm 51:1–11). That last line is not a formula; he had watched the Spirit leave Saul.

What sacrifice cannot do. The psalm knows what the man cannot bring: “For you will not delight in sacrifice, or I would give it; you will not be pleased with a burnt offering. The sacrifices of God are a broken spirit; a broken and contrite heart, O God, you will not despise” (Psalm 51:16–17). He had good reason to know it. There was no sacrifice in the law for deliberate murder or adultery; those carried the death penalty, and no offering covered them. The man had nothing to bring.

The LORD also has put away your sin. The answer comes in the same breath as the confession. There is no interval, no probation, no series of works to be completed first. He says I have sinned and is told in the next sentence that it is dealt with. Put away is the language of removal: the sin taken off him and carried elsewhere.

You shall not die. This reverses the verdict David gave in verse 5. He said the man deserved to die, and he was right; the law agreed with him twice over. And he does not die. Somebody else does, and the whole Bible is about how that comes to be just.

How Paul reads it. Paul answers with this very year of David’s life. He quotes Psalm 32, David’s own account of that silence and its ending, as the description of every believer’s pardon: blessed is the man against whom the Lord will not count his sin (Romans 4:6–8). And he explains how a holy God could do that: God had passed over former sins, and at the cross he put Christ forward as a propitiation (a sacrifice that turns away his just anger), to show that he is both just and the one who justifies whoever has faith in Jesus (Romans 3:25–26). David’s pardon was real the moment Nathan spoke it; it was paid for centuries later, when Christ died outside the walls of the same city.

The child who is born to you shall die. Then, immediately after the pardon, the consequence. The two must be held together, because this is where a great deal of shallow teaching about forgiveness breaks. The sin is put away and the sword still comes; both are said by the same prophet in the same conversation, and neither cancels the other. Forgiveness does not remove the consequences. It removes the sin. David is not going to be cut off as Saul was, or lose the covenant, or be abandoned; and his family is going to be torn apart for the rest of his life, beginning with a baby.

In everyday life. Anyone who has come to God with something truly destructive and been truly forgiven, and then found the wreckage still there in the morning, is standing in this verse. The relationship is restored; the consequences run their course. Confession today takes David’s shape: name the sin to God as sin, without the list of pressures that explain it, and believe his word that it is put away (1 John 1:9). Then, where others were wronged, put right what can still be put right, as Zacchaeus did when he offered fourfold (Luke 19:8). Some wrongs, like this one, can never be undone; the confession is still owed, and so is the honesty.

Was it fair for the child to die for David’s sin? Each person answers for his own guilt (Ezekiel 18:20), and the child was not punished for David’s guilt. The death was God’s judgment on David, who had treated life lightly, and God as the Giver of life may take it when he wills. The child was not lost: David says I shall go to him (v. 23).

Textual note. In verse 14 the Hebrew literally says David scorned the enemies of the LORD, probably a scribe’s reverent way of avoiding writing that a man scorned God; the KJV reads given great occasion to the enemies of the LORD to blaspheme. Either way the point is that his sin brought God’s name into contempt.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Nathan went to his house. And the LORD afflicted the child that Uriah's wife bore to David, and he became sick.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Nathan’s work is done, and the LORD himself strikes the child, so that the word spoken that day begins to come true at once.

Then Nathan went to his house. The prophet goes home, and the writer calls Bathsheba Uriah’s wife one last time.

The LORD afflicted the child. The writer does not say that the child simply fell ill; he says the LORD struck him, using a verb for a blow, so that no one could put the sickness down to chance. There is nothing more for a prophet to say, and what follows (vv. 16–23) is between David and God.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 16–23 — I Shall Go to Him
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Faith pleads while there is hope, and accepts God’s answer when it comes. David seeks God for the child, fasting and lying on the ground for seven days, and will not be raised or fed (vv. 16–17). When the child dies, his servants are afraid to tell him (v. 18), but he understands, rises, washes, changes his clothes, worships in the house of the LORD and then eats (vv. 19–20). To his bewildered servants he explains: while the child lived, who knew whether the LORD would be gracious? Now he cannot bring him back; “I shall go to him, but he will not return to me” (vv. 21–23).
verseByVerse.theology: Seven days on the ground while there was any possibility, and not one day after. He is not callous and he is not resigned; he prayed as long as praying could change anything, and when it could not, he got up and went to worship.
verseByVerse.examples: For those who grieve: David's servants were afraid to tell him, and then bewildered by how he took it. People in grief rarely behave as others expect, and they need presence more than explanations.

verseByVerse.quote: David therefore sought God on behalf of the child. And David fasted and went in and lay all night on the ground. And the elders of his house stood beside him, to raise him from the ground, but he would not, nor did he eat food with them. On the seventh day the child died. And the servants of David were afraid to tell him that the child was dead, for they said, "Behold, while the child was yet alive, we spoke to him, and he did not listen to us. How then can we say to him the child is dead? He may do himself some harm." But when David saw that his servants were whispering together, David understood that the child was dead. And David said to his servants, "Is the child dead?" They said, "He is dead." Then David arose from the earth and washed and anointed himself and changed his clothes. And he went into the house of the LORD and worshiped. He then went to his own house. And when he asked, they set food before him, and he ate. Then his servants said to him, "What is this thing that you have done? You fasted and wept for the child while he was alive; but when the child died, you arose and ate food." He said, "While the child was still alive, I fasted and wept, for I said, 'Who knows whether the LORD will be gracious to me, that the child may live?' But now he is dead. Why should I fast? Can I bring him back again? I shall go to him, but he will not return to me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
David pleads with God for the child while there is hope, and when the child dies he rises, worships and rests his grief on the hope of going where the child has gone. His prayer and his acceptance both rest on what God is like.

David therefore sought God on behalf of the child. He has been told plainly by a prophet what will happen, and he prays anyway. It is not disobedience: he does not argue with Nathan or deny the word. He lies on the floor and asks God to show mercy, on the ground he gives two verses on: who knows whether the LORD will be gracious to me? He is not claiming a promise. He is appealing to what God is like.

The servants of David were afraid. Seven days of this. His household cannot get him off the floor or get him to eat, and when the child dies they are afraid of what the news will do to him. They conclude, reasonably, that it will break him, and stand in the corridor whispering, unable to go in.

Then David arose from the earth. The order of what he does is deliberate and not what anyone expected. He washes, anoints himself and changes his clothes, laying aside the signs of mourning. He goes into the house of the LORD and worships. Then he goes home and eats. Worship comes before the meal: the first place he goes after seven days on the floor and the death of his son is into the presence of the God who told him this would happen.

Who knows whether the LORD will be gracious to me? His servants ask a fair question, and he gives an honest account of the seven days. He never had a promise. He had a word of judgment and a knowledge of God’s character, and on the strength of the second he spent a week begging against the first. While there was a possibility, he prayed with everything he had.

Can I bring him back again? What David refuses is what grief most wants to do: to keep up the protest after the outcome is settled. He is not being cold; he wept on a floor for a week. He is saying that the fasting had a purpose, the purpose is finished, and continuing would be doing something to himself rather than for the child. There is hard-won wisdom in that, and it belongs to people who have prayed properly. He gave everything while it could matter, and he will not punish himself now that it cannot.

I shall go to him, but he will not return to me. This is the sentence people come to this chapter for, and it should be handled slowly and without a trace of glibness, because those who need it are usually holding something unbearable. It does not say the child will be restored to him in this life; that is the very thing he denies. What he says is that he is going where the child is. The movement is one way, and it is David who is travelling.

How much weight will that sentence bear? Some read it as no more than a statement about death: I shall die as he has died, and go to the grave where he is. That reading is possible and should be admitted. But it is hard to square with its effect on the man. He has been on the ground for a week, and this sentence is what gets him up, washed and into the house of God to worship. A remark that everybody dies eventually is no comfort, and it does not explain the change in him. What is certain is this: David, who knew as much about God as anyone in the Old Testament, faced with the death of an infant under a stated judgment on his own sin, looked forward and not back, expected to be with him, and got up and worshipped.

The character of God. David’s whole hope in this chapter rests on the character of God, not on the child’s record, which is the only ground anybody has ever had. He asked whether the LORD would be gracious, and the answer he had received about himself was that the LORD had put away his sin. The God who does that is the God he expects to find the child with.

Christ and the children. And beside it stands the Lord Jesus, who said, “Let the children come to me; do not hinder them, for to such belongs the kingdom of God” (Mark 10:14), and was indignant with the disciples for getting in the way.

Honest comfort. Pretending Scripture says more than it does is not kindness. Anyone standing where David stood should be given what it does give, the settled conviction of a grieving father who knew God well and the character of the God who put away his sin the moment he named it: no less, and nothing invented.

To the bereaved. One more word to a bereaved mother or father. David got up on the seventh day, but this passage is not a timetable for grief. The same man wept for Absalom with a cry the whole army heard (18:33), and Jesus wept at a friend’s grave though he was about to raise him (John 11:35). Tears that go on are not unbelief. What David shows is where to carry them: to the God who is gracious, in the hope of going where the child has gone.

Where Christians differ: do infants who die go to heaven? Scripture does not set out a full doctrine, and Christians have answered differently. Some read David’s words as meaning only that he would join his son in death. Many in the Reformed tradition have held that God saves all who die in infancy, by his grace in Christ, pointing to his mercy, to the fact that infants have not rejected him, and to Jesus’ welcome of little children, “for to such belongs the kingdom of heaven” (Matthew 19:14). Others leave the question open. This commentary’s view: with the 1689 London Baptist Confession and the Westminster Confession (both at 10.3), elect infants dying in infancy are regenerated and saved by Christ through the Spirit, who works when and where and how he pleases. Many believers, with good reason, hope that God’s mercy embraces every child who dies so young, though Scripture does not say so in so many words. Grieving parents may rest their little ones in God’s hands with real hope.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 24–31 — And the LORD Loved Him
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Grace has the last word over the worst chapter of David’s life. David comforts Bathsheba, now called by her own name, and she bears Solomon, and the LORD loves him and sends Nathan with a second name, Jedidiah, “beloved of the LORD” (vv. 24–25). Meanwhile Joab has taken Rabbah’s water supply and summons the king to come and take the city himself (vv. 26–28). David finally goes out to the war, takes Rabbah and its king’s heavy crown, puts the people to work, and returns to Jerusalem with everything Nathan said still ahead of him (vv. 29–31).
verseByVerse.theology: Grace has the last word in the chapter, but it does not erase what went before: the child of this marriage is loved by God, and the house is still under judgment.
verseByVerse.examples: Finishing a job someone else neglected and then handing them the credit can be generosity or it can be leverage. With Joab it is hard to tell which, and probably it is both.

verseByVerse.quote: Then David comforted his wife, Bathsheba, and went in to her and lay with her, and she bore a son, and he called his name Solomon. And the LORD loved him and sent a message by Nathan the prophet. So he called his name Jedidiah, because of the LORD. Now Joab fought against Rabbah of the Ammonites and took the royal city. And Joab sent messengers to David and said, "I have fought against Rabbah; moreover, I have taken the city of waters. Now then gather the rest of the people together and encamp against the city and take it, lest I take the city and it be called by my name." So David gathered all the people together and went to Rabbah and fought against it and took it. And he took the crown of their king from his head. The weight of it was a talent of gold, and in it was a precious stone, and it was placed on David's head. And he brought out the spoil of the city, a very great amount. And he brought out the people who were in it and set them to labor with saws and iron picks and iron axes and made them toil at the brick kilns. And thus he did to all the cities of the Ammonites. Then David and all the people returned to Jerusalem.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God gives a new son out of the ruins and declares his love for him, and David at last goes out to finish the war he should never have left. Grace has the last word in the chapter, though everything Nathan said still lies ahead.

David comforted his wife, Bathsheba. The first grace is small and easy to miss. It is the first time since 11:3 that she is called by her name and not the wife of Uriah, and the first sign anywhere in the account that anyone thought about what this had been like for her. She has been summoned by a king, made pregnant, widowed, married as soon as the mourning was over, and has now buried a baby, and until now everything in her story has been done to her by somebody else. He comforts her. It does not repair anything, but it matters.

And the LORD loved him. The second grace is at the end of the worst chapter of the man’s life. This child is born of a marriage that began in adultery and murder, in a household under an announced judgment, to the woman whose first husband David killed. And God loves him: not tolerates, not permits, but loves, and the writer says it flatly, without explanation, in the sentence that gives his name.

He called his name Solomon. Solomon will inherit the throne, build the house David was not allowed to build, and be the son through whom the covenant of chapter 7 runs. Matthew, opening the New Testament with the genealogy of Jesus Christ, writes him into the line with the fact still attached: “David was the father of Solomon by the wife of Uriah” (Matthew 1:6). The New Testament refuses to tidy this up; it puts the murdered man’s name in the family tree of the Messiah.

So he called his name Jedidiah. God sends the prophet back with a name. Nathan’s last visit brought you are the man and a sentence of judgment; this time he brings a name for the baby, Jedidiah, “beloved of the LORD”. The same prophet, the same house, the same God: that is the shape of the chapter in two visits.

The beloved Son. Solomon was a son of David whom the LORD loved, but he too would fall. The name looks further, to the Son of David over whom the Father said, “This is my beloved Son, with whom I am well pleased” (Matthew 3:17), and in whom sinners from households as broken as David’s are made God’s beloved (Ephesians 1:6).

I have taken the city of waters. Meanwhile the war has gone on. Joab has taken the water supply, so the city cannot hold out, and his message can be read two ways. On the surface it is loyalty: come and finish it, so the credit is yours. Kings were touchy about this, and generals were wise to be careful. Underneath it is something else: lest I take the city and it be called by my name. He is telling the king that he could take the city and let everyone know who did it, and is choosing not to. Remember what has passed between these two men since they last corresponded: a letter ordering Uriah’s death, carried out and never mentioned again. This is a man who knows the king’s secret, calling him out to the war he should have gone to in the first place.

David gathered all the people together. He goes. The chapter that began with a prophet and a lamb ends with the king finally doing what 11:1 said kings do in the spring.

The weight of it was a talent of gold. A talent was about 34 kilograms (75 pounds), not a weight a man wears; it was presumably held over his head on occasion, or only its precious stone was set in David’s crown (see the box below).

Then David and all the people returned to Jerusalem. The chapter ends with the war finished, the crown on the right head and the king home, with everything Nathan said still ahead of him.

Uncertain wording. Their king (v. 30) translates Hebrew malkam, which can also be read as Milcom, the god of the Ammonites (1 Kings 11:5), and many think the crown belonged to his image, which would better suit its great weight; it was placed on David’s head may then mean the precious stone. Both readings are possible.

Uncertain wording. The last verse is genuinely disputed, and it is better to say so than to choose confidently. The Hebrew of verse 31 can be read as forced labour, the people put to work with saws and picks and axes and at the brick kilns, which is how the ESV and most modern versions take it. The Chronicler’s parallel (1 Chronicles 20:3) has a verb that normally means sawed, though many think a one-letter copying slip has turned set into sawed, and the verse in Samuel can also be read as the people being killed with those implements, as the older English versions took it, which would make it an atrocity. The difference turns on a preposition and a single letter, and honest scholars have long divided on it. The same writer reported the killing of two-thirds of the Moabite prisoners without flinching (8:2), so he would probably have said plainly if this were a massacre, and forced labour is what conquerors normally imposed; that reading is at least as likely. It is not possible to be certain, and pretending to be would be worse than the difficulty.
verseByVerse.note: The “royal city” and “city of waters” that Joab took (vv. 26-27) were probably the lower town and its water supply; the citadel still had to fall when David came.

12.theology:
Nathan brings a case, not an accusation (vv. 1-6). David hears it in office, as the judge 8:15 says he was, and gives judgment under oath. Nobody in the story has died, yet his instant sentence is death, with repayment at the law's fourfold rate for a stolen sheep (Ex. 22:1). His own last clause is the sharpest sentence in the chapter: because he had no pity.

An indictment made of gifts (vv. 7-9). God's charge reminds David of all he has been given and offers more, and then names the murder as David's own, though an Ammonite arrow did it. God would have given him more; he did not ask; he took. And the distance he put between himself and the killing counted for nothing before God.

The judgments match the crime (vv. 10-12). He used a sword to solve a problem, and the sword will live in his family. He took a wife in secret, and wives will be taken from him before the sun. And the hardest clause is out of your own house: the judgment is his sons.

One sentence, and the pardon in the same breath (v. 13). No excuse and no request for time, and the direction is right: against the LORD, which Psalm 51 sets out at greater length. The law provided no sacrifice for premeditated murder or adultery, and David had nothing to bring. You shall not die reverses the verdict he gave in verse 5, which was correct. He does not die. Somebody else does: the Son of David, on whom the LORD laid the iniquity of us all (Isaiah 53:6), so that God is just in pardoning (Romans 3:25-26).

Forgiveness and consequence (vv. 13-14). The same prophet says both in the same conversation, and neither cancels the other. David keeps the covenant and the relationship is restored; the consequences run their course.

Prayer against a word already given (vv. 16-23). David appeals not to a promise but to God's character, prays while it could matter, and goes first to worship when it no longer can. His hope for the child rests on that same character, the God who put away his sin the moment he named it; and beside it stands the Lord Jesus saying let the children come to me (Mark 10:14).

And the LORD loved him (vv. 24-25). Bathsheba is called by her name and comforted, and the child of that marriage, born in a house under an announced judgment, is loved by God. Nathan, whose last visit was you are the man, comes back carrying Jedidiah, and Matthew writes the whole history into the Messiah's line: David was the father of Solomon by the wife of Uriah (Matt. 1:6). The grace of God reaches into the very marriage that began in sin.

An unfinished war finished (vv. 26-31). Joab's message is loyal on the surface, and underneath it reminds the king what Joab knows about him, and the king at last goes out to the war he should have fought from the start. How he treated the conquered city (v. 31) is disputed; this commentary takes the forced-labour reading as at least as likely, without claiming certainty.
12.examples:
Then: A prophet walked into a throne room with a lawsuit about a stolen lamb, and the king, doing his job, in office, under oath, lost his temper and sentenced the defendant to death and fourfold repayment before he was told the defendant's name. In the years that followed, four of his own sons died.

Now: Three things. Nathan's method is the first: he did not accuse a man who had already killed to protect this secret. He got him to pronounce his own verdict, on a case he could judge clearly because he did not yet see that it was about himself. Anybody who has to tell someone something true and unwelcome should study that. The second is verse 13 and verse 14 held together: the sin was put away in the same breath as the confession, with no probation and nothing to complete first, and the sword still came. Forgiveness does not remove the consequences, and anyone who has been genuinely pardoned and then found the wreckage still there in the morning is reading the right chapter. And the third is verse 23, for anybody carrying a grief like his: he prayed with everything he had while it could still matter, and he stopped when it could not, and what got him off the floor was not resignation but the expectation that he was going where the child had gone.

keyVerse.quote: David said to Nathan, “I have sinned against the LORD.” And Nathan said to David, “The LORD also has put away your sin; you shall not die.”
keyVerse.note: This is the hinge of David’s life and of the whole book. A confession with no excuses meets a pardon with no delay: two words in Hebrew, and the sin is put away. The man who had pronounced death on himself does not die, and the rest of Scripture explains how a just God could say so, through the Son of David who died in the place of sinners.

12.reflection:
David was furious at the rich man in Nathan’s story but blind to the same sin in himself (vv. 5–7). Why is it so much easier to be outraged at others than to see ourselves? How does the gospel make it possible to hear “you are the man” without despair?

God’s charge against David is a list of gifts, with the offer, “if this were too little, I would add to you as much more” (v. 8). How does remembering God’s generosity expose sin and cure discontent? What does Romans 8:32 add?

David is forgiven at once, yet the child dies and the sword will not leave his house (vv. 13–14). How would you explain the difference between forgiveness and consequences to someone who has been forgiven but still lives with the wreckage of a sin?

David prayed hard while there was hope, and then rose, worshipped and said, “I shall go to him” (vv. 16–23). What does his grief teach about prayer, about accepting God’s answer, and about the hope believers can offer parents whose child has died?

13.title: Amnon, Tamar, Absalom
13.text: <sup>1</sup>Now Absalom, David's son, had a beautiful sister, whose name was Tamar. And after a time Amnon, David's son, loved her.<sup>2</sup>And Amnon was so tormented that he made himself ill because of his sister Tamar, for she was a virgin, and it seemed impossible to Amnon to do anything to her.<sup>3</sup>But Amnon had a friend, whose name was Jonadab, the son of Shimeah, David's brother. And Jonadab was a very crafty man.<sup>4</sup>And he said to him, "O son of the king, why are you so haggard morning after morning? Will you not tell me?" Amnon said to him, "I love Tamar, my brother Absalom's sister."<sup>5</sup>Jonadab said to him, "Lie down on your bed and pretend to be ill. And when your father comes to see you, say to him, 'Let my sister Tamar come and give me bread to eat, and prepare the food in my sight, that I may see it and eat it from her hand.'"<sup>6</sup>So Amnon lay down and pretended to be ill. And when the king came to see him, Amnon said to the king, "Please let my sister Tamar come and make a couple of cakes in my sight, that I may eat from her hand."<sup>7</sup>Then David sent home to Tamar, saying, "Go to your brother Amnon's house and prepare food for him."<sup>8</sup>So Tamar went to her brother Amnon's house, where he was lying down. And she took dough and kneaded it and made cakes in his sight and baked the cakes.<sup>9</sup>And she took the pan and emptied it out before him, but he refused to eat. And Amnon said, "Send out everyone from me." So everyone went out from him.<sup>10</sup>Then Amnon said to Tamar, "Bring the food into the chamber, that I may eat from your hand." And Tamar took the cakes she had made and brought them into the chamber to Amnon her brother.<sup>11</sup>But when she brought them near him to eat, he took hold of her and said to her, "Come, lie with me, my sister."<sup>12</sup>She answered him, "No, my brother, do not violate me, for such a thing is not done in Israel; do not do this outrageous thing.<sup>13</sup>As for me, where could I carry my shame? And as for you, you would be as one of the outrageous fools in Israel. Now therefore, please speak to the king, for he will not withhold me from you."<sup>14</sup>But he would not listen to her, and being stronger than she, he violated her and lay with her.<sup>15</sup>Then Amnon hated her with very great hatred, so that the hatred with which he hated her was greater than the love with which he had loved her. And Amnon said to her, "Get up! Go!"<sup>16</sup>But she said to him, "No, my brother, for this wrong in sending me away is greater than the other that you did to me." But he would not listen to her.<sup>17</sup>He called the young man who served him and said, "Put this woman out of my presence and bolt the door after her."<sup>18</sup>Now she was wearing a long robe with sleeves, for thus were the virgin daughters of the king dressed. So his servant put her out and bolted the door after her.<sup>19</sup>And Tamar put ashes on her head and tore the long robe that she wore. And she laid her hand on her head and went away, crying aloud as she went.<sup>20</sup>And her brother Absalom said to her, "Has Amnon your brother been with you? Now hold your peace, my sister. He is your brother; do not take this to heart." So Tamar lived, a desolate woman, in her brother Absalom's house.<sup>21</sup>When King David heard of all these things, he was very angry.<sup>22</sup>But Absalom spoke to Amnon neither good nor bad, for Absalom hated Amnon, because he had violated his sister Tamar.<sup>23</sup>After two full years Absalom had sheepshearers at Baal-hazor, which is near Ephraim, and Absalom invited all the king's sons.<sup>24</sup>And Absalom came to the king and said, "Behold, your servant has sheepshearers. Please let the king and his servants go with your servant."<sup>25</sup>But the king said to Absalom, "No, my son, let us not all go, lest we be burdensome to you." He pressed him, but he would not go but gave him his blessing.<sup>26</sup>Then Absalom said, "If not, please let my brother Amnon go with us." And the king said to him, "Why should he go with you?"<sup>27</sup>But Absalom pressed him until he let Amnon and all the king's sons go with him.<sup>28</sup>Then Absalom commanded his servants, "Mark when Amnon's heart is merry with wine, and when I say to you, 'Strike Amnon,' then kill him. Do not fear; have I not commanded you? Be courageous and be valiant."<sup>29</sup>So the servants of Absalom did to Amnon as Absalom had commanded. Then all the king's sons arose, and each mounted his mule and fled.<sup>30</sup>While they were on the way, news came to David, "Absalom has struck down all the king's sons, and not one of them is left."<sup>31</sup>Then the king arose and tore his garments and lay on the earth. And all his servants who were standing by tore their garments.<sup>32</sup>But Jonadab the son of Shimeah, David's brother, said, "Let not my lord suppose that they have killed all the young men, the king's sons, for Amnon alone is dead. For by the command of Absalom this has been determined from the day he violated his sister Tamar.<sup>33</sup>Now therefore let not my lord the king so take it to heart as to suppose that all the king's sons are dead, for Amnon alone is dead."<sup>34</sup>But Absalom fled. And the young man who kept the watch lifted up his eyes and looked, and behold, many people were coming from the road behind him by the side of the mountain.<sup>35</sup>And Jonadab said to the king, "Behold, the king's sons have come; as your servant said, so it has come about."<sup>36</sup>And as soon as he had finished speaking, behold, the king's sons came and lifted up their voice and wept. And the king also and all his servants wept very bitterly.<sup>37</sup>But Absalom fled and went to Talmai the son of Ammihud, king of Geshur. And David mourned for his son day after day.<sup>38</sup>So Absalom fled and went to Geshur, and was there three years.<sup>39</sup>And the spirit of the king longed to go out to Absalom, because he was comforted about Amnon, since he was dead.
13.overview:
Where we are. Nathan has just told David that, though his sin is forgiven, “the sword shall never depart from your house”, and that the LORD will raise up evil against him “out of your own house” (12:10–11). Chapters 13 to 20 show that word coming true, and it begins at once, among David’s own children.

The message. Sin is learned in families, and a forgiven man may still watch the harvest of what he sowed. David saw a woman who was not his and took her, then arranged a killing to cover it; now his firstborn takes his half-sister, and his third son arranges a killing. The chapter shows desire that calls itself love for what it is, and shows that silence in the face of wrong, from a brother, a cousin and above all a king, is itself a failure of justice.

Why it was said. Israel’s history does not flatter its kings (see the introduction). Later readers, watching the house of David fail again and again, needed to know that the throne’s troubles came from sin inside it, that God’s word through Nathan was true, and that the promise of chapter 7 would be kept by God in spite of David’s house, not because of it.

How the chapter makes its case. Amnon is sick with desire for Tamar, and his cousin Jonadab, a very crafty man, supplies the plan: feign illness and ask the king to send her (vv. 1–6). David sends her; in an emptied room Amnon seizes her, and she pleads from the law, from her own future and from his good, but he will not listen and violates her, then hates her and has her thrown out, and she tears her royal robe and goes away crying aloud (vv. 7–19). Absalom tells her to keep quiet, David is very angry and does nothing, and Absalom waits two silent years before having Amnon killed at a sheepshearing feast (vv. 20–29). A false report says all the king’s sons are dead; Jonadab, who knew all along, corrects it; Absalom flees to Geshur, and after three years David’s heart longs for the murderer (vv. 30–39).

Where it leads. The chapter leads to Christ chiefly by the need it exposes. Israel’s king was meant to be the one who “delivers the needy when he calls, the poor and him who has no helper” (Psalm 72:12), and every man in Tamar’s life failed her, her father most of all. The promise waited for a Son of David who would “judge the poor” with righteousness (Isaiah 11:4). Jesus is that King. He does not hush up the shamed but bore shame himself, “despising the shame” (Hebrews 12:2), and he will judge the world, so that nothing done in a locked room goes unanswered. His love is also the opposite of Amnon’s: where Amnon took and then discarded, “Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her” (Ephesians 5:25).

For us. Strong desire is not the same as love: love seeks the other’s good and gives itself, while appetite uses and discards. Wrongs in a family or a church must never be hushed up to protect a name, and those who have been wronged need to hear that the shame is not theirs. And anyone who, like David, feels his own sin has silenced him should know that the way back is not silence but honest confession, and the mercy that puts sin away (12:13).
13.theology:
The judgment of chapter 12, arriving (vv. 1-2). This is the household of many wives (3:2-5; 5:13) producing what such a household produces, in a kingdom whose law had warned its king in advance. The sons' sins match David's own exactly, and this is the first part of out of your own house to come true.

What the chapter teaches about desire (vv. 2, 15). A man who is troubled only because he cannot get at a woman, and not because it is wrong to want her, is not in love. And appetite satisfied does not become affection; it becomes disgust, and he turns it not on himself, who is responsible, but on her, because the sight of her reminds him of what he did.

Tamar's dignity (vv. 12-19). She argues from the law, from what it will do to her and to him, and offers a way out; she is not heard, twice; and then she refuses to let the deed be hidden. The book records her arguments in full, calls the deed nebalah, a disgraceful outrage, and calls her desolate, a word used of ruined cities. The story moves on without her, but the book does not treat her as unimportant.

Very angry, and nothing else (v. 21). Every sentence David could have spoken to Amnon had already been spoken to him by a prophet.
