He is silent because he has disqualified himself, and his sons know it. That is what chapter 12's judgment actually looks like: not God striking David, but David unable to act.

The King Tamar needed. Israel's king was meant to be the protector of those with no one else, and the royal psalm prays for a son of David who delivers the needy when he calls, the poor and him who has no helper, and in whose sight their blood is precious (Psalm 72:12-14). Every man in Tamar's house failed her, the king most of all. The promise of chapter 7 never rested on that house's goodness; it waited for the Son of David who would judge the poor with righteousness (Isaiah 11:4), who did not look away from the shamed or hush them up, and who will one day judge the world in justice (Acts 17:31), so that nothing done in a locked room goes unanswered.

Commands others carry out (vv. 22-29). Absalom waits two years in civil silence, then dresses a murder in the language of the battlefield and lets his servants do it, as David wrote a letter and Joab did it. Sin is learned in families, and the method as well as the appetite is passing from father to sons.

Jonadab, and the last verse (vv. 32-39). The man who devised the plan against Tamar saw the murder coming for two years and said nothing. And the chapter ends with no justice anywhere: a daughter desolate, a firstborn dead, and a father whose grief fades into longing for the murderer. The next chapter is Joab noticing that longing.
13.examples:
Then: A young woman argued for her life in a locked room, from the law, from what it would cost her, from what it would make of the man holding her, and finally by offering to marry him if he would only ask her father first; and when he had finished she tore the robe that marked her as a king's daughter and walked through the capital crying aloud so that nobody could pretend it had not happened. Her father was very angry and did nothing.

Now: Three things. Verse 15 is the one to remember: hatred follows the act at once, because appetite satisfied turns to disgust, and the man turns that disgust on his victim, never on himself. Anyone tempted to believe that getting the thing will settle it should notice how fast it turns. Second, Jonadab, who never lifts a hand and is on hand at both disasters with a clever word. Some people do all their damage by supplying a method to someone who had only an appetite. And third, David's silence. He lost the standing to say "this is wrong" and be heard, and he lost it years earlier, in a different room, over a different woman. Even so, the way back was the one he had already been shown: not silence, but owning his own sin before his sons and trusting the mercy that had put it away (12:13).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Desire that calls itself love is shown for what it is before anything is done. Amnon, David’s firstborn, makes himself ill over his half-sister Tamar, and the writer notes that what troubles him is not that wanting her is wrong but that she is guarded (vv. 1–2). His cousin Jonadab, a very crafty man, sees his haggard face, draws out the secret and at once supplies a method: pretend to be ill and ask the king to send Tamar to cook for him (vv. 3–5). Amnon does it, and the king agrees without a question (v. 6). The sword Nathan foretold has entered David’s house.
verseByVerse.theology: The narrator diagnoses it before Amnon acts. What he calls love in verse 1 he calls torment in verse 2, and the obstacle named is not that she is his sister but that she is guarded.
verseByVerse.examples: A friend who hears that we want something wrong and helps us plan it is no friend. The kindest thing Jonadab could have said was no.

verseByVerse.quote: Now Absalom, David's son, had a beautiful sister, whose name was Tamar. And after a time Amnon, David's son, loved her. And Amnon was so tormented that he made himself ill because of his sister Tamar, for she was a virgin, and it seemed impossible to Amnon to do anything to her. But Amnon had a friend, whose name was Jonadab, the son of Shimeah, David's brother. And Jonadab was a very crafty man. And he said to him, "O son of the king, why are you so haggard morning after morning? Will you not tell me?" Amnon said to him, "I love Tamar, my brother Absalom's sister." Jonadab said to him, "Lie down on your bed and pretend to be ill. And when your father comes to see you, say to him, 'Let my sister Tamar come and give me bread to eat, and prepare the food in my sight, that I may see it and eat it from her hand.'" So Amnon lay down and pretended to be ill. And when the king came to see him, Amnon said to the king, "Please let my sister Tamar come and make a couple of cakes in my sight, that I may eat from her hand."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The sword Nathan foretold enters David’s house: his firstborn burns for his half-sister, and a crafty cousin shows him how to get her alone. Before anything happens, the writer shows that Amnon’s “love” is appetite, and that the plan comes from a man who will never have to lay a hand on her.

Absalom, David’s son … Amnon, David’s son. Three of David’s children appear in one verse, and the writer names each one as David’s. Tamar and Absalom are children of Maacah; Amnon, the firstborn, is their half-brother by Ahinoam (3:2–3). This is what the household of 3:2–5 and 5:13 actually produced: six sons at Hebron by six women, more at Jerusalem, under a law that had warned Israel’s king not to multiply wives (Deuteronomy 17:17).

The sword begins. Nathan said the sword would never depart from this house and that evil would be raised up out of your own house (12:10–11). It begins here, and the sons’ sins match the father’s closely. David saw a woman who was not his and took her; his firstborn is about to do the same. David arranged a killing to cover it; his third son will arrange one too.

It seemed impossible to Amnon. Verse 1 calls it love, as Amnon would have. Verse 2 calls it torment, and then names the obstacle, and notice what the obstacle is not. It is not that she is his sister. It is that she is a virgin daughter of the king, and so guarded. As Amnon sees it, the only problem is how to get to her. A man frustrated by the difficulty of getting at a person, and not by the wrongness of wanting to, is not in love, and the writer establishes it before anything happens.

Jonadab was a very crafty man. He is David’s nephew, son of David’s brother Shimeah, and so a cousin of the princes. The Hebrew word is not wicked but wise in its shrewd sense: clever, able to see how a thing can be arranged, and crafty catches it well. Keep him in view; he reappears at the end of the chapter knowing more than anyone else in the room.

My brother Absalom’s sister. Amnon does not say my sister. Perhaps he is putting a little distance between himself and the relationship; perhaps it is simply how a large royal household spoke, naming full brothers and sisters by their mother’s son.

Lie down on your bed and pretend to be ill. The plan takes a sentence, and the craft is in its plainness. A sick prince is visited by the king, and a sick man’s wish for particular food from a particular hand is exactly what an invalid asks and a father grants without thinking. It works on David’s affection for his son, brings Tamar unaccompanied because the king himself sends her, and puts her in a private room with a plausible reason. Nobody has to be lied to except David, and he will not question it. Amnon carries it out word for word, and the king walks straight into it.

Jonadab’s guilt. Be clear about what Jonadab has done. A prince has told him he is consumed with wanting his own half-sister, and he does not talk him out of it, warn anybody or walk away. He supplies a method at once. He never lays a hand on her; he does not have to.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 7–19 — He Would Not Listen to Her
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A king’s daughter is betrayed by every man around her, and refuses to let the wrong be hidden. Sent by her father, Tamar cooks for her “sick” brother, who clears the room and seizes her (vv. 7–11). She pleads from the law of Israel, from her own future and from his good, and offers any other way, but he will not listen and, being stronger, violates her (vv. 12–14). At once his desire turns to hatred, and he has her thrown out and the door bolted, a second wrong she names as worse than the first (vv. 15–17). She tears the robe of the king’s virgin daughters and goes away crying aloud (vv. 18–19).
verseByVerse.theology: Her speech is the most intelligent thing anybody says in this chapter. She argues from the law, from what it will do to her, from what it will do to him, and then offers him a way out that costs her everything and saves them both: ask the king.
verseByVerse.examples: What it does not mean: the silence later forced on Tamar by others is neither consent nor peace. She protested in words, and then in the street, and Scripture keeps both protests on record.

verseByVerse.quote: Then David sent home to Tamar, saying, "Go to your brother Amnon's house and prepare food for him." So Tamar went to her brother Amnon's house, where he was lying down. And she took dough and kneaded it and made cakes in his sight and baked the cakes. And she took the pan and emptied it out before him, but he refused to eat. And Amnon said, "Send out everyone from me." So everyone went out from him. Then Amnon said to Tamar, "Bring the food into the chamber, that I may eat from your hand." And Tamar took the cakes she had made and brought them into the chamber to Amnon her brother.
verseByVerse.commentary:
David sends his daughter into the trap, and every ordinary kindness and every ordinary authority is turned to Amnon’s purpose.

Then David sent home to Tamar. The father sends her. He suspects nothing, which is not much of a defence, because the whole scheme depended on his not asking why a grown prince needed his half-sister to come and cook in his bedroom. He has never had to think hard about Amnon.

She took dough and kneaded it. The writer slows down over the cooking: she kneads the dough, makes the cakes in his sight, bakes them and empties out the pan. Amnon had asked for exactly this, so that he could watch her (v. 6). She is doing an ordinary kindness for a brother she believes is ill, and every detail of it is being used against her.

Send out everyone from me. Amnon refuses the food, which was never the point, and clears the room. There were others present until now, servants at least, and a prince ordering a room emptied is not questioned. Then that I may eat from your hand draws her alone into the inner chamber. Every stage has used ordinary authority, a father’s and then a prince’s, to arrange something nobody would have allowed if they had seen what it was.

verseByVerse.quote: But when she brought them near him to eat, he took hold of her and said to her, "Come, lie with me, my sister." She answered him, "No, my brother, do not violate me, for such a thing is not done in Israel; do not do this outrageous thing. As for me, where could I carry my shame? And as for you, you would be as one of the outrageous fools in Israel. Now therefore, please speak to the king, for he will not withhold me from you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Seized by her brother, Tamar pleads with him from the law of Israel, from what it will do to her, from what it will make of him, and finally by offering any other way. It is the best speech in the chapter, made by someone with a hand already on her.

Come, lie with me, my sister. He uses the word sister while he does it. She answers my brother, reminding him what they are to each other.

Such a thing is not done in Israel. Her first argument is not personal: she appeals to what the nation is. Outrageous thing translates nebalah, the strong word used of the worst offences in Israel, of the atrocity at Gibeah (Judges 19:23) and of Achan’s sin (Joshua 7:15). Her words also echo the story of Dinah, where Shechem’s act is called “an outrageous thing in Israel … for such a thing must not be done” (Genesis 34:7). That story ended with Dinah’s full brothers taking revenge with the sword, and a reader who catches the echo can already guess what Tamar’s full brother will do (vv. 28–29).

Where could I carry my shame? Then herself. In that society a woman in her position had no future after this. It is not a figure of speech: she is describing the rest of her life, and verse 20 proves her right.

As one of the outrageous fools in Israel. Then him. Standing in a closed room with a man stronger than she is, she takes the trouble to tell him what this will make of him. The word is nabal, the name of the fool of 1 Samuel 25, and it does not mean a silly man but a man with no moral sense at all.

Please speak to the king, for he will not withhold me from you. Last of all she offers to marry him: to spend her life with the man now holding her, if only he will not do it this way. She has appealed to the law, to her own future, to his good and to another way of getting what he says he wants. There is nothing left to say.

Could Tamar have married Amnon? The law forbade a man to marry his half-sister (Leviticus 18:9, 11; 20:17), so this is most likely not a legal proposal but a desperate plea, anything that might stop him. Some have suggested that royal practice differed from the law, but the text does not say so. What is not in doubt is what it cost her to say it.

verseByVerse.quote: But he would not listen to her, and being stronger than she, he violated her and lay with her.
verseByVerse.commentary:
None of her pleading reaches him: he will not listen, and being stronger than she, he rapes her.

But he would not listen to her. Literally “he would not listen to her voice”, the first of two refusals (v. 16). Appetite that has already decided does not hear counsel. Proverbs describes a young man walking a road he has been warned about, deaf the whole way, “as an ox goes to the slaughter” (Proverbs 7:22). It could have been written about this room.

Being stronger than she, he violated her and lay with her. Three facts in the order the writer chose: he was stronger, he violated her, he lay with her. The verb translated violated means to humble or force, and the sentence leaves no doubt that this was rape. There is no description and no lingering. It is stated the way a report is stated, and the brevity is a kind of respect.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Amnon hated her with very great hatred, so that the hatred with which he hated her was greater than the love with which he had loved her. And Amnon said to her, "Get up! Go!" But she said to him, "No, my brother, for this wrong in sending me away is greater than the other that you did to me." But he would not listen to her.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The moment it is done, Amnon’s desire turns to hatred, and he throws out the woman he said he loved, a second wrong that Tamar rightly calls worse than the first. What he had was never love, and this verse proves it.

Amnon hated her with very great hatred. The hatred comes at once, not later or after reflection: the sentence puts it straight after the act. It was appetite, as the writer told us in verse 2, and appetite satisfied does not become affection; it becomes disgust, and the disgust has to be aimed at someone. He will not aim it at himself, so he aims it at her. She is now the evidence: every time he looks at her he sees what he did, and he calls that hating her. Scripture states this mark of such sin here once, exactly. A man will wreck a family to get a thing, find it turned to ash moments after he has it, and be unable to bear the person he took, because she is the proof of what he did.

When love is really appetite. Our culture tends to treat strong desire as the truest thing about a person: what you feel intensely must be real, and to deny it is to deny yourself. Amnon felt intensely; he made himself ill with it. But love wants the good of the beloved, while appetite wants the beloved for itself and, once it has had her, has no further use for her. That is why the turn from desire to hatred takes one verse. The modern world has rightly learned to ask whether a person consented, and Tamar plainly did not. The chapter asks a further question, what the desire was for, which consent alone cannot answer. Scripture neither despises desire nor simply obeys it; it judges it by the love it serves (see the note on Song of Songs 8:6–7).

Love that gives itself. The opposite of Amnon’s way is shown in a single clause: “Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her” (Ephesians 5:25). Appetite takes the other person and keeps itself. Love gives itself and keeps the other.

Get up! Go! Two words in Hebrew, barked at her.

This wrong in sending me away is greater than the other. Her argument is legal, and it is correct. The law required a man who violated an unbetrothed virgin to marry her and never divorce her (Deuteronomy 22:28–29). Harsh as that sounds to modern ears, its purpose was to protect the woman, giving her a household and a standing instead of leaving her discarded, and a parallel law lets her father refuse the marriage (Exodus 22:16–17), so it was, most think, a protection she could claim, not a sentence laid on her. Being put out of the door is a second destruction on top of the first, and she says so.

But he would not listen to her. The second refusal is recorded in the same words as the first (v. 14). The writer will not let it be missed.

verseByVerse.quote: He called the young man who served him and said, "Put this woman out of my presence and bolt the door after her." Now she was wearing a long robe with sleeves, for thus were the virgin daughters of the king dressed. So his servant put her out and bolted the door after her. And Tamar put ashes on her head and tore the long robe that she wore. And she laid her hand on her head and went away, crying aloud as she went.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Amnon has her thrown out like rubbish, and Tamar tears the robe of a king’s virgin daughter and goes through the city mourning aloud, refusing to let the wrong be hidden.

Put this woman out of my presence. He will not use her name or speak to her. He gives an order about an object to a servant, in her hearing; the Hebrew says only this.

Bolt the door after her. The bolting is told twice, in the order and in the doing (vv. 17–18). To anyone in the house it would look as though she were the one being thrown out for some fault of her own, and Amnon means it to look that way. The door shuts her out of the life she had, and shuts him in with what he has done.

A long robe with sleeves. The writer stops the story to tell us what she is wearing, which means it matters. It was the dress of the king’s unmarried daughters, a uniform anyone in Jerusalem would recognise at a distance, and the same phrase describes the coat Joseph’s father gave him (Genesis 37:3).

Tamar put ashes on her head. Everything she does is a recognised act of mourning, done in the street: ashes on the head, the garment torn, the hand laid on the head, and the loud crying that was the sound of grief. She tears the robe that says she is a virgin daughter of the king, because she is not one any more, and she lets everybody see it.

Crying aloud as she went. She had every reason to go home quietly. Instead she made it impossible for the household to pretend: whatever was going to be done about this, it would not be done in the dark. It is a brave thing, and it is the last free act she performs in the book.

Uncertain wording. The rare Hebrew phrase behind long robe with sleeves occurs only here and in the story of Joseph (Genesis 37:3), and its exact meaning is not known. Older English versions made it a garment “of divers colours” here and a coat “of many colours” for Joseph. The second word seems to refer to the extremities, the palms or the soles, so many modern versions think of a robe reaching to the wrists and ankles; others suggest it was richly ornamented. Whatever its exact look, the writer tells us what mattered: it marked her as a virgin daughter of the king.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 20–29 — Absalom Spoke to Amnon Neither Good Nor Bad
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Silence in the face of wrong becomes the seedbed of murder. Absalom takes Tamar into his house but tells her to keep quiet, and she lives there desolate (v. 20). David is very angry and does nothing (v. 21). Absalom says nothing to Amnon, good or bad, because he hates him (v. 22). Two years later he holds a sheepshearing feast, invites the king knowing he will decline, and presses until David sends Amnon and all the king’s sons (vv. 23–27). When Amnon is merry with wine, Absalom’s servants strike him down at their master’s command, and the other princes flee (vv. 28–29).
verseByVerse.theology: Two silences sit side by side: a father's, who has lost the standing to speak, and a brother's, who is waiting. Neither of them is peace.
verseByVerse.examples: Anger that does nothing is not justice. David felt the right thing and did nothing with it, and the cost of his inaction fell on the one person in the story who had done no wrong.

verseByVerse.quote: And her brother Absalom said to her, "Has Amnon your brother been with you? Now hold your peace, my sister. He is your brother; do not take this to heart." So Tamar lived, a desolate woman, in her brother Absalom's house.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Absalom takes his sister in but tells her to keep quiet, and Tamar lives on in his house, a desolate woman. His words do several things at once, and only one of them is kind.

Has Amnon your brother been with you? It is hardly a question. The torn robe and the ashes have told him, and the fact that he names Amnon unprompted suggests he had some idea this was coming.

Hold your peace, my sister. He takes her in, and that is real: she lives in his house from this day. But he has just watched his sister walk through the city tearing her clothes, and his instruction is silence: not “I will get justice for you”, not “we are going to the king”, but be quiet, do not take this to heart. Two things are probably true at once. A brother is trying to spare her more public exposure, and a man who has already decided what he will do needs the matter to go quiet so that he can do it in two years’ time. Either way, she is silenced by the person protecting her.

A desolate woman. This is the writer’s own word for her, and the last thing said about her own life. The Hebrew shomemah is not a word about feelings; it is used of ruined cities and of land laid waste after an army has been through it. Tamar is the town Amnon sacked, and she stays that way. Her name appears once more: Absalom calls his daughter Tamar, and of that daughter it is said, she was a beautiful woman (14:27). Nothing else. No marriage, no children, no restoration.

Not left behind. She is the only person in the chapter who behaves well throughout: arguing rightly, warning the offender for his own sake, offering a way out, protesting the second wrong as well as the first and refusing to let it be hidden. And she is the one whose life is over. The narrative moves on to her brothers, because its subject is the house of David and the judgment on it. But the book knows what was done to her: it records her arguments in full, calls the deed nebalah, and calls her desolate. The story moves on without her; the book does not treat her as unimportant.

If this has happened to you. If you have suffered what Tamar suffered, hear what this chapter says. The shame is Amnon’s, not hers: Scripture calls the deed nebalah and calls him the fool, and never hints that she was to blame. She said no, and it is recorded. Her brother told her to keep quiet and her father did nothing, and the book sets down both as failures, not as wisdom. Abuse is never to be tolerated, and never hushed up for the sake of a family’s name, a church’s reputation or anyone’s comfort. If you are in danger, seek safety at once, and tell someone who can act: the police, a doctor, a trusted pastor or elder. And the Son of David is not like David here. He sees what was done, he does not look away, and he himself endured the cross, despising the shame (Hebrews 12:2), so that shame would not have the last word over anyone who trusts him.

verseByVerse.quote: When King David heard of all these things, he was very angry.
verseByVerse.commentary:
David hears it all and is very angry, and then does nothing, because every rebuke he might give Amnon had already been spoken to him.

He was very angry. That is the whole of the father’s response: anger, and nothing after it. No summons, no judgment, no protection ordered for Tamar, no punishment, not even a recorded word to Amnon. The king who administered justice and equity to all his people (8:15) hears that his firstborn has raped his daughter, becomes very angry, and does nothing.

What could David say? Favouritism may have played its part (see the textual note below), but beneath it lay a deeper reason, which everybody in the palace knew. What was David going to say to Amnon? That a king’s son may not take a woman he has decided he wants? That a man in power may not use it to get a woman into a private room? Every sentence available to him had already been spoken to him, by a prophet, in this same palace, about a woman called Bathsheba. He is not silent because he does not care. He is silent because he has disqualified himself, and his sons know it. The judgment of chapter 12 is not that God strikes David down; it is that David can no longer act.

Lost standing. That is what a father can lose: not necessarily his children’s love or obedience, but the standing to say “this is wrong” and be heard. Yet silence was not his only course. The way back was the one he had already been shown: to own his sin before his sons, trust the mercy that had put it away (12:13), and then act for his daughter as a king and a father should.

Textual note. The Hebrew text stops at very angry. The Greek Septuagint and a manuscript of Samuel found at Qumran both carry an additional clause that supplies the reason: “But he would not punish his son Amnon, because he loved him, since he was his firstborn.” Whether or not that sentence belongs in the text, it describes what happened.

verseByVerse.quote: But Absalom spoke to Amnon neither good nor bad, for Absalom hated Amnon, because he had violated his sister Tamar.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Absalom’s two years of polite silence towards Amnon are not forgiveness but murder in preparation.

Neither good nor bad. Not a word in either direction for two full years. He does not accuse him, quarrel with him or conspicuously avoid him. He is civil, and at every family occasion behaves exactly as a brother behaves. The writer explains it in the same sentence: for Absalom hated Amnon.

Planned silence. This is not restraint, and it is not forgiveness. It is a man who has decided on murder and understands that the way to arrange one is to give nobody the slightest reason to remember his grievance. Two years of speaking neither good nor bad is a colder thing than a rage. There may also have been more than revenge in it. Amnon was the firstborn and heir; Chileab, the second son (3:3), is never heard of again and had probably died; so with Amnon dead, Absalom stood next in line for the throne, as the coming chapters show he knew.

Hatred kept quiet. The law had named exactly this: “You shall not hate your brother in your heart, but you shall reason frankly with your neighbor” (Leviticus 19:17). Absalom does neither, and Jesus traced murder back to this very place, anger nursed in the heart (Matthew 5:21–22). A grievance kept silent and fed is not peace. The safer course is the frank word, spoken early.

verseByVerse.quote: After two full years Absalom had sheepshearers at Baal-hazor, which is near Ephraim, and Absalom invited all the king's sons. And Absalom came to the king and said, "Behold, your servant has sheepshearers. Please let the king and his servants go with your servant." But the king said to Absalom, "No, my son, let us not all go, lest we be burdensome to you." He pressed him, but he would not go but gave him his blessing.
verseByVerse.commentary:
After two years Absalom holds a sheepshearing feast and invites the king, needing him to decline.

After two full years. Long enough for Amnon to stop watching him and for the court to suppose the matter forgotten. Baal-hazor was probably a hill about fifteen miles north of Jerusalem, near a town called Ephraim, where Absalom kept his flocks: far enough away for a feast of several days, and far from the king.

Absalom had sheepshearers. Sheepshearing was the great festival of the shepherd’s year, a harvest feast with a great deal to eat and more to drink. Nabal was holding one when David’s men came asking for provisions (1 Samuel 25:2–8).

Please let the king and his servants go. Absalom invites the king first, and whether he meant it is debated. What is certain is that he needed a refusal, because David’s presence would have made the thing impossible, and he needed the refusal to come from the king’s side. David declines out of consideration, lest we be burdensome to you, and sends his blessing instead. It is the answer Absalom was counting on, and the king’s courtesy becomes the opening for the request that follows.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Absalom said, "If not, please let my brother Amnon go with us." And the king said to him, "Why should he go with you?" But Absalom pressed him until he let Amnon and all the king's sons go with him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Absalom asks for Amnon instead, and David, uneasy enough to ask why, gives way all the same.

If not, please let my brother Amnon go. This was the request the first one was built to set up. If the king would not come himself, it was natural for the crown prince to represent him; asking for Amnon looked like an honour, not a trap.

Why should he go with you? David asks the right question. Somewhere in him is still an instinct that this is odd: of all the sons, this is the one Absalom has singled out, and there is a reason these two should not be alone together in the country.

But Absalom pressed him. David asks the question and does not press it; he gives way, as he gave way when Amnon asked for Tamar. Twice in this chapter he has been asked for something that should have made him uneasy, and twice he has handed over a child to a request he did not examine.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Absalom commanded his servants, "Mark when Amnon's heart is merry with wine, and when I say to you, 'Strike Amnon,' then kill him. Do not fear; have I not commanded you? Be courageous and be valiant." So the servants of Absalom did to Amnon as Absalom had commanded. Then all the king's sons arose, and each mounted his mule and fled.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Absalom has Amnon killed at the feast, dressing a drunken murder in the language of the battlefield and leaving the deed to his servants. The first blow of the sword Nathan foretold (12:10) falls inside the king’s house.

Mark when Amnon’s heart is merry with wine. The plan itself is squalid: wait until the man is drunk, and strike him at the table.

Be courageous and be valiant. Absalom dresses it in the vocabulary of war: Do not fear; have I not commanded you? These are words spoken to soldiers before an engagement, words given to Joshua (Joshua 1:9) and used by Joab before battle with the Ammonites (10:12), and here they steady a group of servants for the murder of an unarmed man at a party. He is giving them, and himself, an excuse: this is not an assassination but a brave deed done under orders. And note who takes the risk. He commands and they do it, exactly as David wrote a letter and Joab did it (11:14–17). Sin is learned in families, and the method as well as the appetite is passing from father to sons.

Each mounted his mule and fled. The other princes ride for their lives, and they are right to: they have just watched one brother kill another, and none of them knows where it stops. The mule was the mount of the royal family in David’s time. Absalom will ride one to his death (18:9), and Solomon will be made king riding David’s own (1 Kings 1:33). The princes flee on the animals that mark them as the king’s sons.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 30–39 — The Spirit of the King Longed to Go Out
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The chapter ends in grief, flight and a longing with no justice in it. A rumour tells David that all his sons are dead, and he lies on the ground in mourning (vv. 30–31). Jonadab, who knew all along, assures him that only Amnon is dead, by Absalom’s long-settled intent, and the returning princes prove him right (vv. 32–36). Absalom flees to his grandfather Talmai, king of Geshur, and stays three years (vv. 37–38). As grief for Amnon fades, the king’s heart longs for the son who murdered him (v. 39). Nothing has been judged, and nothing has been healed.
verseByVerse.theology: The house of David weeps together for the first time in the chapter, over a death that every one of its failures helped to cause.
verseByVerse.examples: The chapter ends with a father grieving a murdered son and longing for the murderer, and the next four chapters grow out of that longing.

verseByVerse.quote: While they were on the way, news came to David, "Absalom has struck down all the king's sons, and not one of them is left." Then the king arose and tore his garments and lay on the earth. And all his servants who were standing by tore their garments. But Jonadab the son of Shimeah, David's brother, said, "Let not my lord suppose that they have killed all the young men, the king's sons, for Amnon alone is dead. For by the command of Absalom this has been determined from the day he violated his sister Tamar. Now therefore let not my lord the king so take it to heart as to suppose that all the king's sons are dead, for Amnon alone is dead." But Absalom fled. And the young man who kept the watch lifted up his eyes and looked, and behold, many people were coming from the road behind him by the side of the mountain. And Jonadab said to the king, "Behold, the king's sons have come; as your servant said, so it has come about." And as soon as he had finished speaking, behold, the king's sons came and lifted up their voice and wept. And the king also and all his servants wept very bitterly. But Absalom fled and went to Talmai the son of Ammihud, king of Geshur. And David mourned for his son day after day. So Absalom fled and went to Geshur, and was there three years. And the spirit of the king longed to go out to Absalom, because he was comforted about Amnon, since he was dead.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A false report that all the king’s sons are dead is corrected by Jonadab, who knew all along what was coming; Absalom flees to his grandfather in Geshur, and after three years David’s heart longs for the son who murdered his firstborn. Nothing is judged, and nothing is healed.

Not one of them is left. The rumour arrives before the survivors do, and it is wrong. David tears his clothes and lies on the ground, as he lay on the ground while his baby was dying (12:16). The writer is not likely to have chosen the detail by accident.

Jonadab the son of Shimeah. Then Jonadab walks back into the story, and what he says is chilling. Before any survivor arrives he knows the number of dead is one. He knows the name, he knows whose command it was, and he knows the motive and dates it exactly: from the day he violated his sister Tamar. This is the man who wrote the plan that put Tamar in that bedroom. He has spent two years watching Absalom say neither good nor bad, understanding perfectly what the silence meant, and he said nothing, not to David and not to Amnon, his friend, whom he could have warned. Now he steps forward with the correct information at the moment when it makes him look indispensable to a grieving king.

What crafty means. The writer called him crafty in verse 3, and over two years has shown us what the word means. He never once acts. He arranges, he watches, and he is present with the right sentence at the right moment. He is one of the most quietly frightening figures in the book, and he never touches anybody. He says Amnon alone is dead twice, which is the only kindness he offers, and as your servant said, so it has come about: he cannot help pointing out that he was right. Then the house of David weeps together, the only thing in this chapter they do together.

Talmai the son of Ammihud, king of Geshur. Talmai is Absalom’s grandfather: his mother Maacah was Talmai’s daughter (3:3). So the murderer goes to his mother’s father, a foreign king beyond David’s reach. He has somewhere to go because his father married a foreign princess years before, probably for political reasons.

The spirit of the king longed to go out to Absalom. The last verse of the chapter is one of the saddest sentences about David anywhere. Three years pass. The grief for Amnon fades (the writer says so flatly, and it is what grief does), and what is left is longing for the son who is alive. Set that beside what he did about Tamar. He was very angry about his daughter and did nothing; he mourned his firstborn and then stopped; and what remains, three years on, is a father’s ache for the son who murdered the other one.

Nothing resolved. There is no justice anywhere in this. Amnon was never punished and is now beyond punishment. Absalom has not been tried, charged, pardoned or condemned; he is simply out of the country. Tamar is in a house, desolate, and nobody has mentioned her since verse 20. The king of Israel, whose task was justice for all his people, cannot bring himself to do anything about a rape and a murder in his own family, and misses the murderer. The next chapter is Joab noticing that longing and deciding to use it.

A Father who does both. David could neither judge his son nor truly be reconciled to him; he could only long. The gospel shows a Father whose love for the banished is not weaker than David’s, but who does not leave justice undone. At the cross he shows himself “just and the justifier of the one who has faith in Jesus” (Romans 3:26).

Uncertain wording. The Hebrew of verse 39 is compressed. The verb can mean to long or pine for, but also to be spent or come to an end, so some translate it that David’s anger, or his urge to march out against Absalom, came to an end. Most English versions read it as longing, which fits the opening of the next chapter (14:1), though that verse is itself not quite certain (see the note there). On either reading, David’s grief has faded and Absalom is on his mind.
verseByVerse.note: Geshur was a small kingdom north-east of the Sea of Galilee, home of Absalom’s mother.

keyVerse.quote: Then Amnon hated her with very great hatred, so that the hatred with which he hated her was greater than the love with which he had loved her.
keyVerse.note: One sentence exposes what Amnon had called love. Appetite that has had what it wanted has no further use for the person, and turns its disgust on its victim instead of on itself. Set beside the Son of David, who loved his bride and gave himself up for her, the verse shows the whole difference between a love that takes and a love that gives.

13.reflection:
Amnon called his feeling love, yet it turned to hatred the moment it was satisfied (vv. 1–2, 15). How can we tell love from appetite, in ourselves and in our culture? What does Christ’s self-giving love (Ephesians 5:25) show us?

Jonadab never touched Tamar, but he supplied the plan, and for two years he watched the murder coming and said nothing (vv. 3–5, 32–33). In what ways can we share in wrongs we never commit with our own hands?

Tamar’s brother told her to keep quiet, and her father was very angry but did nothing (vv. 20–21). Why do families and churches so often hush up wrongs? What would it look like to protect the wronged instead of a reputation?

David had lost the standing to rebuke his son because of his own sin. What does this teach about the reach of our sins into other people’s lives? Where does the gospel offer a way back to someone who feels disqualified from speaking?

14.title: Joab's Stratagem; Absalom's Return
14.text: <sup>1</sup>Now Joab the son of Zeruiah knew that the king's heart went out to Absalom.<sup>2</sup>And Joab sent to Tekoa and brought from there a wise woman and said to her, "Pretend to be a mourner and put on mourning garments. Do not anoint yourself with oil, but behave like a woman who has been mourning many days for the dead.<sup>3</sup>Go to the king and speak thus to him." So Joab put the words in her mouth.<sup>4</sup>When the woman of Tekoa came to the king, she fell on her face to the ground and paid homage and said, "Save me, O king."<sup>5</sup>And the king said to her, "What is your trouble?" She answered, "Alas, I am a widow; my husband is dead.<sup>6</sup>And your servant had two sons, and they quarreled with one another in the field. There was no one to separate them, and one struck the other and killed him.<sup>7</sup>And now the whole clan has risen against your servant, and they say, 'Give up the man who struck his brother, that we may put him to death for the life of his brother whom he killed.' And so they would destroy the heir also. Thus they would quench my coal that is left and leave to my husband neither name nor remnant on the face of the earth."<sup>8</sup>Then the king said to the woman, "Go to your house, and I will give orders concerning you."<sup>9</sup>And the woman of Tekoa said to the king, "On me be the guilt, my lord the king, and on my father's house; let the king and his throne be guiltless."<sup>10</sup>The king said, "If anyone says anything to you, bring him to me, and he shall never touch you again."<sup>11</sup>Then she said, "Please let the king invoke the LORD your God, that the avenger of blood kill no more, and my son be not destroyed." He said, "As the LORD lives, not one hair of your son shall fall to the ground."<sup>12</sup>Then the woman said, "Please let your servant speak a word to my lord the king." He said, "Speak."<sup>13</sup>And the woman said, "Why then have you planned such a thing against the people of God? For in giving this decision the king convicts himself, inasmuch as the king does not bring his banished one home again.<sup>14</sup>We must all die; we are like water spilled on the ground, which cannot be gathered up again. But God will not take away life, and he devises means so that the banished one will not remain an outcast.<sup>15</sup>Now I have come to say this to my lord the king because the people have made me afraid, and your servant thought, 'I will speak to the king; it may be that the king will perform the request of his servant.<sup>16</sup>For the king will hear and deliver his servant from the hand of the man who would destroy me and my son together from the heritage of God.'<sup>17</sup>And your servant thought, 'The word of my lord the king will set me at rest,' for my lord the king is like the angel of God to discern good and evil. The LORD your God be with you!"<sup>18</sup>Then the king answered the woman, "Do not hide from me anything I ask you." And the woman said, "Let my lord the king speak."<sup>19</sup>The king said, "Is the hand of Joab with you in all this?" The woman answered and said, "As surely as you live, my lord the king, one cannot turn to the right hand or to the left from anything that my lord the king has said. It was your servant Joab who commanded me; it was he who put all these words in the mouth of your servant.<sup>20</sup>In order to change the course of things your servant Joab did this. But my lord has wisdom like the wisdom of the angel of God to know all things that are on the earth."<sup>21</sup>Then the king said to Joab, "Behold now, I grant this; go, bring back the young man Absalom."<sup>22</sup>And Joab fell on his face to the ground and paid homage and blessed the king. And Joab said, "Today your servant knows that I have found favor in your sight, my lord the king, in that the king has granted the request of his servant."<sup>23</sup>So Joab arose and went to Geshur and brought Absalom to Jerusalem.<sup>24</sup>And the king said, "Let him dwell apart in his own house; he is not to come into my presence." So Absalom lived apart in his own house and did not come into the king's presence.<sup>25</sup>Now in all Israel there was no one so much to be praised for his handsome appearance as Absalom. From the sole of his foot to the crown of his head there was no blemish in him.<sup>26</sup>And when he cut the hair of his head (for at the end of every year he used to cut it; when it was heavy on him, he cut it), he weighed the hair of his head, two hundred shekels by the king's weight.<sup>27</sup>There were born to Absalom three sons, and one daughter whose name was Tamar. She was a beautiful woman.<sup>28</sup>So Absalom lived two full years in Jerusalem, without coming into the king's presence.<sup>29</sup>Then Absalom sent for Joab, to send him to the king, but Joab would not come to him. And he sent a second time, but Joab would not come.<sup>30</sup>Then he said to his servants, "See, Joab's field is next to mine, and he has barley there; go and set it on fire." So Absalom's servants set the field on fire.<sup>31</sup>Then Joab arose and went to Absalom at his house and said to him, "Why have your servants set my field on fire?"<sup>32</sup>Absalom answered Joab, "Behold, I sent word to you, 'Come here, that I may send you to the king, to ask, "Why have I come from Geshur? It would be better for me to be there still." Now therefore let me go into the presence of the king, and if there is guilt in me, let him put me to death.'"<sup>33</sup>Then Joab went to the king and told him, and he summoned Absalom. So he came to the king and bowed himself on his face to the ground before the king, and the king kissed Absalom.
14.overview:
Where we are. Absalom has spent three years in Geshur since he had Amnon murdered, and chapter 13 ended with David’s grief for his firstborn fading into longing for the son who killed him. Joab notices, and acts.

The message. A true word about God’s mercy can be used to bring about what God has not approved. Joab borrows Nathan’s method, a story that makes the king pass judgment on himself, but for his own purpose, and his hired speaker says one of the great sentences of the Old Testament: God “devises means so that the banished one will not remain an outcast” (v. 14). David brings Absalom home with no justice, no repentance and no real reconciliation, and the half-measure ends in a kiss with not one word spoken.

Why it was said. The sword Nathan foretold was now working through David’s house (see the introduction), and Israel needed to see how the rebellion of chapters 15 to 18 grew: not only from Absalom’s ambition, but from a king who would neither judge nor forgive, and from advisers who told him what he wanted to hear.

How the chapter makes its case. Joab hires a wise woman of Tekoa, dresses her as a long-grieving widow and scripts her (vv. 1–3). She brings the king the case of a widow whose one son killed the other and whose clan now demands the survivor’s life, and presses him until he swears by the LORD to protect the killer (vv. 4–11). Then she turns the case on the king’s own banished son, speaks of water spilled on the ground and of the God who devises means, and, asked directly, admits that Joab sent her (vv. 12–20). David lets Joab bring Absalom home but will not see him, and the narrator pauses on Absalom’s beauty, his heavy hair and his daughter Tamar (vv. 21–27). After two years Absalom burns Joab’s barley to force a hearing, dares the king to judge him, and is received with a kiss (vv. 28–33).

Where it leads. The chapter leads to Christ by promise and by contrast. The woman’s sentence is truer than she knew: God did not accept the loss of his banished people but devised the means of bringing them home, and the means was his own Son, who has reconciled us “in his body of flesh by his death” (Colossians 1:22). Yet God’s means, unlike David’s, deal with the sin instead of ignoring it: justice is done at the cross, and the sinner comes home in repentance. David’s wordless kiss looks like the father’s kiss in Jesus’ parable (Luke 15:20), but there the son had come home saying, “Father, I have sinned” (Luke 15:21), and the kiss sealed a real return.

For us. Test the words that move us, not only by how true or how well put they are, but by who sent them and what they are being used for. Do not mistake distance for peace, or a welcome without repentance for love. The God who devised such costly means for our return gives us the courage, by his Spirit, to have the honest conversation David never had.
14.theology:
Nathan's method, Joab's purpose (vv. 1-20). A petitioner, a case that is not what it appears, a king who gives judgment and finds it applies to him: it is chapter 12 repeated deliberately, and the only difference is who sent her. Nathan told David what he did not want to hear, and he submitted; Joab told him what he did want to hear, and he went along. The first produced repentance; the second will produce a rebellion. The test of a word that reaches us is not how skilfully it is put, or even whether it moves us, but whether it comes from God and leads us towards him. A word we are glad to hear deserves at least as much scrutiny as one we resent.

Water spilled on the ground (v. 14). Death is beyond human recovery, and much of human religion is an attempt to gather up the water. God did not accept the loss and did not leave it to us: he devised a means, and it cost him his Son (Col. 1:21-22). The woman meant only that the dead stay dead, so the living should be spared. The verse means far more than she did: the God who will not let the banished remain outcasts is the God of the whole Bible's story, from the garden of Eden to the heavenly city.

What her argument leaves out. The means God devises deal with sin; they involve a price paid and, on our side, repentance, as David's own restoration in chapter 12 shows. Absalom never repents, here or anywhere. A true sentence about God's mercy can be quoted accurately in the service of an outcome God has not authorised, and that is far more common than open error.

Neither justice nor mercy (v. 24). No trial, no verdict, and no welcome either: a house in Jerusalem and a closed door. Mephibosheth was received at the king's table for nothing more than being Jonathan's son; Absalom is kept outside it, and the in-between that looks like restraint is the one course that guarantees disaster. It is easy to understand. David could not execute his son and could not bear to sit across a table from him, and many parents, friends and churches have made the same choice for the same reasons. But distance that is never discussed is not peace, and it does not heal.

Looks and memory (vv. 25-27). The narrator places Absalom's beauty directly after the closed door, because the country is about to choose this man, and the reader has learned from Saul and Eliab what outward appearance is worth (1 Sam. 16:7). Yet he also named his daughter Tamar: whatever else is true of him, he did not forget what was done to his sister.

Arson, a challenge, and a kiss (vv. 28-33). Absalom learns that destruction gets results, and that others will carry the risk for him. His if there is guilt in me is a challenge, not a confession. And the kiss makes things look right and settles nothing; the very next verse is after this Absalom got himself a chariot and horses, and fifty men to run before him. Set it beside the father in Jesus' parable who runs and kisses his son (Luke 15:20-21): there the son has come home saying I have sinned, and the kiss seals a real return. Here no one has said anything at all.
14.examples:
Then: A general hired an actress, dressed her as a widow and wrote her a speech, and she manoeuvred the king of Israel into swearing a public oath about an imaginary son, and in the middle of the performance said one of the truest sentences in the Old Testament about the mercy of God, in order to get a murderer home without a trial.

Now: Two things, and both are uncomfortable. The first is that a true statement about God can be used for a purpose God has not approved, and the more true it is the better it works. He devises means so that the banished one will not remain an outcast is the gospel, and the means he devises deal with the sin rather than waving it through, which is the part the speech omits. Test not only whether a thing is true, but what it is being used for. And the second is verse 24: David could not bring himself to punish and could not bring himself to forgive, so he chose the middle course, and it looked like restraint and was the only option that could not work. Distance maintained and never discussed is not peace. It is a wound with a lid on it, and the lid comes off. The God who devised means for our own return, at such cost, is the one who gives us the courage, by his Spirit, to have the conversation David never had.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Joab sets out to bring Absalom home by making the king judge his own case. Seeing that David’s mind is on his banished son (v. 1), he hires a wise woman from Tekoa, dresses her as a long-grieving widow and puts the words in her mouth (vv. 2–3). She tells of two sons who fought in a field, one now dead and the other demanded by the whole clan for blood vengeance, which would quench her last coal and wipe out her husband’s name (vv. 4–7). Step by step she presses the king, from a vague promise, to protection, to an oath by the LORD that not one hair of her son shall fall (vv. 8–11).
verseByVerse.theology: The same technique can carry the word of God or a general's scheme. What made Nathan's parable a word from God was not its craft but its sender.
verseByVerse.examples: In everyday life, a promise drawn out under pressure still binds the one who gave it, which is why people who want something from us press for one. David would have done well to stop at his first answer.

verseByVerse.quote: Now Joab the son of Zeruiah knew that the king's heart went out to Absalom.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Joab sees that the king’s mind is set on Absalom, and decides to act on it. The longing with which chapter 13 ended becomes an opening for a man who acts on what he notices.

Joab the son of Zeruiah knew. Zeruiah was David’s sister, so Joab is the king’s nephew as well as his commander. The last verse of chapter 13 said the spirit of the king longed to go out to Absalom. Joab has worked it out, and Joab is a man who acts on what he works out.

Why Joab wants him back. The text does not say, and the honest answer is that we do not know. It may be simple concern for a grieving king he has served for decades. It is more likely political: with Amnon dead, Absalom is the likely heir, and while he is in exile nobody knows who will be the next king. A general has an interest in knowing that. Chapter 18 will show what Joab thinks of Absalom when the man becomes inconvenient, and it does not suggest affection.

Uncertain wording. The Hebrew says only that the king’s heart was “on” Absalom, and some translators read it as “against” him. Either way his son is constantly on his mind, and the rest of the chapter shows how divided that mind is: David lets Absalom come home, but will not see his face for two full years (vv. 24, 28).

verseByVerse.quote: And Joab sent to Tekoa and brought from there a wise woman and said to her, "Pretend to be a mourner and put on mourning garments. Do not anoint yourself with oil, but behave like a woman who has been mourning many days for the dead. Go to the king and speak thus to him." So Joab put the words in her mouth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Joab hires a wise woman, dresses her as a long-grieving widow and puts the words in her mouth: Nathan’s method, without Nathan’s sender.

Joab sent to Tekoa. Tekoa was a village about ten miles south of Jerusalem, the home of Amos more than two centuries later.

A wise woman. In that world this was something like a recognised role: another wise woman, at Abel of Beth-maacah in chapter 20, talks Joab out of destroying her town. These were women known locally for judgment and for the ability to speak well. Joab hires her, dresses her for the part and tells her what to say.

Do not anoint yourself with oil. Oil on the skin and hair was part of ordinary grooming in a dry land, and mourners went without it, as David had while his child was dying, resuming it when the child died (12:20). Joab wants her to look like a woman whose grief is old, not fresh tears but the worn look of many days, because her case must stir a king who has himself been grieving and longing for years (13:37–39).

A familiar pattern. A reader who has been paying attention will recognise what is being set up. A petitioner brings the king a case that is not what it appears to be; the king gives judgment, and the judgment turns out to apply to himself. That is exactly what Nathan did two chapters ago, and it broke David open. The difference is the sender. Nathan came because the LORD sent Nathan to David (12:1); this woman comes because Joab put the words in her mouth. Hold that distinction through the whole chapter. The method is identical and the results could hardly be more different, and the reason is not the method but who sent the messenger.

verseByVerse.quote: When the woman of Tekoa came to the king, she fell on her face to the ground and paid homage and said, "Save me, O king." And the king said to her, "What is your trouble?" She answered, "Alas, I am a widow; my husband is dead. And your servant had two sons, and they quarreled with one another in the field. There was no one to separate them, and one struck the other and killed him. And now the whole clan has risen against your servant, and they say, 'Give up the man who struck his brother, that we may put him to death for the life of his brother whom he killed.' And so they would destroy the heir also. Thus they would quench my coal that is left and leave to my husband neither name nor remnant on the face of the earth."
verseByVerse.commentary:
She brings the king a carefully invented case, a widow whose one son has killed the other and whose clan now demands the killer’s life, built at every point to make him easier to pity than Absalom.

Save me, O king. She comes straight to the king as the last court of appeal, which any subject could do when the elders at home could not or would not protect them. The cry is one word in Hebrew, hoshi‘ah, the word Israel cried to God in trouble and the root of “Hosanna” (Psalm 118:25). The king was meant to be God’s instrument in answering it.

Alas, I am a widow. Every element of the story is chosen. She is a widow, so no man protects her interest. There were two sons and now there is one. The killing happened in a field with nobody to separate them, which makes it a quarrel that went wrong, not a planned murder, with no witnesses to say otherwise. Every detail makes her son easier to excuse than Absalom, who planned his brother’s death for two years, gave the order to servants and had it done at a feast in front of the family.

The whole clan has risen. The clan is invoking blood vengeance, the custom by which a murdered man’s nearest relative put the killer to death. It was real, and the law of Israel regulated it instead of abolishing it. There were cities of refuge precisely for the case she describes, a death without premeditation (Numbers 35:9–15), and the clan is refusing to allow the distinction.

My coal that is left. Then the picture that does the work. A household kept a fire going and banked the coals overnight; if the last coal went out, there was no fire in the morning. One surviving son is the last live coal in a dead man’s house. Put it out and the family is finished: neither name nor remnant, no inheritance, nothing on the earth to show that the man ever lived. It is an argument for the dead husband as much as the living son, and it is beautifully judged.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the king said to the woman, "Go to your house, and I will give orders concerning you." And the woman of Tekoa said to the king, "On me be the guilt, my lord the king, and on my father's house; let the king and his throne be guiltless." The king said, "If anyone says anything to you, bring him to me, and he shall never touch you again." Then she said, "Please let the king invoke the LORD your God, that the avenger of blood kill no more, and my son be not destroyed." He said, "As the LORD lives, not one hair of your son shall fall to the ground."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Pressing step by step, she draws from the king first a promise, then his protection, and at last an oath by the LORD that her son will not be touched, before he sees where it leads.

On me be the guilt. When David promises only to give orders, she offers to carry any guilt herself. Sparing a killer from the avenger could look like leaving blood unpunished, which the law said polluted the land (Numbers 35:33), and she releases the king from that fear before he can voice it.

Not one hair of your son shall fall to the ground. Each answer he gives, she accepts and asks for a little more. The first is vague, a promise to see to it. The second is better, a promise to intervene, and still not enough. So she presses a third time, and there it is: an oath in the name of the LORD, covering every hair of the son’s head, that cannot be taken back. She would not leave without it.

What David does not yet know. He does not yet know what he has done. Nathan’s story took six verses; hers has taken eight, and she has been more thorough, because Nathan needed only a verdict and she needed an oath.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The trap closes, and a true word about God is put to a borrowed use. Holding the king’s oath, the woman turns it on him: he has convicted himself, for he will spare another family’s heir while his own banished son stays in exile (vv. 12–13). Death is like water spilled on the ground, she says, but God devises means so that the banished one will not remain an outcast (v. 14). She flatters the king as one like the angel of God (vv. 15–17), and when he asks whether Joab’s hand is in this, she admits it at once (vv. 18–20). Her sentence is the gospel in small, but her use of it leaves out justice and repentance.
verseByVerse.theology: Whatever use the woman made of it, verse 14 is one of the great sentences of the Old Testament, and it is entirely true. God does not leave the banished where they are; he plans their way home.
verseByVerse.examples: She is challenged only at the end, and then tells the truth at once. A moving story and a little flattery had carried a king a long way before anyone asked who sent them.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the woman said, "Please let your servant speak a word to my lord the king." He said, "Speak." And the woman said, "Why then have you planned such a thing against the people of God? For in giving this decision the king convicts himself, inasmuch as the king does not bring his banished one home again. We must all die; we are like water spilled on the ground, which cannot be gathered up again. But God will not take away life, and he devises means so that the banished one will not remain an outcast. Now I have come to say this to my lord the king because the people have made me afraid, and your servant thought, 'I will speak to the king; it may be that the king will perform the request of his servant. For the king will hear and deliver his servant from the hand of the man who would destroy me and my son together from the heritage of God.' And your servant thought, 'The word of my lord the king will set me at rest,' for my lord the king is like the angel of God to discern good and evil. The LORD your God be with you!" Then the king answered the woman, "Do not hide from me anything I ask you." And the woman said, "Let my lord the king speak." The king said, "Is the hand of Joab with you in all this?" The woman answered and said, "As surely as you live, my lord the king, one cannot turn to the right hand or to the left from anything that my lord the king has said. It was your servant Joab who commanded me; it was he who put all these words in the mouth of your servant. In order to change the course of things your servant Joab did this. But my lord has wisdom like the wisdom of the angel of God to know all things that are on the earth."
verseByVerse.commentary:
She turns the king’s oath on himself: if another family’s heir may be spared, why is the nation’s heir still banished? Then she speaks a sentence that holds the gospel in small, that God devises means to bring the banished home, and uses it to bring back a man who never repents. Asked straight out, she admits that Joab sent her.

Please let your servant speak a word. Having got what she came for, she asks to say one thing more, and the trap closes. The king has just sworn to protect a man he has never met, who killed his own brother in a village he has never visited, on the ground that a family should not lose its heir, while his own heir sits in a foreign country under no sentence at all.

The king convicts himself. By his own judgment, from his own mouth, under oath, he is inconsistent. And she widens it: against the people of God. The succession of the house of David is not a private family matter but a national question, and everybody in Israel knows there is now one obvious heir, and he is in Geshur.

Like water spilled on the ground. Verse 14 deserves to be read slowly. She is arguing that Amnon cannot be brought back, so killing Absalom achieves nothing. But the image is bigger than her argument. Pour a jug of water onto dry ground and try to collect it: you cannot, not most of it, not some of it. It is gone into the dust. That is what death is like, and the picture is exact. Everybody knows it, and everybody spends life not thinking about it.

He devises means. Then the verse turns to hope. God devises means: the verb is about planning, working something out deliberately, and what he works out is a way to bring the banished one home. That sentence is the gospel in Old Testament words, and it should be said plainly.

It cost him his Son. The whole human problem is in the first half of the verse: the water is spilled, the loss cannot be undone, and nobody can gather it up. Much of human religion is an attempt to gather up the water. The second half says that God did not accept the loss and did not leave it to us. He devised a means; it took most of the length of the Bible to arrive, and it cost him his Son. Paul describes it in just these terms: we were alienated and hostile in mind, and have been reconciled, brought back, by the death of Christ (Colossians 1:21–22). The banished do not remain outcasts, because God took the trouble to arrange it.

Who is saying it. And it is being said, at this moment, by a woman in borrowed mourning clothes, reciting a speech written by Joab, to procure the unconditional return of a man who murdered his brother and is never once recorded as sorry. Both things are true, and holding them together is the lesson of the chapter.

The missing price. Here is what her argument leaves out. The means God devises do not simply overlook the sin. They involve a price paid and a sin dealt with, and on the human side they involve repentance. David himself is the proof: he was restored in chapter 12, and the restoration came by way of I have sinned against the LORD (12:13). Absalom says nothing of the kind, here or anywhere; when he finally speaks, in verse 32, what he offers is not repentance but a challenge.

Right theology, wrong use. So the theology is right and the application is wrong, and the warning is serious, because this is far more common than open error. True things about God’s mercy can be quoted accurately in the service of an outcome God has not authorised. The sentence is genuine; the use of it is not.

Like the angel of God. Then the flattery, laid on thickly: like the angel of God to discern good and evil, said here and again in verse 20. It is the kind of thing a king hears often enough to stop noticing, and she uses it to close the deal. There is a bleak irony in it that she cannot have intended. The man being told he is like an angel of God at discerning good and evil has sat for ten verses failing to discern that the woman in front of him is acting.

Is the hand of Joab with you in all this? He works it out and asks straight, and she admits it straight. Give her that: challenged, she does not keep up the pretence, and names Joab at once.

How little it changes. David now knows that the whole thing was staged, that the widow is not a widow, that the two sons never existed and that his general has manoeuvred him into an oath. Nathan’s parable ended with I have sinned. This one ends with David telling Joab to fetch Absalom. He has been manipulated, and he lets it stand, because he wanted the outcome anyway. That is the real difference between the two parables. Nathan told David something he did not want to hear, and David submitted to it. Joab told him something he wanted to hear, and David went along with it. The first produced repentance; the second will produce a rebellion.

Doesn’t a loving God simply welcome everyone home? Many people today believe exactly what this woman argued: God is love, so of course the banished come home, and talk of judgment or repentance only spoils it. It sounds generous. But look where that idea led in this house. David took it, and gave Absalom a return with no reckoning and then a kiss with nothing beneath it, and the result was not reconciliation but rebellion. A welcome that never deals with the wrong is not a deeper love but a thinner one, and it leaves the wronged, Tamar here, out of the story altogether. H. Richard Niebuhr, in The Kingdom of God in America, summed up a whole style of preaching in one sentence: “A God without wrath brought men without sin into a kingdom without judgment through the ministrations of a Christ without a cross.” The gospel is more radical than that, not less. God does bring the banished home, but he devises the means, and the means is a cross, where wrong is not overlooked but borne. That is why his welcome can be free to us without being cheap, and why, unlike David’s kiss, it actually reconciles.

Uncertain wording. The Hebrew of verse 14 is difficult in places, and translations vary. Where the ESV has God will not take away life, the KJV has “neither doth God respect any person”, and others take the clause as saying what God does not desire. The heart of the sentence is not in doubt: God devises means so that the banished one will not remain an outcast.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 21–27 — Let Him Not Come Into My Presence
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: David brings his son home and then shuts the door on him, choosing neither justice nor mercy. He tells Joab to fetch the young man Absalom, and Joab thanks him at length (vv. 21–22). Absalom returns from Geshur, but the king orders that he live apart and not come into his presence (vv. 23–24). The narrator then pauses on Absalom: no one in Israel so praised for his looks, without blemish from head to foot, his yearly haircut weighed for all to know (vv. 25–26). He had three sons, and a daughter he named Tamar, after the sister whose wrong began it all (v. 27).
verseByVerse.theology: Justice was what the case required, and if mercy was to be shown it had to be real: received, restored, welcome at the table. David chooses neither, and the arrangement he does choose is the one guaranteed to feed a proud man's grievance for two years.
verseByVerse.examples: The hair is weighed and recorded without comment. In chapter 18 his head is caught in an oak, very likely by this hair, and he dies there.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the king said to Joab, "Behold now, I grant this; go, bring back the young man Absalom." And Joab fell on his face to the ground and paid homage and blessed the king. And Joab said, "Today your servant knows that I have found favor in your sight, my lord the king, in that the king has granted the request of his servant." So Joab arose and went to Geshur and brought Absalom to Jerusalem. And the king said, "Let him dwell apart in his own house; he is not to come into my presence." So Absalom lived apart in his own house and did not come into the king's presence. Now in all Israel there was no one so much to be praised for his handsome appearance as Absalom. From the sole of his foot to the crown of his head there was no blemish in him. And when he cut the hair of his head (for at the end of every year he used to cut it; when it was heavy on him, he cut it), he weighed the hair of his head, two hundred shekels by the king's weight. There were born to Absalom three sons, and one daughter whose name was Tamar. She was a beautiful woman.
verseByVerse.commentary:
David lets Absalom come home but refuses to see him, giving him neither justice nor mercy, and the narrator pauses on the beauty that will soon win Israel and on the daughter named Tamar.

Bring back the young man Absalom. He is a grown man with a murder behind him, and his father still speaks of him as a youth. Joab thanks the king at length, and it costs him nothing.

He is not to come into my presence. This is the decision that shapes everything that follows. David has brought home a man who arranged the murder of the crown prince, and has neither tried him nor pardoned him. There is no charge and no acquittal; there is a house in Jerusalem and a closed door.

Not justice. Absalom killed Amnon, and there was never a trial, a hearing or a verdict, and nobody has mentioned Tamar again. A king whose one recorded qualification was that he administered justice and equity to all his people (8:15) has now failed to administer any at all, twice, in his own family. And the law left no doubt about a planned killing: it allowed no ransom for the life of a murderer (Numbers 35:31), and its cities of refuge sheltered only one who killed without intent (Numbers 35:11–12), exactly the distinction the woman’s story had blurred.

Not mercy. Nor did he extend mercy. If the man was to be forgiven, then forgive him: receive him, restore him, eat with him. That is what forgiveness is, and Mephibosheth received it from this same king for nothing more than being Jonathan’s son (chapter 9).

The worst of both. Instead there is a third course, the worst available. The man is home, at liberty, in the capital, with a household, time on his hands and a grievance that grows every day, and no way to resolve anything because he cannot get into the room. David’s instinct is not hard to understand. He cannot execute his son, and he cannot bring himself to sit across a table from the man who killed his other son. So he does something in between, which feels like a reasonable compromise and is in fact the one option that guarantees disaster.

In everyday life. Anyone who has managed a broken relationship by keeping the person at arm’s length, not confronting, not restoring, just keeping a distance that never gets discussed, can see here where that leads. An arrangement that looks peaceful while the wrong is left unsettled holds for a while and then comes apart, and the result is worse than the original problem.

No blemish in him. The narrator stops to describe him, which he rarely does. No blemish is the word used of sacrificial animals, and it means physically perfect; there is nobody in the country better looking. The reader has been here before. Saul was so handsome that there was not a man among the people of Israel more handsome than he (1 Samuel 9:2), and when Samuel looked at Eliab and thought, surely this is the one, he was told, man looks on the outward appearance, but the LORD looks on the heart (1 Samuel 16:7). The writer puts the description here, straight after the closed door, because the country is about to choose this man.

He weighed the hair of his head. Then the hair, and the writer weighs it: two hundred shekels. It is a great deal of hair, and the note that he cut it only when it became too heavy to carry is not admiration. A man who weighs his own hair every year and lets people know the figure is telling you something about himself.

The King with no beauty that we should desire him. Israel’s true King would come without Absalom’s advantages: “he had no form or majesty that we should look at him, and no beauty that we should desire him” (Isaiah 53:2). Absalom drew a nation by his looks and led it to ruin; Christ drew no one by his looks, and gave his life for the people who turned away from him.

One daughter whose name was Tamar. He named his daughter after his sister. Nothing else is said. The three sons are not named, and a later verse implies they died (18:18), but the daughter has a name, and it is Tamar, and she is beautiful. That is the only memorial his sister receives in this book, and her brother gave it to her. Whatever else is true of Absalom, and a great deal is, he did not forget what was done to her.
verseByVerse.note: Absalom’s yearly haircut weighed 200 shekels, about 5 pounds.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 28–33 — So He Set the Field on Fire
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A peace is made without repentance or justice, and it settles nothing. For two years Absalom lives in Jerusalem without seeing the king (v. 28). Joab twice ignores his messages, so Absalom has his servants set Joab’s barley on fire, and the commander comes at once (vv. 29–31). Absalom complains that he was better off in Geshur and demands to see the king: if there is guilt in him, let the king put him to death (v. 32). David summons him, Absalom bows to the ground, and the king kisses him, with no recorded word from either man (v. 33).
verseByVerse.theology: Five years after the murder, father and son have still not spoken about it. A silence managed that long does not become peace; it becomes a grievance.
verseByVerse.examples: Real reconciliation names the wrong. David's kiss names nothing, and within a chapter the peace it made has unravelled. The welcome home the gospel offers does name the wrong, and pays for it at the cost of a cross, and that is why it holds.

verseByVerse.quote: So Absalom lived two full years in Jerusalem, without coming into the king's presence. Then Absalom sent for Joab, to send him to the king, but Joab would not come to him. And he sent a second time, but Joab would not come. Then he said to his servants, "See, Joab's field is next to mine, and he has barley there; go and set it on fire." So Absalom's servants set the field on fire. Then Joab arose and went to Absalom at his house and said to him, "Why have your servants set my field on fire?" Absalom answered Joab, "Behold, I sent word to you, 'Come here, that I may send you to the king, to ask, "Why have I come from Geshur? It would be better for me to be there still." Now therefore let me go into the presence of the king, and if there is guilt in me, let him put me to death.'" Then Joab went to the king and told him, and he summoned Absalom. So he came to the king and bowed himself on his face to the ground before the king, and the king kissed Absalom.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Shut out for two years, Absalom burns Joab’s field to force a hearing, dares the king to judge him or receive him, and is kissed without a word spoken on either side: a peace that settles nothing.

Two full years in Jerusalem.
