Add it up: three years in Geshur, two years in Jerusalem behind a closed door, five years since he killed Amnon, and in all that time not one conversation with his father about any of it. Nobody has told him he is forgiven, and nobody has told him he is condemned. There has been no hearing, no sentence, no reconciliation, no explanation. He has simply been managed, and what that does to a proud man over two years is the whole of the next chapter.

Joab would not come to him. Joab, who went to Geshur to fetch him, will not now cross the city to see him. He wanted the heir back in the country; having achieved it, he has no further use for the man and twice leaves his messages unanswered.

Go and set it on fire. So Absalom burns the barley. He is a prince of Israel who cannot get a meeting, and his answer is arson against the commander of the army, destroying a standing crop belonging to a man who has just done him a considerable favour. Note the pattern, for it is the second time: Amnon was killed by Absalom’s servants on Absalom’s order, and the field is burned by Absalom’s servants on Absalom’s order. Absalom gives instructions and other people carry the risk.

What Absalom learns. Joab comes at once, and Absalom has learned something. Two polite requests were ignored; destroying something valuable brought the commander of the army to his door. A man who discovers that so young is dangerous.

It would be better for me to be there still. On its own terms the complaint is fair. In exile he at least knew where he stood; here he does not, and a foreign country was better than his father’s capital with the door shut. David created this, and Absalom is describing accurately what the half-measure feels like from inside.

If there is guilt in me, let him put me to death. This is often read as courage or even repentance, and it is neither. There is guilt in him: he arranged a murder in front of witnesses and fled the country for three years, and no one has ever disputed it. So the offer is not an offer but a challenge, made by a man who knows exactly what his father will do, which is nothing. He has watched David fail to act about Tamar and about Amnon, and he forces the choice: put me on trial, or receive me. He is not saying “I did wrong”; he is saying “either kill me or stop pretending.” Nowhere in this chapter, or anywhere else in the book, is Absalom recorded as sorry for anything.

The king kissed Absalom. The chapter ends with a kiss, the most ambiguous gesture in the book. Look at what does not happen. Nothing is said: no recorded word from either man, no question, no accusation, no confession, no condition. Absalom comes in, goes down on the floor, and is kissed. All that has been achieved is that things now look right. The prince is received at court, the awkwardness is over, and nobody has to explain anything, while Tamar is still in a house somewhere, Amnon is still dead, and nothing whatever has been dealt with. The very next verse begins, After this Absalom got himself a chariot and horses, and fifty men to run before him (15:1).

Not the prodigal’s welcome. The kiss looks like everything a reader wants. It is what the father does in Jesus’ parable, running down the road to his returning son (Luke 15:20). But there the son had come home saying I have sinned, and the kiss sealed a real return. Here there is no repentance behind it and no justice done, and both men know it. The Father’s welcome in the gospel is warmer than David’s, not colder, and it rests on a sin dealt with at the cross, not left unspoken.

Why it does not hold. A surface peace laid over a wound that was never cleaned does not hold. It holds long enough for everyone to relax, and then it comes apart, and here it takes the kingdom with it.

keyVerse.quote: We must all die; we are like water spilled on the ground, which cannot be gathered up again. But God will not take away life, and he devises means so that the banished one will not remain an outcast.
keyVerse.note: In the middle of a staged performance, a hired speaker puts the whole human problem and the whole of God’s answer into two sentences. Death is beyond human recovery, but God does not accept the loss: he plans a way home for the banished, and in Christ that plan cost him his Son. The chapter turns on the gap between this truth and its misuse, for God’s means deal with sin, while David’s welcome for Absalom simply ignored it.

14.reflection:
Joab used Nathan’s method, a story that led the king to judge himself, but the results could hardly have been more different (vv. 1–20; 12:1–13). Why does it matter who sends a message, and not only how skilfully it is put? How can we test the words that move us?

“He devises means so that the banished one will not remain an outcast” (v. 14). How does God’s means of bringing us home in Christ deal with sin, where David’s welcome for Absalom simply ignored it?

David would neither punish Absalom nor forgive him, but kept him at a distance for two years (vv. 24, 28). Where are we tempted to manage a broken relationship by distance that is never discussed? What would an honest conversation require of us?

The chapter ends with a kiss and no words (v. 33). How does it differ from the father’s kiss in Luke 15:20–21? What makes a reconciliation real?

15.title: Absalom's Rebellion and David's Flight
15.text: <sup>1</sup>After this Absalom got himself a chariot and horses, and fifty men to run before him.<sup>2</sup>And Absalom used to rise early and stand beside the way of the gate. And when any man had a dispute to come before the king for judgment, Absalom would call to him and say, "From what city are you?" And when he said, "Your servant is of such and such a tribe in Israel,"<sup>3</sup>Absalom would say to him, "See, your claims are good and right, but there is no man designated by the king to hear you."<sup>4</sup>Then Absalom would say, "Oh that I were judge in the land! Then every man with a dispute or cause might come to me, and I would give him justice."<sup>5</sup>And whenever a man came near to pay homage to him, he would put out his hand and take hold of him and kiss him.<sup>6</sup>Thus Absalom did to all of Israel who came to the king for judgment. So Absalom stole the hearts of the men of Israel.<sup>7</sup>And at the end of four years Absalom said to the king, "Please let me go and pay my vow, which I have vowed to the LORD, in Hebron.<sup>8</sup>For your servant vowed a vow while I lived at Geshur in Aram, saying, 'If the LORD will indeed bring me back to Jerusalem, then I will offer worship to the LORD.'"<sup>9</sup>The king said to him, "Go in peace." So he arose and went to Hebron.<sup>10</sup>But Absalom sent secret messengers throughout all the tribes of Israel, saying, "As soon as you hear the sound of the trumpet, then say, 'Absalom is king at Hebron!'"<sup>11</sup>With Absalom went two hundred men from Jerusalem who were invited guests, and they went in their innocence and knew nothing.<sup>12</sup>And while Absalom was offering the sacrifices, he sent for Ahithophel the Gilonite, David's counselor, from his city Giloh. And the conspiracy grew strong, and the people with Absalom kept increasing.<sup>13</sup>And a messenger came to David, saying, "The hearts of the men of Israel have gone after Absalom."<sup>14</sup>Then David said to all his servants who were with him at Jerusalem, "Arise, and let us flee, or else there will be no escape for us from Absalom. Go quickly, lest he overtake us quickly and bring down ruin on us and strike the city with the edge of the sword."<sup>15</sup>And the king's servants said to the king, "Behold, your servants are ready to do whatever my lord the king decides."<sup>16</sup>So the king went out, and all his household after him. And the king left ten concubines to keep the house.<sup>17</sup>And the king went out, and all the people after him. And they halted at the last house.<sup>18</sup>And all his servants passed by him, and all the Cherethites, and all the Pelethites, and all the six hundred Gittites who had followed him from Gath, passed on before the king.<sup>19</sup>Then the king said to Ittai the Gittite, "Why do you also go with us? Go back and stay with the king, for you are a foreigner and also an exile from your home.<sup>20</sup>You came only yesterday, and shall I today make you wander about with us, since I go I know not where? Go back and take your brothers with you, and may the LORD show steadfast love and faithfulness to you."<sup>21</sup>But Ittai answered the king, "As the LORD lives, and as my lord the king lives, wherever my lord the king shall be, whether for death or for life, there also will your servant be."<sup>22</sup>And David said to Ittai, "Go then, pass on." So Ittai the Gittite passed on with all his men and all the little ones who were with him.<sup>23</sup>And all the land wept aloud as all the people passed by, and the king crossed the brook Kidron, and all the people passed on toward the wilderness.<sup>24</sup>And Abiathar came up, and behold, Zadok came also with all the Levites, bearing the ark of the covenant of God. And they set down the ark of God until the people had all passed out of the city.<sup>25</sup>Then the king said to Zadok, "Carry the ark of God back into the city. If I find favor in the eyes of the LORD, he will bring me back and let me see both it and his dwelling place.<sup>26</sup>But if he says, 'I have no pleasure in you,' behold, here I am, let him do to me what seems good to him."<sup>27</sup>The king also said to Zadok the priest, "Are you not a seer? Go back to the city in peace, with your two sons, Ahimaaz your son, and Jonathan the son of Abiathar.<sup>28</sup>See, I will wait at the fords of the wilderness until word comes from you to inform me."<sup>29</sup>So Zadok and Abiathar carried the ark of God back to Jerusalem, and they remained there.<sup>30</sup>But David went up the ascent of the Mount of Olives, weeping as he went, barefoot and with his head covered. And all the people who were with him covered their heads, and they went up, weeping as they went.<sup>31</sup>And it was told David, "Ahithophel is among the conspirators with Absalom." And David said, "O LORD, please turn the counsel of Ahithophel into foolishness."<sup>32</sup>While David was coming to the summit, where God was worshiped, behold, Hushai the Archite came to meet him with his coat torn and dirt on his head.<sup>33</sup>David said to him, "If you go on with me, you will be a burden to me.<sup>34</sup>But if you return to the city and say to Absalom, 'I will be your servant, O king; as I have been your father's servant in time past, so now I will be your servant,' then you will defeat for me the counsel of Ahithophel.<sup>35</sup>Are not Zadok and Abiathar the priests with you there? So whatever you hear from the king's house, tell it to Zadok and Abiathar the priests.<sup>36</sup>Behold, their two sons are with them there, Ahimaaz, Zadok's son, and Jonathan, Abiathar's son, and by them you shall send to me everything you hear."<sup>37</sup>So Hushai, David's friend, came into the city, just as Absalom was entering Jerusalem.
15.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 14 ended with a kiss: after three years in Geshur and two more shut out of the king’s presence, Absalom was received back by his father (14:33). Nathan had said that the sword would never depart from David’s house (12:10). Amnon is already dead; now the sword is drawn against the king himself.

The message. God’s discipline of his king comes through the king’s own son, and David meets it not by clutching his throne but by putting himself in God’s hands: “let him do to me what seems good to him” (v. 26). The man who steals hearts with flattery gains a kingdom for a few weeks; the man who will not use God, and prays one short prayer, is the one God is keeping. And the rejected king becomes the test of every heart around him: who goes, and who stays.

Why it was said. Israel needed to see that the sorrows of David’s house were the word of the LORD through Nathan coming true, and that the promise of chapter 7 did not rest on the king’s popularity or success (see the introduction). Later readers, in exile and with no king at all, needed the picture of a rejected king leaving his city in tears, and of the God who would bring him back.

How the chapter makes its case. Absalom steals the hearts of Israel at the gate with sympathy that costs him nothing (vv. 1–6), uses a vow as cover, and is proclaimed king at Hebron with Ahithophel at his side (vv. 7–12). David leaves Jerusalem rather than have it fought over, and Ittai the foreigner swears to go with him “whether for death or for life” (vv. 13–23). The ark is sent back, because David will not use God as a charm, and the king climbs the Mount of Olives barefoot and weeping, praying that Ahithophel’s counsel be turned into foolishness (vv. 24–31). At the summit the answer is already walking towards him: Hushai, sent back into the city just as Absalom enters it (vv. 32–37).

Where it leads. The chapter leads to Christ by pattern, and the Gospels trace the same road. A son of David crosses the Kidron and goes up the Mount of Olives in sorrow, betrayed by a trusted friend who ate his bread, with a small loyal company and a surrender to the Father’s will (Psalm 41:9; John 13:18; 18:1; Luke 22:39–42). The pattern also shows the difference: David went up under the consequences of his own sin, while Jesus went up without sin, to bear the sins of others, rebels included. And Ittai’s “whether for death or for life” is the answer every disciple gives to the rejected King.

For us. Be wary of the voice that promises everything and has never had to decide anything. When much is lost, leave the outcome with God, do the next sensible thing, and pray for the one thing that matters most. And when the King is rejected and the crowd has gone the other way, be found walking with him.
15.theology:
A true grievance, aimed (vv. 1-6). Absalom never calls the king unjust, which would be a lie anyone could refute. He names a genuine failure, a kingdom with more cases than one man can hear, and lets every litigant draw the conclusion himself. In four years the writer never shows him judging one case: he promises what nobody could deliver to all of them, and is never tested. The writer's verdict is one word, stole.

Religion as cover, and a father who does not ask (vv. 7-9). He picks the one request his father cannot examine without looking impious, and for the third time in three chapters David hands over something precious to a request he does not look at.

Why Ahithophel went (v. 12). The book never says, but it lays the pieces where a careful reader will find them (23:34; 11:3): he may well have been Bathsheba’s grandfather. Nothing in chapter 11 was ever really over.

A king who gives a city away (vv. 14-23). He will not have Israelites killed over walls he built, and what follows is not panic but a sequence of clear decisions. And the foreigners keep faith: Uriah the Hittite, Obed-edom the Gittite, Ittai the Gittite, each set beside an Israelite who failed at the same point.

The ark goes back (vv. 25-26). Israel once carried the ark into battle as a charm and lost it (1 Sam. 4), and David learned in chapter 6 that it is not equipment. He will not claim to know the outcome either: let him do to me what seems good to him echoes Joab's words before battle with the Ammonites (10:12). Yet in the same breath he sets up his network of priests and runners. Neither cancels the other, and the chapter will not let a reader choose between them.

The road the Son of David would take (v. 30). He crossed the Kidron and went up the Mount of Olives, betrayed by a man who ate at his table, and a psalm of David about betrayal says it: even my close friend in whom I trusted, who ate my bread, has lifted his heel against me (Ps. 41:9), which the Lord Jesus quoted in the upper room about Judas (John 13:18). Jesus went out over the Kidron (John 18:1) and up the Mount of Olives (Luke 22:39). And Ahithophel set his house in order and hanged himself (17:23), the only person in Scripture to die that way apart from the man who betrayed Christ (Matt. 27:5). David went up the hill under the consequences of his own sin; the greater Son of David went up it without sin, to bear the sins of others.

One sentence, aimed where it will be decided (vv. 31-32). David prays about the counsel, not the army, and the next verse begins behold. The prayer is answered not by lightning but by a friend in a torn coat who agrees to walk into a captured city, and the kingdom turns on him.
15.examples:
Then: A king who could have defended the strongest city in the country walked out of it barefoot with his head covered, weeping, and when the priests brought the ark of God out to go with him he sent it back inside, into the hands of the son who wanted him dead, because he would not carry God about as a lucky charm even to keep his throne.

Now: Two things. Recognise Absalom's method, because it is still how such men work: find a real failure, tell everyone their complaint is justified without ever examining it, promise what you will never be required to deliver, and behave as though you were one of the crowd. The test of the man offering to fix it is whether he has ever decided anything that cost him a supporter. And verse 31 is the practical one: when everything is going wrong at once, most people pray about the whole of it, which is another way of praying about none of it. David worked out where the thing would actually be decided, prayed for that single point, and then walked up the hill and met the answer coming down. He could pray like that on the worst day of his life, under consequences he had brought on himself, because the LORD had already put away his sin and was still his God; and believers who do not know how to pray have the Spirit's own help in it (Romans 8:26).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–12 — So Absalom Stole the Hearts of the Men of Israel
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Absalom takes the kingdom by stealing it, and the theft works because it is built on a real grievance and costs him nothing. He takes the trappings of a king (v. 1), then for four years stands at the gate, asks each man where he is from, tells him his case is good, laments that the king has no one to hear him, and stops him bowing with a kiss (vv. 2–6). When the hearts are his, he asks leave to pay a vow at Hebron, the city of David’s first anointing (vv. 7–9). Secret messengers wait for the trumpet, two hundred unwitting guests lend him the look of Jerusalem’s support, and Ahithophel, David’s own counsellor, joins him at the altar (vv. 10–12).
verseByVerse.theology: Absalom's appeal works because it is built on something true. A real grievance is the most persuasive tool a demagogue has, and the hardest to answer, because the honest reply has to begin by admitting it.
verseByVerse.examples: Be wary of anyone who uses a religious reason to avoid questions. A vow, a prayer meeting or a sense of calling can be entirely genuine, and it can also be the one errand nobody dares to examine.

verseByVerse.quote: After this Absalom got himself a chariot and horses, and fifty men to run before him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
No sooner is Absalom forgiven than he begins to make himself a king, and his chariot and runners announce it to the whole city.

After this. After the kiss (14:33). The reconciliation is followed at once by a man buying the equipment of a king. A chariot, horses and fifty men running ahead of him through the streets is not transport but a royal procession, and everyone who saw it understood what it meant. Adonijah will do exactly the same before his own bid for the throne (1 Kings 1:5).

What Samuel warned. The writer has recorded this before. The first thing on Samuel’s list of what a king would do was: “he will take your sons and appoint them to his chariots and to be his horsemen and to run before his chariots” (1 Samuel 8:11).

verseByVerse.quote: And Absalom used to rise early and stand beside the way of the gate. And when any man had a dispute to come before the king for judgment, Absalom would call to him and say, "From what city are you?" And when he said, "Your servant is of such and such a tribe in Israel," Absalom would say to him, "See, your claims are good and right, but there is no man designated by the king to hear you." Then Absalom would say, "Oh that I were judge in the land! Then every man with a dispute or cause might come to me, and I would give him justice."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Absalom wins men by telling every litigant he is right and blaming the king for the lack of a hearing: a real grievance turned against his father, with a promise that costs him nothing.

Absalom used to rise early. Every day, before anyone else, he stands by the road into the gate, where cases were heard and business done, and intercepts people on their way in. Whatever else Absalom is, he is not lazy. And his opening question is personal: “From what city are you?” He asks a man where he is from before he asks what he wants, the oldest technique there is, and it works every time.

Your claims are good and right. Almost nothing he says is a lie, which is what makes it dangerous. He tells every man his case is a winner, without hearing the other side, without evidence, and without the slightest intention of deciding anything.

No man designated by the king. This is probably true. The sentence that summed up David’s whole reign was “David administered justice and equity to all his people” (8:15): not the conquests or the tribute, but that people could get a hearing. By now the kingdom stretches from Egypt to the Euphrates, one man cannot hear its cases, and people who have walked three days go home unheard. Their complaint is real, and Absalom has found it. He does not accuse his father of injustice, which anyone could dispute; he points at a genuine failure and lets each man conclude that the king does not care about him. He takes a true grievance and aims it at his father.

Oh that I were judge in the land! The offer costs him nothing, because it is entirely hypothetical. In four years at that gate Absalom is never shown judging a single case: never hearing both parties, never weighing evidence, never giving a ruling that disappoints anybody. It is the permanent advantage of the man who is responsible for nothing: he can promise everyone what nobody could deliver to all of them, and never be tested. The moment he has to judge, half the people at that gate become his enemies, because in every dispute somebody loses.

The charm of the man who has never had to decide. Absalom, all sympathy and no cost, would have thrived in our age. The historian Daniel Boorstin, writing in the early 1960s, described the celebrity as a person known for being well known, and warned that a culture fed on images would come to prefer the image to the real thing. We often do. We are drawn to the critic over the builder and the candidate over the office-holder, because promises are always prettier than decisions. Absalom stole hearts precisely because he had never had to disappoint anyone.

The true Son of David. Christ did the reverse. When a crowd wanted to make him king by force, he withdrew (John 6:15). He told people hard things they did not want to hear, and lost followers by it (John 6:66). And when judgment had to be given, he did the one thing no flatterer will do: he took the verdict on himself. Absalom kissed every man at the gate to win his heart; Christ won hearts by giving his life.

What it does not mean. Not that every complaint about those in charge is rebellion. The grievance at the gate was real, and leaders who do not hear such complaints leave the door open for someone who will exploit them. Absalom’s sin was not in noticing the wound but in using it to steal loyalty for himself.

verseByVerse.quote: And whenever a man came near to pay homage to him, he would put out his hand and take hold of him and kiss him. Thus Absalom did to all of Israel who came to the king for judgment. So Absalom stole the hearts of the men of Israel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Absalom refuses the homage due to a prince and kisses each man instead, and by this daily, calculated warmth he steals the hearts of Israel.

Take hold of him and kiss him. A man bows to a prince, as he should, and the prince catches him before he gets down, takes him by the hand and kisses him. It says: do not bow to me, we are equals. It is entirely calculated. Behind it lies another kiss, his father’s (14:33), and Absalom has learned exactly what a kiss can be made to do.

Thus Absalom did to all of Israel. This was a habit kept up day after day, and notice who was won: men “who came to the king for judgment”, people with an unsettled grievance, the very ones most ready to believe the king had failed them. Paul warns of the same craft in the church: “by smooth talk and flattery they deceive the hearts of the naive” (Romans 16:18).

Absalom stole the hearts of the men of Israel. “Stole” is the writer’s own verdict in one word: not won, not earned, but taken from the one they belonged to. The same Hebrew idiom is used when Jacob deceived Laban (Genesis 31:20, where Jacob literally stole the heart of Laban). Absalom both won their affection and fooled them.

verseByVerse.quote: And at the end of four years Absalom said to the king, "Please let me go and pay my vow, which I have vowed to the LORD, in Hebron. For your servant vowed a vow while I lived at Geshur in Aram, saying, 'If the LORD will indeed bring me back to Jerusalem, then I will offer worship to the LORD.'" The king said to him, "Go in peace." So he arose and went to Hebron.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Absalom covers his rebellion with a vow, the one request his father cannot question, and David, as so often with his sons, lets him go without asking anything.

At the end of four years. Four years of standing at a gate (on the number, see the textual note below).

Let me go and pay my vow. The cover story is invented piety, and well chosen. A vow is between a man and God; it cannot be checked; and to refuse it would make the king look irreligious. Absalom has picked the only request his father cannot examine without seeming impious.

While I lived at Geshur in Aram. Geshur was the small Aramean kingdom east of the Sea of Galilee, his mother’s homeland, where he fled after killing Amnon (3:3; 13:37–38). The vow he describes is shaped like Jacob’s at Bethel: “If God will be with me … so that I come again to my father’s house in peace, then the LORD shall be my God” (Genesis 28:20–21). Absalom borrows the words of a patriarch’s faith to dress a conspiracy.

Go in peace. The third time. David sent Tamar to Amnon’s house without a question (13:7). He let Amnon go to the sheepshearing after one question he did not press (13:26–27). And now he sends the son who has held court at his gate for four years off to his own first capital, with a blessing, having asked nothing. The king who judged all Israel never seems able to look closely at his own sons; of Adonijah the next book says, “His father had never at any time displeased him by asking, ‘Why have you done thus and so?’” (1 Kings 1:6).

Textual note. The Hebrew as it stands says “forty years”, which cannot be right in this reign; the Greek, the Syriac and Josephus all read four, and most modern versions, including the ESV, follow them.

verseByVerse.quote: But Absalom sent secret messengers throughout all the tribes of Israel, saying, "As soon as you hear the sound of the trumpet, then say, 'Absalom is king at Hebron!'" With Absalom went two hundred men from Jerusalem who were invited guests, and they went in their innocence and knew nothing. And while Absalom was offering the sacrifices, he sent for Ahithophel the Gilonite, David's counselor, from his city Giloh. And the conspiracy grew strong, and the people with Absalom kept increasing.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Absalom launches his rebellion at an altar in Hebron, with the tribes primed, two hundred unwitting guests for show, and David’s own counsellor at his side.

Absalom is king at Hebron! The years at the gate now pay: he knows men in every tribe and can reach them all at once. And the choice of Hebron shows what he intends. David was anointed king there, first of Judah and then of all Israel (2:4; 5:3); it is the ancient covenant town where Abraham is buried; and Absalom himself was born there (3:2–3). Proclaiming a king at Hebron says the throne has gone back to where it started.

They went in their innocence. Two hundred men from the capital were invited to a religious feast and found out what they were part of when the trumpet sounded. The writer says it twice in one clause: “in their innocence”, and “knew nothing”. They are hostages of a kind: prominent men of Jerusalem publicly at Absalom’s side, whose presence tells the country that the capital has gone over.

While Absalom was offering the sacrifices. The rebellion is launched at an altar. The sacrifices give the gathering its public reason, cover the arrival of men from every tribe, and lend the new king the look of God’s approval. “And the conspiracy grew strong”: once worship had made it respectable, more joined it by the hour.

Ahithophel the Gilonite, David’s counselor. This is the worst news in the chapter, and chapter 16 will say why: “the counsel that Ahithophel gave was as if one consulted the word of God” (16:23). He is the finest political mind in Israel, and he has been David’s for years.

Why does Ahithophel go? The book never says, but it leaves the pieces where a careful reader will find them. Ahithophel is from Giloh. One of David’s mighty men is “Eliam the son of Ahithophel the Gilonite” (23:34). And the woman on the roof was “Bathsheba, the daughter of Eliam, the wife of Uriah the Hittite” (11:3). If it is the same Eliam, as many think, Ahithophel was Bathsheba’s grandfather, and Uriah, also on that list of the thirty, was the husband of his granddaughter, killed to cover the king’s sin. He has sat in that council chamber giving faultless advice for years to the man who did it, and said nothing. The moment there is another king, he is gone before he is asked twice. Nothing in chapter 11 was ever really over.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 13–23 — Wherever My Lord the King Shall Be
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: When the hearts of Israel go after Absalom, David shows his own heart by refusing to fight for his city, and the crisis shows who will walk with him. He leaves at once so that Jerusalem will not be put to the sword, and his servants answer that they are ready for whatever he decides (vv. 13–15). He leaves ten concubines to keep the house and reviews the loyal column at the last house (vv. 16–18). Ittai the Gittite, a foreigner who arrived only yesterday, refuses to be released and swears to be with the king “whether for death or for life” (vv. 19–22). The whole land weeps aloud as the king crosses the Kidron towards the wilderness (v. 23).
verseByVerse.theology: He leaves rather than let Jerusalem be fought over. Whatever else is true of these chapters, that decision costs him a kingdom and saves a city.
verseByVerse.examples: Faithfulness is often found where it is least expected. The newcomer from Gath keeps faith when the king's own son and counsellor do not, and the book wants its Israelite readers to notice.

verseByVerse.quote: And a messenger came to David, saying, "The hearts of the men of Israel have gone after Absalom." Then David said to all his servants who were with him at Jerusalem, "Arise, and let us flee, or else there will be no escape for us from Absalom. Go quickly, lest he overtake us quickly and bring down ruin on us and strike the city with the edge of the sword." And the king's servants said to the king, "Behold, your servants are ready to do whatever my lord the king decides."
verseByVerse.commentary:
David leaves Jerusalem at once, not in panic but to spare the city a siege, and his servants put themselves wholly at his disposal.

The hearts of the men of Israel have gone after Absalom. The same phrase as verse 6: what Absalom stole, David has now lost.

Arise, and let us flee. He decides in a sentence. Jerusalem is defensible. He took it himself from a garrison that thought it could hold out with the blind and the lame (5:6–9), and he has fortified it since. He has the Cherethites and the Pelethites, the royal bodyguard under Benaiah, foreign professionals probably from Crete and Philistia (8:18); he has six hundred soldiers from Gath; and he has Joab.

Strike the city with the edge of the sword. He could fight for it, and he says why he will not. A siege of Jerusalem would be Israelites killing Israelites over a wall David built, and the people inside would pay for it. So he walks out of his own capital and gives it away rather than have it fought over.

Not panic. The decision has been read as panic. But look at what he does in the next twenty verses: he sends the ark back with a reasoned speech, posts two priests in the city to send him news, identifies Ahithophel as the decisive threat, prays about it, and sends a friend back to work against Absalom from inside. A panicking man does not do those things in that order.

Your servants are ready. His officials answer at once and completely: they will do “whatever my lord the king decides”. On the day the hearts of Israel go after Absalom, the men nearest David stay with him, and the next verses name them, group by group.

verseByVerse.quote: So the king went out, and all his household after him. And the king left ten concubines to keep the house. And the king went out, and all the people after him. And they halted at the last house. And all his servants passed by him, and all the Cherethites, and all the Pelethites, and all the six hundred Gittites who had followed him from Gath, passed on before the king.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The king leaves his palace in the care of ten defenceless women and reviews the loyal column as it passes out of the city.

The king left ten concubines. The sentence reads like housekeeping, but remember them. They have done nothing and chosen nothing, and in chapter 16 Absalom will do to them in public, on the roof, exactly what Nathan said would be done (16:21–22; 12:11). Afterwards they lived shut up until the day they died (20:3).

They halted at the last house. At the edge of the city the king stops and lets the whole company file past him, as a commander reviews his troops: his household, his officials, the royal guard, and the six hundred men from Gath. He sees who has come, and the reader is shown that he still has a loyal core. The Cherethites, Pelethites and Gittites (see the note on vv. 13–15) are foreigners, and they march at the front.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the king said to Ittai the Gittite, "Why do you also go with us? Go back and stay with the king, for you are a foreigner and also an exile from your home. You came only yesterday, and shall I today make you wander about with us, since I go I know not where? Go back and take your brothers with you, and may the LORD show steadfast love and faithfulness to you." But Ittai answered the king, "As the LORD lives, and as my lord the king lives, wherever my lord the king shall be, whether for death or for life, there also will your servant be." And David said to Ittai, "Go then, pass on." So Ittai the Gittite passed on with all his men and all the little ones who were with him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
David releases a foreign officer from a lost cause, and Ittai answers with an oath to share the king’s lot, whether it means death or life.

Ittai the Gittite. The finest thing in the chapter is a conversation with a foreigner. Ittai is from Gath, Goliath’s city, the town where David himself twice took refuge (1 Samuel 21:10; 27:2). He commands six hundred men, the very number David had in the wilderness, and he has been in the country for a matter of days.

Go back and stay with the king. David means Absalom. He is telling this man to go and serve the winner, and he is not being bitter; he is releasing a foreign officer from a quarrel that is not his. “I go I know not where”: he is honest about what he is offering, with no destination, no plan, no prospect. And he sends him off with a blessing in the covenant words, steadfast love and faithfulness, the same blessing he sent to Jabesh-gilead when he first became king at Hebron (2:6).

Wherever my lord the king shall be. Any reader of the Old Testament will hear the echo. Ruth, a Moabite woman, said something very like it on a road out of Moab: “where you go I will go, and where you lodge I will lodge. Your people shall be my people, and your God my God. Where you die I will die, and there will I be buried” (Ruth 1:16–17). Ittai says the same in a soldier’s words. He swears by the LORD, the God of a country he has barely lived in, and by the king, and he names the two possibilities in the order that matters: “whether for death or for life.” He puts death first.

Those who left. Now set him beside the men who are not there. Ahithophel, the wisest man in Israel, has gone. Absalom, the king’s son, is leading the rebellion. Two hundred prominent men of Jerusalem are at Hebron. Amasa, David’s nephew, will command Absalom’s army (17:25). And a Philistine officer who arrived yesterday will not leave.

Faithful foreigners. The book keeps doing this, and it is not accidental. Obed-edom the Gittite took the ark into his house when Israel was afraid of it (6:10–11). Uriah the Hittite would not sleep in his own bed while the ark was in a field (11:11). Ittai the Gittite goes into exile with a king he has barely known. Three foreigners, each set beside Israelites who failed at the same point: a foretaste of the day when those who were “far off” are brought near to the Son of David (Ephesians 2:13).

All the little ones who were with him. He has brought his family. He is not a mercenary taking a contract; he has moved his household onto the losing side of a civil war.

Following a rejected king. Ittai’s oath is the shape of discipleship (Luke 9:23), and Paul gave his answer in other words: “For to me to live is Christ, and to die is gain” (Philippians 1:21).

verseByVerse.quote: And all the land wept aloud as all the people passed by, and the king crossed the brook Kidron, and all the people passed on toward the wilderness.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The king leaves his city amid a nation’s tears, crossing the Kidron towards the wilderness where he once hid from Saul.

Toward the wilderness. The whole countryside stands along the road weeping aloud as the column passes. The road east from the Kidron climbs the Mount of Olives and drops to the Jordan through the wilderness of Judah, the dry country where David hid from Saul years before. The king is going back to where he started, a fugitive again.

The king crossed the brook Kidron. A thousand years later another son of David went out of that city at night, over the same brook, with a small group of followers, on his way to be betrayed, and John records the crossing: Jesus “went out with his disciples across the brook Kidron” (John 18:1). The likeness will grow closer before this chapter ends (see the note on vv. 24–31).
verseByVerse.note: The brook Kidron runs east of Jerusalem, between the city and the Mount of Olives.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 24–31 — Let Him Do to Me What Seems Good to Him
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: David entrusts his throne to God without trying to control him, and joins that trust to every sensible step. The priests bring out the ark, and David sends it back: if he finds favour with the LORD, the LORD will bring him back; if not, “let him do to me what seems good to him” (vv. 24–26). He posts Zadok and Abiathar in the city, with their sons as messengers, and will wait at the fords (vv. 27–29). Then he climbs the Mount of Olives barefoot, head covered and weeping, with all his people weeping behind him (v. 30). Told that Ahithophel has joined the conspiracy, he prays one precise sentence: that the LORD would turn Ahithophel’s counsel into foolishness (v. 31).
verseByVerse.theology: Trust in God is not the same as holding on to the signs of his presence. David lets the ark go and keeps hold of God.
verseByVerse.examples: Let him do to me what seems good to him is a prayer for the worst day of a life, and here it is prayed by a man suffering for his own sin. Submission to God is not only for the innocent, and he does not refuse it from the guilty.

verseByVerse.quote: And Abiathar came up, and behold, Zadok came also with all the Levites, bearing the ark of the covenant of God. And they set down the ark of God until the people had all passed out of the city. Then the king said to Zadok, "Carry the ark of God back into the city. If I find favor in the eyes of the LORD, he will bring me back and let me see both it and his dwelling place. But if he says, 'I have no pleasure in you,' behold, here I am, let him do to me what seems good to him." The king also said to Zadok the priest, "Are you not a seer? Go back to the city in peace, with your two sons, Ahimaaz your son, and Jonathan the son of Abiathar. See, I will wait at the fords of the wilderness until word comes from you to inform me." So Zadok and Abiathar carried the ark of God back to Jerusalem, and they remained there. But David went up the ascent of the Mount of Olives, weeping as he went, barefoot and with his head covered. And all the people who were with him covered their heads, and they went up, weeping as they went. And it was told David, "Ahithophel is among the conspirators with Absalom." And David said, "O LORD, please turn the counsel of Ahithophel into foolishness."
verseByVerse.commentary:
David sends the ark back, leaving his throne wholly to God’s pleasure while making every prudent arrangement, then climbs the Mount of Olives in tears and prays one precise prayer against Ahithophel’s counsel.

Carry the ark of God back into the city. Bringing the ark out with the king was the obvious thing to do, kindly meant: the presence of God should go with the true king. David sends it back, and it is worth seeing what that costs and what it proves. Israel had done the other thing once, and this book told the story at length. Beaten at Aphek, the elders said, “Let us bring the ark of the covenant of the LORD here from Shiloh, that it may come among us and save us”, and the whole camp shouted when it arrived; they lost thirty thousand men and the ark itself in a single day (1 Samuel 4:3–11). David knows that story better than anybody, and he learned in chapter 6, in the hardest possible way, that the ark is not a piece of equipment to be moved about at convenience. So here, running for his life, he is offered the one thing that would look most like God’s endorsement, and he sends it home, to stay in Jerusalem in Absalom’s hands. He will not use God as a lucky charm even when it might save his throne, and he gives the reason: if God means to bring him back, God will bring him back, and the box is not what does it.

The God who is useful. Most religion, ancient and modern, is an attempt to make God useful: a charm for the battle, a sponsor for the cause, a therapist for the anxious, a blessing on the life we had already planned. Plenty of irreligion does the same with other things, asking a career, a romance or a movement to do for us what only God can. Israel at Aphek carried the ark into battle as a charm, and lost it. David, with far more to lose, sends it back. He would rather have God on God’s terms, with no promise of the throne, than God’s furniture on his own. That is the difference between faith and religion used as a tool. The one says, “let him do to me what seems good to him”; the other says, in effect, let him do what seems good to me. And the deepest reason a believer can let go of the box is that God did not treat us as useful. Christ did not come for what he could get from us, and a person loved like that can stop trying to use God and begin to trust him.

Let him do to me what seems good to him. This is the harder half. He would like to come back (v. 25), but he will not pretend to know that he will, nor arrange matters to force it. Joab said the same sentence once before in this book, drawn up between two armies before the Ammonite city: “may the LORD do what seems good to him” (10:12). Do everything a man can do, and then leave the result where it belongs. David is a fugitive from his own son, and he is not bargaining. He does not remind God of the promise of chapter 7, though he could. He is saying: I want to come back, I have no claim, and whatever he decides is right. It is one of the high points of his life, and it comes on the worst day of it.

With your two sons. In the same breath he sets up an intelligence network. The priests go back with the ark, which is legitimate and expected, and their sons will carry messages out to the fords. Nobody will question priests staying in the city with the ark, and nobody watches the sons of priests. Both things are David at once: he refuses to manipulate God, and he makes every arrangement a competent man would make. Neither cancels the other, and the chapter will not let a reader choose between them.

Barefoot and with his head covered. The king of Israel is walking up a hill outside his own capital with no shoes on, his head covered in mourning and shame (see mourning customs), crying aloud where everyone can see him, and the whole column behind him has covered their heads and is crying too. He is probably about sixty. He captured that city, and he is leaving it barefoot because his son wants him dead and the country agreed. Psalm 3 is headed “A Psalm of David, when he fled from Absalom his son”, and it shows what he carried up that hill: “Many are rising against me”, and yet “I lay down and slept; I woke again, for the LORD sustained me” (Psalm 3:1, 5).

Over the Kidron, up the Mount of Olives. Now the likeness to Christ, which lies in the events themselves and is not a decoration added to them. David has crossed the Kidron and is going up the Mount of Olives, betrayed by his closest counsellor, a man who ate at his table. A psalm of David, which many think has Ahithophel in mind, speaks of exactly that: “Even my close friend in whom I trusted, who ate my bread, has lifted his heel against me” (Psalm 41:9), and the Lord Jesus quoted it in the upper room, of Judas, on the night he was betrayed (John 13:18). Jesus went out over the Kidron (John 18:1) and up the Mount of Olives (Luke 22:39). Two chapters from now Ahithophel “set his house in order and hanged himself” (17:23); the only other person in Scripture who dies that way is the man who betrayed Christ (Matthew 27:5). The greater Son of David went up that same slope in anguish, with a small group of loyal and bewildered followers, and prayed, “not my will, but yours, be done” (Luke 22:42), which is what David has just said to Zadok in other words.

Where the likeness ends. The likeness has a limit, and the limit is the gospel. David climbed that hill under the consequences of his own sin, as Nathan had said he would (12:10–11). The Son of David climbed it without sin, betrayed for no wrong of his own, to bear the sins of others in his body on the tree (1 Peter 2:22–24). David came back to his throne by way of a battle in which his son died; Christ came back from the dead to his throne by way of a cross on which he died himself, for those who had rebelled against him.

O LORD, please turn the counsel of Ahithophel into foolishness. One sentence of prayer on a hillside, and it is exactly right. It does not inform God of the situation, rehearse the injustice, or ask in general for the rebellion to fail. It names the single thing that will decide the war. Absalom has the numbers, the capital, the ark and the momentum; what he does not yet have is a good decision, and the man who can give him one has just arrived. If Ahithophel’s advice is taken, David is dead within a day; chapter 17 shows the advice, and it would have worked. So he prays about the counsel, not the army. Anyone who has prayed vaguely in a crisis because the crisis was too big to think about should look at that sentence.

Uncertain wording. David’s question to Zadok in verse 27, “Are you not a seer?”, is hard to read. A seer was the older word for a prophet (1 Samuel 9:9), and Zadok is called one nowhere else. Some take it as a reminder that a priest could seek God’s guidance for the king; others read the Hebrew as “Do you see?” or simply “Look”, introducing the instructions that follow. The practical sense is the same: go back, and be my eyes in the city.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 32–37 — And Behold, Hushai Came to Meet Him
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The answer to David’s prayer arrives before he reaches the top of the hill. Hushai the Archite meets him at the summit, his coat torn and dirt on his head (v. 32). David sees what he is for: not to share the road, where he would be a burden, but to go back, profess loyalty to Absalom and defeat Ahithophel’s counsel from inside (vv. 33–34), passing everything he hears to the priests and their two sons (vv. 35–36). The chapter ends with two men entering Jerusalem at the same moment: Absalom, with an army and the wisest counsellor in Israel, and Hushai, David’s friend, alone (v. 37).
verseByVerse.theology: God's answers to prayer usually come through people. Hushai is the answer to verse 31, and he arrives with dirt on his head, not yet knowing it.
verseByVerse.examples: And David does both things at once. He prays a specific prayer and then uses every means available (a friend inside the palace, two priests, two runners) without treating the second as a substitute for the first.

verseByVerse.quote: While David was coming to the summit, where God was worshiped, behold, Hushai the Archite came to meet him with his coat torn and dirt on his head. David said to him, "If you go on with me, you will be a burden to me. But if you return to the city and say to Absalom, 'I will be your servant, O king; as I have been your father's servant in time past, so now I will be your servant,' then you will defeat for me the counsel of Ahithophel. Are not Zadok and Abiathar the priests with you there? So whatever you hear from the king's house, tell it to Zadok and Abiathar the priests. Behold, their two sons are with them there, Ahimaaz, Zadok's son, and Jonathan, Abiathar's son, and by them you shall send to me everything you hear." So Hushai, David's friend, came into the city, just as Absalom was entering Jerusalem.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Before David reaches the top of the hill God’s answer is walking towards him: a grieving friend, whom David sends back into the city to defeat Ahithophel’s counsel from inside.

Behold, Hushai the Archite came. David prayed in verse 31; verse 32 begins “behold”. The writer sets the two side by side and says nothing, which is how he does his most serious work. David asks God to turn Ahithophel’s counsel into foolishness, and before he reaches the summit, “where God was worshiped”, a man is walking up the hill who is the only person in Israel capable of doing it.

You will be a burden to me. Hushai comes in mourning, coat torn and dirt on his head, to grieve with his friend, with no idea what he is walking into. David tells him, kindly enough, that on the road he would only be a burden, perhaps because of his age. Then he sees that this man is the answer to his prayer. He asks him to go back into a captured city, lie to a usurper’s face, take an oath of loyalty he does not mean, and sit in a council chamber where one wrong word means death. (On the rights and wrongs of that deception, see the note on 16:15–23.)

You will defeat for me the counsel of Ahithophel. David already sees how his prayer is going to be answered: through a frightened friend saying the right thing at the right moment in an enemy’s council. That is how God normally answers: not by lightning, but by a friend asked to do something extremely dangerous, who agrees. Prayer and action are not rivals here; the man who has just prayed is the man who gives the instructions.

Tell it to Zadok and Abiathar. The network is complete: a counsellor in the council, two priests to receive his reports, two runners to carry them, and a king waiting at the fords. Every piece of it will be used in chapter 17, and the two runners will end up hiding in a well with a woman spreading grain over its mouth.

Just as Absalom was entering Jerusalem. The timing of the last verse is exact. Two men walk into Jerusalem at the same moment from opposite directions. One is a prince arriving to take a throne, with an army behind him and the wisest counsellor in Israel at his side. The other is a man with a torn coat, alone, who has agreed to risk his life as a spy. The kingdom turns on the second one.

Hushai, David’s friend. The writer calls him “David’s friend” twice in these chapters (also 16:16). It may well be a court title, for “king’s friend” was a recognised office (1 Kings 4:5). It is also simply true, and it is the reason he goes.

keyVerse.quote: But if he says, ‘I have no pleasure in you,’ behold, here I am, let him do to me what seems good to him.
keyVerse.note: This is the heart of the chapter and one of the high points of David’s life, spoken on its worst day. He sends the ark back rather than use God to save his throne, and he leaves the outcome wholly with the LORD, without bargaining and without claiming to know how it will end. It is the posture the greater Son of David took on the same hill: “not my will, but yours, be done” (Luke 22:42).

15.reflection:
Absalom won hearts by telling every man he was right and promising what he never had to deliver (vv. 2–6). Why is that kind of voice so attractive, in public life, in the church or in a family? How does Jesus’ way of winning hearts differ?

David sent the ark back rather than use it to secure his throne (vv. 24–26). In what ways are we tempted to treat God as useful instead of trusting him? What would “let him do to me what seems good to him” look like in something you are facing?

Ittai, a foreigner of one day’s standing, swore to be with the king “whether for death or for life” (v. 21), while men who had known David for years walked away. What does loyalty to a rejected King look like for a follower of Jesus today?

David’s prayer in verse 31 was a single specific sentence, and the answer came walking up the hill, to be carried out at great risk by a friend (vv. 32–34). What does this teach about how to pray in a crisis, and about how God often answers?

16.title: Shimei's Curse and Absalom in Jerusalem
16.text: <sup>1</sup>When David had passed a little beyond the summit, Ziba the servant of Mephibosheth met him, with a couple of donkeys saddled, bearing two hundred loaves of bread, a hundred bunches of raisins, a hundred of summer fruits, and a skin of wine.<sup>2</sup>And the king said to Ziba, "Why have you brought these?" Ziba answered, "The donkeys are for the king's household to ride on, the bread and summer fruit for the young men to eat, and the wine for those who faint in the wilderness to drink."<sup>3</sup>And the king said, "And where is your master's son?" Ziba said to the king, "Behold, he remains in Jerusalem, for he said, 'Today the house of Israel will give me back the kingdom of my father.'"<sup>4</sup>Then the king said to Ziba, "Behold, all that belonged to Mephibosheth is now yours." And Ziba said, "I pay homage; let me ever find favor in your sight, my lord the king."<sup>5</sup>When King David came to Bahurim, there came out a man of the family of the house of Saul, whose name was Shimei, the son of Gera, and as he came he cursed continually.<sup>6</sup>And he threw stones at David and at all the servants of King David, and all the people and all the mighty men were on his right hand and on his left.<sup>7</sup>And Shimei said as he cursed, "Get out, get out, you man of blood, you worthless man!<sup>8</sup>The LORD has avenged on you all the blood of the house of Saul, in whose place you have reigned, and the LORD has given the kingdom into the hand of your son Absalom. See, your evil is on you, for you are a man of blood."<sup>9</sup>Then Abishai the son of Zeruiah said to the king, "Why should this dead dog curse my lord the king? Let me go over and take off his head."<sup>10</sup>But the king said, "What have I to do with you, you sons of Zeruiah? If he is cursing because the LORD has said to him, 'Curse David,' who then shall say, 'Why have you done so?'"<sup>11</sup>And David said to Abishai and to all his servants, "Behold, my own son seeks my life; how much more now may this Benjaminite! Leave him alone, and let him curse, for the LORD has told him to.<sup>12</sup>It may be that the LORD will look on the wrong done to me, and that the LORD will repay me with good for his cursing today."<sup>13</sup>So David and his men went on the road, while Shimei went along on the hillside opposite him and cursed as he went and threw stones at him and flung dust.<sup>14</sup>And the king, and all the people who were with him, arrived weary at the Jordan. And there he refreshed himself.<sup>15</sup>Now Absalom and all the people, the men of Israel, came to Jerusalem, and Ahithophel with him.<sup>16</sup>And when Hushai the Archite, David's friend, came to Absalom, Hushai said to Absalom, "Long live the king! Long live the king!"<sup>17</sup>And Absalom said to Hushai, "Is this your loyalty to your friend? Why did you not go with your friend?"<sup>18</sup>And Hushai said to Absalom, "No, for whom the LORD and this people and all the men of Israel have chosen, his I will be, and with him I will remain.<sup>19</sup>And again, whom should I serve? Should it not be his son? As I have served your father, so I will serve you."<sup>20</sup>Then Absalom said to Ahithophel, "Give your counsel. What shall we do?"<sup>21</sup>Ahithophel said to Absalom, "Go in to your father's concubines, whom he has left to keep the house, and all Israel will hear that you have made yourself a stench to your father, and the hands of all who are with you will be strengthened."<sup>22</sup>So they pitched a tent for Absalom on the roof. And Absalom went in to his father's concubines in the sight of all Israel.<sup>23</sup>Now in those days the counsel that Ahithophel gave was as if one consulted the word of God; so was all the counsel of Ahithophel esteemed, both by David and by Absalom.
16.overview:
Where we are. David has left Jerusalem and climbed the Mount of Olives in tears, praying that Ahithophel’s counsel would be turned into foolishness, and Hushai has gone back into the city just as Absalom enters it (15:30–37). This chapter covers the rest of that same day, on both sides of the hill.

The message. On the day of his humiliation David meets a flatterer, a curser and a betrayal, and the chapter shows both the man and the judgment. He is quick to believe a lie that suits his grief, yet he bears an unjust curse meekly and leaves his cause with the LORD: “It may be that the LORD will look on the wrong done to me”. Meanwhile in Jerusalem the word Nathan spoke is fulfilled to the letter, on the very roof where the sin began. God’s word does not fail, in judgment or in mercy.

Why it was said. Israel needed to see that the disaster in David’s house was neither chance nor merely Absalom’s wickedness, but the LORD’s word through Nathan coming true (12:11–12), and that a king under discipline could still be a man who trusted God (see the introduction).

How the chapter makes its case. Just past the summit Ziba meets David with supplies and a slander against Mephibosheth, and David gives him his master’s estate on the spot (vv. 1–4). At Bahurim Shimei of Saul’s house curses David as a man of blood and pelts him with stones; David holds back Abishai, leaves the matter with the LORD, and reaches the Jordan weary (vv. 5–14). In Jerusalem Hushai talks his way into Absalom’s court with words that mean two things (vv. 15–19), and on Ahithophel’s advice Absalom takes his father’s concubines on the roof “in the sight of all Israel” (vv. 20–22). The chapter closes on what David is up against: counsel prized like the word of God (v. 23).

Where it leads. The chapter leads to Christ by pattern and by the need it exposes. David, cursed on the road out of Jerusalem, refusing the sword drawn in his defence and entrusting himself to God, foreshadows the Son of David who, “when he was reviled, he did not revile in return” and told Peter to put away his sword (1 Peter 2:23; Matthew 26:52–53). But David bore curses he had partly earned, while Christ, who had earned none, “redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us” (Galatians 3:13). And a king whose judgment fails at Ziba’s word, with a son who shames his father in public, shows how much Israel still needed a King who judges rightly and a Son who honours his Father.

For us. When you are attacked, ask before God whether any of it is true, own that part, and leave the rest with him; a forgiven person need not defend himself to the last word. Beware of deciding big matters while hurt and exhausted, on one side of a story. And remember that sin’s damage falls on those with the least say, and that God sees them.
16.theology:
Judging on the worst day (vv. 3-4). Ziba's lie worked because of its timing. He produced generosity at the exact moment a betrayed man was least able to weigh a story, and David, deceived that week by his son and his counsellor, was ready to believe he had been deceived by everyone. Chapter 19 settles the facts: Mephibosheth was in mourning the whole time and says Ziba slandered him (19:24-26). Yet even then David never decides who lied. He splits the land, and the man who had received his greatest act of kindness loses half of it and answers only oh, let him take it all, since my lord the king has come safely home (19:30). Justice given in haste is very hard to undo.

A false charge and a true word (vv. 7-8). Shimei accuses David of shedding the blood of Saul’s house. David is innocent of that, but it is the charge a Benjaminite would believe without evidence. But man of blood is true: not about Saul, but about a Hittite officer at the wall of Rabbah. A bitter partisan shouting out of tribal spite has landed on exactly the right word, and he does not know it. The writer gives him no credit for insight; he is a man kicking somebody who is finally down. God can let a malicious man speak a word that finds its mark without making the malice any less his own.

The word if, and what it does not say (v. 10). If the LORD has said to him, curse David. He does not say Shimei is right, or that the accusation is fair, or that God approves; Shimei will answer for this, and David raises it on his deathbed. He says only that he will not get rid of a trouble until he knows whether God sent it.

Perspective and hope (vv. 11-12). A man who has taken the measure of the real disaster, a son who seeks his life, is not much moved by an insult from a stranger. And his hope is hedged: perhaps God will look on what is done today and repay it with good. He does not announce that God will vindicate him, quote the promise of chapter 7 at anybody, or promise himself an outcome. That is faith with no guarantee attached, and it is the more honest for it. His circumstances are at their lowest and his trust in God is at its clearest, and the two are connected.

The Son of David did it perfectly. When Christ was reviled he did not revile in return, but entrusted himself to the Judge; that is not passivity and not agreement, but handing the case to a judge who cannot be corrupted. David bore curses he had partly earned. Christ, who had earned none, became a curse for us, and that is what frees his people to bear slander without answering it in kind.

Hushai's answers (vv. 18-19). Not a false word in either, and every sentence means the opposite of what Absalom takes it to mean. It is deception, and the book does not pretend otherwise; the question it raises is taken up at the end of the notes on vv. 15-23.

Nathan's word kept (vv. 21-22). Ahithophel's counsel is shrewd politics. Half the country is waiting to see whether this is a real revolt or a family quarrel, and a public act that makes reconciliation impossible tells every waverer that Absalom cannot climb down, so it is safe to join him. But the writer sees more. Every clause of Nathan's sentence (12:11-12) is fulfilled, in the very place where David's sin began. David had been forgiven and his life spared (12:13), yet the consequences God had announced still came. Forgiveness removes the guilt; it does not always remove the consequences.

The cost falls on people who did nothing. The ten concubines chose none of it, were not consulted about the arrangement that made them royal property, and are not consulted now; what happens on that roof happens because two men are using them to make a political point. The book does not forget them (20:3). Sin rarely confines its damage to the people who committed it, and those who pay most are frequently those with the least say. Uriah did not choose it. Tamar did not choose it. These ten women did not choose it.

What David was up against (v. 23). As if one consulted the word of God is an extraordinary estimate of a man's political judgment, and the writer says both David and Absalom rated him so. That is why the prayer on the hillside was aimed where it was: not that the army would fail or that Absalom would repent, but that this man's advice would be turned into foolishness, because nothing else in the rebellion was going to beat him.
16.examples:
Then: One man walked along a hillside throwing stones and dirt at the king of Israel and his bodyguard, shouting that God was paying him back, and the king forbade his officers to touch him, because he could not be certain God had not sent him.

Now: Two things sit oddly together here. Ziba is the warning about judging: David heard one side, from the party who stood to gain, at the moment he was least able to weigh anything. Grief, exhaustion and a recent betrayal are the conditions in which most unjust snap decisions get made, and the wise course is to refuse to decide anything then. And Shimei is the model for being slandered. David neither agreed with the man nor silenced him; he refused to defend himself, and said it may be. What freed him was that he had already faced the real wound, and had already put himself in God's hands. The believer has firmer ground still: Christ took the curse we earned, and his Spirit gives the patience to leave our case with the Judge. And where we have judged as hastily as David did for Ziba, the way back is the same mercy David himself needed.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–4 — All That Belonged to Mephibosheth Is Now Yours
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A gift can carry a lie, and a wounded man is quickest to believe it. Just past the summit Ziba, Mephibosheth’s steward, meets the fleeing king with donkeys, bread, raisins, summer fruit and wine, matched exactly to the need (vv. 1–2). Asked where his master is, he says Mephibosheth has stayed in Jerusalem expecting Israel to give him back his grandfather’s kingdom (v. 3), a story chapter 19 will show to be false. Without a single question, and without hearing the other side, David hands Ziba everything that belonged to Mephibosheth, and Ziba bows and thanks him (v. 4). The king known for justice gives an unjust verdict on the worst day of his life.
verseByVerse.theology: Ziba's gift is real and his story is false. The section shows how a good king came to believe it.
verseByVerse.examples: David hands over the whole estate in one sentence, without hearing the other side, and it concerns the man who had received his own greatest act of grace. When you are tired, grieved and grateful to the person in front of you, that is the moment to send for the other side before you decide anything.

verseByVerse.quote: When David had passed a little beyond the summit, Ziba the servant of Mephibosheth met him, with a couple of donkeys saddled, bearing two hundred loaves of bread, a hundred bunches of raisins, a hundred of summer fruits, and a skin of wine. And the king said to Ziba, "Why have you brought these?" Ziba answered, "The donkeys are for the king's household to ride on, the bread and summer fruit for the young men to eat, and the wine for those who faint in the wilderness to drink." And the king said, "And where is your master's son?" Ziba said to the king, "Behold, he remains in Jerusalem, for he said, 'Today the house of Israel will give me back the kingdom of my father.'" Then the king said to Ziba, "Behold, all that belonged to Mephibosheth is now yours." And Ziba said, "I pay homage; let me ever find favor in your sight, my lord the king."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Ziba meets the fleeing king with generous supplies and a slander against his master, and David, exhausted and hearing only one side, gives him Mephibosheth’s whole estate on the spot.

Ziba the servant of Mephibosheth met him. Ziba is waiting just past the top of the hill, and the timing is no accident. He has worked out which road David will take and got there first, with exactly what a column of exhausted people needs. Two hundred loaves is the same figure Abigail brought down the mountain to stop a massacre (1 Samuel 25:18), and Ziba may well have the precedent in mind. His answer to the king’s question is itemised, thoughtful and matched to the need. Then comes what he really came to deliver, and it is a lie.

The kingdom of my father. We know it is a lie because the book tells us. When David comes back, Mephibosheth comes down to meet him, and “He had neither taken care of his feet nor trimmed his beard nor washed his clothes, from the day the king departed until the day he came back in safety” (19:24). He had been in mourning the whole time. His account is that he told Ziba to saddle a donkey so that he could go with the king, that being lame he could not go without it, and that Ziba “has slandered your servant” (19:26–27). The story is absurd anyway, if anybody stops to think. The rebellion is Absalom’s, nobody is proposing to restore the house of Saul, and Mephibosheth is a man crippled in both feet who has lived for years at David’s table, with no faction, no army and no following.

All that belonged to Mephibosheth is now yours. In one sentence, without a single question or a hearing, the estate of Saul changes hands on the word of the man who gains by it, while the other party is not even sent for. This is the king who “administered justice and equity to all his people” (8:15), on the worst day of his life: barefoot, betrayed, and handed food by the first person all morning to show him any loyalty. Ziba has attached his accusation to his generosity at the exact moment a betrayed man is least able to weigh a story. That explains David without excusing him: a man just deceived by his son and his counsellor is ready to believe he has been deceived by everybody else.

Never put right. The wrong is never properly righted. When David hears the other side he does not apologise, does not restore the estate, and does not decide who was lying. He splits the land, and Mephibosheth answers, “Oh, let him take it all, since my lord the king has come safely home” (19:30). The man given everything for Jonathan’s sake loses half of it to a lie, and does not complain.

Hear both sides. “The one who states his case first seems right, until the other comes and examines him” (Proverbs 18:17). Decisions made in grief or exhaustion, on one side of a story, about someone who is not in the room, are where good people do their worst injustices. How much better is the promised King, who will not judge by what his eyes see or decide disputes by what his ears hear, but with righteousness (Isaiah 11:3–4).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 5–14 — Let Him Alone, and Let Him Curse
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: David bears an unjust curse without striking back, because he will not get rid of a trouble until he knows whether God has sent it. At Bahurim Shimei, of Saul’s family, comes out cursing and throwing stones, calling David a man of blood whom the LORD is paying back for the house of Saul (vv. 5–8). Abishai offers to take off his head, and David refuses: if the LORD has told him to curse, who can object? David’s own son seeks his life, and a Benjaminite’s curses are small beside that; it may be that the LORD will repay him with good (vv. 9–12). Shimei keeps pace along the hillside, cursing and flinging dust, until the weary column reaches the Jordan (vv. 13–14).
verseByVerse.theology: Shimei's charge is false, but one word in it is true, and David has the humility to hear it.
verseByVerse.examples: Here David’s circumstances are at their lowest and his trust in God is at its clearest. He will not silence the man, and he will not pretend to know what God is doing with him: it may be is as far as he will go.

verseByVerse.quote: When King David came to Bahurim, there came out a man of the family of the house of Saul, whose name was Shimei, the son of Gera, and as he came he cursed continually. And he threw stones at David and at all the servants of King David, and all the people and all the mighty men were on his right hand and on his left. And Shimei said as he cursed, "Get out, get out, you man of blood, you worthless man! The LORD has avenged on you all the blood of the house of Saul, in whose place you have reigned, and the LORD has given the kingdom into the hand of your son Absalom. See, your evil is on you, for you are a man of blood." Then Abishai the son of Zeruiah said to the king, "Why should this dead dog curse my lord the king? Let me go over and take off his head." But the king said, "What have I to do with you, you sons of Zeruiah? If he is cursing because the LORD has said to him, 'Curse David,' who then shall say, 'Why have you done so?'" And David said to Abishai and to all his servants, "Behold, my own son seeks my life; how much more now may this Benjaminite! Leave him alone, and let him curse, for the LORD has told him to. It may be that the LORD will look on the wrong done to me, and that the LORD will repay me with good for his cursing today." So David and his men went on the road, while Shimei went along on the hillside opposite him and cursed as he went and threw stones at him and flung dust. And the king, and all the people who were with him, arrived weary at the Jordan. And there he refreshed himself.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Shimei curses David with a charge that is false about Saul but true in a way he does not know, and David refuses Abishai’s sword, bears the curse and leaves his cause with the LORD.

When King David came to Bahurim. Bahurim is a village on the road down to the Jordan, in Benjaminite country, Saul’s tribe. It is where Paltiel turned back weeping when Michal was taken from him (3:16).

He threw stones at David. The picture is grimly funny as well as awful. A man is throwing rocks at a column that contains the professional army of Israel: the Cherethites, the Pelethites, the six hundred Gittites, and the mighty men of chapter 23 who killed lions in pits and held fields alone. They walk on either side of the king, and they let him do it.

All the blood of the house of Saul. Shimei is wrong and right in the same speech, and it matters which is which. The charge is false. David had Saul at his mercy in a cave, cut off only a corner of his robe, and was troubled even about that (1 Samuel 24:4–5). He stood over him asleep with a spear in the ground by his head and would not let Abishai use it (1 Samuel 26:7–11). He executed the Amalekite who claimed to have finished Saul off, and the two men who murdered Ish-bosheth, and buried the head in Abner’s tomb (1:15; 4:12). He sought out Jonathan’s surviving son and fed him at his own table for years (chapter 9). Shimei has picked the charge a Benjaminite would believe without evidence (though he may have in mind the Gibeonite executions of 21:1–9).

You man of blood. And “man of blood” is true. Not about Saul, but about a Hittite officer at the wall of Rabbah, the unnamed soldiers who died in the same assault so that his death would not stand out, and a letter carried by the man it killed. So a bitter partisan, shouting a false accusation out of tribal spite, has hit the one word that is exactly right. Shimei does not know that. He is not a prophet and not being noble; he is kicking somebody who is finally down. But the word lands.

Let me go over and take off his head. Abishai is entirely in character. He offered the same service over Saul asleep at Hachilah: “let me pin him to the earth with one stroke of the spear, and I will not strike him twice” (1 Samuel 26:8). He is a brave man who solves every problem the same way, and it is his brother Joab who does such things when David says no (3:27; 18:14). This dead dog is the phrase Mephibosheth and David both used of themselves in humility (9:8; 1 Samuel 24:14), here turned to pure contempt.

If he is cursing because the LORD has said to him. David’s answer is easy to make either more or less than it is. He does not say Shimei is right or the accusation fair. He allows that a man throwing stones at him may be part of something God is doing. He is not saying God approves of Shimei (see the question below). He simply will not get rid of a trouble until he knows whether God sent it.

My own son seeks my life. Then the argument, devastating in its simplicity: beside what my own child is doing to me today, a stranger from Saul’s tribe throwing rocks is nothing. A man who has taken the measure of the real disaster is not much moved by an insult, and one reason people are so easily wounded by small slights is that they have not honestly faced the large things.

It may be. Three words keep the whole speech honest. He does not announce vindication or promise himself an outcome. That is faith with no guarantee attached, from a man walking downhill barefoot with dirt flying at him, and it is exactly what he said to Zadok that morning about the ark: “If I find favor in the eyes of the LORD … But if he says, ‘I have no pleasure in you,’ behold, here I am” (15:25–26).

Arrived weary at the Jordan. Shimei keeps it up along the slope a long way, and they arrive worn out at the river. The writer lets that be the end of the day: “And there he refreshed himself.”

He did not revile in return. The New Testament shows the same thing done perfectly. Christ, “When he was reviled, he did not revile in return; when he suffered, he did not threaten, but continued entrusting himself to him who judges justly” (1 Peter 2:23): not passivity, but handing the case to a judge who cannot be corrupted. And the Son of David, arrested on the Mount of Olives, told a man with a sword to put it away, though he could have had twelve legions of angels (Matthew 26:52–53). David had Abishai, and refused his sword. It is the same refusal on a smaller scale, with one difference that is the whole gospel: David bore curses he had partly earned, and Christ, who had earned none, “redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us” (Galatians 3:13).

In practice. When someone attacks us unfairly, the natural response is to refute the whole charge, or to let Abishai loose. David’s way is slower: let the critic speak, ask before God whether any word of it is true, own that part, and leave the rest, and the critic, with the LORD (Romans 12:19).
