A forgiven man can do this, because he has nothing left to protect except God’s opinion of him, and that is already settled.

What it does not mean. Not that we must stay within reach of someone who is harming us. David kept walking, and Shimei stayed on the far hillside. Bearing an insult with patience is one thing; remaining where you are being hurt is another, and seeking safety is no failure of faith.

Did God send Shimei to curse? David accepts that God may be humbling him through it; God rules even a sinner’s words to chasten his servant. But Shimei chose his malice and was guilty of it, as David later recognised (1 Kings 2:8–9).

Uncertain wording. The Hebrew of verse 12 is uncertain. As written it seems to say that the LORD will look “on my iniquity”; the reading traditionally spoken aloud in the synagogue is “on my eye” (perhaps meaning his tears), and the early Greek translation has “on my affliction”. The ESV’s “the wrong done to me” gives the likely sense: David hopes that God will see what he is suffering.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 15–23 — In the Sight of All Israel
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: In Jerusalem the judgment Nathan announced is carried out to the letter. Absalom enters the city with Ahithophel (v. 15). Hushai greets him with “Long live the king!” and meets his suspicion with answers that mean one thing to Absalom and another to Hushai (vv. 16–19). Ahithophel advises Absalom to go in to his father’s concubines, so that the breach can never be healed and his followers take heart; a tent is pitched on the roof, and it is done “in the sight of all Israel” (vv. 20–22), as Nathan said it would be (12:11–12). The section ends by telling us how highly that counsel was prized: as if one consulted the word of God (v. 23).
verseByVerse.theology: What happens on the roof fulfils Nathan's sentence of 12:11-12 in public, and in the very place where David's sin began.
verseByVerse.examples: Hushai's double answer is a small masterpiece: every clause is technically about whoever God has chosen, and Absalom hears what he wants to hear. The last verse then measures exactly what David prayed against on the hillside.

verseByVerse.quote: Now Absalom and all the people, the men of Israel, came to Jerusalem, and Ahithophel with him. And when Hushai the Archite, David's friend, came to Absalom, Hushai said to Absalom, "Long live the king! Long live the king!" And Absalom said to Hushai, "Is this your loyalty to your friend? Why did you not go with your friend?" And Hushai said to Absalom, "No, for whom the LORD and this people and all the men of Israel have chosen, his I will be, and with him I will remain. And again, whom should I serve? Should it not be his son? As I have served your father, so I will serve you." Then Absalom said to Ahithophel, "Give your counsel. What shall we do?" Ahithophel said to Absalom, "Go in to your father's concubines, whom he has left to keep the house, and all Israel will hear that you have made yourself a stench to your father, and the hands of all who are with you will be strengthened." So they pitched a tent for Absalom on the roof. And Absalom went in to his father's concubines in the sight of all Israel. Now in those days the counsel that Ahithophel gave was as if one consulted the word of God; so was all the counsel of Ahithophel esteemed, both by David and by Absalom.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Hushai wins Absalom’s trust with words that mean the opposite of what Absalom hears, and on Ahithophel’s advice Absalom takes his father’s concubines on the palace roof, fulfilling Nathan’s word to the letter.

Long live the king! The rebellion enters the capital without a fight, as David intended. Hushai shouts the acclamation twice, louder than anybody in the room, and does not say which king. That will be his whole technique.

Is this your loyalty to your friend? Absalom is nobody’s fool, and his question has a barb: “friend” twice, Hushai’s own title at court (see the note on 15:32–37).

Words with two meanings. There is not a false word in either answer. “Whom the LORD and this people and all the men of Israel have chosen”: the LORD chose David, though Absalom hears an endorsement because the people have just acclaimed him. “Should it not be his son?” sounds like an argument for the son’s right to the throne, and is in fact only a question. “As I have served your father, so I will serve you”: Absalom takes it as a transfer of loyalty, but Hushai has always served David’s interests, and in Absalom’s court he will go on doing exactly that. Every sentence is technically true and means the opposite of what the hearer takes it to mean.

The question it raises. It should be said plainly that this is deception, and the book does not pretend otherwise. Hushai is a spy in a rebel court, and Scripture does not stop here to weigh it. What can be said is that he is in a war, that Absalom would kill him on the spot for an honest answer, and that he belongs with the midwives in Egypt and Rahab at Jericho rather than with Ziba, who lied for an estate (see the box at the end of this note).

Go in to your father’s concubines. Ahithophel’s advice is why David prayed on the hillside. It is cold, brilliant and, on its own terms, correct. Absalom’s problem is not military. Half the country is waiting to see whether this is a real revolt or a family quarrel. Taking the royal harem was the recognised act of a successor (compare 3:7; 12:8; 1 Kings 2:22). Doing it publicly makes peace with his father impossible, so every waverer in Israel now knows that Absalom cannot back down, which means it is safe to join him. It is a plan for burning a bridge, and it works.

In the sight of all Israel. Set it beside Nathan’s words clause by clause: “Behold, I will raise up evil against you out of your own house. And I will take your wives before your eyes and give them to your neighbor, and he shall lie with your wives in the sight of this sun. For you did it secretly, but I will do this thing before all Israel and before the sun” (12:11–12). Out of his own house: his son. Before all Israel: a tent the whole city can see. Before the sun: in daylight, nothing hidden.

They pitched a tent for Absalom on the roof. There is only one palace roof in this book: “he saw from the roof a woman bathing” (11:2). The place where a man looked down and saw something he wanted is where the judgment is carried out, by his own son, on the advice of the man who was probably her grandfather (see the note on 15:10–12). None of this is stated; it is put where an attentive reader will find it.

The cost to the innocent. There is a cost here that falls on people who did nothing. The ten concubines (secondary wives, lawfully bound to the king but of lower standing) were left to keep the house in what read like a housekeeping detail (15:16). Two men are using them to make a political point, and the book does not forget them. When David comes back he provides for them, “but did not go in to them. So they were shut up until the day of their death, living as if in widowhood” (20:3): provided for, but with no life of their own left, perhaps while still young. Sin rarely confines its damage to the people who commit it, and those who pay the most are often those with the least say. The God who records their fate has not overlooked them.

As if one consulted the word of God. The chapter ends by telling us what David is up against. When Ahithophel spoke, both kings did what he said, as they would an oracle. That is why David prayed not that the army would fail or Absalom repent, but that this man’s advice would be turned into foolishness. Yet “No wisdom, no understanding, no counsel can avail against the LORD” (Proverbs 21:30), and the next chapter is David’s prayer being answered, in a council chamber, by a friend in a torn coat.

Where Christians differ. Was Hushai’s deception right? Scripture records it without approving every detail. Many hold that deceiving those bent on murder, in war, is not the false witness the ninth commandment forbids, as with Rahab and the midwives; others, with Augustine and Calvin, hold that every untruth is sin, which God may forgive and overrule.

This commentary’s view. Deceiving those bent on murder is not the lie the ninth commandment forbids, and Hushai stands where Rahab stood, who is commended for her faith (Hebrews 11:31). Either way it is no licence for ordinary lying (Colossians 3:9).

keyVerse.quote: It may be that the LORD will look on the wrong done to me, and that the LORD will repay me with good for his cursing today.
keyVerse.note: Cursed, stoned and humiliated, David refuses Abishai’s sword and leaves his cause with God, with nothing promised and nothing demanded: “it may be”. It is faith without a guarantee, on the worst day of his life, and a small picture of the Son of David who, when he was reviled, entrusted himself to him who judges justly (1 Peter 2:23).

16.reflection:
David gave Ziba Mephibosheth’s estate after hearing one side of the story, while exhausted and hurt (vv. 1–4). When are you most likely to judge people hastily? What would it look like to practise Proverbs 18:17 at home, at church or at work?

Shimei’s charge was false about Saul, yet “man of blood” was true about Uriah (vv. 7–8). How can we listen to unfair criticism for the part that may be true, without being crushed by the rest?

David refused Abishai’s sword and said, “It may be that the LORD will look on the wrong done to me” (vv. 9–12). How does 1 Peter 2:23 show Jesus doing this perfectly, and what would entrusting yourself to God look like in a conflict you face?

The ten concubines paid for sins in which they had no part (vv. 21–22; 20:3). Where do you see the damage of sin falling on the powerless today, and how should Christians respond?

17.title: Ahithophel's Counsel Overthrown
17.text: <sup>1</sup>Moreover, Ahithophel said to Absalom, "Let me choose twelve thousand men, and I will arise and pursue David tonight.<sup>2</sup>I will come upon him while he is weary and discouraged and throw him into a panic, and all the people who are with him will flee. I will strike down only the king,<sup>3</sup>and I will bring all the people back to you as a bride comes home to her husband. You seek the life of only one man, and all the people will be at peace."<sup>4</sup>And the advice seemed right in the eyes of Absalom and all the elders of Israel.<sup>5</sup>Then Absalom said, "Call Hushai the Archite also, and let us hear what he has to say."<sup>6</sup>And when Hushai came to Absalom, Absalom said to him, "Thus has Ahithophel spoken; shall we do as he says? If not, you speak."<sup>7</sup>Then Hushai said to Absalom, "This time the counsel that Ahithophel has given is not good."<sup>8</sup>Hushai said, "You know that your father and his men are mighty men, and that they are enraged, like a bear robbed of her cubs in the field. Besides, your father is expert in war; he will not spend the night with the people.<sup>9</sup>Behold, even now he has hidden himself in one of the pits or in some other place. And as soon as some of the people fall at the first attack, whoever hears it will say, 'There has been a slaughter among the people who follow Absalom.'<sup>10</sup>Then even the valiant man, whose heart is like the heart of a lion, will utterly melt with fear, for all Israel knows that your father is a mighty man, and that those who are with him are valiant men.<sup>11</sup>But my counsel is that all Israel be gathered to you, from Dan to Beersheba, as the sand by the sea for multitude, and that you go to battle in person.<sup>12</sup>So we shall come upon him in some place where he is to be found, and we shall light upon him as the dew falls on the ground, and of him and all the men with him not one will be left.<sup>13</sup>If he withdraws into a city, then all Israel will bring ropes to that city, and we shall drag it into the valley, until not even a pebble is to be found there."<sup>14</sup>And Absalom and all the men of Israel said, "The counsel of Hushai the Archite is better than the counsel of Ahithophel." For the LORD had ordained to defeat the good counsel of Ahithophel, so that the LORD might bring harm upon Absalom.<sup>15</sup>Then Hushai said to Zadok and Abiathar the priests, "Thus and so did Ahithophel counsel Absalom and the elders of Israel, and thus and so have I counseled.<sup>16</sup>Now therefore send quickly and tell David, 'Do not stay tonight at the fords of the wilderness, but by all means pass over, lest the king and all the people who are with him be swallowed up.'"<sup>17</sup>Now Jonathan and Ahimaaz were waiting at En-rogel. A female servant was to go and tell them, and they were to go and tell King David, for they were not to be seen entering the city.<sup>18</sup>But a young man saw them and told Absalom. So both of them went away quickly and came to the house of a man at Bahurim, who had a well in his courtyard. And they went down into it.<sup>19</sup>And the woman took and spread a covering over the well's mouth and scattered grain on it, and nothing was known of it.<sup>20</sup>When Absalom's servants came to the woman at the house, they said, "Where are Ahimaaz and Jonathan?" And the woman said to them, "They have gone over the brook of water." And when they had sought and could not find them, they returned to Jerusalem.<sup>21</sup>After they had gone, the men came up out of the well, and went and told King David. They said to David, "Arise, and go quickly over the water, for thus and so has Ahithophel counseled against you."<sup>22</sup>Then David arose, and all the people who were with him, and they crossed the Jordan. By daybreak not one was left who had not crossed the Jordan.<sup>23</sup>When Ahithophel saw that his counsel was not followed, he saddled his donkey and went off home to his own city. He set his house in order and hanged himself, and he died and was buried in the tomb of his father.<sup>24</sup>Then David came to Mahanaim. And Absalom crossed the Jordan with all the men of Israel.<sup>25</sup>Now Absalom had set Amasa over the army instead of Joab. Amasa was the son of a man named Ithra the Ishmaelite, who had married Abigal the daughter of Nahash, sister of Zeruiah, Joab's mother.<sup>26</sup>And Israel and Absalom encamped in the land of Gilead.<sup>27</sup>When David came to Mahanaim, Shobi the son of Nahash from Rabbah of the Ammonites, and Machir the son of Ammiel from Lo-debar, and Barzillai the Gileadite from Rogelim,<sup>28</sup>brought beds, basins, and earthen vessels, wheat, barley, flour, parched grain, beans and lentils,<sup>29</sup>honey and curds and sheep and cheese from the herd, for David and the people with him to eat, for they said, "The people are hungry and weary and thirsty in the wilderness."
17.overview:
Where we are. Absalom holds Jerusalem and, on Ahithophel’s advice, has burned his bridges on the palace roof (16:20–23). David is somewhere short of the Jordan with a weary column, and Hushai sits in the rebel council, sent there in answer to David’s prayer (15:31–34).

The message. The LORD rules the councils of men. The best plan in Israel is set aside for a worse one, not because anyone is forced, but because “the LORD had ordained to defeat the good counsel of Ahithophel” (v. 14). So David’s one-sentence prayer is answered through a friend’s courage, a young man’s vanity and a woman’s quick wits. No human wisdom can stand against God’s purpose, and he keeps his king through ordinary people doing ordinary, brave things.

Why it was said. Israel needed to know that David’s return was neither luck nor cleverness but the LORD’s doing, as he had promised to establish David’s house (chapter 7), and that the wisest of men are no match for him (see the introduction).

How the chapter makes its case. Ahithophel proposes a swift night strike to kill the king alone, and the council approves (vv. 1–4). Absalom calls Hushai as well, who answers with true facts and wrong conclusions, flattering Absalom with the picture of himself at the head of all Israel (vv. 5–13). The council prefers Hushai, and the writer tells us why (v. 14). Word goes out by a servant girl and two runners, hidden in a well at Bahurim by a quick-thinking woman, and by daybreak David is across the Jordan (vv. 15–22). Ahithophel goes home and hangs himself, and Absalom crosses with Amasa in command (vv. 23–26). At Mahanaim three unlikely men bring beds and food for the weary (vv. 27–29).

Where it leads. The chapter leads to Christ by pattern and by the character of God it reveals. A council in Jerusalem plotting against the LORD’s anointed, overruled by God without anyone being forced, is the pattern of the council that gathered against Jesus, to do “whatever your hand and your plan had predestined to take place” (Acts 4:28). Ahithophel’s cold reckoning, one man’s death for the people’s peace, was spoken again by Caiaphas (John 11:50), and the betrayer who hanged himself foreshadows Judas (Matthew 27:5). In Christ “the foolishness of God is wiser than men” (1 Corinthians 1:25): the cross looked like the triumph of the wicked, and it was God’s plan to save.

For us. Pray specifically, and then look for God’s answer in other people’s ordinary choices. Beware of advice that flatters you. And be among those who bring beds and bread when the King’s people are hungry and weary in the wilderness.
17.theology:
The plan that would have worked (vv. 1-3). Speed, surprise, one target, minimum bloodshed, and the army brought home intact. Kill David and there is no rebellion left to fight, because the Gittites and the mighty men are not fighting for a cause; they are fighting for him. The narrator himself calls it the good counsel, and the chapter cannot be understood unless the reader grants that.

How the worse plan won (vv. 7-13). Hushai grants that Ahithophel's advice is normally right and disputes only this time, because attacking him directly would be fatal. He finds Absalom's weak point within a sentence or two: not tactics but reputation, the fear that a single reverse would empty his support overnight. Then he offers him what Ahithophel's plan withheld, the glory of winning the kingdom in person. Militarily it is a disaster: surprise surrendered, weeks instead of hours, a muster that cannot be hidden, everything staked on one pitched battle. But Absalom is not weighing tactics; he is choosing the plan that puts him at the head of the army. The elders were not stupid; they had simply heard the better speech, and the better speech is what carries a room.

Verse 14: good counsel, God's purpose, and a prayer answered. Three things are packed into the sentence. First, God's own historian calls the plan God overthrew good. Second, the LORD had ordained: not merely permitted or foresaw, but ordained, while every person in the room did exactly what he thought best. Nobody was coerced. Ahithophel gave honest professional judgment, Hushai used his own courage and wit, Absalom exercised a vanity he had cultivated for years, and the elders preferred a better speech. Every human factor is fully accounted for, and still the writer says God ordained the result. Scripture holds these together everywhere without explaining how: Joseph's brothers meant evil and God meant good by the same act (Gen. 50:20), and at the cross men did what God's hand and plan had predestined (Acts 4:28) and were held responsible as lawless men (Acts 2:23). Any account of God’s rule that drops either half, his ordaining or their responsibility, is not what this verse teaches.

Third, this is 15:31 answered, and the way it was answered matters. There was no voice and no sign, and nothing David could have seen; anyone in that council would have seen only politics. David never learns it. He is told only to cross the river at once. He does not get verse 14; we do. That is the honest position of everyone who prays: the answer normally looks exactly like other people making their own decisions for their own reasons, and the sentence explaining what was really happening is not available at the time.

Hushai does not trust his own success (v. 16). He has just won the argument and gained David weeks, yet his message is to cross tonight, in case Absalom changes his mind. Only the river makes the delay safe. Confidence in God's providence did not make him careless; it made him diligent.

Providence through ordinary courage (vv. 17-20). The ordaining of verse 14 was carried out by people who never knew they were part of it. A servant girl walked out of the city with the most dangerous information in Israel, because nobody notices a maid going to the spring. A woman at Bahurim, the same village where Shimei threw stones that morning, thought on the spot of scattering grain over a well. She has no name and gets two verses, and a kingdom depended on her nerve.

Ahithophel calculates one last time (v. 23). This is not despair over a professional slight. He can see the end from where he stands: Absalom will muster, David will have time, there will be a pitched battle and David will win it, and the counsellor who left the king's table will be the first called to account. So he rides home, sets his house in order, and takes his own life, with no rage and no impulse. Scripture records it as the end of a man who put great gifts to the service of betrayal, not as a model. Anyone who has lost someone this way should read the question answered at the end of the notes on vv. 23-26.

The other man who died that way. Ahithophel is the only man in the Old Testament to hang himself. The next in Scripture is the one who sat at the table of the Son of David, ate his bread, took silver, and went and hanged himself (Matt. 27:5). Psalm 41:9 speaks of the close friend who ate David's bread and lifted his heel against him, and Jesus applied that verse to Judas in the upper room (John 13:18). Betrayal by a trusted counsellor, over the Kidron, on the Mount of Olives, ending in a rope: the pattern was written into this book a thousand years before the night it happened again.

Two sons of two sisters (v. 25). Amasa is Joab's cousin and both are David's nephews, so the two armies about to meet are commanded by members of the same family. The name matters later: David confirms Amasa in command in chapter 19 as a peace offering to the rebels, and Joab kills him for it in chapter 20 with the same feigned friendliness and the same wound he used on Abner.

Help from the edges (vv. 27-29). An Ammonite prince, a provincial from Lo-debar, and an old man from across the river come out with beds, basins, wheat, beans, honey and cheese, with no weapons and no money among them, and nobody wins a war with lentils. They come at the very moment the whole country from Dan to Beersheba is mustering behind the king's son. The book has done this from the beginning: Obed-edom, Uriah and Ittai were all outsiders who proved more faithful than insiders. The people who show up are from the edges, and they come not to back a winner but because the people are hungry and weary and thirsty.
17.examples:
Then: The best political mind in Israel proposed a plan that would have ended the war that night with a single death, and the council agreed. Then a young man who liked being consulted asked for one more opinion, and David's friend talked them out of it. And somewhere in a village, a woman put a cloth over a well and scattered grain on it.

Now: Verse 14 is the one to think over slowly, and it is not a comfortable verse. It insists that God ordained the outcome of a meeting in which everyone freely did what he thought best, and it does not explain how. What is practically useful is that David got his answer and never knew it. He prayed ten specific words, and the answer looked like nothing more than a committee preferring a better speech. Most answered prayer is like that. If you are waiting to see God's hand before you believe he has moved, you will usually be waiting for something that only shows up in the account written afterwards; meanwhile you may keep praying, and keep doing the next faithful thing. The woman at Bahurim is what verse 14 looks like from ground level: no name, two verses, an idea she had on the spot, and a kingdom depending on it.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–14 — The LORD Had Ordained to Defeat the Good Counsel
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God overturns the best counsel in Israel by means of a worse one that flatters its hearer. Ahithophel proposes to take twelve thousand men that very night, catch David weary, scatter his people and kill the king alone, bringing the nation back like a bride (vv. 1–3), and Absalom and the elders approve (v. 4). Yet Absalom calls Hushai too (vv. 5–6). Hushai says that “this time” the counsel is not good (v. 7), paints David and his men as enraged bears and seasoned fighters who will turn the first clash into a rout (vv. 8–10), and proposes instead a muster of all Israel with Absalom at its head (vv. 11–13). The council chooses Hushai’s plan, “For the LORD had ordained to defeat the good counsel of Ahithophel” (v. 14).
verseByVerse.theology: The text itself calls Ahithophel's plan the good counsel. Hushai's is worse in every military respect, and it wins because it flatters.
verseByVerse.examples: Here, for one sentence, the only such sentence in the whole rebellion, the writer lifts the curtain on what God was doing, and it answers a prayer prayed barefoot on a hillside two chapters ago.

verseByVerse.quote: Moreover, Ahithophel said to Absalom, "Let me choose twelve thousand men, and I will arise and pursue David tonight. I will come upon him while he is weary and discouraged and throw him into a panic, and all the people who are with him will flee. I will strike down only the king, and I will bring all the people back to you as a bride comes home to her husband. You seek the life of only one man, and all the people will be at peace." And the advice seemed right in the eyes of Absalom and all the elders of Israel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Ahithophel proposes a swift and sound plan, to strike that night and kill only the king, and the whole council approves it; the chapter depends on seeing that it would have worked.

Let me choose twelve thousand men. Twelve thousand is a strike force, not an army: enough to overwhelm a column of refugees and small enough to move fast. And “tonight” is the heart of the plan. David crossed the Kidron this morning; he is somewhere short of the Jordan, on foot, with women and children and a weeping crowd.

While he is weary and discouraged. Ahithophel knows exactly what state David is in, because he has sat in his council for years. Then the surgical part: “I will strike down only the king.” He has grasped what Absalom has not, that this is not a war between two armies but a question about one man.

As a bride comes home to her husband. The plan is not only effective but, on its own terms, humane: one death instead of a battle, the army home intact, no Israelite killing another, the nation returning like a bride. Ahithophel is proposing an assassination to prevent a civil war, he is right on the facts and the timing, and it would have worked.

All the elders of Israel. The plan is approved not by Absalom alone but by the tribal leaders who have gone over to him, very likely some of the same men who once anointed David king at Hebron (5:3). This is a proper council of the nation, and Ahithophel has carried it.

The life of only one man. Ahithophel’s reckoning, one death so that “all the people will be at peace”, was heard again a thousand years later in another Jerusalem council, from Caiaphas: “it is better for you that one man should die for the people, not that the whole nation should perish” (John 11:50). God overthrew Ahithophel’s plan; Caiaphas’s cold calculation he made the means of his own, and “upon him was the chastisement that brought us peace” (Isaiah 53:5).

Uncertain wording. The Hebrew of verse 3 is compressed and hard to follow; read literally it says something like like the return of the whole is the man whom you seek. The ESV, with most modern versions, follows the early Greek translation and its picture of a bride. Either way the sense is clear: kill one man, and the nation comes back.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Absalom said, "Call Hushai the Archite also, and let us hear what he has to say." And when Hushai came to Absalom, Absalom said to him, "Thus has Ahithophel spoken; shall we do as he says? If not, you speak." Then Hushai said to Absalom, "This time the counsel that Ahithophel has given is not good."
verseByVerse.commentary:
With the matter settled, Absalom calls for a second opinion and tells Hushai the whole plan, and Hushai, on the spot, disputes it without attacking the man who gave it.

Call Hushai the Archite also. It is settled. Then comes the sentence on which the kingdom turns, and it looks like nothing at all: let us hear from the other one too. Absalom is not suspicious of Ahithophel; he likes to be consulted and cannot quite bring himself to act on a finished decision. Why he says it, the writer does not tell us. Verse 14 tells us who was behind it.

If not, you speak. Absalom tells Hushai the whole plan before asking him, the worst thing he could have done: Hushai now knows exactly what threatens David and how little time he has, and can shape his answer to undo it. But he has no time to prepare and no second chance.

This time the counsel that Ahithophel has given is not good. He answers with total confidence, and adds two words: “this time”. To attack Ahithophel, whose advice is treated like the word of God (16:23), would be fatal; Hushai concedes everything about the counsellor and disputes only this occasion.

verseByVerse.quote: Hushai said, "You know that your father and his men are mighty men, and that they are enraged, like a bear robbed of her cubs in the field. Besides, your father is expert in war; he will not spend the night with the people. Behold, even now he has hidden himself in one of the pits or in some other place. And as soon as some of the people fall at the first attack, whoever hears it will say, 'There has been a slaughter among the people who follow Absalom.' Then even the valiant man, whose heart is like the heart of a lion, will utterly melt with fear, for all Israel knows that your father is a mighty man, and that those who are with him are valiant men.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Hushai takes true facts about David and his men and draws the wrong conclusion from them, playing on the rebels’ fear that the old king may yet prove stronger.

True facts, wrong conclusions. Every single thing Hushai says is true, and every conclusion he draws from it is wrong. David’s men are mighty men (chapter 23 lists them), David is expert in war, and a bear robbed of her cubs is an exact picture of those six hundred men at this moment. All of which is precisely why Ahithophel wanted to strike tonight, before they have slept or crossed the river. Hushai takes the same facts and turns them into a reason to wait.

There has been a slaughter. Then the hook, aimed straight at what Absalom cares about: if the first attack goes even slightly wrong, word will spread that his men are being slaughtered, and his support will evaporate overnight. That is a fear about reputation, not tactics, and Absalom has spent four years at a gate building a reputation one handshake at a time.

Like the heart of a lion. The pictures pile up: a bear robbed of her cubs, a lion-hearted man melting with fear. Even the bravest of Absalom’s men, Hushai says, will lose heart, “for all Israel knows that your father is a mighty man”. He plays on the doubt every rebel carries, that the old king may yet prove stronger than the new one.

verseByVerse.quote: But my counsel is that all Israel be gathered to you, from Dan to Beersheba, as the sand by the sea for multitude, and that you go to battle in person. So we shall come upon him in some place where he is to be found, and we shall light upon him as the dew falls on the ground, and of him and all the men with him not one will be left. If he withdraws into a city, then all Israel will bring ropes to that city, and we shall drag it into the valley, until not even a pebble is to be found there."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Hushai proposes a muster of all Israel with Absalom at its head, a plan that sounds overwhelming, flatters the prince, and wins David the time he needs.

That you go to battle in person. Now the flattery, and it is enormous. “From Dan to Beersheba” is the formula for the entire nation. “As the sand by the sea for multitude” is the language of God’s promise to Abraham (Genesis 22:17), applied to Absalom’s army. And then: “that you go to battle in person.” In Ahithophel’s version somebody else wins the kingdom and hands it to Absalom; in Hushai’s, Absalom rides at the head of the largest army ever assembled in Israel and wins it himself. Militarily it is a disaster: it surrenders surprise, gives David weeks instead of hours, needs a muster that cannot be hidden, and stakes the whole rebellion on one pitched battle. But Absalom is not asking which plan is sounder. He is choosing the one in which he leads the army himself.

As the dew falls on the ground. Dew settles everywhere at once and leaves nothing uncovered: an army so large that David cannot be missed wherever he hides. What it leaves unsaid is that such an army takes weeks to gather, and time is the one thing Hushai is trying to win for David.

We shall drag it into the valley. The last verse is not a plan at all but poetry. Nobody drags a city into a valley with ropes. It is a picture of total, effortless victory, exactly what a proud man wants to hear about himself. Ahithophel gave a plan; Hushai gave a vision.

verseByVerse.quote: And Absalom and all the men of Israel said, "The counsel of Hushai the Archite is better than the counsel of Ahithophel." For the LORD had ordained to defeat the good counsel of Ahithophel, so that the LORD might bring harm upon Absalom.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The council chooses the worse plan because it flatters, and the writer draws back the curtain: the LORD had ordained it, in answer to David’s prayer, to bring disaster on Absalom.

The counsel of Hushai the Archite is better. They vote for the worse plan unanimously, and they are not stupid. They have just heard a better speech. The man with the correct answer spoke in numbers and hours; the man with the wrong answer spoke of the sand by the sea and the king at the head of the nation. The better argument lost to the more flattering one, and that does not happen only in ancient councils.

The good counsel of Ahithophel. Here the writer stops the story to tell us what has actually been happening, and there are three things in it. First, “the good counsel of Ahithophel”: God’s own historian, in the very sentence that describes God overthrowing it, calls the plan good. It was the right plan, competently argued, by the best mind in Israel.

The LORD had ordained. Second, “the LORD had ordained to defeat” it: not merely permitted it, or foresaw it, but ordained it. The outcome of that council was settled before anybody spoke, and nobody in it was coerced. Ahithophel gave his honest judgment, Hushai used his own intelligence and courage, Absalom indulged his vanity freely, and the elders were persuaded by a better speech. Every human factor is accounted for, and God still ordained the result. Scripture holds these together everywhere and never explains how: Joseph’s brothers meant evil and God meant good, and both are said of the same act (Genesis 50:20).

A prayer answered. Third, two chapters ago a barefoot man going up the Mount of Olives with his head covered prayed, “O LORD, please turn the counsel of Ahithophel into foolishness” (15:31). This verse is that prayer being answered, and the writer wants us to see it. And look how: not by a voice or a sign, but through a friend’s courage, a young man’s vanity, and a room of elders who liked one speech better than another. Anyone in that council would have seen only politics; at no moment is God visible.

At the cross. The same truth stands at the centre of the gospel. Herod, Pilate and the peoples gathered against Jesus “to do whatever your hand and your plan had predestined to take place” (Acts 4:28), and they were still “lawless men”, responsible for what they did (Acts 2:23). The worst council in history was ruled by God, and what looked like the defeat of the Son of David was the plan by which he saved his people.

Do we really choose by reason? We like to think we weigh the evidence and follow it. The philosopher David Hume, no friend of Christianity, was blunter: “Reason is, and ought only to be the slave of the passions.” Much modern psychology has agreed at least with the first half: we decide with our loves and then recruit our arguments. Scripture said it long before Hume: “Keep your heart with all vigilance, for from it flow the springs of life” (Proverbs 4:23).

The gospel does not flatter. The gospel never flatters: it does not promise that we will drag the city into the valley, but tells us we cannot save ourselves. Such a message is not believed because it pleases a proud heart, so when it is believed, something has happened to the heart first: “The Lord opened her heart to pay attention to what was said by Paul” (Acts 16:14). God changes what we love, and then reason, freed from vanity, can finally see.

In everyday life. David never learns this. He is told that night only that he must cross the river at once. He does not get verse 14; we do. That is the honest situation of anyone who prays: the answer, if it comes, will normally look like other people making their own decisions for their own reasons. Pray anyway, and specifically, and trust the God who rules the rooms we cannot see into.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 15–22 — A Woman Spread a Covering Over the Well
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God’s answer to David’s prayer is carried the last mile by the courage of hidden, ordinary people. Hushai tells the priests both plans and urges that David cross the Jordan that very night (vv. 15–16). A servant girl takes the message to Jonathan and Ahimaaz at En-rogel; a boy sees them and tells Absalom, and they run to a house at Bahurim, where a woman hides them in a well under a covering spread with grain and sends the pursuers the wrong way (vv. 17–20). The runners reach David, and by daybreak not one of his people is left on the near bank of the Jordan (vv. 21–22).
verseByVerse.theology: Everything now depends on ordinary people doing something dangerous: a servant girl carrying messages, two young men in a hole in the ground, and a woman with a handful of grain.
verseByVerse.examples: Courage here does not look heroic. It looks like a woman in her own courtyard keeping her voice steady while soldiers ask questions, because she has decided whose side she is on.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Hushai said to Zadok and Abiathar the priests, "Thus and so did Ahithophel counsel Absalom and the elders of Israel, and thus and so have I counseled. Now therefore send quickly and tell David, 'Do not stay tonight at the fords of the wilderness, but by all means pass over, lest the king and all the people who are with him be swallowed up.'" Now Jonathan and Ahimaaz were waiting at En-rogel. A female servant was to go and tell them, and they were to go and tell King David, for they were not to be seen entering the city. But a young man saw them and told Absalom. So both of them went away quickly and came to the house of a man at Bahurim, who had a well in his courtyard. And they went down into it. And the woman took and spread a covering over the well's mouth and scattered grain on it, and nothing was known of it. When Absalom's servants came to the woman at the house, they said, "Where are Ahimaaz and Jonathan?" And the woman said to them, "They have gone over the brook of water." And when they had sought and could not find them, they returned to Jerusalem. After they had gone, the men came up out of the well, and went and told King David. They said to David, "Arise, and go quickly over the water, for thus and so has Ahithophel counseled against you." Then David arose, and all the people who were with him, and they crossed the Jordan. By daybreak not one was left who had not crossed the Jordan.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Hushai sends urgent word to cross the Jordan that night, and the message reaches David through a servant girl, two runners and a quick-thinking woman who hides them in a well.

Thus and so did Ahithophel counsel. Hushai gets the message out at once, reporting both plans. Note his caution: his counsel has won and has probably bought David weeks, but he does not trust his own success for one night: “by all means pass over”, tonight, in case Absalom changes his mind.

A female servant. The network set up in chapter 15 now works as designed, and its first link is a servant girl. She walks out of the city with the most dangerous information in Israel in her head. Nobody notices a maid going to the spring at En-rogel, which is precisely why she is the one sent.

A young man saw them. Then it goes wrong: a boy sees them and reports it. They run into a courtyard at Bahurim, the village where Shimei came out throwing stones earlier that day, and climb down a well.

Scattered grain on it. One verse, and the kingdom hangs on it. Two strangers drop into the household’s well with pursuers behind them. She covers the mouth, and then, which shows what kind of person she is, scatters grain over the covering, so that any soldier walking into the yard sees an ordinary courtyard with grain spread out to dry. That detail was part of no plan; she thought of it while it was happening.

They have gone over the brook of water. She speaks to armed men on her own doorstep, calmly, and sends them off in a believable direction. If her voice shakes, or one of them decides to look under the grain, two young men die in a well, David is not warned, and Absalom may yet take Ahithophel’s advice. Her name is not recorded. Here is what the ordaining of verse 14 looked like on the ground: a woman with a handful of grain, thinking fast, in a village.

Not one was left. By dawn the river is behind them, and the writer counts: “By daybreak not one was left who had not crossed the Jordan.” A whole community, children included, crosses at night, and nobody is left on the wrong bank. On the night of his arrest the greater Son of David guarded his own in the same way: “Of those whom you gave me I have lost not one” (John 18:9).

Where Christians differ. Was the woman wrong to mislead the soldiers? Scripture records her words without comment. She was hiding men from armed pursuers who meant to kill the king, much as Rahab hid the spies (Joshua 2:4–6), and Rahab is commended for her faith (Hebrews 11:31). Many hold that misleading those bent on murder is not the false witness the ninth commandment forbids; others hold that every untruth is sin, which God may forgive and overrule.

This commentary’s view. Misleading those bent on murder is not the lie the ninth commandment forbids (see the note on 16:15–23). Faithful Christians differ here, and neither view is a licence for ordinary lying (Colossians 3:9).

Uncertain wording. The word translated “brook” in verse 20 occurs only here in the Old Testament, and its exact meaning is not known. Most take it as a small stream or channel of water. The point is clear enough: she sends the pursuers on, across the water and away from the well.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 23–26 — He Set His House in Order and Hanged Himself
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The wisest man in Israel sees the end of the rebellion before anyone else, and takes his own life, while the two sides gather for battle. Ahithophel, his counsel rejected, rides home, sets his house in order and hangs himself (v. 23). David reaches Mahanaim, the fortified town across the Jordan, and Absalom crosses after him with all Israel (v. 24). Absalom has put Amasa over the army in place of Joab, and the writer gives his family tree, which shows that the two commanders are cousins, both nephews of David (v. 25). The rebel army camps in the land of Gilead (v. 26).
verseByVerse.theology: Ahithophel is not despairing at a setback. He has just watched the council choose the losing plan, and he can see how it will end, both for Absalom and for a man who has publicly betrayed David.
verseByVerse.examples: One chapter ago his advice was reckoned as the word of God. Great ability is no protection against a life that ends in ruin when it has been put to the service of betrayal.

verseByVerse.quote: When Ahithophel saw that his counsel was not followed, he saddled his donkey and went off home to his own city. He set his house in order and hanged himself, and he died and was buried in the tomb of his father. Then David came to Mahanaim. And Absalom crossed the Jordan with all the men of Israel. Now Absalom had set Amasa over the army instead of Joab. Amasa was the son of a man named Ithra the Ishmaelite, who had married Abigal the daughter of Nahash, sister of Zeruiah, Joab's mother. And Israel and Absalom encamped in the land of Gilead.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Seeing his counsel rejected, Ahithophel calmly puts his affairs in order and hangs himself, while David reaches Mahanaim and Absalom crosses the Jordan with Amasa, David’s nephew, in command.

When Ahithophel saw that his counsel was not followed. One of the coldest verses in Scripture. This is not despair over a professional slight. Ahithophel can see the whole thing to the end: Absalom will muster, David will have time to organise across the Jordan, there will be a pitched battle, and David will win it. And when David wins, the first man called to account will be the counsellor who left the king’s table for the son’s. So he calculates, as he has calculated everything else. He is a dead man either way, and he prefers to arrange it himself.

He saddled his donkey. The sequence of verbs is what makes it terrible. He saddled his donkey; he rode home to Giloh; he “set his house in order”, settling his affairs and providing for his family; and then he took his own life. There is no rage in any of that, and no impulse. He was buried in his father’s tomb, which suggests his family did not treat him as disgraced. All that ability, counsel prized “as if one consulted the word of God” (16:23), and he is dead in a house at Giloh because a vain young man liked a better speech.

Like Judas. The writer has been preparing one more likeness since chapter 15. Ahithophel is the only man in the Old Testament who hangs himself. The only other in Scripture is the man who sat at the table of the Son of David, ate his bread, took silver to betray him, and “went and hanged himself” (Matthew 27:5). A psalm of David, very possibly with Ahithophel in mind, says, “Even my close friend in whom I trusted, who ate my bread, has lifted his heel against me” (Psalm 41:9), and Jesus quoted it in the upper room of Judas (John 13:18). Brilliance that turns against the LORD’s anointed ends, both times, in the same dark place.

Then David came to Mahanaim. Mahanaim lies across the Jordan in Gilead, and its name has a history: Jacob met the angels of God there and called the place Two Camps, shortly before he faced Esau (Genesis 32:1–2). It had also been Ish-bosheth’s capital (2:8), a defensible town far from Jerusalem.

Amasa over the army instead of Joab. Amasa’s parentage is given because it matters: he is Joab’s cousin, and both are David’s nephews. The two armies about to fight are commanded by the sons of two sisters. Remember the name: David will confirm Amasa’s appointment in chapter 19 as a peace offering to the rebels, and Joab will kill him for it in chapter 20.

Is suicide a sin, and is it unforgivable? Taking one’s own life breaks the sixth commandment, a grave sin against the God who gives life (Exodus 20:13). But it is not the unforgivable sin; that is the settled rejection of Christ (Mark 3:28–29). A true believer who dies this way, in despair or illness of mind, is not cut off from the grace that saves sinners, for salvation rests on Christ’s work, not on the state of our last moment (Romans 8:38–39).

If you are struggling. Anyone thinking of ending their life should speak to someone today: a pastor or biblical counsellor first, a trusted friend, and a doctor for a medical check-up (taking medicine is no failure of faith). Anyone in immediate danger should call the local emergency number now, the same day.

Uncertain wording. This Nahash (v. 25) is almost certainly not the Ammonite king. 1 Chronicles 2:16 names Zeruiah and Abigail as David’s sisters, so Nahash may have been their mother, or their mother’s first husband.

Textual note. The Hebrew here calls Ithra “the Israelite” (as the KJV has it), while 1 Chronicles 2:17 calls him an Ishmaelite, which the ESV follows, probably rightly, since an ordinary Israelite father would hardly need his nation named.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 27–29 — Three Men Brought Beds and Bowls
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: At the lowest point of David’s reign, help comes from the edges. Three men meet him at Mahanaim: Shobi, son of the Ammonite king Nahash, from Rabbah; Machir of Lo-debar, who once sheltered Mephibosheth; and old Barzillai the Gileadite (v. 27). They bring beds, basins and pots, wheat, barley and flour, beans and lentils, honey, curds, sheep and cheese (vv. 28–29), and they give their reason in plain words: “The people are hungry and weary and thirsty in the wilderness.” It is not a war chest but care for exhausted people, and through it God sustains his king.
verseByVerse.theology: Each of these men has a history with David, and chapter 9 and chapter 10 lie behind two of them. Kindness shown years before is being repaid at the lowest point of the reign.
verseByVerse.examples: What they bring is domestic rather than military, and they bring it because the people are hungry. Practical care for the weary is never a small thing in this book.

verseByVerse.quote: When David came to Mahanaim, Shobi the son of Nahash from Rabbah of the Ammonites, and Machir the son of Ammiel from Lo-debar, and Barzillai the Gileadite from Rogelim, brought beds, basins, and earthen vessels, wheat, barley, flour, parched grain, beans and lentils, honey and curds and sheep and cheese from the herd, for David and the people with him to eat, for they said, "The people are hungry and weary and thirsty in the wilderness."
verseByVerse.commentary:
At Mahanaim three unlikely men, an Ammonite prince, the man who sheltered Mephibosheth and an old Gileadite, bring beds and food to David’s exhausted people, simply because they are hungry and weary.

Shobi the son of Nahash. Three men come out to meet a defeated king, and behind at least two of them lies an old kindness now being repaid. The first is a son of Nahash, the Ammonite king whose death set off chapter 10, when his son Hanun shamed David’s envoys and started a war (10:1–4). Shobi comes from Rabbah, the city Joab was besieging while David was on the roof, at whose wall Uriah was killed. He is from the house David tried to show kindness to and was insulted for, from the city where David committed his worst act, and he has come out with food.

Machir the son of Ammiel from Lo-debar. The second was last seen in chapter 9: Mephibosheth lived in his house for all the years nobody in Jerusalem thought about him (9:4–5). The man who took in the last of the old dynasty, when the new king might have wanted him dead, now supplies the new king when his own son has driven him out. Whatever Machir is, he is consistent: he looks after whoever has been driven out.

Barzillai the Gileadite. The third is Barzillai, a very old and very rich man from Gilead, to whom chapter 19 will give one of the finest speeches in the book (19:31–39).

Beds, basins, and earthen vessels. Read the list: no weapons, no money. It is what you send to people who have walked a long way and are sleeping outdoors: something to lie on, something to cook in, and food for a few thousand exhausted people. And the writer gives their reason in their own words, not that the king’s cause is just, but “The people are hungry and weary and thirsty in the wilderness.”

Who came, and who did not. Israel has just thrown David out, and his nephew commands the rebel army. What arrives at Mahanaim is a foreigner, a provincial and an old man from across the river, with bedding. As with Obed-edom, Uriah and Ittai (see the note on 15:19–22), at the lowest point of the reign the people who show up are from the edges.

Serving the rejected King. These three men served a king in exile by feeding his weary people. Jesus says the same is still possible: “I was hungry and you gave me food … as you did it to one of the least of these my brothers, you did it to me” (Matthew 25:35, 40). The kindness that counts is often as plain as beds, basins and lentils, brought to tired people by those nobody expected.
verseByVerse.note: Mahanaim, east of the Jordan, had been Ish-bosheth’s capital, which made it a natural refuge for a government in exile.

keyVerse.quote: And Absalom and all the men of Israel said, “The counsel of Hushai the Archite is better than the counsel of Ahithophel.” For the LORD had ordained to defeat the good counsel of Ahithophel, so that the LORD might bring harm upon Absalom.
keyVerse.note: This is one of the few places where the writer stops the story to tell us what God was doing, and it explains the whole rebellion. A council of free and responsible men chose the worse plan, and the LORD had ordained that they would, in answer to David’s prayer on the Mount of Olives (15:31). The same truth stands at the cross, where men did their worst and God accomplished his plan to save.

17.reflection:
Ahithophel’s plan was sound, yet the council chose Hushai’s because it flattered Absalom (vv. 11–14). Where are you most open to advice that flatters you? How does the gospel, which never flatters, free us to hear the truth?

“The LORD had ordained to defeat the good counsel of Ahithophel” (v. 14), yet everyone in the room chose freely. How does this truth, and its fulfilment at the cross (Acts 4:27–28), steady you when events seem to lie in the hands of powerful or foolish people?

David’s prayer in 15:31 was answered through Hushai’s courage, a servant girl, two runners and an unnamed woman with a handful of grain (vv. 15–22). What does this teach about how God usually answers prayer, and about the worth of hidden faithfulness?

Shobi, Machir and Barzillai brought beds and food because “The people are hungry and weary and thirsty in the wilderness” (v. 29). Who around you is weary, and what practical kindness could you bring them this week?

18.title: The Death of Absalom
18.text: <sup>1</sup>Then David mustered the men who were with him and set over them commanders of thousands and commanders of hundreds.<sup>2</sup>And David sent out the army, one third under the command of Joab, one third under the command of Abishai the son of Zeruiah, Joab's brother, and one third under the command of Ittai the Gittite. And the king said to the men, "I myself will also go out with you."<sup>3</sup>But the men said, "You shall not go out. For if we flee, they will not care about us. If half of us die, they will not care about us. But you are worth ten thousand of us. Therefore it is better that you send us help from the city."<sup>4</sup>The king said to them, "Whatever seems best to you I will do." So the king stood at the side of the gate, while all the army marched out by hundreds and by thousands.<sup>5</sup>And the king ordered Joab and Abishai and Ittai, "Deal gently for my sake with the young man Absalom." And all the people heard when the king gave orders to all the commanders about Absalom.<sup>6</sup>So the army went out into the field against Israel, and the battle was fought in the forest of Ephraim.<sup>7</sup>And the men of Israel were defeated there by the servants of David, and the loss there was great on that day, twenty thousand men.<sup>8</sup>The battle spread over the face of all the country, and the forest devoured more people that day than the sword.<sup>9</sup>And Absalom happened to meet the servants of David. Absalom was riding on his mule, and the mule went under the thick branches of a great oak, and his head caught fast in the oak, and he was suspended between heaven and earth, while the mule that was under him went on.<sup>10</sup>And a certain man saw it and told Joab, "Behold, I saw Absalom hanging in an oak."<sup>11</sup>Joab said to the man who told him, "What, you saw him! Why then did you not strike him there to the ground? I would have been glad to give you ten pieces of silver and a belt."<sup>12</sup>But the man said to Joab, "Even if I felt in my hand the weight of a thousand pieces of silver, I would not reach out my hand against the king's son, for in our hearing the king commanded you and Abishai and Ittai, 'For my sake protect the young man Absalom.'<sup>13</sup>On the other hand, if I had dealt treacherously against his life (and there is nothing hidden from the king), then you yourself would have stood aloof."<sup>14</sup>Joab said, "I will not waste time like this with you." And he took three javelins in his hand and thrust them into the heart of Absalom while he was still alive in the oak.<sup>15</sup>And ten young men, Joab's armor-bearers, surrounded Absalom and struck him and killed him.<sup>16</sup>Then Joab blew the trumpet, and the troops came back from pursuing Israel, for Joab restrained them.<sup>17</sup>And they took Absalom and threw him into a great pit in the forest and raised over him a very great heap of stones. And all Israel fled every one to his own home.<sup>18</sup>Now Absalom in his lifetime had taken and set up for himself the pillar that is in the King's Valley, for he said, "I have no son to keep my name in remembrance." He called the pillar after his own name, and it is called Absalom's monument to this day.<sup>19</sup>Then Ahimaaz the son of Zadok said, "Let me run and carry news to the king that the LORD has delivered him from the hand of his enemies."<sup>20</sup>And Joab said to him, "You are not to carry news today. You may carry news another day, but today you shall carry no news, because the king's son is dead."<sup>21</sup>Then Joab said to the Cushite, "Go, tell the king what you have seen." The Cushite bowed before Joab, and ran.<sup>22</sup>Then Ahimaaz the son of Zadok said again to Joab, "Come what may, let me also run after the Cushite." And Joab said, "Why will you run, my son, seeing that you will have no reward for the news?"<sup>23</sup>"Come what may," he said, "I will run." So he said to him, "Run." Then Ahimaaz ran by the way of the plain, and outran the Cushite.<sup>24</sup>Now David was sitting between the two gates, and the watchman went up to the roof of the gate by the wall, and when he lifted up his eyes and looked, he saw a man running alone.<sup>25</sup>The watchman called out and told the king. And the king said, "If he is alone, there is news in his mouth." And he drew nearer and nearer.<sup>26</sup>The watchman saw another man running. And the watchman called to the gate and said, "See, another man running alone!" The king said, "He also brings news."<sup>27</sup>The watchman said, "I think the running of the first is like the running of Ahimaaz the son of Zadok." And the king said, "He is a good man and comes with good news."<sup>28</sup>Then Ahimaaz cried out to the king, "All is well." And he bowed before the king with his face to the earth and said, "Blessed be the LORD your God, who has delivered up the men who raised their hand against my lord the king."<sup>29</sup>And the king said, "Is it well with the young man Absalom?" Ahimaaz answered, "When Joab sent the king's servant, your servant, I saw a great commotion, but I do not know what it was."<sup>30</sup>And the king said, "Turn aside and stand here." So he turned aside and stood still.<sup>31</sup>And behold, the Cushite came, and the Cushite said, "Good news for my lord the king! For the LORD has delivered you this day from the hand of all who rose up against you."<sup>32</sup>The king said to the Cushite, "Is it well with the young man Absalom?" And the Cushite answered, "May the enemies of my lord the king and all who rise up against you for evil be like that young man."<sup>33</sup>And the king was deeply moved and went up to the chamber over the gate and wept. And as he went, he said, "O my son Absalom, my son, my son Absalom! Would I had died instead of you, O Absalom, my son, my son!"
18.overview:
Where we are. Absalom holds Jerusalem, but the LORD has turned Ahithophel’s counsel to foolishness (17:14), and David has crossed the Jordan to Mahanaim, where friends fed his weary people (17:27–29). The time Hushai bought has been used, and now the battle comes.

The message. The LORD keeps the king he chose, and rebellion against God’s anointed ends in death; yet the victory brings David no joy, because the rebel was his son. The chapter holds justice and grief together without letting go of either. Absalom’s fall is just, David’s love for him is real, and a father’s love, however deep, cannot save a son who has rebelled. “Would I had died instead of you” is the cry of a love that cannot pay.

Why it was said. Israel needed to see that God’s choice of king stands against every usurper, and that the sword Nathan foretold (12:10) was no empty threat (see the introduction). Generations of readers who would watch the house of David torn by its own sons needed to know both that God keeps his promise and that sin within a family costs what it costs.

How the chapter makes its case. David organises his army, is kept from the field by his own men, and orders all three commanders, in the hearing of everyone, to deal gently with Absalom (vv. 1–5). The forest of Ephraim swallows twenty thousand men (vv. 6–8). Absalom hangs by the head in an oak; a nameless soldier refuses any price to touch him, and Joab kills him himself and has him buried under a heap of stones, a world away from the pillar he had raised to his own name (vv. 9–18). Two runners come to a king waiting between the gates with one question; Ahimaaz cannot answer it and the Cushite does (vv. 19–32). The chapter ends on a father’s lament on the stairs (v. 33).

Where it leads. The chapter leads to Christ by the need it exposes, and by contrast. David longed to die in his son’s place and could not, and his death would have changed nothing in Absalom’s heart. A thousand years later the Son of David did die in the place of rebels, and his death achieved what it was for: “while we were enemies we were reconciled to God by the death of his Son” (Romans 5:10). Absalom hung in a tree under the curse he had earned; Christ hung on a tree under the curse we had earned (Galatians 3:13). David on the stairs is not a picture of the cross but of the longing the cross answers.

For us. When powerful people ask us to do what they will not put their own name to, the nameless soldier shows the way: a clear word from the King, held steadily. Our name is not kept by monuments we raise but by the God who writes it in heaven. And parents grieving a wayward child may grieve as David did, without shame, and bring their child to a Father who did not spare his own Son.
18.theology:
An order that could not be obeyed (v. 5). David gives his command aloud, at the gate, to all three commanders, with the whole army filing past, because he knows what Joab does with an inconvenient man. It works, in a way: an ordinary infantryman can quote it back to the commander-in-chief. Yet the order is also indefensible. Absalom is a grown man who murdered his brother, stole a kingdom and shamed his father before the nation, and an army cannot be sent to win a battle against an enemy it has been told not to hurt. For my sake does not claim the order is right; it asks a favour. Love for a child can be real and still be no guide to justice.

The bitter end (v. 8). Twenty thousand dead in a forest. Ahithophel’s plan would have cost one life, David’s (17:2). Abner had asked across a valley years before, shall the sword devour forever? The rejection of the king God chose ends, as such rebellion does, in waste.

The writer plants a detail and does not point to it (v. 9). The text says Absalom's head was caught, not his hair. But four chapters earlier the writer stopped to weigh that hair (14:25-26), and now its owner hangs between heaven and earth, belonging to neither, while the royal mule walks out from under him. Every reader makes the connection; the text never asserts it. Judgment in this book often comes through the very things a man was proudest of.

The case for Joab, and what is left of it (vv. 10-15). Absalom alive would have been a permanent rallying point, and Joab is not wrong about the politics. But he had a direct, public order from his king, and he set it aside, as he did with Abner and will do with Amasa. Each time there is a real political argument, and each time Joab decides that his judgment outranks the king's. David never punishes him; he cannot, and says so at 3:39 and again on his deathbed (1 Kings 2:5-6). The clearest conscience in the chapter belongs to a man with no name. Joab offers ten pieces of silver; the soldier says not for a thousand. He is not haggling; he means that no sum would make him do it. He quotes the king's order back with the names in it, and then tells his commander to his face that when the reckoning came, you yourself would have stood aloof. He is right: Joab has spent a career giving orders and letting other men carry the risk. Joab's reply, I will not waste time like this with you, is not an argument. He does not dispute the order or claim he did not hear it. He puts three javelins into a helpless man and has ten armour-bearers finish the body, spreading the act across eleven men so that no one of them can be held responsible. And the other side of Joab belongs in the record too: the moment Absalom is dead he sounds the recall, and thousands go home alive.

Two monuments (vv. 17-18). A pit under a heap of stones is the marker of a man who died under judgment, as with Achan and the king of Ai. Beside it stands the pillar Absalom raised to his own name because he had no son to remember him. He spent his life on being seen, and the last thing recorded of him is a stone with his name on it. If his sons had died young, as most readers take it, he was also a man who had buried his children, and that should temper any verdict passed on him.

Kindness, and the courage to say it (vv. 19-32). Joab, who has just killed the king's son, will not let young Ahimaaz carry the news, in one of his few kind acts in this book. He has seen what happens to the man who brings David such news: the Amalekite who came to Ziklag with Saul's crown was executed. So he sends a Cushite, a foreigner and probably a slave, who goes without being asked whether he wants to. Ahimaaz runs anyway, arrives first, and cannot say it. He knows exactly what happened, and he says he saw a commotion and does not know what it was. Wanting to be the one who arrives is not the same as being ready to speak. And David's single question shows where his heart is. Twenty thousand dead, the kingdom his again, and he does not ask about the battle or whether Ittai survived. He has been sitting between two gates all day, ready to read good news into the way a man runs. Ahimaaz shouts shalom, all is well, and David asks whether there is shalom for Absalom. The answer is no.

The lament (v. 33). Grief speaks like this. It circles, it does not develop, it says the one true thing again. The word is not “the rebel”; it is my son. Every reason to hate him is true, and not one of them weighs with David now.

Would I had died instead of you. The oldest wish of love, and in David's mouth it is useless: had he died in that forest, nothing in Absalom's heart would have changed, and the exchange would have purchased nothing. A father can want to take his son's place; he cannot do it, and he cannot make it mean anything if he does. Here the verse points beyond David to Christ, and it helps us only if we keep the difference between the two clear.

A thousand years later another Son of David, in David's own city, went out to die for rebels who had stolen the hearts of a kingdom from its rightful King and wanted a throne that was not theirs. He did not merely wish to die in their place; he did it. And the difference is not only that it happened but that it worked: while we were enemies we were reconciled to God by the death of his Son (Rom. 5:10). David on that staircase is not a picture of the cross. He is a picture of the longing the cross answers, and the one thing he wanted most was impossible for him and was not impossible for God.

For parents of a wayward child. Many who read this verse are mothers and fathers with a son or daughter who has turned against them or against God, and some have stood at a grave like this one. Scripture does not tell David to stop loving the boy, and it does not call his grief weakness. Nor does it pretend he had been a faultless father: he had indulged and neglected by turns, and Absalom's choices were still Absalom's own. Both are usually true, and neither guilt nor excuse is the place to stay. While the child lives, keep praying and keep the door open; the father in Jesus' parable was watching the road and ran when he saw his son (Luke 15:20). And where a child has died far off, the grieving may leave the question with the Judge of all the earth, who will do what is just (Genesis 18:25), and who did not spare his own Son but gave him up for us all (Romans 8:32).
18.examples:
Then: A king told his commanders, in front of his whole army, to deal gently with the man who had taken his throne, and when a soldier found that man hanging helpless in a tree and refused a thousand pieces of silver to touch him, the commander-in-chief killed him himself.

Now: The nameless soldier is the model, and what makes him one is not courage in the abstract. He had a clear word from his king, quoted accurately, and he could see exactly what the man pressuring him was like. You yourself would have stood aloof is the line to remember the next time somebody powerful asks you to do what they will not put their own name to. The Christian stands on a clearer word from a better King, who did not stand aloof but bore the reckoning himself, and whose Spirit gives the steadiness to say no. Ahimaaz, who ran faster than the man with the real message and then could not open his mouth, is the gentler warning: wanting to carry the news is not the same as being willing to say it. And the lament does not need improving. Scripture records five my sons in one verse without tidying any of them away. A parent who still loves a child who has broken their heart is not being foolish; David was that parent on those stairs.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–8 — The Forest Devoured More People
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The rebellion is ended in battle, and the cost is terrible. David, organising his refugees into an army, divides it into three and is persuaded by his own men not to go out, because he is the one man the enemy needs to kill (vv. 1–4). At the gate he orders all three commanders, in the hearing of the whole army, to deal gently with Absalom, an order that shows a father’s love and cannot be obeyed by soldiers sent to win (v. 5). In the forest of Ephraim Israel’s hurried muster breaks, and the broken country devours more men than the sword: twenty thousand dead (vv. 6–8).
verseByVerse.theology: He gives the order publicly and to all three commanders at once, because he knows perfectly well that one of them will kill his son if he can. He is trying to make it impossible.
verseByVerse.examples: The terrain does most of the killing. Broken ground turns a hurried national muster into a rout, which is exactly what Hushai's plan exposed Absalom's army to and Ahithophel's would have avoided.

verseByVerse.quote: Then David mustered the men who were with him and set over them commanders of thousands and commanders of hundreds. And David sent out the army, one third under the command of Joab, one third under the command of Abishai the son of Zeruiah, Joab's brother, and one third under the command of Ittai the Gittite. And the king said to the men, "I myself will also go out with you." But the men said, "You shall not go out. For if we flee, they will not care about us. If half of us die, they will not care about us. But you are worth ten thousand of us. Therefore it is better that you send us help from the city." The king said to them, "Whatever seems best to you I will do." So the king stood at the side of the gate, while all the army marched out by hundreds and by thousands. And the king ordered Joab and Abishai and Ittai, "Deal gently for my sake with the young man Absalom." And all the people heard when the king gave orders to all the commanders about Absalom. So the army went out into the field against Israel, and the battle was fought in the forest of Ephraim. And the men of Israel were defeated there by the servants of David, and the loss there was great on that day, twenty thousand men. The battle spread over the face of all the country, and the forest devoured more people that day than the sword.
verseByVerse.commentary:
David, back in command, is kept from the field by his own men, and sends them into battle with an order no army could obey: deal gently with the rebel. The battle that follows ends the rebellion at a terrible price.

Then David mustered the men who were with him. David the professional soldier is back. Three chapters ago he walked barefoot out of Jerusalem in tears (15:30); now, using every hour Hushai bought him, he has organised the refugees who crossed the Jordan in the dark into an army.

Under the command of Ittai the Gittite. The third division goes to the Philistine who arrived only days ago. Ittai had said, wherever my lord the king shall be, whether for death or for life (15:21), and David has given him a third of the army. That is what David thought of the speech.

You shall not go out. His men refuse to let him fight, and their argument is cold and correct: this war is about one man, exactly as Ahithophel said (17:2–3). If half the army dies it changes nothing; if David dies it is over. Set that against 11:1: the time when kings go out to battle... But David remained at Jerusalem. He stayed home then and should have gone; he offers to go now and is told to stay. All the trouble since began with that first decision to stay at home.

Deal gently for my sake. Everything in the chapter runs into this order. David names all three commanders and gives it aloud at the gate as the whole army marches past, and the writer makes sure we notice: all the people heard. That is not carelessness. David has known Joab for decades and knows what he does with a rebel, having watched him kill Abner at the gate of Hebron (3:27). So he makes the order public, where it cannot be denied or quietly not heard.

The young man Absalom. Yet the order is also a serious failure; both things are true. The young man Absalom is what David called him when he brought him back from Geshur (14:21). He is a grown man, probably in his thirties, who has murdered his brother, stolen a kingdom, driven out his father and lain with his father’s concubines on a roof in front of the nation (16:22). An army cannot be sent to win a battle and told to be gentle with the enemy’s leader; every soldier on that road understands the arithmetic even if David will not. And for my sake does not even claim the order is right. It asks a personal favour.

Against Israel… twenty thousand men. The writer will not soften it: this is civil war, David’s men against their own nation. Ahithophel had offered twelve thousand men, one night, one death, and the nation brought home like a bride (17:1–3). This is the alternative that was chosen instead.

The forest devoured more people that day than the sword. The forest of Ephraim lay east of the Jordan, not far from Mahanaim, and not in the hill country of Ephraim west of the river; it probably took its name from Ephraimites who had settled or claimed land in Gilead (compare Judges 12:1–6). It is broken ground of ravines, scrub, rocks and trees, the worst terrain for a large army that does not know it, and Absalom’s muster was farmers and townsmen called up in a hurry, fighting professionals on ground the professionals chose. Once such a line breaks, men run in panic into the trees, fall into ravines, get lost and are hunted down in ones and twos.

The bitter end. Devoured is a word for eating, the picture Abner used when he called across a valley years before: Shall the sword devour forever? Do you not know that the end will be bitter? (2:26). The bitter end is a wood full of dead Israelites: rejecting the king God chose ends, as such rebellion does, in waste.

Textual note. In verse 3 most Hebrew manuscripts read for now there are ten thousand like us; some ancient manuscripts and translations read you are worth ten thousand of us, which the ESV and most modern versions follow. The Hebrew words for “now” and “you” sound alike and differ by one letter; either way, the king matters more than any number of his soldiers.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 9–18 — The King's Command Concerning You
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The rebel prince dies helpless, at the hand of the one man who will not obey the king. Absalom is caught by the head in an oak, and the royal mule walks out from under him (v. 9). A soldier refuses Joab’s reward, quoting the king’s order and telling Joab to his face that he would have left him to take the blame (vv. 10–13). Joab kills Absalom with three javelins, has ten armour-bearers finish him, recalls the army, and throws the body into a pit under a heap of stones (vv. 14–17). Beside that grave the writer sets the pillar Absalom raised to his own name (v. 18).
verseByVerse.theology: The writer records Absalom's end without a word of comment, and lets what he said four chapters earlier about Absalom's hair do its own work.
verseByVerse.examples: A man who refuses to do wrong for a thousand pieces of silver, and says why to his commander's face, needs no name to be remembered.

verseByVerse.quote: And Absalom happened to meet the servants of David. Absalom was riding on his mule, and the mule went under the thick branches of a great oak, and his head caught fast in the oak, and he was suspended between heaven and earth, while the mule that was under him went on. And a certain man saw it and told Joab, "Behold, I saw Absalom hanging in an oak." Joab said to the man who told him, "What, you saw him! Why then did you not strike him there to the ground? I would have been glad to give you ten pieces of silver and a belt." But the man said to Joab, "Even if I felt in my hand the weight of a thousand pieces of silver, I would not reach out my hand against the king's son, for in our hearing the king commanded you and Abishai and Ittai, 'For my sake protect the young man Absalom.' On the other hand, if I had dealt treacherously against his life (and there is nothing hidden from the king), then you yourself would have stood aloof." Joab said, "I will not waste time like this with you." And he took three javelins in his hand and thrust them into the heart of Absalom while he was still alive in the oak.
