And ten young men, Joab's armor-bearers, surrounded Absalom and struck him and killed him. Then Joab blew the trumpet, and the troops came back from pursuing Israel, for Joab restrained them. And they took Absalom and threw him into a great pit in the forest and raised over him a very great heap of stones. And all Israel fled every one to his own home. Now Absalom in his lifetime had taken and set up for himself the pillar that is in the King's Valley, for he said, "I have no son to keep my name in remembrance." He called the pillar after his own name, and it is called Absalom's monument to this day.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Absalom hangs helpless in an oak, and Joab, brushing aside a soldier who quotes the king’s order back at him, kills him. The man who lived to be seen ends in a pit under a heap of stones, beside the pillar he raised to his own name.

His head caught fast in the oak. Say first what the text says: his head, not his hair. Riding at speed under low branches, he was caught by the head, the mule kept going, and he was left hanging. Then notice what the writer has done. Four chapters earlier he stopped the story to describe Absalom’s hair, cut once a year when it grew too heavy, and weighed (14:25–26), and made no point of it. Now its owner hangs by the head in a tree. The writer plants things and waits; every reader makes the connection, it is almost certainly intended, and the text still does not assert it.

Suspended between heaven and earth. The phrase is exact in more than one way: between the two, belonging to neither, held by nothing he chose. And the mule is the royal mount; Solomon will be set on David’s own mule to be proclaimed king (1 Kings 1:33). Absalom is riding the animal of a king, and it walks out from under him.

Why then did you not strike him? Joab’s reaction is instant, and shows he had already decided. He does not ask whether the man is sure, but why he did not kill him, and names a price on the spot: ten pieces of silver and a belt, a mark of honour.

A thousand pieces of silver. The best speech in the chapter is made by a man with no name. Joab offers ten pieces of silver; the soldier would not do it for a thousand. He is not haggling or being pious: no sum would turn this into a thing he would do. His reason is the king’s order, given in our hearing and quoted back with the names in it. That is why David gave it at the gate: an ordinary soldier can now quote it, accurately, to the commander-in-chief.

You yourself would have stood aloof. The second half is devastating. There is nothing hidden from the king, and when the reckoning came for the death of his son, Joab would have stood aloof, let the soldier hang for it alone and said nothing about the ten pieces of silver. He has taken his commander’s measure precisely and says so to his face, and he is right: Joab has spent his career giving orders and letting other men carry the risk.

I will not waste time like this with you. That is Joab’s entire answer, and it is not an argument; he does not dispute the order or claim not to have heard it. He does it himself: three javelins into the heart of a man hanging helpless in a tree. Then ten armour-bearers finish the body, spreading the act across eleven men, so that no single one can be held responsible.

The case for Joab. It has to be put, because it is not nothing. Absalom alive would be a permanent rallying point, and David is a father who cannot see it. Joab is thinking of the kingdom, and he is not wrong about the politics. But he heard a direct, public order from his king, and he disobeyed it and killed the king’s son.

The third time. Abner at the gate of Hebron, in peacetime, in a city of refuge (3:27); Absalom here; Amasa in two chapters (20:10). Each time Joab decides that his judgment outranks the king’s. David never punishes him. He cannot: he needs him, and says so at 3:39, these men, the sons of Zeruiah, are more severe than I, and he is still saying it on his deathbed, when he tells Solomon to deal with what he could not (1 Kings 2:5–6).

Then Joab blew the trumpet. That is the other side of the man. The moment Absalom is dead he sounds the recall, and thousands of Israelites who would have been hunted through that forest go home. He did the same at Gibeon when Abner called across the valley (2:28).

A very great heap of stones. A pit in a wood and a pile of rocks is not a burial but a disposal, and Israel knew what it meant. Over Achan they raised over him a great heap of stones (Joshua 7:26), and over the king of Ai likewise (Joshua 8:29): the heap marks a man who died under judgment. He is not laid in a tomb, and his father, waiting at Mahanaim, is not asked.

Hanged on a tree. The law said that a man put to death and hanged on a tree was under God’s curse, and must not be left there overnight (Deuteronomy 21:22–23). The writer of Samuel draws no line from that law to Absalom, but a reader of the whole Bible can hardly miss what Paul does with it: “Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us” (Galatians 3:13). The rebel son hung in a tree under the curse he had earned; the obedient Son hung on a tree under the curse we had earned, and was raised.

Absalom’s monument. The placing is deliberate and merciless: two memorials in consecutive verses, the heap the army raised and the pillar Absalom raised for himself, in the King’s Valley near the capital, while he was alive, named after himself. (The carved tomb in Jerusalem’s Kidron Valley now called Absalom’s Pillar was cut many centuries later, in Roman times, and is not his.)

I have no son. The reason is strange, because we were told he had three sons and a daughter (14:27). The sons are never named or mentioned again, and the plain sense is probably that they died young. If so, he had buried three sons, and here is a man building a stone with his own name on it because there will be nobody after him. Pause there before passing any verdict on him.

He called the pillar after his own name. The pillar sums the man up. He spent his life on being seen: the chariot and the fifty runners, the hair, the kisses at the gate, the tent on the roof (15:1–6; 16:22). The last thing recorded about him is a stone with his name on it, so that people would keep saying it. His sister’s memorial was a daughter he named after her (14:27). His own was a rock.

The monuments we build to ourselves. Few of us commission a stone, but much of modern life is a quieter version of Absalom’s pillar: the career that must leave a mark, the personal brand, the life curated to be seen. We call it legacy, but underneath there is often Absalom’s reasoning: nobody will keep my name, so I must keep it myself. Shelley’s poem “Ozymandias” imagines a traveller finding the broken statue of a great king in an empty desert, its pedestal still ordering the mighty to look on his works and despair, with nothing left to look at. That is what self-made names come to. The surprise is that God offers the very thing Absalom built. To people with no children to carry their name, Isaiah promised “a monument and a name better than sons and daughters; I will give them an everlasting name that shall not be cut off” (Isaiah 56:5), and the Hebrew word for monument there is the word used of Absalom’s pillar. Jesus told his disciples to “rejoice that your names are written in heaven” (Luke 10:20). A name kept by God does not need a stone.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 19–32 — Is It Well with the Young Man Absalom?
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Victory has come, but the king cares about only one thing, and the news must be carried to him. Joab will not let Ahimaaz carry word of the king’s son’s death and sends a Cushite instead, but Ahimaaz insists, runs by the plain and arrives first (vv. 19–23). David waits between the gates, reading good news into the way a man runs (vv. 24–27). Ahimaaz cries “All is well” but cannot answer the king’s one question (vv. 28–30). The Cushite answers it, in the polite form of a wish that all the king’s enemies might be like that young man (vv. 31–32).
verseByVerse.theology: The king asks one question, and asks it twice, and it is not about the battle. Twenty thousand men are dead in a forest, and he wants to know about one of them.
verseByVerse.examples: Joab, who is not a sentimental man, twice tried to stop Ahimaaz for the young man’s own sake. Ahimaaz arrived first, and when the king’s question came he could not bring himself to answer it.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Ahimaaz the son of Zadok said, "Let me run and carry news to the king that the LORD has delivered him from the hand of his enemies." And Joab said to him, "You are not to carry news today. You may carry news another day, but today you shall carry no news, because the king's son is dead." Then Joab said to the Cushite, "Go, tell the king what you have seen." The Cushite bowed before Joab, and ran. Then Ahimaaz the son of Zadok said again to Joab, "Come what may, let me also run after the Cushite." And Joab said, "Why will you run, my son, seeing that you will have no reward for the news?" "Come what may," he said, "I will run." So he said to him, "Run." Then Ahimaaz ran by the way of the plain, and outran the Cushite. Now David was sitting between the two gates, and the watchman went up to the roof of the gate by the wall, and when he lifted up his eyes and looked, he saw a man running alone. The watchman called out and told the king. And the king said, "If he is alone, there is news in his mouth." And he drew nearer and nearer. The watchman saw another man running. And the watchman called to the gate and said, "See, another man running alone!" The king said, "He also brings news." The watchman said, "I think the running of the first is like the running of Ahimaaz the son of Zadok." And the king said, "He is a good man and comes with good news." Then Ahimaaz cried out to the king, "All is well." And he bowed before the king with his face to the earth and said, "Blessed be the LORD your God, who has delivered up the men who raised their hand against my lord the king." And the king said, "Is it well with the young man Absalom?" Ahimaaz answered, "When Joab sent the king's servant, your servant, I saw a great commotion, but I do not know what it was." And the king said, "Turn aside and stand here." So he turned aside and stood still. And behold, the Cushite came, and the Cushite said, "Good news for my lord the king! For the LORD has delivered you this day from the hand of all who rose up against you." The king said to the Cushite, "Is it well with the young man Absalom?" And the Cushite answered, "May the enemies of my lord the king and all who rise up against you for evil be like that young man."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The king’s whole heart is in one question, and two runners show two ways of carrying hard news: one cannot bring himself to say it, the other says it without knowing what it will cost. And Joab, of all people, tries to spare a young man the task.

Let me run and carry news to the king. Ahimaaz, who hid in a well at Bahurim for the king (17:18–19), has earned the right to ask. His message, the LORD has delivered him from the hand of his enemies, is true and a victory report, and it says nothing about a body in a pit.

You are not to carry news today. Joab, who has just killed the king’s son, will not let this young man report his death. It is one of his few kind acts in this book, and a clear-eyed one. He knows what happens to a man who brings David that news: the Amalekite who came to Ziklag with Saul’s crown, expecting a reward, was executed on the spot (1:10–15). The king’s son is dead: Joab names it plainly, the only time he says it.

The Cushite bowed before Joab. So he sends a foreigner instead. A Cushite is a man from the lands south of Egypt, probably a slave or a mercenary, expendable in a way that the son of the high priest is not. He bows and goes without a word. He was not asked whether he wanted to.

Why will you run, my son? Joab tries again, calling him my son: you will have no reward for the news. Whatever you think you are running towards, it is not there.

By the way of the plain. He goes anyway, by the flat route through the Jordan valley, longer but quicker, and overtakes the man who left first. It has been his war too, and he wants to be the one who arrives. He has not thought about what he will say when he gets there.

Between the two gates. The king sits in the gateway, between the inner and outer gates, where he cannot see anything himself. He reads the runner as any commander would: a man alone is a messenger, whereas men in numbers would mean a rout.

He is a good man and comes with good news. The next line is heartbreaking. From a watchman’s description of the way a man runs, he draws the conclusion he wants. He has sat between the gates all day with one question in his head, looking for any reason to believe the answer will be the one he wants.

All is well. Ahimaaz shouts it as he arrives: shalom. His formal report is good theology: he gives the credit to God and says nothing untrue.

Is it well with the young man Absalom? The only question David has. The kingdom is his again, and he does not ask about the battle, or Joab, or whether Ittai survived, or how many of the twenty thousand were his own. He asks about one man, and calls him what he has always called him. And there is a terrible play on words in the Hebrew: Ahimaaz shouted shalom, and David asks whether there is shalom for Absalom. The same word, and the answer is no.

I do not know what it was. Ahimaaz cannot say it. He knows exactly what happened, he was told plainly that the king’s son is dead, and he says he saw a commotion and does not know what it was. It is a lie, and entirely understandable; anyone who has had to break such news will recognise the moment. Joab knew he could not do it. One curt order, and Ahimaaz is put to one side. Wanting to carry the news is not the same as being ready to say it.

Be like that young man. The Cushite answers the question. He does not say he is dead; he uses the accepted form, a wish rather than a report: may all the king’s enemies end as that young man has. It is meant kindly, it is the plainest possible answer, and that young man gives David back his own words. Sent by a commander who did not explain, to a king he does not know, the Cushite says the correct thing in the correct form and expects to be thanked.

Uncertain wording. Ahimaaz’s answer in verse 29 is awkward in Hebrew, running literally something like at the sending of the king’s servant Joab and your servant. The ESV takes it as Joab sending the Cushite (“the king’s servant”) and Ahimaaz (“your servant”). Some hear in the tangled sentence a young man stumbling over what he cannot say. The sense is clear: he claims to have left before he knew what had happened.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The chapter ends not on victory but on a father’s grief. David turns from the messenger, climbs to the room over the gate and weeps, saying “my son” five times in one verse and wishing he had died in Absalom’s place. Every reason to condemn Absalom is true, and none of them weighs with David now. His wish is the oldest longing of love, and it was impossible for him. It points beyond him to the Son of David who did die for rebels.
verseByVerse.theology: My son, five times in one verse. It is not rhetoric; it is the way grief actually speaks.
verseByVerse.examples: Anyone who has wept like this over a child, or over anyone loved and lost, will find nothing here that tells them to stop. God gave this verse room in Scripture, and he gives grief room still.

verseByVerse.quote: And the king was deeply moved and went up to the chamber over the gate and wept. And as he went, he said, "O my son Absalom, my son, my son Absalom! Would I had died instead of you, O Absalom, my son, my son!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The victory ends in a father’s broken grief for his rebel son, and David’s wish to have died in Absalom’s place is love that cannot pay, a longing that only the cross answers.

Went up to the chamber over the gate. The chamber over the gate is a small room above the gateway, the nearest thing to privacy in a fortified town. He turns from the messenger without a word, climbs the stairs, and breaks.

As he went. He is saying it on the stairs, aloud, where the guards at the gate can hear every word. That detail matters: Joab will throw it at him in the next chapter.

My son, my son. Count them: my son five times in one verse, Absalom three times, and in the next chapter he is still saying it (19:4), eight times in two verses. This is not the lament for Saul and Jonathan, a poem written down and taught to the people of Judah (1:17–27). This is a man on a staircase saying the same two words over and over because there is nowhere else for them to go. Grief speaks like this. It circles. It does not develop or move on to a second point. It says the one true thing again.

O my son Absalom. Not “the rebel”, nor Absalom the son of Maacah, as the book introduced him (3:3); not the man who murdered Amnon, drove his father out of Jerusalem, and would have killed him yesterday had the battle gone the other way. My son. Every reason to hate him is true, and David is thinking of none of them. That is what a father is. And the first readers would hear Nathan behind it: the sword shall never depart from your house (12:10). The child of Bathsheba, then Amnon, now Absalom: this is the third son David has lost since that day.

Would I had died instead of you. The oldest wish of love: let it have been me. In David’s mouth it is useless, and he must have known it. Had he died in that forest, Absalom would have been a rebel king with his brother’s blood on him and nothing changed in his heart, and the exchange would have purchased nothing at all.

For rebels who were his enemies. Here the verse opens onto something larger, and it should be said carefully, because it helps only if the difference between David and Christ is kept clear. A thousand years later another Son of David, in David’s own city, went out to die for rebels who had stolen the hearts of a kingdom away from its rightful King and were his enemies by their own choice. He did not merely wish to die for them. He did it.

A death that worked. And the difference is not only that his death happened but that it worked. David’s substitution would have been a gesture that saved nobody. Christ’s death achieved what it was for: “while we were enemies we were reconciled to God by the death of his Son” (Romans 5:10). The rebels came home.

Not a picture of the cross. So David on that staircase is not a picture of the cross. He is a picture of the longing the cross answers: a father who wanted to die in his son’s place and could not, crying out over a kingdom he had won and a boy he had lost. The one thing he wanted most in the world was impossible for him. It was not impossible for God.

keyVerse.quote: And the king was deeply moved and went up to the chamber over the gate and wept. And as he went, he said, “O my son Absalom, my son, my son Absalom! Would I had died instead of you, O Absalom, my son, my son!”
keyVerse.note: The battle is won and the kingdom restored, yet the chapter’s last word is a father’s grief, and it shows what David’s heart had been fixed on all day. His wish to die in his son’s place is the oldest longing of love, and it was impossible for him; it was not impossible for God, whose Son did die in the place of rebels.

18.reflection:
David ordered his commanders to deal gently with Absalom “for my sake” (v. 5). Where can love for someone close to us blind us to what is just? How do we keep both love and justice in view?

The nameless soldier refused a reward because he had heard the king’s word, and he saw that Joab “would have stood aloof” (vv. 12–13). When have you been pressed to do something that the person pressing you would not own? What helps us stand firm?

Absalom raised a pillar so that his name would be remembered (v. 18). What are the “monuments” people build to themselves today? What difference does it make that God promises to keep our names (Luke 10:20)?

David cried, “Would I had died instead of you” (v. 33). How does his longing help us see what Christ actually did for rebels like us (Romans 5:10)? How might it comfort a parent who grieves for a wayward child?

19.title: The Return of the King
19.text: <sup>1</sup>It was told Joab, "Behold, the king is weeping and mourning for Absalom."<sup>2</sup>So the victory that day was turned into mourning for all the people, for the people heard that day, "The king is grieving for his son."<sup>3</sup>And the people stole into the city that day as people steal in who are ashamed when they flee in battle.<sup>4</sup>The king covered his face, and the king cried with a loud voice, "O my son Absalom, O Absalom, my son, my son!"<sup>5</sup>Then Joab came into the house to the king and said, "You have today covered with shame the faces of all your servants, who have this day saved your life and the lives of your sons and your daughters and the lives of your wives and your concubines,<sup>6</sup>because you love those who hate you and hate those who love you. For you have made it clear today that commanders and servants are nothing to you, for today I know that if Absalom were alive and all of us were dead today, then you would be pleased.<sup>7</sup>Now therefore arise, go out and speak kindly to your servants, for I swear by the LORD, if you do not go, not a man will stay with you this night, and this will be worse for you than all the evil that has come upon you from your youth until now."<sup>8</sup>Then the king arose and took his seat in the gate. And the people were all told, "Behold, the king is sitting in the gate." And all the people came before the king. Now Israel had fled every man to his own home.<sup>9</sup>And all the people were arguing throughout all the tribes of Israel, saying, "The king delivered us from the hand of our enemies and saved us from the hand of the Philistines, and now he has fled out of the land from Absalom.<sup>10</sup>But Absalom, whom we anointed over us, is dead in battle. Now therefore why do you say nothing about bringing the king back?"<sup>11</sup>And King David sent this message to Zadok and Abiathar the priests: "Say to the elders of Judah, 'Why should you be the last to bring the king back to his house, when the word of all Israel has come to the king?<sup>12</sup>You are my brothers; you are my bone and my flesh. Why then should you be the last to bring back the king?'<sup>13</sup>And say to Amasa, 'Are you not my bone and my flesh? God do so to me and more also, if you are not commander of my army from now on in place of Joab.'"<sup>14</sup>And he swayed the heart of all the men of Judah as one man, so that they sent word to the king, "Return, both you and all your servants."<sup>15</sup>So the king came back to the Jordan, and Judah came to Gilgal to meet the king and to bring the king over the Jordan.<sup>16</sup>And Shimei the son of Gera, the Benjaminite, from Bahurim, hurried to come down with the men of Judah to meet King David.<sup>17</sup>And with him were a thousand men from Benjamin. And Ziba the servant of the house of Saul, with his fifteen sons and his twenty servants, rushed down to the Jordan before the king,<sup>18</sup>and they crossed the ford to bring over the king's household and to do his pleasure. And Shimei the son of Gera fell down before the king, as he was about to cross the Jordan,<sup>19</sup>and said to the king, "Let not my lord hold me guilty or remember how your servant did wrong on the day my lord the king left Jerusalem. Do not let the king take it to heart.<sup>20</sup>For your servant knows that I have sinned. Therefore, behold, I have come this day, the first of all the house of Joseph to come down to meet my lord the king."<sup>21</sup>Abishai the son of Zeruiah answered, "Shall not Shimei be put to death for this, because he cursed the LORD's anointed?"<sup>22</sup>But David said, "What have I to do with you, you sons of Zeruiah, that you should this day be as an adversary to me? Shall anyone be put to death in Israel this day? For do I not know that I am this day king over Israel?"<sup>23</sup>And the king said to Shimei, "You shall not die." And the king gave him his oath.<sup>24</sup>And Mephibosheth the son of Saul came down to meet the king. He had neither taken care of his feet nor trimmed his beard nor washed his clothes, from the day the king departed until the day he came back in safety.<sup>25</sup>And when he came to Jerusalem to meet the king, the king said to him, "Why did you not go with me, Mephibosheth?"<sup>26</sup>He answered, "My lord, O king, my servant deceived me, for your servant said to him, 'I will saddle a donkey for myself, that I may ride on it and go with the king.' For your servant is lame.<sup>27</sup>He has slandered your servant to my lord the king. But my lord the king is like the angel of God; do therefore what seems good to you.<sup>28</sup>For all my father's house were but men doomed to death before my lord the king, but you set your servant among those who eat at your table. What further right have I, then, to cry to the king?"<sup>29</sup>And the king said to him, "Why speak any more of your affairs? I have decided: you and Ziba shall divide the land."<sup>30</sup>And Mephibosheth said to the king, "Oh, let him take it all, since my lord the king has come safely home."<sup>31</sup>Now Barzillai the Gileadite had come down from Rogelim, and he went on with the king to the Jordan, to escort him over the Jordan.<sup>32</sup>Barzillai was a very aged man, eighty years old. He had provided the king with food while he stayed at Mahanaim, for he was a very wealthy man.<sup>33</sup>And the king said to Barzillai, "Come over with me, and I will provide for you with me in Jerusalem."<sup>34</sup>But Barzillai said to the king, "How many years have I still to live, that I should go up with the king to Jerusalem?<sup>35</sup>I am this day eighty years old. Can I discern what is pleasant and what is not? Can your servant taste what he eats or what he drinks? Can I still listen to the voice of singing men and singing women? Why then should your servant be an added burden to my lord the king?<sup>36</sup>Your servant will go a little way over the Jordan with the king. Why should the king repay me with such a reward?<sup>37</sup>Please let your servant return, that I may die in my own city near the grave of my father and my mother. But here is your servant Chimham. Let him go over with my lord the king, and do for him whatever seems good to you."<sup>38</sup>And the king answered, "Chimham shall go over with me, and I will do for him whatever seems good to you, and all that you desire of me I will do for you."<sup>39</sup>Then all the people went over the Jordan, and the king went over. And the king kissed Barzillai and blessed him, and he returned to his own home.<sup>40</sup>The king went on to Gilgal, and Chimham went on with him. All the people of Judah, and also half the people of Israel, brought the king on his way.<sup>41</sup>Then all the men of Israel came to the king and said to the king, "Why have our brothers the men of Judah stolen you away and brought the king and his household over the Jordan, and all David's men with him?"<sup>42</sup>All the men of Judah answered the men of Israel, "Because the king is our close relative. Why then are you angry over this matter? Have we eaten at all at the king's expense? Or has he given us any gift?"<sup>43</sup>And the men of Israel answered the men of Judah, "We have ten shares in the king, and in David also we have more than you. Why then did you despise us? Were we not the first to speak of bringing back our king?" But the words of the men of Judah were fiercer than the words of the men of Israel.
19.overview:
Where we are. Absalom is dead under a heap of stones, and David is weeping in the room over the gate at Mahanaim (18:33). The rebellion is over. Now the king has to come home, to a nation that so recently chose someone else.

The message. Winning a battle is not the same as restoring a kingdom. The chapter shows a rejected king returning to the people who rejected him, and how he receives them: mercy to an enemy who confesses, half a measure of justice to a slandered friend, honour to a loyal old man, and silence over a quarrel that will one day tear the nation apart. God is keeping his promise to David, but David’s return, full of grace and full of flaws, shows that David cannot heal his people.

Why it was said. Later readers lived with a divided kingdom (1 Kings 12) and with the memory of how David’s reign ended (1 Kings 2). They needed to see where the crack began, and to see that even David’s best mercy did not last (see the introduction). The chapter teaches them to look for a better King.

How the chapter makes its case. The army slinks home ashamed while the king mourns, and Joab, who killed Absalom, tells David the truth; the king rises and sits in the gate (vv. 1–8). The tribes argue about bringing him back, and David wins Judah through the priests and by offering Amasa the command in Joab’s place (vv. 9–15). At the Jordan Shimei, who cursed him, confesses and is spared under oath (vv. 16–23). Mephibosheth, in mourning since the day the king left, shows that Ziba lied, and David divides the land between them (vv. 24–30). Barzillai declines a place at court with honest words about old age and sends Chimham instead (vv. 31–40). The chapter ends with Israel and Judah quarrelling over who brought the king back (vv. 41–43).

Where it leads. The chapter leads to Christ by pattern and by the need it exposes. A king comes back across the Jordan and decides what to do with rebels. David’s pardon of Shimei was real and did not last; his son was told to undo it (1 Kings 2:8–9). Christ’s pardon rests on his own blood and is spoken by a King who does not die: “there is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus” (Romans 8:1). David judged Mephibosheth’s case in haste; the Son of David will not judge by what his eyes see (Isaiah 11:3–4). And where David’s tribes quarrelled over him, God promised one King over a reunited people (Ezekiel 37:22–24), and Christ “himself is our peace, who has made us both one” (Ephesians 2:14). Mephibosheth, who wanted the king more than the land, shows what that King’s mercy does to a heart.

For us. A true rebuke is worth hearing even from someone with no right to give it. Those who live by a pardon they did not earn should be quick to show mercy and to keep their word. Old age, honestly faced, is no loss of worth in a kingdom where everyone is carried home. And small quarrels about who was honoured first are worth ending before they harden.
19.theology:
Stealing into the city (vv. 1-4). David’s men fought a hastily called-up national army in broken country and beat it, and saved the throne, and they come home in ones and twos, not meeting anyone's eye, because the lament was said aloud over the gate and the whole army heard it. Nobody said a word to them; no word was needed. A leader's private grief, however right, is never wholly private.

Joab is right, and Joab is the reason (vv. 5-7). The man who killed Absalom against a public order now orders the king to stop grieving, and every clause is true. His list of the household that would have died is accurate, since Absalom had already taken ten of the concubines on a roof. You love those who hate you is unfair as a statement about David's heart and exact as a description of what his behaviour has told everyone outside the room, and Joab is careful to claim only the second. The ultimatum is insolence, and it is also true: if the army walks out tonight, David has won a battle and lost a kingdom in the same week. This is the pattern of Joab throughout: he says the right thing, and he is the reason it needs saying.

And the king gets up (v. 8). Spoken to like that by the man who killed his son, he does not answer back or have him removed. Nothing here says the grief is over; it will not be over for the rest of his life. A duty owed to other people has been put in front of what he wants to do, which is what the office requires and what grief makes nearly impossible. The New Testament never asks anybody to stop grieving; it asks them not to grieve as others do who have no hope (1 Thess. 4:13). The grief stays. It does not get to run the household.

Amasa, and what it costs (v. 13). Offering the rebel general the royal command is a political masterstroke, since nothing reassures defeated rebels faster than seeing their own commander promoted rather than hanged. It is also personal, the one thing David can do about Joab. And it is Amasa's death warrant, because Joab does not give up a post; he kills the man who is given it.

Shimei, and the oath David did not keep (vv. 18-23). Shimei’s confession uses the right words, no one can tell whether he means them, and he is already bargaining with it. David's answer is magnificent: a secure man does not need to make an example of anybody, and a reign that resumes with a hanging at the river has told the whole country what to expect. But years later, dying, David names this very day to Solomon and tells him to bring Shimei's grey head down with blood (1 Kings 2:8-9). The book records both scenes and reconciles neither, and the notes on vv. 16-30 weigh the defences offered for David’s last instruction.

A pardon that holds. A king comes home across a river and decides what to do with those who rebelled, and the reader of the whole Bible cannot help setting the scene beside another King. David's word to Shimei was real and did not last; his son was told to undo it. Christ's pardon is spoken by a King who does not die and leave instructions, and it rests not on his mood on a day of celebration but on his own blood: no one will snatch them out of my hand (John 10:28), and there is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus (Romans 8:1). And Mephibosheth, who would rather have the king than the land, is a fair picture of what that pardon does to a heart; Paul counted everything loss because of the surpassing worth of knowing Christ Jesus my Lord (Philippians 3:8).

Half-justice (vv. 24-30). Mephibosheth's weeks of unwashed mourning, kept alone in a city under Absalom's control, and the plain fact that he cannot walk, settle the question. Yet the king who administered justice and equity to all his people (8:15) splits the land between the liar and the man he lied about, and does not want to hear more, because revisiting the judgment would mean admitting he made it carelessly. This is the second time in the book that David has fallen short of that description; the first was with Tamar. Mephibosheth's answer, let him take it all, is the last thing he says in Scripture, and nobody is obliged to believe he meant it. But he kept mourning when nobody was watching, walked in with no accusation prepared, and said his family deserved death and had been given a table instead. He never asked for the land in chapter 9 either.

Barzillai and honest old age (vv. 31-39). The power of his speech is its honesty. He does not pretend to be too humble for a court or make a show of declining an honour; he gives a plain account of what age has taken, judgment, taste and music, and concludes the offer would be wasted on him. He earned the place, and he can see that in Jerusalem he would be an old man who needs looking after. So he asks for a grave beside his parents, and then, having asked nothing for himself, asks for his son. Old age in Scripture is not a time to pretend, but neither is it a time when a person stops giving: he cannot use the offer, so he hands it to the next generation. David never forgot it (1 Kings 2:7).

The first crack (vv. 41-43). Both sides have a real point. Judah is the king's own tribe; Israel is ten-elevenths of the nation and raised the question first (vv. 9-10). Neither is lying and neither is listening, and David says nothing at all. Out of this quarrel comes Sheba's revolt in the very next verse, and two generations later the same words split the kingdom for good (1 Kings 12:16). A squabble at a river crossing about who escorted the king is the first visible crack in the thing that finally breaks Israel in half. Every large division starts somewhere this size.
19.examples:
Then: An eighty-year-old man who had fed a king's starving army at the risk of everything he owned was offered a permanent place at the royal table. He turned it down because he could no longer taste food or enjoy music, asked only to be buried near his parents, and sent his son in his place.

Now: Joab is the study in receiving a true rebuke from somebody with no right to give it. He had disobeyed a public order and killed the king's son, and he was still correct, and David got up and did what he said. Whether the person telling you is entitled to is a separate question from whether they are right, and most of us answer the first to avoid the second. Someone who knows he lives by a pardon he did not earn can afford to hear the truth from anybody. Barzillai is the study in knowing what you can no longer use: not false modesty but an honest inventory, and then asking for the next generation instead of yourself. And the quarrel at the end is the warning. Nobody in it was lying. It was about precedence and who was asked first, and the sentence shouted in it split the kingdom two generations later.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–15 — You Have Today Covered with Shame the Faces of All Your Servants
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Grief that is right in itself can still fail the people who depend on you, and the king must rise to his duty before the kingdom can be restored. David’s victorious army creeps back into the city like a beaten one, because the king is mourning aloud for the man they killed (vv. 1–4). Joab, who killed him, tells David that his grief has shamed his servants and will cost him the army by nightfall, and David gets up and sits in the gate (vv. 5–8). The tribes argue while nobody acts, so David sends the priests to stir Judah and offers Amasa, the rebel general, the command in Joab’s place (vv. 9–15).
verseByVerse.theology: Joab’s rebuke is brutal, every word of it is true, and it comes from the man who caused the grief he is ordering the king to stop. Both facts stand.
verseByVerse.examples: David does what Joab says. He gets up and goes to sit where the army can see him, because the men who saved his kingdom deserve to see their king.

verseByVerse.quote: It was told Joab, "Behold, the king is weeping and mourning for Absalom." So the victory that day was turned into mourning for all the people, for the people heard that day, "The king is grieving for his son." And the people stole into the city that day as people steal in who are ashamed when they flee in battle. The king covered his face, and the king cried with a loud voice, "O my son Absalom, O Absalom, my son, my son!" Then Joab came into the house to the king and said, "You have today covered with shame the faces of all your servants, who have this day saved your life and the lives of your sons and your daughters and the lives of your wives and your concubines, because you love those who hate you and hate those who love you. For you have made it clear today that commanders and servants are nothing to you, for today I know that if Absalom were alive and all of us were dead today, then you would be pleased. Now therefore arise, go out and speak kindly to your servants, for I swear by the LORD, if you do not go, not a man will stay with you this night, and this will be worse for you than all the evil that has come upon you from your youth until now." Then the king arose and took his seat in the gate. And the people were all told, "Behold, the king is sitting in the gate." And all the people came before the king. Now Israel had fled every man to his own home. And all the people were arguing throughout all the tribes of Israel, saying, "The king delivered us from the hand of our enemies and saved us from the hand of the Philistines, and now he has fled out of the land from Absalom. But Absalom, whom we anointed over us, is dead in battle. Now therefore why do you say nothing about bringing the king back?" And King David sent this message to Zadok and Abiathar the priests: "Say to the elders of Judah, 'Why should you be the last to bring the king back to his house, when the word of all Israel has come to the king? You are my brothers; you are my bone and my flesh. Why then should you be the last to bring back the king?' And say to Amasa, 'Are you not my bone and my flesh? God do so to me and more also, if you are not commander of my army from now on in place of Joab.'" And he swayed the heart of all the men of Judah as one man, so that they sent word to the king, "Return, both you and all your servants." So the king came back to the Jordan, and Judah came to Gilgal to meet the king and to bring the king over the Jordan.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The victory turns to shame because the king will not stop mourning, until Joab, the very man who caused his grief, tells him the truth; David rises to his duty and begins to win back the tribes that rejected him.

As people steal in who are ashamed. The sentence is terrible, and exact. These men won, and twenty thousand of the enemy are dead. Yet they come back through the gate the way a beaten army comes home, quietly, in ones and twos, not meeting anybody’s eye, because the king they fought for is upstairs crying over the man they killed. Nobody has said a word to them; no word was needed. The lament over the gate was said aloud, and David is still saying my son, five times in 18:33 and three more here.

Then Joab came into the house to the king. Joab says the hardest thing anybody says to David in the whole book. Note who is speaking: the man publicly told to deal gently with Absalom, who put three javelins into him. Joab caused this grief and now orders the king to stop it, and every word he says is true.

The lives of your sons and your daughters. His list names what would have happened had the battle gone the other way, and he is right. Absalom had already taken ten of those concubines on a roof (16:22); he was not going to spare the rest of the household.

You love those who hate you and hate those who love you. This cuts deepest. It is unfair as a statement about David’s heart, and entirely fair as a description of what his behaviour has communicated, and that distinction is the whole of Joab’s argument. He tells the king not what he feels but what everyone outside the room has been given to understand. Then comes the knife: the king would be pleased if Absalom lived and they had all died. Every man in the army has worked that out; only Joab would say it.

For I swear by the LORD. Then an ultimatum, sworn in God’s name by a general to his king. It is insolence, and it is also true. An army that believes its king despises it does not stay, and if those men walk out tonight, David has won a battle and lost a kingdom in the same week.

Then the king arose and took his seat in the gate. Remarkably, the king does it. He does not answer back, defend himself or have Joab removed. He walks down and sits in the gate, where every man coming in can see him. It is not a change of feeling: the grief will not be over for the rest of his life. He has put the duty he owes to other people in front of what he wants to do, which is what the office requires and what grief makes nearly impossible.

Why do you say nothing about bringing the king back? Meanwhile the tribes argue and nobody acts. They anointed Absalom, he is dead in a pit, and nobody wants to be first to propose fetching David, because everyone backed the other side so recently.

You are my bone and my flesh. David uses the priests Zadok and Abiathar again, the same two men who ran his intelligence during the flight (15:35–36). And he uses the phrase the tribes used to him at Hebron when they made him king, we are your bone and flesh (5:1), quoting the nation’s own words back to his own tribe. Judah is the awkward case: Absalom launched the revolt from Hebron, Judah’s own town (15:10), and the tribe is now the most compromised and most nervous in Israel. So Judah comes down to Gilgal (v. 15), by the Jordan, where Israel first camped in the land (Joshua 4:19) and where Samuel once gathered the people to renew the kingdom under Saul (1 Samuel 11:14–15). The king’s return begins where kingship had been renewed before.

Commander of my army from now on in place of Joab. David at last moves against Joab. Amasa led the force that fought in the forest of Ephraim (17:25), and David offers him the royal command permanently, under the oath “God do so to me and more also”: may God punish me if I do not keep my word. Two things are going on at once. It is a political masterstroke, for nothing would reassure the defeated rebels faster than seeing their own general promoted rather than executed. And it is personal: Joab killed David’s son against a direct order and then humiliated him in his own room, and this is the one thing David can do about it.

Amasa’s death warrant. Without knowing it, David is also signing Amasa’s death warrant. Joab does not give up a post; he kills the man who is given it, and the reader who remembers Abner at the gate of Hebron knows how chapter 20 ends.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 16–30 — Shall Anyone Be Put to Death in Israel This Day?
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The returning king meets an enemy and a slandered friend, and shows both the grace and the limits of his rule. Shimei, who cursed him, hurries down with a thousand Benjaminites and confesses his sin (vv. 16–20). Abishai wants his head, but David will not let the day of his return be stained with blood and gives Shimei his oath, an oath he will later undermine (vv. 21–23). Mephibosheth, unwashed in mourning since the day the king left, shows that Ziba lied (vv. 24–28). David hurriedly divides the land between them, and Mephibosheth gives up his share, content that the king is home (vv. 29–30).
verseByVerse.theology: The pardon at the Jordan is genuine in the moment, and it does not hold. The book records both the oath and the deathbed instruction, and leaves the tension standing.
verseByVerse.examples: Mephibosheth's appearance makes his account far more credible than Ziba's, yet David will not reverse his judgment. The man who was wronged does not argue; what matters to him is that the king is home.

verseByVerse.quote: And Shimei the son of Gera, the Benjaminite, from Bahurim, hurried to come down with the men of Judah to meet King David. And with him were a thousand men from Benjamin. And Ziba the servant of the house of Saul, with his fifteen sons and his twenty servants, rushed down to the Jordan before the king, and they crossed the ford to bring over the king's household and to do his pleasure. And Shimei the son of Gera fell down before the king, as he was about to cross the Jordan, and said to the king, "Let not my lord hold me guilty or remember how your servant did wrong on the day my lord the king left Jerusalem. Do not let the king take it to heart. For your servant knows that I have sinned. Therefore, behold, I have come this day, the first of all the house of Joseph to come down to meet my lord the king." Abishai the son of Zeruiah answered, "Shall not Shimei be put to death for this, because he cursed the LORD's anointed?" But David said, "What have I to do with you, you sons of Zeruiah, that you should this day be as an adversary to me? Shall anyone be put to death in Israel this day? For do I not know that I am this day king over Israel?" And the king said to Shimei, "You shall not die." And the king gave him his oath. And Mephibosheth the son of Saul came down to meet the king. He had neither taken care of his feet nor trimmed his beard nor washed his clothes, from the day the king departed until the day he came back in safety. And when he came to Jerusalem to meet the king, the king said to him, "Why did you not go with me, Mephibosheth?" He answered, "My lord, O king, my servant deceived me, for your servant said to him, 'I will saddle a donkey for myself, that I may ride on it and go with the king.' For your servant is lame. He has slandered your servant to my lord the king. But my lord the king is like the angel of God; do therefore what seems good to you. For all my father's house were but men doomed to death before my lord the king, but you set your servant among those who eat at your table. What further right have I, then, to cry to the king?" And the king said to him, "Why speak any more of your affairs? I have decided: you and Ziba shall divide the land." And Mephibosheth said to the king, "Oh, let him take it all, since my lord the king has come safely home."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The returning king meets the man who cursed him and the friend who was slandered: he spares the one under oath and hears the other, but his mercy will not last and his justice is only half done, while Mephibosheth’s answer shows a heart that wants the king more than the land.

Hurried to come down with the men of Judah. The man who threw stones (16:5–13) hurried to be at the river first. He cursed the LORD’s anointed in public when he was sure David was finished; David is not finished, and Shimei has perhaps a day to get in front of him before somebody else raises the subject.

A thousand men from Benjamin. He brings a thousand men of Saul’s own tribe. That is not repentance but a delegation: a king does not execute a man standing in front of a thousand of his tribesmen on the first day of a reconciliation. Ziba is there too, with his whole household, having done extremely well out of the rebellion (16:1–4).

Your servant knows that I have sinned. He says the right words, and says them first. It is a proper confession, and no one can tell from outside whether he means it. What can be observed is the sentence he attaches to it: the first of all the house of Joseph to come down. (“The house of Joseph” here stands for the northern tribes, among whom Benjamin was counted.) He is already bargaining: I got here before the north, so remember it in my favour.

Shall not Shimei be put to death for this? Abishai, for the third time in these books, offers to kill somebody: Saul asleep in the camp (1 Samuel 26:8), Shimei on the hillside (16:9), and now Shimei at the Jordan. A brave and useful man with one idea, this time he is quoting the law: cursing the LORD’s anointed was a capital matter (Exodus 22:28). He has a case.

Shall anyone be put to death in Israel this day? David’s answer is magnificent, though he will not hold to it to the end of his life. This is the day the kingdom came back, and executions do not belong in it; a reign that resumes with a hanging at the river has told the whole country what to expect. Do I not know that I am this day king over Israel? A secure man does not need to make an example of anybody. It is the same instinct that spared Saul twice.

The king gave him his oath. He swears it, the strongest undertaking available to him. Now the honest difficulty, which should not be smoothed over. Years later, dying, David gives Solomon his final instructions, and Shimei is on the list: and there is also with you Shimei the son of Gera... who cursed me with a grievous curse on the day when I went to Mahanaim. But when he came down to meet me at the Jordan, I swore to him by the LORD, saying, “I will not put you to death with the sword.” Now therefore do not hold him guiltless... bring his gray head down with blood to Sheol (1 Kings 2:8–9). He remembers the oath and this exact day, and tells his son to do what he promised not to do himself.

The attempts to excuse it. No reading of that makes it admirable. Some argue that Shimei’s later conduct forfeited the protection, that the oath bound David personally and not the crown, and that a king owes a duty to justice as well as to his word. Those arguments are not worthless, but they amount to keeping the letter of an oath while arranging for its substance to be broken by somebody else. The book records both scenes and does not reconcile them. The mercy at the Jordan is real; the deathbed instruction is real. He was capable of both.

Mephibosheth the son of Saul came down. Then the man Ziba lied about, Saul’s grandson (son in Hebrew can mean any descendant), and he hardly needs to say a word. He has not cared for his feet, trimmed his beard or washed his clothes since the morning David walked out. Those are signs of mourning, kept for weeks in a city under Absalom’s control, where anybody could see them. The man Ziba described was waiting to be given his grandfather’s kingdom (16:3). This man has been mourning for the king since the day he left.

Why did you not go with me, Mephibosheth? The king’s question has an edge. The answer is complete, and turns on the one fact everybody knew: he cannot walk. He asked Ziba to saddle a donkey so that he could follow, and Ziba took the donkeys loaded with food, got there first and told a story. The lameness that made him harmless in chapter 9 made him helpless here. And his plea is not a demand for justice. Calling the king like the angel of God, as the woman of Tekoa did (14:17, 20), he leaves the matter with him: his whole family were men doomed to death, and instead he was given a seat at the king’s table. Against that, what claim could he press?

You and Ziba shall divide the land. The ruling is a bad one, and it should be said plainly. Mephibosheth’s account explains everything and Ziba’s does not. Ziba’s story required a crippled pensioner with no faction and no army to expect the tribes to crown him during a coup by David’s own son, and David gave Ziba the estate for that story in one sentence. Now, at the proper hearing, he splits the land between the liar and the man he lied about. Why speak any more of your affairs? He does not want to hear it: he has a kingdom to reassemble, and revisiting the judgment would mean admitting he made it carelessly. This is the king who administered justice and equity to all his people (8:15), and this is the second time in the book that he falls short of that description: first with Tamar, now here.

Let him take it all. The last thing Mephibosheth says in Scripture is the best line in the chapter. Slandered, robbed of his inheritance and half vindicated by a king who will not look properly at the evidence, he answers that Ziba can have the whole estate, because the king is home. Nobody is obliged to believe he meant it. But look at the man who says it: he kept mourning when there was no advantage in it, walked in without an accusation prepared, said his family deserved death and had been given a table instead, and when half robbed gave up the other half. He asked for nothing in chapter 9 either.

A better King. David’s pardon was real and did not last; his judgment was hurried. The Son of David pardons by his own blood, and no one will snatch his people out of his hand (John 10:28); he will not judge by what his eyes see or decide by what his ears hear (Isaiah 11:3). And Mephibosheth’s answer is what his mercy does to a heart: Paul counted everything as loss “because of the surpassing worth of knowing Christ Jesus my Lord” (Philippians 3:8).

Uncertain wording. The first words of verse 18 are brief and unusual in Hebrew, literally something like and the crossing crossed. The ESV takes the rare word to mean a ford, so that Ziba’s party crossed the river to help bring the king’s household over; older English versions took it as a ferry boat. Either way the picture is the same: Ziba and his men were busily at the river, making themselves useful, when Shimei fell at the king’s feet.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 31–40 — How Many Years Have I Still to Live?
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: An old man who risked everything for the king declines his reward with honesty and grace. Barzillai, eighty and very wealthy, who fed the king’s army at Mahanaim, escorts him to the Jordan, and David invites him to live at court (vv. 31–33). Barzillai answers with a plain account of what age has taken from him, asks only to die near his parents’ grave, and offers Chimham in his place (vv. 34–38). The king kisses and blesses him, and he goes home, while the king goes on to Gilgal (vv. 39–40). David never forgot him.
verseByVerse.theology: This is one of the finest passages on old age in Scripture, and its power is the honesty with which an old man counts what has gone.
verseByVerse.examples: He asks nothing for himself except a grave near his parents, and the son he sends in his place is remembered in a place name four hundred years later.

verseByVerse.quote: Now Barzillai the Gileadite had come down from Rogelim, and he went on with the king to the Jordan, to escort him over the Jordan. Barzillai was a very aged man, eighty years old. He had provided the king with food while he stayed at Mahanaim, for he was a very wealthy man. And the king said to Barzillai, "Come over with me, and I will provide for you with me in Jerusalem." But Barzillai said to the king, "How many years have I still to live, that I should go up with the king to Jerusalem? I am this day eighty years old. Can I discern what is pleasant and what is not? Can your servant taste what he eats or what he drinks? Can I still listen to the voice of singing men and singing women? Why then should your servant be an added burden to my lord the king? Your servant will go a little way over the Jordan with the king. Why should the king repay me with such a reward? Please let your servant return, that I may die in my own city near the grave of my father and my mother. But here is your servant Chimham. Let him go over with my lord the king, and do for him whatever seems good to you." And the king answered, "Chimham shall go over with me, and I will do for him whatever seems good to you, and all that you desire of me I will do for you." Then all the people went over the Jordan, and the king went over. And the king kissed Barzillai and blessed him, and he returned to his own home. The king went on to Gilgal, and Chimham went on with him. All the people of Judah, and also half the people of Israel, brought the king on his way.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Barzillai, who risked everything for the king, declines the king’s reward with honest words about old age, asks only for a grave near his parents, and hands the honour to the next generation; and the king never forgot him.

Barzillai the Gileadite. He is one of the three men who brought bedding and cheese to Mahanaim when David arrived with nothing (17:27–29). Eighty years old and very rich, he fed an army, and a third fact is implied: he backed the losing side of a civil war at his own expense, at an age when nobody would have blamed him for staying out of it. Had Absalom won, an old landowner in Gilead who had provisioned David’s army would have kept neither his estate nor his life.

Come over with me. David offers him a place at court, the highest thing he has to give, exactly what he gave Mephibosheth.

How many years have I still to live? One of the finest speeches in the Old Testament is entirely about being old. He is not being morbid but doing arithmetic: what would be the point of uprooting himself now? Then the inventory, three questions, each naming something that has gone. Can I discern what is pleasant and what is not? Judgment, in the ordinary sense of appreciating things properly. Can your servant taste what he eats or what he drinks? His palate has gone, and a court is a place of feasts. Can I still listen to the voice of singing men and singing women? His hearing, or his appetite for music, or both. This is the saddest, because David is a musician, and Barzillai is saying that the best thing about the king’s table is a thing he can no longer enjoy.

A rare honesty. He does not pretend to be too humble for a court, or claim he is more useful at home. He gives a plain, rather bleak account of what age has taken and concludes that the offer would be wasted on him. Most of us would take the seat and pretend to enjoy the singing.

Why then should your servant be an added burden? The sentence many people cannot say. He has earned the place, and he can see that what he would actually be, in Jerusalem, is an old man who needs looking after. He would rather not be that.

Why does growing old feel like losing your worth? Barzillai asks his question with dignity; many old people today ask it with dread. A culture that measures people by what they produce and how independent they are has little to say to someone who can no longer do either, and so the deepest fear of age is often not pain but being a burden. Where assisted dying is legal, that fear is among the reasons people most often give for asking for it. Scripture does not deny the losses Barzillai lists. It simply refuses to let them settle anyone’s worth. Israel’s God says, “even to your old age I am he, and to gray hairs I will carry you. I have made, and I will bear; I will carry and will save” (Isaiah 46:4). Notice who carries whom. Every one of us began life as a burden to somebody for years, and we were made that way, to be carried. The church is told, “Bear one another’s burdens, and so fulfill the law of Christ” (Galatians 6:2), because Christ first carried ours, all the way to the cross. In his kingdom, being carried is not a failure. It is how everyone gets home.

Near the grave of my father and my mother. He will walk the king a little way over the Jordan and no further; even the escort is measured out. The one thing he asks for is a grave: to die in his own city, near where his parents are buried. Not a title, not land, not a position. And then, having asked nothing for himself, he asks for somebody else: here is your servant Chimham, probably his son (1 Kings 2:7 speaks of the sons of Barzillai). He cannot use the offer; the next generation can.

Geruth Chimham. It was not a small thing. Four hundred years later, when Jerusalem has fallen and the last Judeans are fleeing to Egypt, Jeremiah notes where they stopped: they went and stayed at Geruth Chimham near Bethlehem (Jeremiah 41:17). The name probably means “the lodging-place of Chimham”. David probably gave the family land near Bethlehem, his own town, and the name outlasted the kingdom.

The king kissed Barzillai and blessed him. A kiss at a river, and an old man walks back up into Gilead to die at home. It is the last we hear of him, except that on his deathbed, giving Solomon the list of people to deal with, David includes one instruction that is not about revenge: but deal loyally with the sons of Barzillai the Gileadite, and let them be among those who eat at your table, for with such loyalty they met me when I fled from Absalom your brother (1 Kings 2:7). He never forgot the cheese and the bedding.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 41–43 — The Words of the Men of Judah Were Fiercer
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The kingdom is barely restored before its tribes quarrel over the king, and the first crack in the nation appears. The men of Israel complain that Judah has stolen the king away and brought him over the Jordan without them (v. 41). Judah answers that the king is their close relative and that they have taken nothing from him (v. 42). Israel claims ten shares in the king and reminds Judah that they spoke first, but Judah’s words are fiercer still (v. 43). David says nothing, and the quarrel leads straight into Sheba’s revolt in the next chapter.
verseByVerse.theology: The rebellion is over, and the argument that starts here is worse, because it is not about Absalom. It is ten tribes against one, over precedence, and both sides are partly right.
verseByVerse.examples: The chapter ends by telling us how heated the exchange was, not how it was settled, because it was not settled, and the very next verse is a rebel’s trumpet. Quarrels about who was honoured first rarely stay small.

verseByVerse.quote: Then all the men of Israel came to the king and said to the king, "Why have our brothers the men of Judah stolen you away and brought the king and his household over the Jordan, and all David's men with him?" All the men of Judah answered the men of Israel, "Because the king is our close relative. Why then are you angry over this matter? Have we eaten at all at the king's expense? Or has he given us any gift?" And the men of Israel answered the men of Judah, "We have ten shares in the king, and in David also we have more than you. Why then did you despise us? Were we not the first to speak of bringing back our king?" But the words of the men of Judah were fiercer than the words of the men of Israel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The kingdom is barely restored before its tribes quarrel over who honoured the king first, and in that quarrel, left unanswered by David, lies the first crack that will one day split Israel in two.

Then all the men of Israel came to the king. The war is over and the argument begins at once, about precedence: Judah escorted the king across the river, and the other tribes were not invited. The word they use is stolen, the same verb the writer used of Absalom stealing the hearts of the men of Israel (15:6). They accuse Judah of doing to the king what Absalom did to them.

Because the king is our close relative. Judah’s answer has two parts. The first is honest and unhelpful: of course we brought him home, he is ours. The second is defensive: we have taken nothing and received no favours. That is true, but it does not answer the complaint.

We have ten shares in the king. Israel’s reply is arithmetic: ten tribes to your one. And their last question is fair: they were the first to speak of bringing back the king. Verses 9 and 10 recorded the northern tribes arguing about it while Judah said nothing, and David had to send the priests to prod Judah into moving. So both sides have a real point. Judah is the king’s tribe; Israel is most of the nation and raised the question first. Neither is lying, and neither is listening.

But the words of the men of Judah were fiercer. The chapter does not say who was right or what the king decided; David says nothing at all. It says only that Judah shouted louder, because the argument had no outcome.

The first crack. The next chapter opens with a man from Benjamin blowing a trumpet: we have no portion in David, and we have no inheritance in the son of Jesse; every man to his tents, O Israel! (20:1). Sheba’s rebellion comes straight out of this quarrel and is over in a chapter; the quarrel is not. Two generations later, when Rehoboam has answered the north with a threat about scorpions, the ten tribes walk out saying almost the same words: What portion do we have in David? We have no inheritance in the son of Jesse. To your tents, O Israel! (1 Kings 12:16). The kingdom splits at that sentence and never comes back together. So this squabble at a river crossing, about who was asked first, whose relative he is and who felt slighted, is the first visible crack in what finally breaks Israel in half. Every large division starts somewhere this size.

One King over one people. The prophets did not leave the crack unhealed. Ezekiel promised that God would make the divided people one nation again, with one king over them all: My servant David shall be king over them, and they shall all have one shepherd (Ezekiel 37:22–24). That promise is kept in Christ, who gathers into one flock people far more divided than Judah and Israel: “he himself is our peace, who has made us both one” (Ephesians 2:14). Quarrels about precedence among his people deny what he died to make.

keyVerse.quote: And Mephibosheth said to the king, “Oh, let him take it all, since my lord the king has come safely home.”
keyVerse.note: Slandered, robbed and only half vindicated, Mephibosheth gives up the rest of his land because the king himself has returned. In a chapter of bargaining, quarrelling and half-justice, his words show a heart that wants the king more than the king’s gifts, which is what the mercy of the greater Son of David does to those who receive it.

19.reflection:
Joab, who had caused David’s grief, told him the truth about what it was doing to his people, and David got up and acted (vv. 5–8). Why is it hard to hear a true rebuke from someone we resent? What helps us listen anyway?

David spared Shimei with an oath, yet later told Solomon to deal with him (v. 23; 1 Kings 2:8–9). How is Christ’s pardon different from David’s? How should being forgiven by him shape the way we forgive?

Barzillai spoke honestly about what age had taken from him, and asked for his son rather than for himself (vv. 34–37). What can we learn from him about growing old, and about how the church should value those who need carrying?

The quarrel between Israel and Judah was about who honoured the king first, and it led to rebellion and, later, to division (vv. 41–43). Where do such small rivalries appear among Christians? How does Christ, our peace, help us end them?

20.title: Sheba's Revolt and the Wise Woman of Abel
20.text: <sup>1</sup>Now there happened to be there a worthless man, whose name was Sheba, the son of Bichri, a Benjaminite. And he blew the trumpet and said, "We have no portion in David, and we have no inheritance in the son of Jesse; every man to his tents, O Israel!"<sup>2</sup>So all the men of Israel withdrew from David and followed Sheba the son of Bichri. But the men of Judah followed their king steadfastly from the Jordan to Jerusalem.<sup>3</sup>And David came to his house at Jerusalem. And the king took the ten concubines whom he had left to care for the house and put them in a house under guard and provided for them, but did not go in to them. So they were shut up until the day of their death, living as if in widowhood.<sup>4</sup>Then the king said to Amasa, "Call the men of Judah together to me within three days, and be here yourself."<sup>5</sup>So Amasa went to summon Judah, but he delayed beyond the set time that had been appointed him.<sup>6</sup>And David said to Abishai, "Now Sheba the son of Bichri will do us more harm than Absalom. Take your lord's servants and pursue him, lest he get himself to fortified cities and escape from us."<sup>7</sup>And there went out after him Joab's men and the Cherethites and the Pelethites, and all the mighty men. They went out from Jerusalem to pursue Sheba the son of Bichri.<sup>8</sup>When they were at the great stone that is in Gibeon, Amasa came to meet them. Now Joab was wearing a soldier's garment, and over it was a belt with a sword in its sheath fastened on his thigh, and as he went forward it fell out.<sup>9</sup>And Joab said to Amasa, "Is it well with you, my brother?" And Joab took Amasa by the beard with his right hand to kiss him.<sup>10</sup>But Amasa did not observe the sword that was in Joab's hand. So Joab struck him with it in the stomach and spilled his entrails to the ground without striking a second blow, and he died. Then Joab and Abishai his brother pursued Sheba the son of Bichri.<sup>11</sup>And one of Joab's young men took his stand by Amasa and said, "Whoever favors Joab, and whoever is for David, let him follow Joab."<sup>12</sup>And Amasa lay wallowing in his blood in the highway. And anyone who came by, seeing him, stopped. And when the man saw that all the people stopped, he carried Amasa out of the highway into the field and threw a garment over him.<sup>13</sup>When he was taken out of the highway, all the people went on after Joab to pursue Sheba the son of Bichri.<sup>14</sup>And Sheba passed through all the tribes of Israel to Abel of Beth-maacah, and all the Bichrites assembled and followed him in.<sup>15</sup>And all the men who were with Joab came and besieged him in Abel of Beth-maacah. They cast up a mound against the city, and it stood against the rampart, and they were battering the wall to throw it down.<sup>16</sup>Then a wise woman called from the city, "Listen! Listen! Tell Joab, 'Come here, that I may speak to you.'"<sup>17</sup>And he came near her, and the woman said, "Are you Joab?" He answered, "I am." Then she said to him, "Listen to the words of your servant." And he answered, "I am listening."<sup>18</sup>Then she said, "They used to say in former times, 'Let them but ask counsel at Abel,' and so they settled a matter.<sup>19</sup>I am one of those who are peaceable and faithful in Israel. You seek to destroy a city that is a mother in Israel. Why will you swallow up the heritage of the LORD?"<sup>20</sup>Joab answered, "Far be it from me, far be it, that I should swallow up or destroy!<sup>21</sup>That is not true. But a man of the hill country of Ephraim, called Sheba the son of Bichri, has lifted up his hand against King David. Give up him alone, and I will withdraw from the city." And the woman said to Joab, "Behold, his head shall be thrown to you over the wall."<sup>22</sup>Then the woman went to all the people in her wisdom. And they cut off the head of Sheba the son of Bichri and threw it out to Joab. So he blew the trumpet, and they dispersed from the city, every man to his home. And Joab returned to Jerusalem to the king.<sup>23</sup>Now Joab was in command of all the army of Israel; and Benaiah the son of Jehoiada was in command of the Cherethites and the Pelethites;<sup>24</sup>and Adoram was in charge of the forced labor; and Jehoshaphat the son of Ahilud was the recorder;<sup>25</sup>and Sheva was secretary; and Zadok and Abiathar were priests;<sup>26</sup>and Ira the Jairite was also David's priest.
20.overview:
Where we are. David is on his way back to Jerusalem, and the tribes have just quarrelled at the Jordan over who brought him home, with Judah shouting loudest (19:41–43). Amasa, Absalom’s general, has been promised Joab’s command.

The message. The kingdom David has regained is restored but not healed. A worthless man with a trumpet splits the nation along the very line on which it will one day break for good; ten innocent women pay for an earlier sin; and a murderer kills his rival and is left at the head of the army. God keeps David on his throne, and even uses a wise woman to spare a city, but David cannot purge the evil inside his own house and government. The chapter makes us long for a King who can.

Why it was said. The first readers knew how the story ended: a kingdom torn in two under Rehoboam over a slogan and a grievance about forced labour (1 Kings 12; see the introduction). This chapter shows them that both were already present in David’s day, and that the house of David needed more than a restored throne.

How the chapter makes its case. Sheba the son of Bichri blows a trumpet and the north walks out, while Judah stays with the king; David returns and shuts away the ten concubines for life (vv. 1–3). Amasa is slow to muster Judah, David sends Abishai after Sheba, and Joab kills Amasa with a kiss and a sword at Gibeon; the army halts at the body until it is covered, then follows Joab (vv. 4–13). Sheba is besieged in Abel of Beth-maacah, and a wise woman calls Joab to the wall, saves the city and has Sheba’s head thrown over it (vv. 14–22). The chapter closes with David’s officials, with Joab’s name first and a new office for forced labour (vv. 23–26).

Where it leads. The chapter leads to Christ by the need it exposes and by promise. Sheba’s slogan names a division that is never healed in the Old Testament, but the prophets promised one King over a reunited people (Ezekiel 37:22–24), and Jesus died “to gather into one the children of God who are scattered abroad” (John 11:52). David could not judge the violent man at the top of his own government; the Son of David will judge with perfect righteousness. And where Joab’s army threw a cloak over a crime so that the march could go on, God covers sin by forgiving it, at the cost of his Son.

For us. Be wary of whoever hands people words for a grievance they already feel, and remember that in Christ no believer is without a portion. Do not cover wrongs simply so that business can carry on; what Christ has covered can be confessed in the open. And like the woman of Abel, speak plain, wise words to the powerful, even without a title.
20.theology:
The slogan that outlives the man (v. 1). Sheba did not create the grievance. He found ten tribes freshly humiliated at the river and handed them words for what they already felt, which is all such men ever do. He loses within the chapter; his slogan wins two generations later.

The King who mends the split. Sheba’s slogan names a division that is never healed within the Old Testament. The prophets saw the cure in a coming son of David: one king shall be king over them all, and they shall be no longer two nations, with my servant David as their one shepherd (Ezekiel 37:22, 24). The New Testament finds that King in Jesus, who died to gather into one the children of God who are scattered abroad (John 11:52) and broke down the wall between Jew and Gentile (Ephesians 2:14). In him nobody need shout that they have no portion in David: every believer has an inheritance kept in heaven (1 Peter 1:4), and quarrels over precedence, as old as that river crossing, meet a Son of David who washed his disciples' feet.

Why a king had concubines at all (v. 3). A reader will ask it. A concubine was a wife of lower rank, without the full standing of a wife. Scripture records the practice without approving it: the law forbade Israel's king to multiply wives (Deuteronomy 17:17), the pattern from creation is one man and one woman (Genesis 2:24), and Jesus returns to that beginning (Matthew 19:4-6). Nearly every polygamous household in the Old Testament breeds rivalry and grief, and David's is the plainest case. The ten women shut in a house for life, living as if in widowhood, are its saddest result.

David still will not use Joab (v. 6). He gives the order to Abishai and goes round Joab through his brother, which is a weak arrangement, since Abishai has spent his life doing what Joab does, and the troops who march out are called Joab's men. David's assessment of the danger is right, though: Absalom wanted the throne, but Sheba wants the country in two pieces.

Worse than Abner (vv. 8-10). The method is the same: the greeting, the hand on the beard, the single blow to the stomach. But Abner was an enemy commander who had killed Joab's brother; Amasa is the commander of the royal army, appointed by David under oath only days before. This is a serving officer murdering the man the king set over him, in front of the troops, to get his job back, and verse 23 records that he got it. David's one attempt to discipline Joab was to give his post to someone else, and Joab answered it with a sword.

The body in the road (vv. 12-13). The army stops dead at the sight of the king's commander lying in his own blood, until someone drags him into a field and throws a cloak over him, and then the column moves on. The writer makes no comment of his own, and needs none: for the army the problem was never the death, but that it could be seen. Covering a wrong is not the same as dealing with it, and David, years later and dying, still cannot deal with it himself (1 Kings 2:5).

The wise woman of Abel (vv. 16-22). Unlike the woman of Tekoa, who was found, dressed and scripted by Joab, this woman has no employer and no script.
