She tells Joab what the town is, a place of counsel; establishes that she and it are loyal; and then names what he is about to do: destroy a mother in Israel and swallow up the heritage of the LORD. The land is not his to destroy, because every town is part of an inheritance God gave. Joab, who has just killed a man in a road, backs down at once. She is the third woman in this history, after Abigail and the woman of Tekoa, to turn events with nothing but words, and she asks nothing for herself.

A new office, and what it becomes (v. 24). Adoram over the forced labour is not in the chapter 8 list; the kingdom has acquired conscripted labour and a minister to run it. Under Solomon it becomes vast, and when he dies the northern tribes ask Rehoboam to lighten the hard service of your father and his heavy yoke (1 Kings 12:4). He refuses, and they stone Adoram (1 Kings 12:18). So both halves of the final split are already in this chapter: the slogan in verse 1 and the grievance in verse 24.

The list is a mercy and an indictment (vv. 23-26). It mirrors the one at the end of chapter 8, which came after the conquests. This one comes after Bathsheba, Amnon, Tamar, Absalom, the flight, the forest and Sheba, and says the same thing in the same form. The government works, and the ordinary business of governing goes on, which is how God generally keeps the world running after a catastrophe. Yet the two things that will destroy the kingdom are already inside the administration and drawing a salary: Joab at the top, unpunished, and Adoram over the forced labour, unnoticed.
20.examples:
Then: A woman with no office, no name recorded, and no one who sent her leaned over a city wall while the army of Israel was battering it down, called the commander-in-chief to come and talk, and stopped the siege. Then she went inside and persuaded the whole city to do the hard thing she had promised on their behalf.

Now: Sheba is the study in how a fracture happens. He had no case and no following, and it did not matter, because the grievance was already there and all he supplied was a sentence for it. Watch who hands people words for what they are already feeling, and remember that in the Son of David nobody is without a portion. The body in the road is a warning of another kind: once it was covered nobody had to decide anything, which is exactly how institutions, churches included, handle a thing they have no intention of dealing with. And the woman of Abel is the best example of the three. She did not plead, and asked nothing for herself. She told a violent man what his action really was, and then she went and did the part that cost something. Courage of that kind does not need a title.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–3 — We Have No Portion in David
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Out of the quarrel at the Jordan comes a new revolt, and the cost of earlier sin falls on the innocent. Sheba, a worthless man of Benjamin, blows a trumpet and gives the humiliated northern tribes a slogan: no portion in David, every man to his tents (v. 1). The north follows him, while Judah stays with the king all the way to Jerusalem (v. 2). David comes home and shuts the ten concubines, violated publicly by Absalom, in a guarded house, providing for them but never going in to them; they live out their lives as if widows (v. 3).
verseByVerse.theology: The last sentence of the previous chapter was that Judah shouted louder than Israel. This is what happens next: one man with a trumpet finds ten tribes already angry and gives them a slogan.
verseByVerse.examples: Words matter. A slogan shouted by a nobody in a moment of wounded pride outlived him and, two generations later, broke the kingdom in two.

verseByVerse.quote: Now there happened to be there a worthless man, whose name was Sheba, the son of Bichri, a Benjaminite. And he blew the trumpet and said, "We have no portion in David, and we have no inheritance in the son of Jesse; every man to his tents, O Israel!" So all the men of Israel withdrew from David and followed Sheba the son of Bichri. But the men of Judah followed their king steadfastly from the Jordan to Jerusalem. And David came to his house at Jerusalem. And the king took the ten concubines whom he had left to care for the house and put them in a house under guard and provided for them, but did not go in to them. So they were shut up until the day of their death, living as if in widowhood.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A worthless man with a trumpet turns the quarrel at the Jordan into a rebellion, and the north walks away from David along the very line on which the kingdom will one day break; meanwhile ten women who did nothing wrong pay for Absalom’s sin for the rest of their lives.

There happened to be there. The phrasing is almost dismissive, and that is the point. Sheba is nobody: no army, no standing, no faction and no case. The word used of him, worthless, is the one Nabal’s servants used of Nabal (1 Samuel 25:17) and Shimei used of David (16:7). What he has is a trumpet and a sentence, and he is standing in the middle of an argument that was already burning.

We have no portion in David. Twelve words in Hebrew, and they will eventually break the kingdom. No portion and no inheritance are land words, the vocabulary of tribal allotment: the house of David is Judah’s business, and the north has no stake in it. The son of Jesse is a sneer with a history, what Saul called David when he would not use his name (1 Samuel 20:27; 22:7). Every man to his tents is the formula for breaking up a national muster: go home, this is not our war.

Why the slogan caught on. Ten tribes have just been shouted down at a river crossing (19:43), and a man with a trumpet gives them a slogan. He did not create the grievance; he found it fully formed and put words to it, which is all such men ever do.

All the men of Israel withdrew from David. The whole north walks out. The rebellion is over in twenty verses; what matters is that the country divided along the exact line it will divide along permanently: ten tribes on one side, Judah on the other. Two generations from now, when Rehoboam answers a northern delegation with a threat about scorpions, this is what they say as they go: What portion do we have in David? We have no inheritance in the son of Jesse. To your tents, O Israel! (1 Kings 12:16). The kingdom never comes back together. Sheba loses; the slogan wins.

A portion in the Son of David. The slogan names a division that the Old Testament never heals, and a hope it never gives up: one King over one people (Ezekiel 37:22–24). In Jesus, the Son of David, nobody need shout that they have no portion in David. Every believer has “an inheritance that is imperishable, undefiled, and unfading, kept in heaven” (1 Peter 1:4).

The ten concubines. Then the cost of chapter 16, borne by ten women who had done nothing wrong. David had left them to keep the house when he fled (15:16). At Ahithophel’s advice Absalom took them publicly, in the sight of all Israel (16:22), on the roof, which is where the whole business began (11:2).

Put them in a house under guard. There is no good answer. He cannot take them back; the custom of the time, and probably the principle of Deuteronomy 24:4, made that impossible. Nor does he send them away. He provides a house, a guard and food for the rest of their lives, and the writer records the result in one clause: living as if in widowhood. They will not marry, have children or leave that house. They will be fed and housed and forgotten.

Who paid the cost. They chose none of it: not to be royal concubines, not to be left behind, and certainly not the roof. Two men conducted a political argument through their bodies, and the women pay the whole cost, as Uriah, Tamar and twenty thousand men in a forest paid before them. Sin does not confine its damage to the people who commit it. David has his throne again and Absalom is dead; these ten are alive and shut in a house, and that is the last we hear of them.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 4–13 — Is It Well with You, My Brother?
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The king’s one attempt to discipline his general is answered with a sword. Amasa, the new commander, is slow to muster Judah, so David sends Abishai after Sheba, and Joab’s men go too (vv. 4–7). At the great stone in Gibeon, Joab greets Amasa as a brother, takes him by the beard to kiss him and kills him with a single blow, as he once killed Abner (vv. 8–10). A soldier calls the army to follow Joab, but the men stop at the body in the road until it is dragged into a field and covered, and then the pursuit goes on under Joab (vv. 11–13).
verseByVerse.theology: Every element of this repeats Abner's murder: the affectionate greeting, the hand, the stomach, the one blow. Amasa's mistake is Abner's too: he did not look for a weapon in the hand of a man calling him brother.
verseByVerse.examples: The difference is that Amasa is the king's own appointed commander. The army halts at the body because it does not know what has just happened to the chain of command.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the king said to Amasa, "Call the men of Judah together to me within three days, and be here yourself." So Amasa went to summon Judah, but he delayed beyond the set time that had been appointed him. And David said to Abishai, "Now Sheba the son of Bichri will do us more harm than Absalom. Take your lord's servants and pursue him, lest he get himself to fortified cities and escape from us." And there went out after him Joab's men and the Cherethites and the Pelethites, and all the mighty men. They went out from Jerusalem to pursue Sheba the son of Bichri. When they were at the great stone that is in Gibeon, Amasa came to meet them. Now Joab was wearing a soldier's garment, and over it was a belt with a sword in its sheath fastened on his thigh, and as he went forward it fell out. And Joab said to Amasa, "Is it well with you, my brother?" And Joab took Amasa by the beard with his right hand to kiss him. But Amasa did not observe the sword that was in Joab's hand. So Joab struck him with it in the stomach and spilled his entrails to the ground without striking a second blow, and he died. Then Joab and Abishai his brother pursued Sheba the son of Bichri. And one of Joab's young men took his stand by Amasa and said, "Whoever favors Joab, and whoever is for David, let him follow Joab." And Amasa lay wallowing in his blood in the highway. And anyone who came by, seeing him, stopped. And when the man saw that all the people stopped, he carried Amasa out of the highway into the field and threw a garment over him. When he was taken out of the highway, all the people went on after Joab to pursue Sheba the son of Bichri.
verseByVerse.commentary:
David’s one attempt to discipline Joab, by giving his command to Amasa, is answered with a kiss and a sword; the army stops at the body only until it is covered, and then follows the murderer.

But he delayed beyond the set time. Amasa is late with his first task. Perhaps Judah was unwilling to muster for Absalom’s former general; perhaps he was simply slow. What matters is that the delay gives Joab a reason to be in the road at Gibeon.

David said to Abishai. David is still refusing Joab a command and goes round him through his brother, a thin arrangement, since Abishai has spent his whole life doing what Joab does. Joab holds no command, yet the men who march out are called Joab’s men: the army is still his. And David’s assessment is right: Absalom wanted the throne; Sheba wants the country in two pieces.

As he went forward it fell out. Perhaps the sword genuinely worked loose and he picked it up, so that Amasa saw him stand up with a blade in his hand and thought nothing of it; perhaps it was contrived, so that the weapon was in his left hand while his right reached out empty (see the box below). Either way the writer tells us before the greeting, so that we watch the greeting knowing what is in the hand.

Is it well with you, my brother? They are cousins, their mothers sisters (17:25), so brother is no great exaggeration. Taking a man by the beard with the right hand to kiss him was the most intimate greeting between men in that culture. It requires him to stand still and put his face forward; it works only if you are trusted; it occupies the right hand; and it puts the other man’s stomach eighteen inches from your left.

Abner at Hebron. Go back to 3:27: And when Abner returned to Hebron, Joab took him aside into the midst of the gate to speak with him privately, and there he struck him in the stomach, so that he died The same man, the same wound in the same place, the same method. Here the writer adds that he needed no second blow. He knows exactly where to put it. And Amasa’s mistake is Abner’s. Neither saw the weapon, because neither was looking for one: a man who takes you by the beard and calls you brother is not a man you are watching.

Worse than Abner. Abner was the enemy commander, and there was a blood feud, for Abner had killed Asahel (2:23). Amasa is the commander of the royal army, appointed by David personally, under oath, days ago. This is not private vengeance; it is a serving officer murdering the man the king set over him, in front of the troops, to get his job back. And he gets it, as verse 23 records. This is what happens when a king cannot discipline his general. David’s one attempt to act against Joab was to give the command to somebody else, and Joab answered it with a sword.

Whoever favors Joab. He steps over the body and carries on with the campaign. A soldier stands beside the corpse shouting a loyalty formula, and the order of the names is whoever favors Joab, and whoever is for David. Joab first. Slip or not, it accurately describes who is running this army.

All the people stopped. Without a word of his own, the writer comments on the whole business. The army will not walk past. Every man who comes up the road sees the king’s commander lying in his own blood and stops dead, and the column jams. They know what they are looking at. So the young man drags him into a field and throws a cloak over him, and the moment he is covered the army moves again. The problem was never the death; it was that the death could be seen. Get it out of the road, throw something over it, and the campaign proceeds and nobody has to decide anything.

When the only wrong is being seen. The young man with the cloak has a modern instinct. The anthropologist Ruth Benedict, writing about Japan after the Second World War, distinguished cultures governed by guilt, where what matters is what you have done, from cultures governed by shame, where what matters is who saw it. Many observers think the West has been drifting towards the second. Public life becomes reputation management, and a wrong nobody notices hardly seems to count. Joab’s army is that world in miniature: nobody denies the murder; they simply move it out of the road. Scripture also speaks of covering sin, but in the opposite direction. When Adam and Eve hid behind fig leaves, “the LORD God made for Adam and for his wife garments of skins and clothed them” (Genesis 3:21), and skins mean that something died. David himself sang, “Blessed is the one whose transgression is forgiven, whose sin is covered” (Psalm 32:1). God does not throw a cloak over sin so that the march can go on. He forgives it, and the covering cost him his Son. That is why a Christian need not manage appearances: what Christ has covered can be confessed in the open.

Until David’s deathbed. Nothing more is said about Amasa until David is dying and tells Solomon: you also know what Joab the son of Zeruiah did to me, how he dealt with the two commanders of the armies of Israel, Abner the son of Ner, and Amasa the son of Jether, whom he killed, avenging in time of peace for blood that had been shed in war (1 Kings 2:5). Even then he cannot punish Joab himself. He asks his son to.

Uncertain wording. Verse 8 is awkward in Hebrew, and its exact sense has been argued over for centuries: whether the sword fell by accident or by design, and how it came to be in his hand. The ESV’s as he went forward it fell out keeps the Hebrew’s brevity. What is clear is that Joab had a drawn sword in his hand as he reached for Amasa’s beard, and Amasa did not notice it (v. 10).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 14–22 — A City and a Mother in Israel
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A wise woman with no office saves a city by speaking plainly to a violent man. Sheba flees to Abel of Beth-maacah in the far north, and Joab’s army builds a siege mound and batters the wall (vv. 14–15). A woman calls Joab to the wall, reminds him that Abel is a town of counsel, a mother in Israel and part of the LORD’s heritage, and asks why he would swallow it up (vv. 16–19). Joab answers that he wants only Sheba. She persuades the city, Sheba’s head is thrown over the wall, and the army goes home (vv. 20–22).
verseByVerse.theology: She is hired by nobody and scripted by nobody. The woman of Tekoa came with Joab's words in her mouth; this one calls him to the wall on her own authority and argues with him.
verseByVerse.examples: Her argument is not a plea. She tells him what the place is, and then names what he is about to do in words he cannot answer.

verseByVerse.quote: And Sheba passed through all the tribes of Israel to Abel of Beth-maacah, and all the Bichrites assembled and followed him in. And all the men who were with Joab came and besieged him in Abel of Beth-maacah. They cast up a mound against the city, and it stood against the rampart, and they were battering the wall to throw it down. Then a wise woman called from the city, "Listen! Listen! Tell Joab, 'Come here, that I may speak to you.'" And he came near her, and the woman said, "Are you Joab?" He answered, "I am." Then she said to him, "Listen to the words of your servant." And he answered, "I am listening." Then she said, "They used to say in former times, 'Let them but ask counsel at Abel,' and so they settled a matter. I am one of those who are peaceable and faithful in Israel. You seek to destroy a city that is a mother in Israel. Why will you swallow up the heritage of the LORD?" Joab answered, "Far be it from me, far be it, that I should swallow up or destroy! That is not true. But a man of the hill country of Ephraim, called Sheba the son of Bichri, has lifted up his hand against King David. Give up him alone, and I will withdraw from the city." And the woman said to Joab, "Behold, his head shall be thrown to you over the wall." Then the woman went to all the people in her wisdom. And they cut off the head of Sheba the son of Bichri and threw it out to Joab. So he blew the trumpet, and they dispersed from the city, every man to his home. And Joab returned to Jerusalem to the king.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A wise woman with no office and no name calls the commander of Israel to the wall, tells him what he is about to destroy, and saves her city at the cost of one rebel’s head.

To Abel of Beth-maacah. Sheba runs to the far north, near the sources of the Jordan, about as far from Jerusalem as one can get and still be in Israel, and his following has shrunk to his own clan; the ten tribes have gone home.

They cast up a mound against the city. They build a siege ramp against an Israelite town and start knocking the wall in, and a woman shouts down and summons the commander-in-chief of Israel to talk to her.

A wise woman called from the city. She is called a wise woman, the phrase used of the woman of Tekoa, and the difference between them is the whole point. The woman of Tekoa was found by Joab, dressed by Joab and given a speech to recite; the writer says so twice (14:2–3, 19). This one has no employer and no script. She has looked over a wall at a siege ramp and decided to negotiate. The exchange is short and businesslike (I am listening), and Joab stops the assault to have it.

Let them but ask counsel at Abel. She opens by telling him what the town is. Abel had a reputation as a place people came to for a ruling, and there was evidently a proverb about it. Her first move is not a plea but information: you are battering the wall of the place people come to for a ruling, and you asked nobody anything before you started. Israel’s own law of war told an army to offer a city terms of peace before attacking it (Deuteronomy 20:10), and that law was written about foreign towns. This one is Israelite, and nobody had offered it anything.

Three names for what he does. Then three sentences, each putting a name on what he is doing. I am one of those who are peaceable and faithful in Israel: she establishes her right to be heard; she is no rebel, and neither is the town. A city that is a mother in Israel: this is how an important town with dependent villages was spoken of, a place that has daughters. Knock it down and you are not taking a fortress; you are killing a mother and orphaning everything around her.

Why will you swallow up the heritage of the LORD? This is the theological argument, and it settles the matter. The land is not Joab’s to destroy. Every town in Israel is part of an inheritance God distributed, and a general who flattens one is not conducting an operation but consuming what belongs to God. The picture is close to Abner’s at Gibeon: Shall the sword devour forever? (2:26).

Far be it from me. He backs down at once, and even repeats her verb. This is Joab, who killed Abner at a gate, Absalom in a tree and Amasa in a road on the way here. He does not threaten her; he answers the argument on its own terms and states his actual objective, which is one man, and she agrees to it before consulting anybody.

The woman went to all the people in her wisdom. Without office or authority, she persuades the town, and a whole city does what she says. The result is brutal arithmetic: one head over a wall instead of a town under it.

One man instead of a city. The bargain has an echo in the Gospels. When the council feared that Rome would destroy the nation, the high priest reasoned the same way: “it is better for you that one man should die for the people, not that the whole nation should perish” (John 11:50). John saw a meaning in it that Caiaphas never intended. The difference is everything. Sheba was a guilty rebel, given up to save a town from the consequences of his crime. Jesus was innocent, and gave himself up to save the guilty from the consequences of theirs.

The third such woman. She is the third such woman in this history. Abigail came down a mountain track with two hundred loaves and stopped David from slaughtering every male in Nabal’s household, with a theological argument about bloodguilt (1 Samuel 25). The woman of Tekoa changed the succession of Israel with a story. This woman stops the army of Israel from destroying a city with three sentences from a wall. None of them holds any office. And she asks nothing for herself: no terms for her household, no reward. She argues about what the town is and what the land is, and then she goes and does the hard part. We never learn her name.

Uncertain wording. In verse 14 the Hebrew names those who followed Sheba with a word found nowhere else, usually read “the Berites”. The ESV, like several modern versions, reads Bichrites, Sheba’s own clan (he is the son of Bichri), which fits the story well. Who the Berites might have been is unknown. Either way, Sheba’s following has shrunk from all Israel to a handful.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 23–26 — Now Joab Was in Command
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The chapter closes with a list of David’s officials that is both a mercy and an indictment. It mirrors the list in chapter 8: after all the disasters since then, the kingdom still has its government, and ordinary business goes on (vv. 23–26). But the first name is Joab, over the whole army, unpunished for murdering the commander David appointed (v. 23). And a new office has appeared, Adoram over the forced labour (v. 24), the grievance that will one day help to split the kingdom.
verseByVerse.theology: The list mirrors the one at the end of chapter 8 and does the same work: the crisis is over, and the kingdom is in ordered operation again.
verseByVerse.examples: The first name on it is Joab, back at the head of the army days after murdering the king's appointed commander. Order has returned, but not justice. And a new post appears, Adoram over the forced labour, the grievance on which the north will one day secede.

verseByVerse.quote: Now Joab was in command of all the army of Israel; and Benaiah the son of Jehoiada was in command of the Cherethites and the Pelethites; and Adoram was in charge of the forced labor; and Jehoshaphat the son of Ahilud was the recorder; and Sheva was secretary; and Zadok and Abiathar were priests; and Ira the Jairite was also David's priest.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The chapter closes with David’s officials: the government still works, which is God’s mercy, but the murderer Joab heads the list unpunished, and a new office for forced labour holds the grievance that will one day help to split the kingdom.

Joab was in command of all the army of Israel. Days ago the king appointed Amasa to that post, personally, with an oath, from now on in place of Joab (19:13). Joab met Amasa in a road, called him brother, took him by the beard and killed him. And the first name on the list of officials is Joab’s. No inquiry, charge or demotion follows: thirteen verses after the murder, an administrative note records that the murderer has the job.

The verdict on the reign. That is the verdict on the chapter and on the whole reign. David could not touch him. He said so at 3:39 after Abner, these men, the sons of Zeruiah, are more severe than I, and he is still saying it as a dying man, handing the problem to a son who will finally do what he never could (1 Kings 2:5–6).

Adoram was in charge of the forced labor. Then a name that was not on the list in chapter 8 (8:16–18). Adoram’s office is new: somewhere in the intervening years the kingdom has acquired conscripted labour and a minister to run it. Remember that name. Under Solomon the forced labour becomes vast, and when he dies the northern tribes come to Rehoboam with one request: Your father made our yoke heavy. Now therefore lighten the hard service of your father and his heavy yoke on us, and we will serve you (1 Kings 12:4). He refuses, with the line about scorpions. Then King Rehoboam sent Adoram, who was taskmaster over the forced labor, and all Israel stoned him to death with stones (1 Kings 12:18).

Both halves of the split. The same office and, if the years allow it, very possibly the same man. The tribes stone the labour minister and go home with Sheba’s sentence from verse 1 in their mouths. So both halves of the final split are already in this one chapter: the slogan in verse 1 and the grievance in verse 24.

The Cherethites and the Pelethites. They were David’s foreign bodyguard, probably from Crete and Philistia. Ira the “priest” was most likely a royal official or chaplain; the same word is used of David’s sons as chief ministers (8:18).

Two cabinet lists. The list deliberately mirrors the one in chapter 8, which came after the conquests, with the kingdom at its height. This one comes after Bathsheba, Amnon, Tamar, Absalom, the flight, the forest and Sheba, and says the same thing in the same form. The offices are filled; the government works. That is a real mercy: a kingdom that has been through all this still has a cabinet, and the ordinary business of governing goes on, which is how God generally keeps the world running after a catastrophe.

Also an indictment. The list is also an indictment, because of the first name on it and the third. Joab at the top, unpunished; Adoram over the forced labour, unnoticed. The reign is restored, and the two things that will destroy the kingdom are already inside the administration, drawing a salary. Israel would need a King whose government has no such rot at its heart, of whom it is promised that “of the increase of his government and of peace there will be no end… to establish it and to uphold it with justice and with righteousness” (Isaiah 9:7).

keyVerse.quote: And he blew the trumpet and said, “We have no portion in David, and we have no inheritance in the son of Jesse; every man to his tents, O Israel!”
keyVerse.note: Sheba’s rebellion is over within the chapter, but his slogan names the line along which the kingdom will finally break (1 Kings 12:16). It shows that David’s restored throne had not healed his people. Only the greater Son of David gathers a divided people into one, and in him no one need say they have no portion.

20.reflection:
Sheba did not create the north’s grievance; he gave it a slogan (vv. 1–2; compare 19:43). How do slogans and grievances divide families, churches and nations today? How does belonging to Christ change the way we respond to them?

The ten concubines bore the cost of sins they did not commit (v. 3). Who pays for our sins besides ourselves? How does the gospel speak both to those who have been hurt and to those who have caused hurt?

The army stopped at Amasa’s body only until it was covered (vv. 12–13). Where are we tempted to “cover” a wrong so that things can carry on, rather than deal with it? How is God’s covering of sin different (Psalm 32:1)?

The wise woman of Abel had no office, yet she spoke plainly to a violent man and saved her city (vv. 16–22). What does her example teach about courage, wisdom and speaking truth to those in power?

21.title: The Gibeonites' Vengeance; War with Philistines
21.text: <sup>1</sup>Now there was a famine in the days of David for three years, year after year. And David sought the face of the LORD. And the LORD said, "There is bloodguilt on Saul and on his house, because he put the Gibeonites to death."<sup>2</sup>So the king called the Gibeonites and spoke to them. Now the Gibeonites were not of the people of Israel but of the remnant of the Amorites. Although the people of Israel had sworn to spare them, Saul had sought to strike them down in his zeal for the people of Israel and Judah.<sup>3</sup>And David said to the Gibeonites, "What shall I do for you? And how shall I make atonement, that you may bless the heritage of the LORD?"<sup>4</sup>The Gibeonites said to him, "It is not a matter of silver or gold between us and Saul or his house; neither is it for us to put any man to death in Israel." And he said, "What do you say that I shall do for you?"<sup>5</sup>They said to the king, "The man who consumed us and planned to destroy us, so that we should have no place in all the territory of Israel,<sup>6</sup>let seven of his sons be given to us, so that we may hang them before the LORD at Gibeah of Saul, the chosen of the LORD." And the king said, "I will give them."<sup>7</sup>But the king spared Mephibosheth, the son of Saul's son Jonathan, because of the oath of the LORD that was between them, between David and Jonathan the son of Saul.<sup>8</sup>The king took the two sons of Rizpah the daughter of Aiah, whom she bore to Saul, Armoni and Mephibosheth; and the five sons of Merab the daughter of Saul, whom she bore to Adriel the son of Barzillai the Meholathite;<sup>9</sup>and he gave them into the hands of the Gibeonites, and they hanged them on the mountain before the LORD, and the seven of them perished together. They were put to death in the first days of harvest, at the beginning of barley harvest.<sup>10</sup>Then Rizpah the daughter of Aiah took sackcloth and spread it for herself on the rock, from the beginning of harvest until rain fell upon them from the heavens. And she did not allow the birds of the air to come upon them by day, or the beasts of the field by night.<sup>11</sup>When David was told what Rizpah the daughter of Aiah, the concubine of Saul, had done,<sup>12</sup>David went and took the bones of Saul and the bones of his son Jonathan from the men of Jabesh-gilead, who had stolen them from the public square of Beth-shan, where the Philistines had hanged them, on the day the Philistines killed Saul on Gilboa.<sup>13</sup>And he brought up from there the bones of Saul and the bones of his son Jonathan; and they gathered the bones of those who were hanged.<sup>14</sup>And they buried the bones of Saul and his son Jonathan in the land of Benjamin in Zela, in the tomb of Kish his father. And they did all that the king commanded. And after that God responded to the plea for the land.<sup>15</sup>There was war again between the Philistines and Israel, and David went down together with his servants, and they fought against the Philistines. And David grew weary.<sup>16</sup>And Ishbi-benob, one of the descendants of the giants, whose spear weighed three hundred shekels of bronze, and who was armed with a new sword, thought to kill David.<sup>17</sup>But Abishai the son of Zeruiah came to his aid and attacked the Philistine and killed him. Then David's men swore to him, "You shall no longer go out with us to battle, lest you quench the lamp of Israel."<sup>18</sup>After this there was again war with the Philistines at Gob. Then Sibbecai the Hushathite struck down Saph, who was one of the descendants of the giants.<sup>19</sup>And there was again war with the Philistines at Gob, and Elhanan the son of Jaare-oregim, the Bethlehemite, struck down Goliath the Gittite, the shaft of whose spear was like a weaver's beam.<sup>20</sup>And there was again war at Gath, where there was a man of great stature, who had six fingers on each hand, and six toes on each foot, twenty-four in number, and he also was descended from the giants.<sup>21</sup>And when he taunted Israel, Jonathan the son of Shimei, David's brother, struck him down.<sup>22</sup>These four were descended from the giants in Gath, and they fell by the hand of David and by the hand of his servants.
21.overview:
Where we are. The rebellions of Absalom and Sheba are over, and the main story of David’s reign has been told. Chapters 21 to 24 are an appendix arranged by theme rather than date (see the introduction): the famine probably came earlier in the reign, after Mephibosheth was brought to court (chapter 9), and the battles with giants come from various years. This chapter opens the appendix with a national disaster and a list of warriors, a pair mirrored in reverse in chapters 23 and 24.

The message. A promise sworn in the LORD’s name binds, even when it was won by trickery and even centuries later, and breaking it brought guilt on the whole land. The chapter will not make the remedy simple: seven men die for their father’s crime, and God answers only after a grieving mother’s faithfulness moves the king to bury the dead. And the king himself has grown weary. The lamp of Israel has to be guarded by other men, because David cannot keep his people’s light burning by his own strength.

Why it was said. Shimei had cursed David as a “man of blood” who had taken the throne from the house of Saul (16:7–8). This chapter shows honestly how seven of Saul’s descendants died: for Saul’s own bloodguilt, at the demand of the people he had wronged, while David kept faith with Jonathan’s son. Later readers, whose kings survived only because God had promised David a lamp, needed both lessons: God’s name on a promise is not to be trifled with, and the throne stands by God’s faithfulness, not the king’s vigour (see the introduction).

How the chapter makes its case. A three-year famine is traced to Saul’s slaughter of the Gibeonites, whom Israel had sworn to spare; David lets them name the remedy, seven of Saul’s sons are put to death, and Mephibosheth is spared because David keeps his own oath to Jonathan (vv. 1–9). Rizpah, mother of two of the seven, guards the bodies from harvest until the rains, and when David hears of it he gives them, with Saul and Jonathan, a grave in the family tomb; only “after that” does God answer the plea for the land (vv. 10–14). In later wars four giants fall; the old king grows weary, is nearly killed, is rescued by Abishai and kept from battle, and the victories are credited to David and his servants together (vv. 15–22).

Where it leads. To Christ by the need the chapter exposes and by promise. Seven men were handed over against their will for another man’s sin and hanged, and the law called a hanged man cursed (Deuteronomy 21:23); their deaths ended a famine but could not take away guilt. Paul applies that same law to the cross: Christ became “a curse for us” (Galatians 3:13), giving himself freely, the righteous for the unrighteous, and his blood does what theirs could not. And the lamp his men would not let go out became the image of God’s promise to David, “I have prepared a lamp for my anointed” (Psalm 132:17), kept in the Son of David whose kingdom will have no end.

For us. Keep your word, even when keeping it has become costly, because the God whose name is on it has kept every promise to us in Christ. Do not despise the one small faithful thing left to you: Rizpah could only keep the birds away, and it moved a king. And when strength fails, as David’s did, the kingdom does not: it rests on a King who never grows weary.
21.theology:
The oath that held for centuries (v. 2). In Joshua 9 Israel was tricked into a treaty by the Gibeonites, discovered the fraud within three days, and kept the oath anyway because it had been sworn by the LORD (Josh. 9:19). It held through the whole period of the judges. Saul broke it in a fit of national zeal, and nothing in 1 Samuel records the act; we hear of it only here. Why should a whole nation suffer for it? Because the oath was Israel's, sworn by its leaders in God's name, and Saul broke it as Israel's king; Scripture holds a people answerable for what is done in its name until it is put right.

What the text asserts, and what it does not (vv. 3-6). It asserts bloodguilt, the guilt of shedding innocent blood, and God names it: blood shed on the land defiles the land (Num. 35:33), and Saul is beyond execution. It does not assert that God commanded the remedy. There is no oracle; David asks the injured party what they want and agrees in four words, though Israel's law says children are not to be put to death for their fathers (Deut. 24:16). The notes on vv. 1-9 set out what has been said to ease the difficulty. Some of it is probably right, none of it makes the scene comfortable, and the narrator does not try to make it comfortable either. He reports what was asked and done, and then spends five verses on a woman sitting on a rock.

One oath avenged and one oath kept (v. 7). Seven men die because Saul broke a promise sworn in the LORD's name; one crippled man lives, and keeps his place at the king's table, because David keeps one. That is the chapter's real subject: the weight of a promise with God's name on it.

Rizpah (vv. 10-11). A woman with no husband, no standing and no protector, whose family has been destroyed twice, at Gilboa and now at Gibeah, plants herself in public beside the evidence of a royal decision and stays until the rains come. She had been in this book once before, as the woman Ish-bosheth and Abner quarrelled over for political reasons (3:7), and she said nothing then either. Keeping the animals from her sons' bodies is the only thing left she can give them, and she gives it. And something happens because of her: the king hears, and gives the dead the burial the chapter had so far denied them. The writer sets her beside the men of Jabesh-gilead, who walked all night to take Saul's body off a Philistine wall (1 Sam. 31:11-13). Both acted for people who could do nothing for them, and both because the bodies of the dead matter to God.

Where the writer puts God's answer (v. 14). And after that God responded to the plea for the land. After what? The executions were in April; if they had settled it, the rain should have come then. The answer is recorded after Rizpah, after the bones were fetched, after a burial. The writer draws no conclusion, as he never does, but a reader may notice it.

So was it right, and where does it lead? The bloodguilt was real and God named it; the remedy was the Gibeonites' demand and David's decision, and the text never praises it. Many careful readers think David should have asked the LORD before agreeing, as he had asked about the cause, though the narrator does not say so. What no Christian may take from it is that God makes children pay for their parents' sins: the son shall not suffer for the iniquity of the father (Ezekiel 18:20). And the chapter's darkest image is one the gospel answers. The law it strains against says a hanged man is cursed (Deuteronomy 21:23), and Paul applies that very law to the cross: Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us (Galatians 3:13). The seven were handed over against their will for another man's sin. He gave himself, the righteous for the unrighteous (1 Peter 3:18), and his blood does what theirs could not: it takes guilt away, so that the blessing promised to Abraham reaches the nations (Galatians 3:14).

And David grew weary (v. 15). The boy who ran at a giant with a sling is an old man on a battlefield who cannot keep going, and Abishai, the man who wanted to spear Saul in his sleep and behead Shimei, saves him. The sons of Zeruiah were more severe than David, and they also kept him alive.

The lamp of Israel (v. 17). His men swear that he will never go into battle again, out of love and out of plain calculation, and being told by the people who love you that you can no longer do the thing that defined you is a real grief of old age. The phrase they reach for becomes a word for God’s covenant promise to David: God keeps a tribe for Solomon's son that David my servant may always have a lamp before me in Jerusalem (1 Kings 11:36), and says it again at 1 Kings 15:4 and 2 Kings 8:19. Soldiers used it about a tired man on a battlefield, and Scripture carried it for centuries, until the promise was kept in the Son of David.

The Elhanan difficulty (v. 19). Here Elhanan kills Goliath, where 1 Chronicles 20:5 says he killed Goliath's brother. The likeliest explanation is a copyist's slip in Samuel, discussed in the notes on vv. 15-22; it costs nothing to admit, and the narrative of 1 Samuel 17 stands on its own.

By the hand of David and by the hand of his servants (v. 22). David killed none of the four giants, and the credit is given to David and his servants together. That is what a reign looks like at the end: the work goes on, other men do it, and the man who cannot go out any more is still named in the account, because he is why they are there.
21.examples:
Then: A woman whose two sons had been handed over by the king and hanged on a hill spread sackcloth on the rock beside their bodies and stayed there from April until the autumn rains, so that nothing would eat her children. The king heard what she had done, and went and gave them a grave.

Now: Rizpah is the study in doing the only thing left. She could not undo the sentence, appeal it, or bury them, but there was one thing she could do, and she did it for half a year without a word, and it moved a king. Most people faced with a wrong they cannot fix do nothing at all, on the grounds that what they could do would not be enough. Grieving people, too, may find in her that faithful love for the dead is not wasted. The chapter's other subject is the weight of a promise with God's name on it: a treaty extracted by fraud that Israel kept for centuries, and one man's life spared because David remembered what he had sworn to a friend dead for decades. We keep our word because the God whose name is on it keeps his, and every promise he made us is Yes in Christ (2 Corinthians 1:20); where we have broken ours, the way back is to own it and make it right, as this chapter does, at cost.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–9 — There Is Bloodguilt on Saul
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A broken oath brings guilt on the land, and a kept oath saves a life. A three-year famine sends David to the LORD, who names the cause: Saul broke Israel’s ancient oath to the Gibeonites and put them to death (vv. 1–2). David asks the Gibeonites how he may make atonement; they refuse money and ask for seven of Saul’s sons, and David agrees (vv. 3–6). He spares Mephibosheth because of his own oath to Jonathan, and the seven are put to death on the mountain at the beginning of barley harvest (vv. 7–9). The writer records the remedy without praising it, and leaves the reader to weigh it against God’s law.
verseByVerse.theology: The oath Saul broke was the one Israel swore to the Gibeonites in Joshua 9 and kept for centuries, even though it had been obtained by fraud. The bloodguilt is real.
verseByVerse.examples: Keep the distinction the text keeps: David asked the Gibeonites what they wanted and did it. The text does not say God commanded it, and it records God answering the plea for the land only after a burial (v. 14).

verseByVerse.quote: Now there was a famine in the days of David for three years, year after year. And David sought the face of the LORD. And the LORD said, "There is bloodguilt on Saul and on his house, because he put the Gibeonites to death." So the king called the Gibeonites and spoke to them. Now the Gibeonites were not of the people of Israel but of the remnant of the Amorites. Although the people of Israel had sworn to spare them, Saul had sought to strike them down in his zeal for the people of Israel and Judah. And David said to the Gibeonites, "What shall I do for you? And how shall I make atonement, that you may bless the heritage of the LORD?" The Gibeonites said to him, "It is not a matter of silver or gold between us and Saul or his house; neither is it for us to put any man to death in Israel." And he said, "What do you say that I shall do for you?" They said to the king, "The man who consumed us and planned to destroy us, so that we should have no place in all the territory of Israel, let seven of his sons be given to us, so that we may hang them before the LORD at Gibeah of Saul, the chosen of the LORD." And the king said, "I will give them." But the king spared Mephibosheth, the son of Saul's son Jonathan, because of the oath of the LORD that was between them, between David and Jonathan the son of Saul. The king took the two sons of Rizpah the daughter of Aiah, whom she bore to Saul, Armoni and Mephibosheth; and the five sons of Merab the daughter of Saul, whom she bore to Adriel the son of Barzillai the Meholathite; and he gave them into the hands of the Gibeonites, and they hanged them on the mountain before the LORD, and the seven of them perished together. They were put to death in the first days of harvest, at the beginning of barley harvest.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A promise sworn in the LORD’s name, broken by Saul, has brought guilt on the whole land, and the remedy is grim: seven of Saul’s sons die for their father’s crime, while one man lives because David keeps his own oath. God names the guilt; the text does not say that he commanded the remedy.

David sought the face of the LORD. Only after three years of failed harvests does David ask the LORD, and the writer does not say why. A famine was understood to be a covenant matter, since the blessings and curses of Deuteronomy tie rain to obedience, and a king might have been expected to enquire in the first bad year rather than the third. When he does ask, the answer concerns something done before he was king.

Although the people of Israel had sworn to spare them. Go back to Joshua 9. When Israel came into the land, the Gibeonites saw what had happened to Jericho and Ai and decided to survive by fraud: an embassy in worn-out sandals, carrying mouldy bread, claimed to come from a distant country and asked for a treaty. Joshua and the elders did not enquire of the LORD, the text says so explicitly, and they made the treaty and swore to it. Three days later the fraud came out; these were neighbours. The congregation wanted to kill them, and the leaders refused for one reason, which is the whole point: they had sworn by the LORD (Joshua 9:19). Tricked into an oath, they kept it because it had God’s name on it, and the Gibeonites lived among Israel unharmed for centuries as woodcutters and water-carriers for the sanctuary.

In his zeal for the people of Israel and Judah. Then Saul broke it. Nothing in 1 Samuel records the massacre, and the writer gives one clause about the motive. This is the man who would not carry out the ban on Amalek (God’s command to destroy it completely) when God commanded it, and did carry it out on Nob, a town of Israel’s own priests, when nobody commanded it (1 Samuel 22:19). Zeal for Israel, applied to the wrong people, twice.

How shall I make atonement? David speaks of atonement: covering the guilt so that blessing can return, “that you may bless the heritage of the LORD”. Then note his verb, because the moral question of the chapter turns on it. He does not enquire of the LORD what should be done. He was told what the problem was; now he asks the injured party to name the price. They refuse money and disclaim any right to execute anyone, and he presses them again. They name seven of Saul’s sons, to be hanged at Gibeah, Saul’s own town, and David agrees in four words.

What the text says, and what it does not. Honesty here means being exact. It says there was bloodguilt, the guilt of shedding innocent blood, and that God named it. Blood shed on the land was understood to defile the land itself, and Numbers is explicit that “no atonement can be made for the land for the blood that is shed in it, except by the blood of the one who shed it” (Numbers 35:33). Saul is dead and beyond execution, so the Gibeonites ask for his house instead. What the text does not say is that God commanded this. There is no oracle. The remedy is the Gibeonites’ proposal and David’s decision, and when the writer finally records God acting, it is at the end of verse 14, after a burial.

But the king spared Mephibosheth. In the middle of it one man is spared, and the reason is an oath. Seven men die because Saul broke an oath sworn in the LORD’s name; one man lives because David keeps an oath sworn in the LORD’s name (1 Samuel 20:14–17). Break one, and the land does not yield for three years. Keep one, and a crippled man eats at the king’s table while his cousins are executed. The one who may dwell with God is the one who “swears to his own hurt and does not change” (Psalm 15:4). A believer keeps a promise made in good faith even when keeping it has become costly, because God has kept every promise he made to us at far greater cost.

The two sons of Rizpah the daughter of Aiah. Two of the seven belong to Rizpah, and the writer names them. She has been in this book before: the concubine of Saul over whom Ish-bosheth accused Abner, in the quarrel that lost the house of Saul its kingdom (3:7). She was a political question then, argued over by men, and she said nothing.

At the beginning of barley harvest. The last clause is a date, and it is about to matter. Barley harvest is April.

Handed over for another’s sin. Seven men die against their will for what another man did, and their deaths cannot cleanse a single conscience. Christ gave himself freely, “the righteous for the unrighteous, that he might bring us to God” (1 Peter 3:18); the section’s theology develops the contrast.

Was it just for seven sons to die for their father’s sin? Israel’s own law raises the question: “fathers shall not be put to death because of their children, nor shall children be put to death because of their fathers. Each one shall be put to death for his own sin” (Deuteronomy 24:16). Various things have been said to ease it: that the ancient world reckoned bloodguilt to a household, and that Deuteronomy 24 governs the ordinary courts rather than a covenant breach at national level; that these sons may have shared in the killing, since the LORD speaks of bloodguilt “on Saul and on his house” (v. 1), though the text does not say these seven did; and that an oath sworn in God’s name and publicly broken is a different order of thing from a private crime. Some of that is probably right. None of it makes the scene comfortable, and the narrator does not try to. Nor was this human sacrifice in the sense of an offering to God: it was an execution, demanded by the injured party as justice for Saul’s bloodguilt and granted by David. Scripture records the event without making it a pattern.

Uncertain wording. The verb translated “hang” (vv. 6, 9, 13) is rare, used also of the execution in Numbers 25:4, and its exact sense is unknown: it may mean to hang, to impale, or to expose a body with its limbs broken. What is clear is that this was a public execution with the bodies left exposed “before the LORD”, which is why Rizpah’s vigil follows.

Textual note. The five sons were Merab’s; most Hebrew manuscripts read “Michal”, an early copying slip, since Merab married Adriel (1 Samuel 18:19).
verseByVerse.note: Gibeon lay a few miles north-west of Jerusalem, in the territory of Benjamin, Saul's own tribe (Josh. 18:25).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: One grieving woman’s silent faithfulness moves a king, and God answers after the dead are buried. Rizpah, mother of two of the seven, spreads sackcloth on the rock and keeps the birds and beasts from the bodies from harvest until the rains (v. 10). When David hears of it, he fetches the bones of Saul and Jonathan from Jabesh-gilead, whose men had rescued them from a Philistine wall years before (vv. 11–12). All are buried together in the tomb of Saul’s father Kish, and only “after that” does God respond to the plea for the land (vv. 13–14).
verseByVerse.theology: Barley harvest is April, and the rains come in the autumn. For five or six months a mother sat beside seven bodies, two of them her sons, so that they would not be eaten.
verseByVerse.examples: It is Rizpah's doing that ends the chapter properly. Only when the king is told what she has done does he fetch Saul's bones and give them all a grave. A concubine with no power sat on a rock until the king of Israel did the right thing.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Rizpah the daughter of Aiah took sackcloth and spread it for herself on the rock, from the beginning of harvest until rain fell upon them from the heavens. And she did not allow the birds of the air to come upon them by day, or the beasts of the field by night. When David was told what Rizpah the daughter of Aiah, the concubine of Saul, had done, David went and took the bones of Saul and the bones of his son Jonathan from the men of Jabesh-gilead, who had stolen them from the public square of Beth-shan, where the Philistines had hanged them, on the day the Philistines killed Saul on Gilboa. And he brought up from there the bones of Saul and the bones of his son Jonathan; and they gathered the bones of those who were hanged. And they buried the bones of Saul and his son Jonathan in the land of Benjamin in Zela, in the tomb of Kish his father. And they did all that the king commanded. And after that God responded to the plea for the land.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A bereaved mother’s silent vigil over her sons’ bodies, kept for months, moves the king to give the house of Saul an honourable burial, and only after that burial does God answer the prayers for the land. The heart of the chapter is one woman doing something nobody asked her to do.

From the beginning of harvest until rain fell. Everything depends on the timing. Barley harvest is around April; the autumn rains usually come in October or November: perhaps five or six months. She spreads sackcloth, the coarse cloth of mourning, on the rock where the bodies are, and she stays there through a summer with no shelter, into the autumn. She does not go home at night, and there is nobody to take turns with.

She did not allow the birds of the air. The bodies were left exposed, which was the point of the execution, though the law required even a criminal’s body to be buried the same day, for “a hanged man is cursed by God” and the land must not be defiled (Deuteronomy 21:23). So the vultures come by day, and she drives them off. At night the jackals and hyenas come, and she drives them off too, alone, in the dark, beside seven decomposing bodies, two of them her children, for perhaps a hundred and eighty days. She cannot bring them back, and she cannot bury them, for nobody has given her permission. What she can do is stop the animals eating them, and so she does that, the only thing left that she can give them.

Not a word from Rizpah. She does not accuse David, curse the Gibeonites or appeal to anybody; the book records not a single word from her. She is a woman with no husband, no standing, no protector and no legal claim, whose family has been destroyed twice over and whose sons were handed over by the reigning king. Yet she plants herself in public beside the evidence of a royal decision and stays there until the rains come.

When David was told. This is the verse that turns the chapter. Word gets back, as it would; a woman on a rock for five months is not a private act. And what David does next is what the chapter has left undone until now: he buries the dead.

The men of Jabesh-gilead. He goes across the Jordan for Saul’s bones, and the writer takes a whole verse to remind us how they got there. When Saul died on Gilboa, the Philistines fastened his body and his sons’ bodies to the wall at Beth-shan, and the men of Jabesh-gilead walked all night through occupied country, took them down and buried them (1 Samuel 31:11–13), because of the day decades earlier when Saul had saved their town. The first act of David’s reign was a message of thanks to those men for it (2:5–7). So the chapter now sets two acts of loyalty side by side: a town that walked all night to take four bodies off a wall, and a woman who sat on a rock for months to keep the birds off seven more. Both acted for people who could do nothing for them, and both because bodies matter.

After that God responded to the plea for the land. All of them go into the family tomb of Kish: Saul, Jonathan and the seven (see burial customs). Then comes the clause the writer has placed with care. After what? The executions were months earlier, in April; if the hangings had settled the matter, the rain should have come then. The answer is recorded after Rizpah, after the bones were fetched, after seven men and a king and a prince were laid in a grave in Benjamin. The writer does not draw the conclusion, but a reader is entitled to notice that God’s answer follows a burial and not an execution. And the burial happened because a woman with nothing sat on a rock until somebody told the king.

The power of those who have none. We tend to assume that history is moved by the powerful. Nietzsche argued that life itself is the will to power, and much modern thought has followed him in reading every relationship, law and even kindness as a contest over who controls whom. On that view Rizpah should not matter: no vote, no army, no husband, no recorded word. Yet a king who handed her sons over to die is moved by a woman sitting on a rock, and the rain comes after what she set in motion. Scripture keeps telling this kind of story, because this is how God works: “God chose what is weak in the world to shame the strong” (1 Corinthians 1:27). The greatest instance is the one the cynic cannot account for. The decisive act in history was not a seizure of power but a man giving his life up on a cross, and among the first witnesses of his burial were two women who simply watched, as Rizpah watched: “Mary Magdalene and Mary the mother of Joses saw where he was laid” (Mark 15:47). With this God, faithfulness that seems to change nothing is never wasted.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The great giant-killer has grown old, and the light of Israel must now be guarded by others. In a new war with the Philistines David grows weary and is nearly killed by a giant until Abishai saves him; his men swear that he will never go out to battle again, “lest you quench the lamp of Israel” (vv. 15–17). Three more giants fall to Sibbecai, Elhanan and David’s nephew Jonathan (vv. 18–21), and the summary gives the victory to David and his servants together (v. 22). The reign goes on through other hands, held by God’s promise rather than the king’s strength.
verseByVerse.theology: The man who killed a giant as a boy is nearly killed by one as an old man, and is saved by his nephew. His army then keeps him from the field, and the name they give him, the lamp of Israel, becomes a word for God’s promise to David.
verseByVerse.examples: Verse 19 is a well-known difficulty, set out in the notes below. Saying a reading is uncertain is better than inventing a certainty.

verseByVerse.quote: There was war again between the Philistines and Israel, and David went down together with his servants, and they fought against the Philistines. And David grew weary. And Ishbi-benob, one of the descendants of the giants, whose spear weighed three hundred shekels of bronze, and who was armed with a new sword, thought to kill David. But Abishai the son of Zeruiah came to his aid and attacked the Philistine and killed him. Then David's men swore to him, "You shall no longer go out with us to battle, lest you quench the lamp of Israel." After this there was again war with the Philistines at Gob. Then Sibbecai the Hushathite struck down Saph, who was one of the descendants of the giants. And there was again war with the Philistines at Gob, and Elhanan the son of Jaare-oregim, the Bethlehemite, struck down Goliath the Gittite, the shaft of whose spear was like a weaver's beam. And there was again war at Gath, where there was a man of great stature, who had six fingers on each hand, and six toes on each foot, twenty-four in number, and he also was descended from the giants. And when he taunted Israel, Jonathan the son of Shimei, David's brother, struck him down. These four were descended from the giants in Gath, and they fell by the hand of David and by the hand of his servants.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The giant-killer has grown old and nearly dies at a giant’s hand; now his men fight his battles and guard him as the lamp of Israel, and their victories are counted as his and theirs together. These skirmishes, from various years, show a reign carried on by other hands and kept by God’s promise.

And David grew weary. Three words, and they are the end of something. This is the man who ran at a giant with a sling and came back with the head, who struck down the Philistines from Geba to Gezer (5:25). Now he is an old man on a battlefield who cannot keep going.

Thought to kill David. A descendant of the giants, with a heavy spear and new equipment, sees the king of Israel struggling and moves in. His spearhead alone weighs three hundred shekels, about three and a half kilos, half the weight of Goliath’s (1 Samuel 17:7). The symmetry needs no comment: a boy killed a Philistine giant in the Valley of Elah and made his name doing it; decades later a Philistine giant nearly kills the same man because he is too tired to defend himself. The “descendants of the giants” were of the Rephaim, a people of great stature in Canaan, like the Anakim (Deuteronomy 2:11); the six-fingered man of verse 20 was one of them. They are not to be confused with the Nephilim of Genesis 6.

But Abishai the son of Zeruiah came to his aid. Abishai saves his life: the man who wanted to spear Saul in his sleep and twice to behead Shimei, and whose brother Joab murdered three men. When David is down with a giant standing over him, Abishai is the one who gets there. The sons of Zeruiah were more severe than David, and they also kept him alive.

You shall no longer go out with us to battle. His own men take him off the battlefield. They swear it, which makes it binding, and they do it out of love and out of arithmetic: he is worth ten thousand of them, as they told him before the battle in the forest of Ephraim (18:3), and Israel would not survive his death in a skirmish. It is still a hard verse. Being told by the people who love you that you can no longer do the thing that defined you is one of the recognisable griefs of growing old, and the writer places it right after “David grew weary”.

The lamp of Israel. The phrase they choose becomes a word for God’s covenant promise. A lamp burning in a house meant the household still lived. When the kingdom is torn from Solomon’s son, God keeps one tribe for him “that David my servant may always have a lamp before me in Jerusalem” (1 Kings 11:36). It is said again of Abijam (1 Kings 15:4), and again when Judah deserves destruction: “the LORD was not willing to destroy Judah, for the sake of David his servant, since he promised to give a lamp to him and to his sons forever” (2 Kings 8:19). The lamp is the promise of chapter 7 in a single image, a light God undertakes not to let go out. Soldiers used the word about a tired man on a battlefield, Scripture carried it for centuries, and the promise it carries, “I have prepared a lamp for my anointed” (Psalm 132:17), is kept in the Son of David whose kingdom will have no end (Luke 1:33). His men had to guard David’s light; Christ’s light no one can put out (John 1:5).

When he taunted Israel. It is the same Hebrew verb as Goliath’s defiance in the valley for forty days (1 Samuel 17:10), and a nephew of David’s kills this man for it.

By the hand of David and by the hand of his servants. The summary is generous, and it is the point of putting these four skirmishes here at all. David killed none of them. He was nearly killed by the first, saved by his nephew, and then kept from the battlefield; Sibbecai, Elhanan and Jonathan killed the other three. Yet the credit is given to David and his servants together, in one phrase, without distinction. That is what a reign looks like near its end: the work goes on and other men do it, and the old man who cannot go out any more is still named in the account, because he is the reason they are there. The next chapter is his psalm, and the one after that lists his mighty men by name.

Uncertain wording. Two phrases are uncertain. “The giants” (vv. 16, 18, 20, 22) translates a Hebrew word, rapha, that may name a people (the Rephaim) or a single ancestor of these men; either way they belonged to a remembered race of very tall warriors around Gath. And in verse 16 the Hebrew says only that Ishbi-benob was “girded with new”, without a noun; “sword” is supplied by the translators as the likeliest meaning, though it may have been new armour of some kind.

Textual note. Verse 19 is one of the best-known textual difficulties in the Old Testament, and the honest thing is to lay it out. It says Elhanan killed Goliath the Gittite, and describes his spear in the exact words of 1 Samuel 17:7. But 1 Samuel 17 says David killed Goliath, in one of the most detailed narratives in the book, and 1 Chronicles, recording the same list, reads: “Elhanan the son of Jair struck down Lahmi the brother of Goliath the Gittite, the shaft of whose spear was like a weaver’s beam” (1 Chronicles 20:5). There are three positions. The first, which most translators and commentators take, is that the Samuel text has suffered a copyist’s slip and Chronicles preserves the original: the Hebrew words involved are easily confused in the older script, and a scribe’s eye dropping “the brother of” is a recognised kind of error. On this reading Elhanan killed Goliath’s brother, and there is no conflict. The second, a minority view, is that Chronicles is a later attempt to smooth out an awkward verse. The third, occasionally suggested, is that Elhanan was David’s original name; there is no real evidence for it, the men have different fathers, and it should be set aside. The likeliest explanation is a copying error in a name, which textual criticism, the careful comparing of manuscripts, exists to detect; admitting it costs nothing, and the account of David and Goliath in 1 Samuel 17 stands on its own.
verseByVerse.note: The father's name in v. 19, Jaare-oregim, probably shows a second copying slip: oregim means "weavers" and seems to have been picked up from "weaver's beam" at the end of the verse, while 1 Chronicles 20:5 has simply Jair.

keyVerse.quote: But Abishai the son of Zeruiah came to his aid and attacked the Philistine and killed him. Then David’s men swore to him, “You shall no longer go out with us to battle, lest you quench the lamp of Israel.”
keyVerse.note: The giant-killer has grown old, and his life now depends on other men. Their phrase, “the lamp of Israel”, becomes Scripture’s image for God’s promise that David’s line will not go out (1 Kings 11:36), a promise that rested not on David’s strength but on God’s faithfulness, and is kept in Jesus, the Son of David.

21.reflection:
Israel kept its oath to the Gibeonites for centuries, though it had been won by fraud, and Saul’s breaking of it brought guilt on the whole land (vv. 1–2). Why does a promise made in God’s name matter so much? Are there promises you are tempted to treat as cancelled because keeping them has become costly?

The text tells us that God named the guilt but not that he commanded the remedy, and Israel’s own law said children must not die for their fathers (Deuteronomy 24:16). How should we read a hard passage like this honestly, without explaining the difficulty away or concluding that God is unjust?

Rizpah could not undo what had happened; all she could do was keep the birds and beasts away, and she did it for months until the king heard (vv. 10–14). Where are you tempted to do nothing because what you can do seems too small? What does her story teach about faithfulness that seems to change nothing?

David grew weary and had to be rescued and kept from battle, yet the victories were counted as his and his servants’ together (vv. 15–22). How do you respond to the loss of strength or role, in yourself or in others? How does it help to know that the lamp of David rests on God’s promise in Christ, not on the king’s strength?

22.title: David's Song of Deliverance
22.text: <sup>1</sup>And David spoke to the LORD the words of this song on the day when the LORD delivered him from the hand of all his enemies, and from the hand of Saul.<sup>2</sup>He said, "The LORD is my rock and my fortress and my deliverer,<sup>3</sup>my God, my rock, in whom I take refuge, my shield, and the horn of my salvation, my stronghold and my refuge, my savior; you save me from violence.<sup>4</sup>I call upon the LORD, who is worthy to be praised, and I am saved from my enemies.<sup>5</sup>"For the waves of death encompassed me, the torrents of destruction assailed me;<sup>6</sup>the cords of Sheol entangled me; the snares of death confronted me.<sup>7</sup>"In my distress I called upon the LORD; to my God I called. From his temple he heard my voice, and my cry came to his ears.<sup>8</sup>"Then the earth reeled and rocked; the foundations of the heavens trembled and quaked, because he was angry.<sup>9</sup>Smoke went up from his nostrils, and devouring fire from his mouth; glowing coals flamed forth from him.<sup>10</sup>He bowed the heavens and came down; thick darkness was under his feet.<sup>11</sup>He rode on a cherub and flew; he was seen on the wings of the wind.<sup>12</sup>He made darkness around him his canopy, thick clouds, a gathering of water.<sup>13</sup>Out of the brightness before him coals of fire flamed forth.<sup>14</sup>The LORD thundered from heaven, and the Most High uttered his voice.<sup>15</sup>And he sent out arrows and scattered them; lightning, and routed them.<sup>16</sup>Then the channels of the sea were seen; the foundations of the world were laid bare, at the rebuke of the LORD, at the blast of the breath of his nostrils.<sup>17</sup>"He sent from on high, he took me; he drew me out of many waters.<sup>18</sup>He rescued me from my strong enemy, from those who hated me, for they were too mighty for me.<sup>19</sup>They confronted me in the day of my calamity, but the LORD was my support.<sup>20</sup>He brought me out into a broad place; he rescued me, because he delighted in me.<sup>21</sup>"The LORD dealt with me according to my righteousness; according to the cleanness of my hands he rewarded me.<sup>22</sup>For I have kept the ways of the LORD and have not wickedly departed from my God.<sup>23</sup>For all his rules were before me, and from his statutes I did not turn aside.<sup>24</sup>I was blameless before him, and I kept myself from guilt.<sup>25</sup>And the LORD has rewarded me according to my righteousness, according to my cleanness in his sight.<sup>26</sup>"With the merciful you show yourself merciful; with the blameless man you show yourself blameless;<sup>27</sup>with the purified you deal purely, and with the crooked you make yourself seem tortuous.<sup>28</sup>You save a humble people, but your eyes are on the haughty to bring them down.<sup>29</sup>For you are my lamp, O LORD, and my God lightens my darkness.<sup>30</sup>For by you I can run against a troop, and by my God I can leap over a wall.<sup>31</sup>This God— his way is perfect; the word of the LORD proves true; he is a shield for all those who take refuge in him.<sup>32</sup>"For who is God, but the LORD? And who is a rock, except our God?<sup>33</sup>This God is my strong refuge and has made my way blameless.<sup>34</sup>He made my feet like the feet of a deer and set me secure on the heights.<sup>35</sup>He trains my hands for war, so that my arms can bend a bow of bronze.<sup>36</sup>You have given me the shield of your salvation, and your gentleness made me great.<sup>37</sup>You gave a wide place for my steps under me, and my feet did not slip;<sup>38</sup>I pursued my enemies and destroyed them, and did not turn back until they were consumed.<sup>39</sup>I consumed them; I thrust them through, so that they did not rise; they fell under my feet.<sup>40</sup>For you equipped me with strength for the battle; you made those who rise against me sink under me.<sup>41</sup>You made my enemies turn their backs to me, those who hated me, and I destroyed them.<sup>42</sup>They looked, but there was none to save; they cried to the LORD, but he did not answer them.<sup>43</sup>I beat them fine as the dust of the earth; I crushed them and stamped them down like the mire of the streets.<sup>44</sup>"You delivered me from strife with my people; you kept me as the head of the nations; people whom I had not known served me.<sup>45</sup>Foreigners came cringing to me; as soon as they heard of me, they obeyed me.<sup>46</sup>Foreigners lost heart and came trembling out of their fortresses.<sup>47</sup>"The LORD lives, and blessed be my rock, and exalted be my God, the rock of my salvation,<sup>48</sup>the God who gave me vengeance and brought down peoples under me,<sup>49</sup>who brought me out from my enemies; you exalted me above those who rose against me; you delivered me from men of violence.<sup>50</sup>"For this I will praise you, O LORD, among the nations, and sing praises to your name.<sup>51</sup>Great salvation he brings to his king, and shows steadfast love to his anointed, to David and his offspring forever."
22.overview:
Where we are. The appendix (chapters 21 to 24) is built around two poems, and this is the first: David’s song of deliverance, which is Psalm 18 almost word for word. Its heading dates it to the deliverance “from the hand of Saul”, decades earlier, probably somewhere around chapters 5 to 8. Yet it stands here, after ten chapters recording the collapse of David’s household.

The message. The LORD is a rock that does not move, even when the man standing on it falls. When his servant cries out, God comes down in overwhelming power to rescue one man, “because he delighted in me”; he equips him, makes him great by his gentleness, and binds his steadfast love to David and his offspring for ever. The book does not end with the wreckage; it ends with this song.

Why it was said. David sang it as a young king newly safe from Saul. Whoever placed it here wrote for readers who knew everything in chapters 11 to 20, and later readers lived under kings who mostly failed, and then with no king at all (see the introduction). They needed to hear that what David believed in the caves was still true after he had failed, because it rested on God, not on David.

How the chapter makes its case. David piles up names for God, all of them meaning safety (vv. 1–4). Death closes over him like floodwater and rope, and he cries out (vv. 5–7). God answers with an earthquake and a storm, bowing the heavens and riding a cherub (vv. 8–16), and all of it is for one man: “he drew me out of many waters” (vv. 17–20). David speaks of his righteousness, and of how God deals with the merciful, the crooked, the humble and the proud (vv. 21–28). God is his lamp and his rock, trains his hands and makes him great by gentleness (vv. 29–37). Real victories follow, over enemies and over strife within Israel (vv. 38–46), and the song ends in praise to the living God and in the promise to David’s offspring (vv. 47–51).

Where it leads. To Christ by promise and by pattern. The last line, steadfast love “to his anointed, to David and his offspring forever”, is the promise of chapter 7, and it runs past David to the Son of David; Zechariah blessed God for “a horn of salvation for us in the house of his servant David” (Luke 1:69). Paul hears verse 50 fulfilled as the Gentiles come in to praise God (Romans 15:9). Only one Son of David could sing of clean hands without reserve, and his righteousness is credited to those who trust him. And the cords of death that closed over David could not hold the one God raised up, “loosing the pangs of death” (Acts 2:24).

For us. Everyone runs somewhere when the fear comes; this song names the only refuge that holds when the waters rise. The God who shakes creation attends to one person in trouble, and he does it because he delights in his own. And for anyone who has failed badly, the book’s last word on David is a reminder that the rock does not move when the man on it falls.
22.theology:
Why it is here (v. 1). An editor who had chapter 11 in front of him reached back decades and put this song at the end. He recorded the whole collapse without excusing a line of it, and then closed with what David believed the whole way through, because it was still true afterwards.

The righteousness claim, faced (vv. 21-25). The man who speaks of the cleanness of my hands is in the book that records what those hands did. The verse notes give three answers. The compilers placed the psalm after chapter 11, so they did not read it as a claim to sinless perfection. The heading names the deliverance from Saul, and on that question David's hands were clean. And blameless in the Old Testament means undivided allegiance, not sinlessness: David never served another god. Kings sums him up the same way: he did what was right all his days, except in the matter of Uriah the Hittite (1 Kings 15:5).

And what he did when he fell. The same man prayed Psalm 51, and any account of David that keeps only one of the two psalms is false. These verses are not comfortable and should not be made to seem so. Yet a Christian hears in them a voice that can say them without reserve. Only one Son of David had wholly clean hands, and it is his righteousness, not David's, that God credits to sinners who trust him (Romans 3:22; 2 Corinthians 5:21). David sang verses 21 to 25 as a forgiven man; believers sing them in Christ.
