Your gentleness made me great (v. 36). After twenty verses of strength and equipment, the word David chooses for what made him is gentleness: God stooping down to a man who did not deserve it. That is the centre of the song.

The LORD lives (v. 47). The closing praise rests not on God's power or goodness, though the song praises both, but on his being alive. Paul quotes verse 50 first among four Old Testament texts showing that the nations coming in was always the plan (Rom. 15:9). Many readers hear Paul placing the words in the Messiah's own mouth: David's greater Son, having confirmed God's promises, praises the Father among the nations as they come in.
22.examples:
Then: The men who compiled Israel's history had recorded, without excusing a line of it, a king's adultery, the murder he arranged, his daughter's rape, the killing of one son by another, a rebellion that drove him barefoot out of his own capital, and a body left lying in a public road. Then they reached back decades to a song he had sung as a young fugitive and put it at the end of the book.

Now: Verse 36 is the one to take away. If you had to say in a few words what made you, what would you name? David had a great deal to choose from (the anointing, the giant, the throne, the empire, the trained hands and the bronze bow, all of which he mentions), and what he says is your gentleness made me great. The placement speaks too. Somebody who knew everything in chapters 11 to 20 decided that the last word on this life would not be the wreckage. Not because the wreckage was not real; they wrote ten chapters of it. Because what he had believed as a young man in a cave was still true about God after he had failed as badly as a man can fail. For anyone who has failed badly, that is where the way back begins.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–20 — He Drew Me Out of Many Waters
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: When his servant cries out, God comes down in power to rescue him, because he delights in him. David sings on the day the LORD delivered him from Saul and all his enemies, and piles up names for God that all mean safety: rock, fortress, deliverer, shield, refuge (vv. 1–4). Death closes over him like floodwater and rope, and he cries out to the LORD, who hears him (vv. 5–7). The answer is an earthquake: God bows the heavens, rides a cherub, thunders from heaven and lays bare the sea bed (vv. 8–16). And all of it arrives at one man: “he drew me out of many waters”, into a broad place, “because he delighted in me” (vv. 17–20).
verseByVerse.theology: Psalm 18 is the same song with almost the same heading. The differences between the two are the sort that arise when a song is copied and sung for generations.
verseByVerse.examples: The theophany, God’s visible coming, shakes creation, and the point of it is a man being pulled out of water. That is the logic of the whole psalm: the God whose approach bows the heavens comes down for one person.

verseByVerse.quote: And David spoke to the LORD the words of this song on the day when the LORD delivered him from the hand of all his enemies, and from the hand of Saul. He said, "The LORD is my rock and my fortress and my deliverer, my God, my rock, in whom I take refuge, my shield, and the horn of my salvation, my stronghold and my refuge, my savior; you save me from violence.
verseByVerse.commentary:
David begins by naming what God has been to him, a rock and fortress and shield, and the book sets this song at its end so that God’s faithfulness, not David’s failures, has the last word.

From the hand of Saul. The heading dates the song to the deliverance from Saul, decades earlier, and yet it stands here in the appendix, after everything: after the roof and Bathsheba and the letter Uriah carried; after Nathan and the dead child; after Amnon and Tamar; after the pit in the forest and a father over the gate saying my son five times; after a man with a trumpet splitting the country, a body lying in a road at Gibeon, and ten women shut in a house until they died. The book has spent ten chapters recording the collapse of this man’s household, and it does not end there. It ends with his song. That is a theological decision (see the note on vv. 50–51).

The LORD is my rock and my fortress. Verses 2–3 give name after name for God, and every one is about safety. Rock is ground that does not shift under your feet. Fortress is the high strong place, and David spent years living in actual ones. Deliverer is the one who gets you out, and a shield is what stands between you and the blow. Horn of my salvation pictures a charging animal’s strength turned to your side. Zechariah took up the phrase when he blessed God for raising up “a horn of salvation for us in the house of his servant David” (Luke 1:69): the strength David found in God came to his house in a person.

My God, my rock. The possessive is on all of them: my rock, my fortress, my God. This is not God in the abstract but what one man has found him to be. The vocabulary is a fugitive’s: the words of a man who spent years in caves at Adullam and Engedi and the Wilderness of Ziph, and who learned that a stronghold is only as good as the God in it.

What it means to take refuge. To many modern ears “refuge” sounds like weakness: faith as a hiding place for people who cannot face life. But nobody lives without a refuge. Everyone has somewhere to run when the fear comes at three in the morning: money, a good name, a person, our own competence. Proverbs sees it exactly: “A rich man’s wealth is his strong city, and like a high wall in his imagination” (Proverbs 18:11). The question is never whether you take refuge, but in what, and whether it holds when the waters rise. That refuge now has a name. The psalm about the LORD’s Anointed ends, “Blessed are all who take refuge in him” (Psalm 2:12), and he is safe to run to because he went into the flood himself. The waves of death that closed over David broke over Christ on the cross, so that “there is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus” (Romans 8:1). Taking refuge is something you do, not a mood. When the fear comes this week, notice where you run first, and then run to him in plain words: Lord, this is what I am afraid of, and I am putting it in your hands.
verseByVerse.note: Psalm 18 opens with a line not found here: I love you, O LORD, my strength.

verseByVerse.quote: I call upon the LORD, who is worthy to be praised, and I am saved from my enemies. "For the waves of death encompassed me, the torrents of destruction assailed me; the cords of Sheol entangled me; the snares of death confronted me. "In my distress I called upon the LORD; to my God I called. From his temple he heard my voice, and my cry came to his ears.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Before he tells of the danger, David names the God worth calling on; then death closes over him like water and rope, he cries out, and God hears.

I call upon the LORD, who is worthy to be praised. Verse 4 is the whole song in one line, given before the story starts: he called, and he was saved. The order matters for anyone in trouble: David does not wait until he is out of the waters to call God worthy of praise; the praise is how he tells the story of the waters.

The cords of Sheol entangled me. The trouble comes in pictures of water and rope, of drowning and being caught (vv. 5–6). Sheol is the place of the dead, and its cords are death’s grip already on him. He called, and God heard (v. 7). There was no temple yet, so his temple here is God’s heavenly dwelling. A man cried out in trouble, and the answer is an earthquake.

Not held by it. These cords closed over David and let him go. They closed fully over the Son of David, and could not keep him: “God raised him up, loosing the pangs of death, because it was not possible for him to be held by it” (Acts 2:24). Because he went down into those waters and came out, the cry of verse 7 is safe on the lips of anyone joined to him.

verseByVerse.quote: "Then the earth reeled and rocked; the foundations of the heavens trembled and quaked, because he was angry. Smoke went up from his nostrils, and devouring fire from his mouth; glowing coals flamed forth from him. He bowed the heavens and came down; thick darkness was under his feet. He rode on a cherub and flew; he was seen on the wings of the wind. He made darkness around him his canopy, thick clouds, a gathering of water. Out of the brightness before him coals of fire flamed forth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God answers one man’s cry by coming down as he came at Sinai, in fire, smoke and darkness, and creation shakes at his coming.

He bowed the heavens and came down. The ground moves and the foundations of the heavens tremble. Smoke comes from God’s nostrils and fire from his mouth; he bends the heavens down like a man pushing a low branch aside, and comes through with darkness under his feet, riding a cherub, moving on the wind (vv. 8–11). The cherubim were the winged figures over the ark, and Israel knew the LORD as the one who is enthroned on the cherubim (1 Samuel 4:4); here the throne itself takes flight. The language is deliberately that of Sinai and the exodus. God came down on a mountain in smoke and fire and darkness, and he came down to Egypt for a nation of slaves, and David puts his own rescue in that vocabulary. The point of the poetry is that God is not detached. When his people cry out, he does not send a message. He comes, and creation notices him coming.

He made darkness around him his canopy. Verses 12–13 hold together two things Israel always said about God’s coming: he is hidden, and he is blazing. He wraps himself in dark rain clouds as a king sits within a pavilion, and yet out of “the brightness before him” coals of fire break out. Moses reminded Israel that at Horeb they heard a voice out of the fire and darkness but “saw no form” (Deuteronomy 4:11–12). No one sees God himself in the storm. They see what he wears, and that is enough to shake them.

Uncertain wording. Where verse 11 has “he was seen on the wings of the wind”, Psalm 18:10 has “he came swiftly”. The two Hebrew verbs differ by a single, very similar letter, so one is probably a copying variant of the other; most think “came swiftly” (or “swooped”) is original. The picture is the same either way: God borne on the storm wind to his servant’s aid.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD thundered from heaven, and the Most High uttered his voice. And he sent out arrows and scattered them; lightning, and routed them. Then the channels of the sea were seen; the foundations of the world were laid bare, at the rebuke of the LORD, at the blast of the breath of his nostrils.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The storm becomes a battle: God’s thunder is his voice and his lightning his arrows, and at his rebuke the sea bed is laid bare as at the exodus.

The LORD thundered from heaven. The lightning bolts are loosed at David’s enemies so that they scatter and run. Israel had seen this happen. When the Philistines came up against Samuel at Mizpah, “the LORD thundered with a mighty sound that day against the Philistines and threw them into confusion” (1 Samuel 7:10), and Hannah had sung, “against them he will thunder in heaven” (1 Samuel 2:10). The Most High is the title of God as ruler over every nation (Genesis 14:19; Deuteronomy 32:8): David’s enemies were not facing a local god but the Lord of the whole earth.

The foundations of the world were laid bare. In verse 16 the sea bed is exposed and the foundations of the world uncovered. That is the sea parting at the exodus, in the language of poetry: the whole created order pulled back like a curtain because God is angry at what has been done to his servant.

verseByVerse.quote: "He sent from on high, he took me; he drew me out of many waters. He rescued me from my strong enemy, from those who hated me, for they were too mighty for me. They confronted me in the day of my calamity, but the LORD was my support. He brought me out into a broad place; he rescued me, because he delighted in me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
All that power arrives at one man: God reaches down, draws him out of the flood and sets him in a broad place, for no reason in David but God’s own delight in him.

He took me. This is the sentence all of that was for (v. 17). The earth has shaken, the heavens have bowed, the sea bed has been laid bare, and the object of the entire operation is one man. The verb drew me out is a rare one, the one behind the name Moses: “I drew him out of the water” (Exodus 2:10). God reaches down through all that and picks one man out of a flood. That is the mystery at the centre of Old Testament prayer, and the psalm states it without apology: the God who shakes creation attends to one person’s crisis, and his greatness is no reason to think he is not paying attention.

In the day of my calamity. The enemies chose their moment. They “confronted” him (the verb of verse 6, where the snares of death confronted him) when he was already down; calamity is the day everything goes wrong at once. But the LORD was my support: the word means a staff or prop, something a man leans his whole weight on, and it did not give way.

He brought me out into a broad place. David admits that his enemies were too mighty for me (v. 18). The Hebrew for distress is a word about narrowness: being hemmed in, squeezed, with nowhere to go. Rescue is the opposite, open ground and room to move. Anybody who has been in trouble knows exactly what the two words describe.

Because he delighted in me. Not because David was useful, or strong, or necessary to a plan. Deuteronomy says the same of Israel: God did not choose them because they were numerous, but “because the LORD loves you” (Deuteronomy 7:7–8). The reason is in God, and it is affection. It is the same delight the Father declared over his Son at the Jordan (Matthew 3:17), and those joined to Christ are loved with it.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 21–37 — Your Gentleness Made Me Great
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God deals with people according to what they are, and the man he equips owes all his strength to God’s gentleness. David speaks of his righteousness and clean hands (vv. 21–25), a claim the book that records chapter 11 does not read as sinlessness but as loyalty to God, vindicated in his long ordeal with Saul. God shows himself merciful to the merciful and seems twisted to the crooked; he saves the humble and brings down the proud (vv. 26–28). He is David’s lamp, his rock and the one who made his way blameless (vv. 29–34). He trained his hands for war and gave him room to stand, and what made David great was God’s gentleness (vv. 35–37).
verseByVerse.theology: The righteousness claim is the hard part of this psalm and should not be explained away, since the same book contains chapters 11 to 20. It concerns covenant loyalty (he never went after other gods) and the one vindication named in the heading: twice he refused to put out his hand against Saul when he could have.
verseByVerse.examples: Verse 36 is the sentence to carry out of this section. Amid the bronze bows and trained hands, he says what actually made him: your gentleness made me great.

verseByVerse.quote: "The LORD dealt with me according to my righteousness; according to the cleanness of my hands he rewarded me. For I have kept the ways of the LORD and have not wickedly departed from my God. For all his rules were before me, and from his statutes I did not turn aside. I was blameless before him, and I kept myself from guilt. And the LORD has rewarded me according to my righteousness, according to my cleanness in his sight.
verseByVerse.commentary:
David’s claim to clean hands is not a claim to sinlessness but to undivided loyalty, vindicated in his long ordeal with Saul; only Christ can say these words without reserve.

According to the cleanness of my hands. The man saying this (v. 21) is in a book which has just spent ten chapters recording what those hands did. He took an officer’s wife, then had the man killed with a letter he carried himself; he failed to act when his daughter was raped and his son murdered. Three things need saying.

The editor knew. First, whoever assembled this book had chapter 11 in front of him and put this psalm in anyway, afterwards. So the people who compiled Israel’s own Scriptures did not understand these verses as a claim to sinless perfection.

What the claim is about. The heading tells you which deliverance is in view: from the hand of all his enemies, and from the hand of Saul. On that question David has a specific record. For years he was hunted by a man he had not wronged, and twice he had him at his mercy: asleep at Hachilah with a spear in the ground beside his head, and in a cave at Engedi. Both times he refused: The LORD forbid that I should put out my hand against the LORD’s anointed (1 Samuel 26:11). His conscience troubled him even for cutting a corner off a robe. On the question the song is about, his hands were clean, he knew it, and God had vindicated him.

I was blameless before him. The second thing is what blameless (v. 24) means in the Old Testament. It is not sinlessness but undivided loyalty: a heart that is not split, that has not gone after other gods, that faces one way. It is the word used of Noah and of Job. It is true of David as of hardly any other king of Israel. He was an adulterer and a murderer, and he never once served another god. The verdict passed on almost every king after him (that he made Israel to sin, kept the high places, the hilltop shrines, went after the Baals) is never passed on David.

When he fell. The third thing is what he did when he fell, and the psalter records that too: “Have mercy on me, O God, according to your steadfast love … Against you, you only, have I sinned and done what is evil in your sight” (Psalm 51:1–4). The same man wrote both. Psalm 51 is not a correction of Psalm 18; they are two true things said by one person, and any account of David that keeps only one of them is false. Scripture puts both in one book without softening either, and these verses should not be made comfortable.

The one who could sing it without reserve. Only one Son of David had wholly clean hands, who could ask his enemies, “Which one of you convicts me of sin?” (John 8:46). God dealt with him not according to his righteousness but according to our sin, and then vindicated him by raising him from the dead. That is why a forgiven sinner may sing these verses in him: “For our sake he made him to be sin who knew no sin, so that in him we might become the righteousness of God” (2 Corinthians 5:21).

verseByVerse.quote: "With the merciful you show yourself merciful; with the blameless man you show yourself blameless; with the purified you deal purely, and with the crooked you make yourself seem tortuous. You save a humble people, but your eyes are on the haughty to bring them down.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God does not change with the person looking at him, but each person finds him according to what they are: merciful to the merciful, baffling to the crooked, saving the humble and bringing down the proud.

With the merciful you show yourself merciful. To the crooked God seems tortuous: twisted, hard to deal with, impossible to get a straight answer from. A devious man finds God devious because he reads God through himself, as a bent ruler measures everything bent. That is why Saul, at the end, could get nothing out of God by dreams or Urim (the priest’s sacred lot) or prophets, and went to a medium. And it is why Pharaoh met a God who kept hardening him.

You save a humble people. Verse 28 holds the whole of Hannah’s song and the whole of Mary’s: God saves the humble and brings the haughty down. Both books that bear Samuel’s name have been arguing it from their opening chapters.

Your eyes are on the haughty to bring them down. God’s eyes are on the proud as well as the humble, and the watching is not idle. The books of Samuel have shown it in one life after another: Goliath, Nabal, Saul and Absalom were each lifted up and each brought down. David himself, at the height of his power, was brought low when he took what was not his (chapters 11–12). The verse is a comfort to the lowly and a warning to anyone, the singer included, who begins to look down on others.

verseByVerse.quote: For you are my lamp, O LORD, and my God lightens my darkness. For by you I can run against a troop, and by my God I can leap over a wall. This God— his way is perfect; the word of the LORD proves true; he is a shield for all those who take refuge in him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The LORD is David’s light and strength, and his way and his word are flawless, a shield not only for kings but for all who take refuge in him.

For you are my lamp, O LORD. His own men called David the lamp of Israel one chapter ago (21:17); here he says who the lamp actually is.

By my God I can leap over a wall. Verse 30 is the confidence of a soldier who knows where his strength comes from: by you he charges a troop, by my God he gets over a wall. The word for “troop” is the one used of the Amalekite raiding band David pursued after Ziklag was burned (1 Samuel 30:8, 15). Neither line is a boast about himself; each begins with God.

The word of the LORD proves true. Verse 31 stops to say why that confidence is safe. His way is perfect: whatever God does is complete and without flaw, even when it does not look so from inside it. Proves true pictures metal refined in the fire and coming out pure. God’s promise to David was tested by years of waiting and danger, and it held. Proverbs repeats the line almost word for word: “Every word of God proves true; he is a shield to those who take refuge in him” (Proverbs 30:5). And the last clause opens the song to everyone: he is a shield for all who take refuge in him, not for kings only.

verseByVerse.quote: "For who is God, but the LORD? And who is a rock, except our God? This God is my strong refuge and has made my way blameless. He made my feet like the feet of a deer and set me secure on the heights.
verseByVerse.commentary:
There is no God and no rock but the LORD, and the blameless way David spoke of is God’s own work in him.

Who is God, but the LORD? The question expects no answer: there is no other god and no other rock. It is Hannah’s confession again, almost in the same words: “There is none holy like the LORD: for there is none besides you; there is no rock like our God” (1 Samuel 2:2). The books of Samuel open and close on the same song, and the God who heard a barren woman is the God who kept a hunted king.

Has made my way blameless. Verse 33 adds a clause that matters after verses 21–25: God made my way blameless. David is not claiming to have produced it himself. In verse 34 his feet are like a deer’s, the animal that can run flat out on rock where a man would break an ankle. He spent years in that terrain being hunted, and the picture is exact.

verseByVerse.quote: He trains my hands for war, so that my arms can bend a bow of bronze. You have given me the shield of your salvation, and your gentleness made me great. You gave a wide place for my steps under me, and my feet did not slip;
verseByVerse.commentary:
Every skill and strength David had was God’s training and gift, and what made him great, he says, was God’s gentleness.

He trains my hands for war. The shepherd who killed Goliath with a sling did not credit his skill to himself, and neither does the king. A “bow of bronze” was probably a bow strengthened with bronze, too stiff for an ordinary man to bend. Psalm 144 opens with the same thanks: “Blessed be the LORD, my rock, who trains my hands for war, and my fingers for battle” (Psalm 144:1). What looks like natural talent and long practice, David calls God’s training.

Your gentleness made me great. Look at what surrounds verse 36: trained hands, a bronze bow, feet like a deer’s, the heights, a shield. Every image in twenty verses has been about strength and equipment, and when he comes to say what actually made him, the word is gentleness: God’s willingness to stoop to a man who did not deserve it. Consider who says it: a boy passed over by his father, a fugitive in caves, an adulterer and murderer forgiven, a father who lost three sons. Looking back over all of it, what he names as having made him is that God was gentle with him. It is the gentleness that came in person, “gentle and lowly in heart” (Matthew 11:29), to those who labour and are heavy laden.

You gave a wide place for my steps. The wide place for his steps in verse 37 is the broad place of verse 20 again. He keeps returning to the picture: room to stand.

Uncertain wording. The word translated “gentleness” is rare, and its form here differs slightly from Psalm 18:35. It is usually understood as God’s gentleness or humility, his stooping down; some translations render it “your help”, taking it from a verb meaning “to answer”. The sense is close either way: God bending to help a man who could not help himself.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 38–51 — To David and His Offspring Forever
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The living God gave the king his victories, and his steadfast love will run on to David’s offspring for ever. David describes real campaigns plainly: enemies pursued and crushed, crying to the LORD with no answer (vv. 38–43). God delivered him from strife with his own people and set him over nations he had not known (vv. 44–46). The closing praise rests on one fact, “The LORD lives”, the God who gave David vengeance instead of letting him take it (vv. 47–49). David will praise him among the nations, words Paul hears fulfilled as the Gentiles come in (v. 50), and the song ends on the promise of chapter 7: steadfast love “to his anointed, to David and his offspring forever” (v. 51).
verseByVerse.theology: The battle language is that of an ancient warrior king describing real campaigns. It should not be softened into metaphor, nor treated as a model for anybody's conduct toward their neighbours.
verseByVerse.examples: The song ends where chapter 7 ended, and reaches past its author. His anointed... David and his offspring forever is the covenant promise, and it runs on to David's greater Son.

verseByVerse.quote: I pursued my enemies and destroyed them, and did not turn back until they were consumed. I consumed them; I thrust them through, so that they did not rise; they fell under my feet. For you equipped me with strength for the battle; you made those who rise against me sink under me. You made my enemies turn their backs to me, those who hated me, and I destroyed them. They looked, but there was none to save; they cried to the LORD, but he did not answer them. I beat them fine as the dust of the earth; I crushed them and stamped them down like the mire of the streets.
verseByVerse.commentary:
David describes real wars plainly, giving the victory to God; this is a king’s song about his nation’s battles, not a pattern for how believers treat their enemies.

I pursued my enemies and destroyed them. Verses 38–43 should be read as what they are: an ancient king describing real campaigns in the vocabulary of his own world. He fought the Philistines, the Ammonites, the Syrians, the Edomites and the Moabites; men died under his feet, and he says so. Even here the grammar keeps giving the work to God: you equipped me, you made them sink.

They cried to the LORD, but he did not answer them. Verse 42 is the dark mirror of verse 7. David cried to the LORD in his distress, and his cry came to God’s ears; his enemies cry and there is no answer. The difference is not in how loudly they called. They had set themselves against the king the LORD had chosen, and no one can fight God’s purpose and count on God’s help in the same breath. It is what happened to Saul at the end (see the note on vv. 26–28).

What it does not mean. Taking it plainly means two things. It is not a model for anybody’s conduct toward their neighbours, though it has been used as one. David was the anointed king of a covenant nation fighting national wars about a thousand years before Christ. The New Testament does not authorise a Christian to speak this way about anybody, and its instruction is the opposite: “Bless those who persecute you; bless and do not curse them” (Romans 12:14). The Son of David won his decisive battle by dying for his enemies. Nor should the passage be dissolved into metaphor to make it comfortable. These were real battles, the psalm is honest about them, and Scripture does not tidy up its own history.

verseByVerse.quote: "You delivered me from strife with my people; you kept me as the head of the nations; people whom I had not known served me. Foreigners came cringing to me; as soon as they heard of me, they obeyed me. Foreigners lost heart and came trembling out of their fortresses.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God rescued David from war within Israel as well as war without, and set the shepherd boy over nations he had never known.

You delivered me from strife with my people. That is not the Philistines. That is Absalom, and Sheba, and the argument at the Jordan: the wars inside Israel. The song puts civil conflict among the things he was delivered from, and anyone who has read the previous twenty chapters knows that it was these, not the foreign wars, that nearly finished him.

You kept me as the head of the nations. The rest of verse 44 and verses 45–46 look outward. Chapter 8 lists the peoples who came under David: the Philistines, Moab, Zobah and the Syrians of Damascus, and Edom. Toi king of Hamath sent his son with gifts, and Hiram king of Tyre built David a house (5:11; 8:9–10). Foreigners came cringing to me: people he had never met submitted as soon as they heard of him, and came trembling out of their fortresses. The song gives the credit where it has given all the rest: you kept me. It is a small foretaste of the Son of David, to whom the Father has promised “the nations your heritage” (Psalm 2:8).

verseByVerse.quote: "The LORD lives, and blessed be my rock, and exalted be my God, the rock of my salvation, the God who gave me vengeance and brought down peoples under me, who brought me out from my enemies; you exalted me above those who rose against me; you delivered me from men of violence.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The whole song rests on this: the LORD is alive, and he, not David, gave the king his vengeance and his victories.

The LORD lives. These words (v. 47) are the foundation of the whole song. He is not an idea, or a national symbol, or a carved thing like Dagon in his temple at Ashdod, which fell on its face (1 Samuel 5:3). He is a living God who hears a man in trouble and comes.

The God who gave me vengeance. David does not say that he took vengeance but that God gave it. That is the line he held when he had Saul at his mercy: “May the LORD avenge me against you, but my hand shall not be against you” (1 Samuel 24:12; see the note on vv. 21–25). He left judgment with God, and God did not fail him. Paul gives Christians the same rule for the wrongs done to them: “never avenge yourselves, but leave it to the wrath of God” (Romans 12:19).

verseByVerse.quote: "For this I will praise you, O LORD, among the nations, and sing praises to your name. Great salvation he brings to his king, and shows steadfast love to his anointed, to David and his offspring forever."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The song ends by reaching beyond its singer: praise among the nations, and God’s steadfast love to his anointed king and to his offspring for ever, a promise kept in Jesus Christ.

Among the nations. Paul argues in Romans that Christ became a servant to the circumcised to confirm the promises given to the patriarchs, “and in order that the Gentiles might glorify God for his mercy”, and he stacks up four Old Testament texts to show that this was always the plan. The first is verse 50: “Therefore I will praise you among the Gentiles, and sing to your name” (Romans 15:9). David sang about praising God among the nations, and Paul reads it as a promise that the nations themselves would come in.

Great salvation he brings to his king. The last verse goes past the man singing it. His king: not me, but the office, and it is God’s, not David’s. Steadfast love: hesed, the word this whole book has been built on, what Jonathan asked for, what Jabesh-gilead showed Saul, what David showed Mephibosheth and tried to show Hanun. Here it is God’s, shown to his anointed, his mashiach or messiah, a word that simply means the man with the oil on him, and in this verse means David. And to David and his offspring forever is chapter 7: “your house and your kingdom shall be made sure forever before me. Your throne shall be established forever” (7:16).

To David and his offspring forever. So the song ends on the promise, and the promise runs past its singer. There is no way to sing of God’s steadfast love to David and his offspring forever without the sentence travelling beyond one lifetime, and it did: through Solomon, through the long line of kings who mostly failed, through the exile when there was no son of David on any throne anywhere, and out the other side to a birth in the town this man came from.

Why the book ends this way. The compilers could have closed with Absalom and written a tragedy about a man who ruined his own house. Instead, having recorded all of it without excusing a line, they reached back decades and put his song near the end. Not because the wreckage was not real; they wrote ten chapters of it. Because this is what he believed the whole way through, and it was still true afterwards. The rock did not move when the man on it fell, and that is why the book closes with a psalm and not with a grave.

keyVerse.quote: He said, “The LORD is my rock and my fortress and my deliverer,
keyVerse.note: The song opens with what David had found God to be, in the words of a man who lived for years in caves and strongholds. Everything after it, the cry, the storm, the rescue and the promise to his offspring, unfolds this one confession, and the book chooses it as the last word on a life that had collapsed: the rock did not move when the man on it fell.

22.reflection:
David gives name after name for God in verses 2–3, and every one of them is about safety. Where do you tend to run first when fear comes? What would it look like this week to take refuge in the LORD in plain words?

The God who shakes the earth and bows the heavens does it to rescue one man, “because he delighted in me” (vv. 8–20). Which do you find harder to believe: that God is that great, or that he pays that much attention to you? How does Christ show us both?

The book places David’s claims of “the cleanness of my hands” (vv. 21–25) after the chapters that record his adultery and murder. How can David say these things, and how do they sound on the lips of Jesus, the only Son of David with wholly clean hands?

David looks back over a life of victories and failures and says, “your gentleness made me great” (v. 36). If you had to say in a few words what has made you, what would you name? Where have you seen God’s gentleness with you?

23.title: David's Last Words and His Mighty Men
23.text: <sup>1</sup>Now these are the last words of David: The oracle of David, the son of Jesse, the oracle of the man who was raised on high, the anointed of the God of Jacob, the sweet psalmist of Israel:<sup>2</sup>"The Spirit of the LORD speaks by me; his word is on my tongue.<sup>3</sup>The God of Israel has spoken; the Rock of Israel has said to me: When one rules justly over men, ruling in the fear of God,<sup>4</sup>he dawns on them like the morning light, like the sun shining forth on a cloudless morning, like rain that makes grass to sprout from the earth.<sup>5</sup>"For does not my house stand so with God? For he has made with me an everlasting covenant, ordered in all things and secure. For will he not cause to prosper all my help and my desire?<sup>6</sup>But worthless men are all like thorns that are thrown away, for they cannot be taken with the hand;<sup>7</sup>but the man who touches them arms himself with iron and the shaft of a spear, and they are utterly consumed with fire."<sup>8</sup>These are the names of the mighty men whom David had: Josheb-basshebeth a Tahchemonite; he was chief of the three. He wielded his spear against eight hundred whom he killed at one time.<sup>9</sup>And next to him among the three mighty men was Eleazar the son of Dodo, son of Ahohi. He was with David when they defied the Philistines who were gathered there for battle, and the men of Israel withdrew.<sup>10</sup>He rose and struck down the Philistines until his hand was weary, and his hand clung to the sword. And the LORD brought about a great victory that day, and the men returned after him only to strip the slain.<sup>11</sup>And next to him was Shammah, the son of Agee the Hararite. The Philistines gathered together at Lehi, where there was a plot of ground full of lentils, and the men fled from the Philistines.<sup>12</sup>But he took his stand in the midst of the plot and defended it and struck down the Philistines, and the LORD worked a great victory.<sup>13</sup>And three of the thirty chief men went down and came about harvest time to David at the cave of Adullam, when a band of Philistines was encamped in the Valley of Rephaim.<sup>14</sup>David was then in the stronghold, and the garrison of the Philistines was then at Bethlehem.<sup>15</sup>And David said longingly, "Oh, that someone would give me water to drink from the well of Bethlehem that is by the gate!"<sup>16</sup>Then the three mighty men broke through the camp of the Philistines and drew water out of the well of Bethlehem that was by the gate and carried and brought it to David. But he would not drink of it. He poured it out to the LORD<sup>17</sup>and said, "Far be it from me, O LORD, that I should do this. Shall I drink the blood of the men who went at the risk of their lives?" Therefore he would not drink it. These things the three mighty men did.<sup>18</sup>Now Abishai, the brother of Joab, the son of Zeruiah, was chief of the thirty. And he wielded his spear against three hundred men and killed them and won a name beside the three.<sup>19</sup>He was the most renowned of the thirty and became their commander, but he did not attain to the three.<sup>20</sup>And Benaiah the son of Jehoiada was a valiant man of Kabzeel, a doer of great deeds. He struck down two ariels of Moab. He also went down and struck down a lion in a pit on a day when snow had fallen.<sup>21</sup>And he struck down an Egyptian, a handsome man. The Egyptian had a spear in his hand, but Benaiah went down to him with a staff and snatched the spear out of the Egyptian's hand and killed him with his own spear.<sup>22</sup>These things did Benaiah the son of Jehoiada, and won a name beside the three mighty men.<sup>23</sup>He was renowned among the thirty, but he did not attain to the three. And David set him over his bodyguard.<sup>24</sup>Asahel the brother of Joab was one of the thirty; Elhanan the son of Dodo of Bethlehem,<sup>25</sup>Shammah of Harod, Elika of Harod,<sup>26</sup>Helez the Paltite, Ira the son of Ikkesh of Tekoa,<sup>27</sup>Abiezer of Anathoth, Mebunnai the Hushathite,<sup>28</sup>Zalmon the Ahohite, Maharai of Netophah,<sup>29</sup>Heleb the son of Baanah of Netophah, Ittai the son of Ribai of Gibeah of the people of Benjamin,<sup>30</sup>Benaiah of Pirathon, Hiddai of the brooks of Gaash,<sup>31</sup>Abi-albon the Arbathite, Azmaveth of Bahurim,<sup>32</sup>Eliahba the Shaalbonite, the sons of Jashen, Jonathan,<sup>33</sup>Shammah the Hararite, Ahiam the son of Sharar the Hararite,<sup>34</sup>Eliphelet the son of Ahasbai of Maacah, Eliam the son of Ahithophel the Gilonite,<sup>35</sup>Hezro of Carmel, Paarai the Arbite,<sup>36</sup>Igal the son of Nathan of Zobah, Bani the Gadite,<sup>37</sup>Zelek the Ammonite, Naharai of Beeroth, the armor-bearer of Joab the son of Zeruiah,<sup>38</sup>Ira the Ithrite, Gareb the Ithrite,<sup>39</sup>Uriah the Hittite: thirty-seven in all.
23.overview:
Where we are. This is the second poem at the centre of the appendix (chapters 21 to 24), set beside the song of chapter 22: the last inspired words of David. After it comes the roll of his mighty men, matching the giant-killers of 21:15–22, with the stories of what a few of them did.

The message. A king who rules justly, in the fear of God, is to his people what sunrise and rain are to the land: a gift they cannot produce for themselves. No king of Israel was that for long, David included, and at the end of his life he rests not on his record but on the everlasting covenant God made with him, “ordered in all things and secure”. The roll of his men shows the same God working through ordinary courage, and it ends, without comment, on the name of the man David had killed.

Why it was said. Later Israel lived under kings who mostly failed to be morning light, and then under no king at all (see the introduction). These words told them what to hope for and what to rest on: not the house of David’s faithfulness but God’s covenant with it. The roll told them, too, that their history would not be told by flattering the king.

How the chapter makes its case. David’s last words come as an oracle, inspired by the Spirit, with a picture of the just ruler as morning light and rain, the covenant he rests on, and the end of the worthless (vv. 1–7). Then the mighty men: the Three, who stood when Israel ran, “and the LORD brought about a great victory” (vv. 8–12); three men who broke through a Philistine garrison for a cup of water from Bethlehem’s well, which David would not drink but poured out to the LORD (vv. 13–17); Abishai and Benaiah (vv. 18–23); and the thirty, from Joab’s dead brother to an Ammonite, ending with “Uriah the Hittite: thirty-seven in all” (vv. 24–39).

Where it leads. To Christ by promise and by the need it exposes. The prophets said a righteous Branch would rise for David (Jeremiah 23:5), and when he was about to be born Zechariah sang that “the sunrise shall visit us from on high” (Luke 1:78). The everlasting covenant David leaned on is the one God kept by raising Jesus from the dead, giving “the holy and sure blessings of David” (Acts 13:34). And the roll ending with Uriah shows why a better King was needed. David would not drink a cup bought with his men’s blood; the Son of David poured out his own blood for his people and handed them the cup (Luke 22:20).

For us. At the end of a life with regrets, the place to rest is where David rested: on a covenant God arranged and God guards, kept in Christ. Those with any authority should remember that a passing wish lands on people who want to please them. And faithfulness in a lentil field, holding the ground when others run, is the kind of courage God still uses.
23.theology:
Presented as a word given (vv. 1-2). Oracle is the formula that introduces prophetic utterance, and the Spirit of the LORD speaks by me; his word is on my tongue claims inspiration outright. The New Testament agrees: Peter says the Holy Spirit spoke through David’s mouth, and at Pentecost calls him a prophet (Acts 1:16; 2:30).

The ruler who is the morning. No king of David's line was this sunrise for long, and the prophets said one would be: a righteous Branch raised up for David, who would reign as king and deal wisely (Jeremiah 23:5), a sun of righteousness rising with healing in its wings (Malachi 4:2). When that son of David was about to be born, Zechariah sang that the sunrise shall visit us from on high (Luke 1:78). And the everlasting covenant David rested on is the one Paul says God kept by raising Jesus from the dead: I will give you the holy and sure blessings of David (Acts 13:34). It is secure because its final King cannot die again.

What the list is (v. 8). The book is nearly over and the writer spends a long passage on soldiers' names and villages. These are the men from the cave: everyone who was in distress, and everyone who was in debt, and everyone who was bitter in soul (1 Sam. 22:2), four hundred failures in a hole in the ground. This is what became of them, and it is a picture of what God can make of people who come to his king with nothing.

Why he would not drink it (vv. 16-17). Pouring the water out to the LORD is a drink offering, not ingratitude. The cup had three men's lives in it, so he gave it to the only one worth what it cost, and accepted the rebuke in it: a leader’s passing wish is never harmless, because others will act on it.

And who else is on it. The roll includes Asahel, long dead; a man from Saul's own village; Zelek the Ammonite; Eliam, very probably Bathsheba's father; and last, Uriah the Hittite, one of the finest soldiers in the country, murdered by the man whose list this is. His name stands in a chapter that opens with David saying the Spirit of the LORD speaks by me. The book holds on to both facts and does not reconcile them for us.
23.examples:
Then: A hunted man in a cave twelve miles from the town he grew up in said aloud, to nobody in particular, that he wished he could have a drink from the well by the gate. Three of his men walked through an enemy army to get it, and he would not put it to his lips, but poured it out as an offering to God because it had their lives in it.

Now: Three things. Verse 5 is where to end up: at the close of a life in which nearly everything that could go wrong in a family did, what he rests on is not an achievement of his own but a covenant God arranged and God guards. Anyone looking back on a life with regrets can rest on the same thing. Second, the well, and the uncomfortable half of it: David never told anybody to go. People with any authority at all should notice how a passing remark lands on those who want to please them, and that somebody else pays the cost. And third, the last line. The book puts the name of the man David had killed at the very end of the roll of his finest soldiers, in the place he earned, and adds nothing. It is more devastating than any verdict it could have written.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–7 — Ordered in All Things and Secure
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: David’s last words picture the king his people need, and rest on the covenant God has made. They come as an oracle: the son of Jesse, raised up by God, anointed, the sweet psalmist of Israel, speaks by the Spirit of the LORD (vv. 1–2). A ruler who rules justly in the fear of God is to his people like sunrise on a cloudless morning and rain that makes the grass sprout (vv. 3–4). David’s own house has not always been so, but God has made with him “an everlasting covenant, ordered in all things and secure” (v. 5). The worthless, by contrast, are like thorns, cleared with iron and burned where they lie (vv. 6–7).
verseByVerse.theology: This is prophetic formula, not memoir. The titles stack up in front of the claim to speak by the Spirit (raised on high, anointed of the God of Jacob, the sweet psalmist of Israel), and every one of them names something given to him.
verseByVerse.examples: At the end of a life he does not rehearse victories or failures. He goes back to chapter 7, a covenant ordered in all things and secure, and that is what he stakes everything on. It is not his own record.

verseByVerse.quote: Now these are the last words of David: The oracle of David, the son of Jesse, the oracle of the man who was raised on high, the anointed of the God of Jacob, the sweet psalmist of Israel: "The Spirit of the LORD speaks by me; his word is on my tongue. The God of Israel has spoken; the Rock of Israel has said to me: When one rules justly over men, ruling in the fear of God, he dawns on them like the morning light, like the sun shining forth on a cloudless morning, like rain that makes grass to sprout from the earth. "For does not my house stand so with God? For he has made with me an everlasting covenant, ordered in all things and secure. For will he not cause to prosper all my help and my desire? But worthless men are all like thorns that are thrown away, for they cannot be taken with the hand; but the man who touches them arms himself with iron and the shaft of a spear, and they are utterly consumed with fire."
verseByVerse.commentary:
In his last inspired words David pictures the just ruler as sunrise and rain to his people, admits that his own house has not matched it, and rests everything on the covenant God made and God keeps; the picture points past him to Christ.

The oracle of David, the son of Jesse. The word is oracle, the formula that introduces a prophetic utterance, the one Balaam uses, and Agur in Proverbs. This is not offered as a memoir or a farewell speech but as a word given. These are his last inspired words as psalmist and prophet, not his last speech; he still speaks in 1 Kings 2.

The four titles. They are worth reading slowly. The son of Jesse is where he started, the name Saul used when he would not say David, and the name Sheba used when he broke the country in half (20:1); he takes it first. The man who was raised on high is passive: somebody else raised him. The anointed of the God of Jacob says that he was anointed king, and whose choice that was. And then the sweet psalmist of Israel. Of everything that could have gone in that fourth place (the king, the conqueror, the founder of a dynasty), the one chosen is that he wrote the nation’s songs. Then he claims inspiration outright: the Spirit speaks by him, as the New Testament agrees (Acts 1:16; 2 Peter 1:21).

He dawns on them like the morning light. Verses 3–4 give his picture of what a king is for, and it is unlike the way power usually describes itself. Both images are of things arriving that people cannot produce for themselves. The first is sunrise on a clear morning: light coming up over ground that has been dark all night, and everything becoming visible. It is not a display of force, just the end of not being able to see. The second is rain on new grass. In that country rain is the difference between a harvest and a famine, and nobody can make it happen. It arrives, and the ground goes green.

Like rain that makes grass to sprout. That is what a ruler who rules justly, in the fear of God, is like to the people under him. David is not describing a strong king or a successful one, but the effect on ordinary people of being governed by somebody honest who is afraid of God. It describes David at his best (David administered justice and equity to all his people, 8:15) and what he failed to be, since Absalom built a rebellion on the claim that nobody at the gate was being heard (15:3). No king in Israel was consistently the morning light for his people, including this one, and the sentence points past all of them. On just leadership in every sphere of life, see on Ephesians 5:21.

Does not my house stand so with God? Whichever way the clause is read (see below), the sentence after it is the same: the everlasting covenant of chapter 7, and it is what the man goes back to at the end of his life. He does not list his victories, mention Goliath or Jerusalem, or rehearse his failures. He goes to the promise.

Ordered in all things and secure. The word for ordered is used for drawing up a battle line or setting out wood on an altar: things arranged deliberately, nothing left loose. The covenant is not a general goodwill but an arrangement, put together with care. And secure means guarded and kept. It will not fail, because its security does not depend on the man it was made with, which David, of all people, has reason to know. He has watched his own house do nearly everything a house can do wrong: a daughter raped by her brother, a son murdered by a son, a rebellion, a child he begged for buried. What he stakes his hope on at the end is not one thing he did. He has made with me: God did it, God arranged it, God keeps it.

Worthless men are all like thorns. Verses 6–7 set the other picture beside it. The just ruler is morning light and rain on grass; worthless men are briars in a field. You cannot clear thorns by hand; you need tools, and in the end you burn them where they lie. They produce nothing and take up ground. The word for worthless is the one used of Nabal, of Sheba the son of Bichri, and of the men who would not have Saul as king: in this book, a settled name for the person who is no good to anybody. So the last words of David are two pictures and a promise: what good government does for people, what is finally done with those who will not have it, and in the middle, holding both, a covenant ordered in all things and secure.

The morning that came. David speaks of the righteous king God promised his house (7:12–16), and no king of David’s line fulfilled it but one. The prophets promised a righteous Branch for David (Jeremiah 23:5) and a sun of righteousness rising with healing in its wings (Malachi 4:2); Zechariah greeted his coming as the sunrise from on high (Luke 1:78), and the risen Christ calls himself “the bright morning star” (Revelation 22:16). The covenant David rested on is secure because its final King cannot die again (Acts 13:34).

Can any power be trusted? Most of us now read every claim to authority with a raised eyebrow, and not without reason. The philosopher Paul Ricoeur called Marx, Nietzsche and Freud the masters of suspicion, because they taught the modern world to ask what interest hides behind every noble word, and a century of tyrants and abusive institutions has taught the same lesson. So a ruler pictured as morning light and rain can sound naive. But these words close a book that has spent ten chapters exposing the man who spoke them. What Scripture refuses is the cynic’s conclusion that authority can only ever crush. It holds out a ruler whose power makes things grow, and then it shows him to us: one who had all authority and used it to wash feet, who “came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many” (Mark 10:45). Suspicion can tell us whom not to trust. It cannot give us anyone to trust. Only a King like that can.

Uncertain wording. Two phrases are uncertain. In verse 1, “the sweet psalmist of Israel” may instead mean “the favorite of the songs of Israel” (the ESV margin), that is, the one Israel’s songs celebrate; either way David is tied to the nation’s praise. In verse 5 the Hebrew of the first clause is difficult. Older English versions read it as a concession, “although my house be not so with God”: my household has not been what I have just described, and yet. Most modern versions read it as a question expecting yes: “does not my house stand so with God?” The two differ more in tone than in effect, because the promise that follows is the same either way.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 8–23 — Shall I Drink the Blood of These Men?
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God won David’s victories through men who stood their ground, and the best of them loved their king enough to risk their lives for a wish. Josheb-basshebeth, Eleazar and Shammah stood when Israel ran, and each time “the LORD brought about a great victory” (vv. 8–12). At Adullam David longs aloud for water from the well of Bethlehem, now held by the Philistines; three men break through the garrison and bring it, and he will not drink it but pours it out to the LORD, because it cost the risk of their blood (vv. 13–17). Abishai and Benaiah, killer of a lion in a pit on a snowy day, win a name beside the Three (vv. 18–23).
verseByVerse.theology: The exploits of the Three all have one shape: a man refuses to run, and then the LORD brought about a great victory. The man’s courage holds the ground and God gives the victory, and the writer keeps both halves.
verseByVerse.examples: The water is the finest thing in the chapter. He said oh, that someone would: a longing, not an order, and three men went through an enemy army for it. Pouring it out was not refusing the gift but giving it to God instead.

verseByVerse.quote: These are the names of the mighty men whom David had: Josheb-basshebeth a Tahchemonite; he was chief of the three. He wielded his spear against eight hundred whom he killed at one time. And next to him among the three mighty men was Eleazar the son of Dodo, son of Ahohi. He was with David when they defied the Philistines who were gathered there for battle, and the men of Israel withdrew. He rose and struck down the Philistines until his hand was weary, and his hand clung to the sword. And the LORD brought about a great victory that day, and the men returned after him only to strip the slain. And next to him was Shammah, the son of Agee the Hararite. The Philistines gathered together at Lehi, where there was a plot of ground full of lentils, and the men fled from the Philistines. But he took his stand in the midst of the plot and defended it and struck down the Philistines, and the LORD worked a great victory. And three of the thirty chief men went down and came about harvest time to David at the cave of Adullam, when a band of Philistines was encamped in the Valley of Rephaim. David was then in the stronghold, and the garrison of the Philistines was then at Bethlehem. And David said longingly, "Oh, that someone would give me water to drink from the well of Bethlehem that is by the gate!" Then the three mighty men broke through the camp of the Philistines and drew water out of the well of Bethlehem that was by the gate and carried and brought it to David. But he would not drink of it. He poured it out to the LORD and said, "Far be it from me, O LORD, that I should do this. Shall I drink the blood of the men who went at the risk of their lives?" Therefore he would not drink it. These things the three mighty men did. Now Abishai, the brother of Joab, the son of Zeruiah, was chief of the thirty. And he wielded his spear against three hundred men and killed them and won a name beside the three. He was the most renowned of the thirty and became their commander, but he did not attain to the three. And Benaiah the son of Jehoiada was a valiant man of Kabzeel, a doer of great deeds. He struck down two ariels of Moab. He also went down and struck down a lion in a pit on a day when snow had fallen. And he struck down an Egyptian, a handsome man. The Egyptian had a spear in his hand, but Benaiah went down to him with a staff and snatched the spear out of the Egyptian's hand and killed him with his own spear. These things did Benaiah the son of Jehoiada, and won a name beside the three mighty men. He was renowned among the thirty, but he did not attain to the three. And David set him over his bodyguard.
verseByVerse.commentary:
David’s victories were won by men who held their ground when others ran, and each time the writer gives the victory to the LORD; the best of them loved their king so much that a passing wish sent them through an enemy garrison, and David honoured their courage by pouring the water out to God.

These are the names of the mighty men whom David had. The book is nearly over, and the writer spends most of the chapter listing soldiers. That is a decision: thirty-seven names, most with a village attached, and what four or five of them did. These are the men who gathered to David at Adullam, “everyone who was in distress, and everyone who was in debt, and everyone who was bitter in soul” (1 Samuel 22:2), and this is what became of them.

His hand clung to the sword. In verses 9–10 Israel ran and Eleazar did not. He fought until his hand locked around the grip and he could not let go, a soldier’s detail and a true one: a man who has held a weapon through a long fight cannot open his fingers afterwards. Then the LORD brought about a great victory, not “Eleazar won a great victory”. The man stood, and God gave the outcome. And the army that ran away came back to strip the slain, which the writer records without comment.

A plot of ground full of lentils. Shammah’s stand (vv. 11–12) has the same shape, and the ground he defends is a lentil field: not a pass or a city gate, but a vegetable patch. It was somebody’s food, the army decided it was not worth dying for, and one man stood in the middle of it. Then the same sentence again: the LORD worked a great victory. The writer does not say the men were irrelevant, and he does not let them keep the credit.

And David said longingly. Verses 13–17 are the best scene in the catalogue, and everything turns on the word longingly. David is at Adullam, about twelve miles from Bethlehem, a fugitive. Bethlehem is his home town, where he watched his father’s sheep and Samuel poured oil on his head, and a Philistine garrison is sitting in it. What he says is not an order, and the writer is careful to show it. It is what a homesick man says when he is tired, and it means: I wish I were home.

Broke through the camp of the Philistines. Twelve miles each way, through an occupied town, past a garrison, to a well in the open by the gate, the most exposed place in Bethlehem, and back again carrying water. Nobody sent them, and there was no military purpose whatever; their commander wanted it, and that was enough.

But he would not drink of it. This has occasionally been read as ingratitude, and it is the opposite. He poured it out to the LORD, the language of a drink offering: he does not tip it away, he offers it. The blood of the men is his reasoning, and it is exactly right. Three men nearly died to fill that cup, and what is in it now is not simply water; it has their lives in it. So he gives it to God, the only one worth what it cost.

A rebuke he takes on himself. He is honest enough not to hide it. He said a careless thing where his men could hear. A leader’s passing wish is never harmless: three of them risked everything for a remark he made without thinking, and he will not benefit from that. Anyone with authority, a parent, a manager, a pastor, should notice how their words land on people who want to please them.

The cup reversed. Here a king refuses a cup bought with his servants’ blood. The Son of David reverses it. He does not let his people die to bring him what he wants; he pours out his own blood for them and puts the cup in their hands: “This cup that is poured out for you is the new covenant in my blood” (Luke 22:20).

Abishai, the brother of Joab. Abishai (vv. 18–19) is the man who wanted to spear Saul in his sleep, twice asked to behead Shimei, and killed the giant standing over David (21:17). He has a name in this list, and he earned it.

A lion in a pit on a day when snow had fallen. Snow in that country is rare enough to be worth recording. Benaiah went down into the pit with the animal, on a day when the footing was bad and the sides slippery, and killed it there (v. 20). His Egyptian (v. 21) is, in Chronicles, five cubits tall, about seven and a half feet, with a spear like a weaver’s beam (1 Chronicles 11:23), which is the Goliath description again: David’s men face giants as he did, and they learned it from him. The man set over the royal guard in verse 23 ends up commanding Solomon’s whole army, and he is the man who finally executes Joab (1 Kings 2:34).

Uncertain wording. The “two ariels of Moab” (v. 20) are uncertain, as the ESV note says. The word may mean “lion of God”, a name for champion warriors, which most take to be the sense here; it is also the word for an altar hearth, and some read “two sons of Ariel”. Benaiah, at any rate, killed two of Moab’s best.

Textual note. Josheb-basshebeth killed eight hundred here, three hundred in 1 Chronicles 11:11: numbers in Hebrew manuscripts were easily miscopied, and a copyist may have been influenced by Abishai’s three hundred in verse 18. The chief’s name differs too (Jashobeam in Chronicles; the KJV renders the Hebrew here “The Tachmonite that sat in the seat”), probably for the same reason. Such slips belong to the copying and leave the account itself trustworthy.
verseByVerse.note: The meaning of the word ariel is uncertain (ESV note).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 24–39 — Uriah the Hittite: Thirty-Seven in All
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The roll of David’s thirty shows who God gathered round his king, and it ends with a name that tells the truth about the king. It begins with Asahel, Joab’s brother, long dead, and runs through men from all over Israel and beyond: a man from Saul’s own town of Gibeah, a probable father of Bathsheba, Zelek the Ammonite, Joab’s armour-bearer (vv. 24–38). The last line is “Uriah the Hittite: thirty-seven in all” (v. 39). The writer adds no comment; he lets the name stand where it belongs, among the finest soldiers in the kingdom.
verseByVerse.theology: The roll is a mixture. Israelites from every tribe, a man from Saul's own village, an Ammonite, a Hittite: the foreigners are on the list of Israel's most honoured soldiers, and so is the brother whose death started Joab's feud.
verseByVerse.examples: The last name on the roll of honour is Uriah. The book has already recorded what was done to him and by whom, and here it adds no comment at all.

verseByVerse.quote: Asahel the brother of Joab was one of the thirty; Elhanan the son of Dodo of Bethlehem, Shammah of Harod, Elika of Harod, Helez the Paltite, Ira the son of Ikkesh of Tekoa, Abiezer of Anathoth, Mebunnai the Hushathite, Zalmon the Ahohite, Maharai of Netophah, Heleb the son of Baanah of Netophah, Ittai the son of Ribai of Gibeah of the people of Benjamin, Benaiah of Pirathon, Hiddai of the brooks of Gaash, Abi-albon the Arbathite, Azmaveth of Bahurim, Eliahba the Shaalbonite, the sons of Jashen, Jonathan, Shammah the Hararite, Ahiam the son of Sharar the Hararite, Eliphelet the son of Ahasbai of Maacah, Eliam the son of Ahithophel the Gilonite, Hezro of Carmel, Paarai the Arbite, Igal the son of Nathan of Zobah, Bani the Gadite, Zelek the Ammonite, Naharai of Beeroth, the armor-bearer of Joab the son of Zeruiah, Ira the Ithrite, Gareb the Ithrite, Uriah the Hittite: thirty-seven in all.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The roll of honour gathers men from Joab’s family, Saul’s home town and Israel’s enemies, and it ends with Uriah the Hittite, named without comment in the place he earned, so that the king’s sin stands in the record beside his glory.

Asahel the brother of Joab. The list begins with a dead man. Asahel was “as swift of foot as a wild gazelle” and would not turn aside, and Abner killed him with the butt of a spear at Gibeon (2:18–23), which started the feud that ended in a murder at the gate of Hebron. He is still on the roll. “The thirty” was the name of the elite company, whose members changed over the years; with the Three, Abishai, Benaiah and replacements such as this, the list reaches thirty-seven (v. 39).

Gibeah of the people of Benjamin. Gibeah (v. 29) is Saul’s home town. A man from Saul’s own village and tribe is among the most honoured soldiers in David’s kingdom: the war between Saul’s house and David’s did not set every man of Benjamin against David.

Eliam the son of Ahithophel the Gilonite. Eliam (v. 34) brings two earlier stories together. Ahithophel of Giloh is the counsellor who went over to Absalom and hanged himself, and chapter 11 said the woman on the roof was “Bathsheba, the daughter of Eliam, the wife of Uriah the Hittite” (11:3). So this man is very probably Bathsheba’s father, and Ahithophel her grandfather, and both are in this chapter: one on the roll of honour, one at the end of a rope in Giloh.

Zelek the Ammonite. Zelek (v. 37) comes from the nation whose king shaved David’s envoys and whose capital David’s army besieged.

Uriah the Hittite. The last name in the list is Uriah the Hittite. The writer has already told the story: a spring afternoon, a roof, a woman washing; a man brought back from the front who would not sleep in his own house because “the ark and Israel and Judah dwell in booths, and my lord Joab and the servants of my lord are camping in the open field” (11:11); a letter he carried to Joab with his own hands; a wall at Rabbah. Now, thirty-seventh and last on the roll of the finest soldiers in the kingdom, there he is. There is no asterisk and no comment, no sentence explaining that this is the man the king had killed. The name simply stands where it belongs.

The writer’s method. That is the writer’s whole method, and this is the purest example of it in either book. He seldom tells us what to think. He recorded Saul’s spear and said nothing; the cart at Uzzah’s death and said nothing; the new wives after 5:12 and said nothing. He put “the thing that David had done displeased the LORD” at the end of chapter 11 as the only editorial sentence in twenty-seven verses. Here he does not even do that. He writes the name and stops.

The list as a whole. Uriah was not a peripheral figure but one of the top thirty-seven soldiers in the country, a foreigner who had thrown in with Israel and Israel’s God so thoroughly that his one recorded speech is about the ark being in a field. He was murdered by the man whose list this is, and his name is on it. The book puts the last words and the last name in the same chapter and leaves the reader holding both.

A better King and a better roll. The holding of both is itself the Bible’s answer: the best king Israel had could write a roll of honour with his victim’s name on it, so the people of God needed a King who would never spend a servant’s life for his own sake, but gave his life for them. His roll is kept too, and every name on it was bought by him. “Rejoice that your names are written in heaven” (Luke 10:20).

keyVerse.quote: For does not my house stand so with God? For he has made with me an everlasting covenant, ordered in all things and secure.
keyVerse.note: At the end of a life in which his own house did nearly everything a house can do wrong, David does not list his victories or rehearse his failures. He goes back to God’s promise of chapter 7, whose security does not depend on the man it was made with, and which God kept in Jesus, the Son of David who cannot die again (Acts 13:34).

23.reflection:
David pictures a just ruler, one who rules “in the fear of God”, as morning light and rain on new grass (vv. 3–4). Why are these such fitting pictures? Where have you seen authority, at home, at work or in the church, make others flourish, and how does Jesus fulfil the picture?

At the end of his life David rests on “an everlasting covenant, ordered in all things and secure” (v. 5), not on his achievements or his record. What do you tend to rest on when you look back over your life? What difference does it make that the covenant depends on God and not on us?

Three men risked their lives for a cup of water because of a wish David spoke aloud, and he poured it out to the LORD rather than drink it (vv. 15–17). What does this teach about the weight of a leader’s words? How does it point, by contrast, to the cup Jesus gives us?

The roll of David’s finest soldiers ends with “Uriah the Hittite” and no comment (v. 39). Why do you think the writer did that? What does it show about how Scripture tells the truth about its heroes, and about our need for a better King?

24.title: The Threshing Floor of Araunah
24.text: <sup>1</sup>Again the anger of the LORD was kindled against Israel, and he incited David against them, saying, "Go, number Israel and Judah."<sup>2</sup>So the king said to Joab, the commander of the army, who was with him, "Go through all the tribes of Israel, from Dan to Beersheba, and number the people, that I may know the number of the people."<sup>3</sup>But Joab said to the king, "May the LORD your God add to the people a hundred times as many as they are, while the eyes of my lord the king still see it, but why does my lord the king delight in this thing?"<sup>4</sup>But the king's word prevailed against Joab and the commanders of the army. So Joab and the commanders of the army went out from the presence of the king to number the people of Israel.<sup>5</sup>They crossed the Jordan and began from Aroer, and from the city that is in the middle of the valley, toward Gad and on to Jazer.<sup>6</sup>Then they came to Gilead, and to Kadesh in the land of the Hittites; and they came to Dan, and from Dan they went around to Sidon,<sup>7</sup>and came to the fortress of Tyre and to all the cities of the Hivites and Canaanites; and they went out to the Negeb of Judah at Beersheba.<sup>8</sup>So when they had gone through all the land, they came to Jerusalem at the end of nine months and twenty days.<sup>9</sup>And Joab gave the sum of the numbering of the people to the king: in Israel there were 800,000 valiant men who drew the sword, and the men of Judah were 500,000.<sup>10</sup>But David's heart struck him after he had numbered the people. And David said to the LORD, "I have sinned greatly in what I have done. But now, O LORD, please take away the iniquity of your servant, for I have done very foolishly."<sup>11</sup>And when David arose in the morning, the word of the LORD came to the prophet Gad, David's seer, saying,<sup>12</sup>"Go and say to David, 'Thus says the LORD, Three things I offer you. Choose one of them, that I may do it to you.'"<sup>13</sup>So Gad came to David and told him, and said to him, "Shall three years of famine come to you in your land? Or will you flee three months before your foes while they pursue you? Or shall there be three days' pestilence in your land? Now consider, and decide what answer I shall return to him who sent me."<sup>14</sup>Then David said to Gad, "I am in great distress. Let us fall into the hand of the LORD, for his mercy is great; but let me not fall into the hand of man."<sup>15</sup>So the LORD sent a pestilence on Israel from the morning until the appointed time. And there died of the people from Dan to Beersheba 70,000 men.<sup>16</sup>And when the angel stretched out his hand toward Jerusalem to destroy it, the LORD relented from the calamity and said to the angel who was working destruction among the people, "It is enough; now stay your hand." And the angel of the LORD was by the threshing floor of Araunah the Jebusite.<sup>17</sup>Then David spoke to the LORD when he saw the angel who was striking the people, and said, "Behold, I have sinned, and I have done wickedly. But these sheep, what have they done? Please let your hand be against me and against my father's house."<sup>18</sup>And Gad came that day to David and said to him, "Go up, raise an altar to the LORD on the threshing floor of Araunah the Jebusite."<sup>19</sup>So David went up at Gad's word, as the LORD commanded.<sup>20</sup>And when Araunah looked down, he saw the king and his servants coming on toward him. And Araunah went out and paid homage to the king with his face to the ground.<sup>21</sup>And Araunah said, "Why has my lord the king come to his servant?" David said, "To buy the threshing floor from you, in order to build an altar to the LORD, that the plague may be averted from the people."<sup>22</sup>Then Araunah said to David, "Let my lord the king take and offer up what seems good to him. Here are the oxen for the burnt offering and the threshing sledges and the yokes of the oxen for the wood.<sup>23</sup>All this, O king, Araunah gives to the king." And Araunah said to the king, "May the LORD your God accept you."<sup>24</sup>But the king said to Araunah, "No, but I will buy it from you for a price. I will not offer burnt offerings to the LORD my God that cost me nothing." So David bought the threshing floor and the oxen for fifty shekels of silver.<sup>25</sup>And David built there an altar to the LORD and offered burnt offerings and peace offerings. So the LORD responded to the plea for the land, and the plague was averted from Israel.
24.overview:
Where we are. This is the last chapter of 2 Samuel and the close of the appendix (chapters 21 to 24; see the introduction). It answers chapter 21: there a famine for Saul’s sin, here a plague for David’s, and each ends when the LORD responded to the plea for the land (21:14; 24:25).

The message. Israel’s strength was never its numbers but its God, and when the king forgets it, the people suffer with him. Yet the God whose judgment falls is the God whose mercy is great: he stops the plague himself, and he stops it at an altar, on ground bought at a price that would become the site of the temple. Sin is answered not by the king doing better but by a sacrifice that God commands and accepts.

Why it was said. Later Israel, ruled by kings who trusted armies and alliances, needed to see where their greatest king’s pride led and how it ended: not in triumph but at an altar, on the ground God chose for his house (see the introduction).

How the chapter makes its case. God, already angry with Israel, incites David, who counts his fighting men over Joab’s protest for nine months and twenty days (vv. 1–9). He confesses, chooses to fall into the hand of the LORD rather than of men, and, as seventy thousand die and God stays the angel’s hand at Jerusalem, pleads for the people he counted as soldiers as his sheep (vv. 10–17). He buys the threshing floor of Araunah rather than take it free, offers sacrifices, and the plague is averted (vv. 18–25).

Where it leads. To Christ by pattern, by the need the chapter exposes, and by the place itself. David asks to bear the judgment for his sheep and cannot; Jesus, the Son of David and the good shepherd, “lays down his life for the sheep” (John 10:11). The plague ends at a sacrifice on Moriah, where Abraham once named the place the LORD will provide (Genesis 22:14), and in the same city God “did not spare his own Son but gave him up for us all” (Romans 8:32), so that judgment stopped on him for good. David would not offer what cost him nothing; God gave what cost him everything.

For us. Do not rest your security in your numbers, whatever you count: they cannot save, and delight in them is a quiet idol. When you have sinned, fall into the hands of the God whose mercy is great, and trust the sacrifice he has provided rather than any payment of your own. Then give him worship that costs you something, gladly, because you were bought with a price.
24.theology:
Who incited David (v. 1)? Samuel says the LORD; Chronicles, written later, says Satan (1 Chronicles 21:1); and David says the choice was his own and takes the blame (v. 10). All three are true at different levels. Satan wanted David to fall and was the near tempter. God, already angry at Israel's sin, did not put evil into David's heart, for he tempts no one (James 1:13); he allowed Satan to work on a pride already there, within limits, and turned the outcome into a judgment. The pattern is Job's: Satan asks leave and executes the disasters, yet Job says the LORD gave, and the LORD has taken away, and the narrator approves the sentence (Job 1:21-22). Chronicles names the near agent and Samuel the ultimate governor, and neither cancels David's guilt. (The Hebrew of 1 Chronicles 21:1 has no article, and a few scholars read it as a human adversary; most translators take it as the name Satan.) Scripture will not let God be a bystander, nor the author of evil, and it does not explain the mechanism: the same tension stood at 17:14, where God ordained the outcome of a council in which every man freely did what he thought best.

These sheep, what have they done? (v. 17). He upgrades his own verdict (foolish in verse 10, wicked here) and then changes the word for the people. Shepherd is what this history has called the office from the day the elders came to Hebron (5:2) and in God's own words in the covenant (7:8). He counted them as soldiers and now calls them sheep, and that one word is the whole correction of the chapter: a census turns people into a figure on a tally, while a shepherd knows them as creatures that cannot look after themselves.
