Then he offers himself, not as a bargain, since he has nothing to trade, but asking that the judgment fall where the guilt is. The offer is refused, because a sinner cannot pay for other sinners. But there is a Son of David who stood over that same city, wept over it, and did what this man could only ask to do.

A threshing floor is the right place (v. 18). Grain is beaten and winnowed there, so it is the standard biblical picture of judgment; and it is also where the harvest is gathered. Judgment and provision happen on the same floor.

Where the book stops (v. 25). The threshing floor where judgment stopped is the ground where Solomon would build the temple, on Mount Moriah, where Abraham once offered Isaac and named the place the LORD will provide. One hill holds Abraham and Isaac and the ram, David and the angel and the fifty shekels, Solomon's temple, and, in the same city outside a wall, a Son of David on whom judgment stopped for good.
24.examples:
Then: A man was offered, free and sincerely, everything he needed to stop a plague that was killing his people (the land, the animals, and a farmer’s own working tools broken up for firewood), and he refused it and counted out fifty shekels of silver, because he would not give God something that had cost him nothing.

Now: Three things. Verse 1 is the one to hold carefully rather than solve: Scripture attributes the same event to God and to Satan and to a man's own choice, and refuses to let go of any of the three, and an account of God’s rule over events that drops one of them is not this book's account. Second, verse 14, which belongs in the memory against a bad day: not that God will go easy, but that if you must be dealt with, you would rather it were by the one whose mercy is great than by anyone else at their kindest. And third, the last sentence. Costless worship is the easiest thing in the world and does not feel like anything at all: nothing given up, nothing missed, nothing difficult. He was entitled to take the land. He paid for it. Not to buy God's favour: the plague stopped because God said it is enough, and the one sacrifice that answers for sin was paid by God himself, who did not spare his own Son. What we give is thanks, and the Spirit who has made us his own is the one who makes us glad to give it.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A king who had learned that the LORD “saves not with sword and spear” now wants to know how many swords he has. Verse 1 sets the event under God’s rule and his anger with Israel; Chronicles names Satan as the tempter; the guilt is David’s (v. 1). Joab, no scrupulous man, sees the pleasure behind the order and objects, but the king’s word prevails (vv. 2–4). For nine months and twenty days the commanders cross the land, from beyond the Jordan north to Dan and the coast and down to Beersheba (vv. 5–8). The total is the whole point: 1,300,000 men who drew the sword (v. 9).
verseByVerse.theology: Chronicles names Satan as the one who incited David; Samuel names the LORD. The Bible attributes one event to both without embarrassment, just as it says of the cross that men did what God's plan had predestined and that they were lawless men (Acts 2:23; 4:28).
verseByVerse.examples: The text never says what was wrong with a census, but the evidence converges: Joab objects; the count is of men who drew the sword; and the law required a ransom to be paid at any census, that there be no plague among them when you number them (Ex. 30:12).

verseByVerse.quote: Again the anger of the LORD was kindled against Israel, and he incited David against them, saying, "Go, number Israel and Judah." So the king said to Joab, the commander of the army, who was with him, "Go through all the tribes of Israel, from Dan to Beersheba, and number the people, that I may know the number of the people." But Joab said to the king, "May the LORD your God add to the people a hundred times as many as they are, while the eyes of my lord the king still see it, but why does my lord the king delight in this thing?" But the king's word prevailed against Joab and the commanders of the army. So Joab and the commanders of the army went out from the presence of the king to number the people of Israel. They crossed the Jordan and began from Aroer, and from the city that is in the middle of the valley, toward Gad and on to Jazer. Then they came to Gilead, and to Kadesh in the land of the Hittites; and they came to Dan, and from Dan they went around to Sidon, and came to the fortress of Tyre and to all the cities of the Hivites and Canaanites; and they went out to the Negeb of Judah at Beersheba. So when they had gone through all the land, they came to Jerusalem at the end of nine months and twenty days. And Joab gave the sum of the numbering of the people to the king: in Israel there were 800,000 valiant men who drew the sword, and the men of Judah were 500,000.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In a year when God is already angry with Israel, David orders a count of his fighting men, taking delight in his own strength rather than the LORD’s, and presses on for nine months against his own general’s protest. God governs the whole event, Satan is its tempter, and the guilt is David’s.

Again the anger of the LORD was kindled against Israel. Why God is angry with Israel the writer does not say; again points back to the famine of chapter 21. The harder problem is that God incited David to do a thing for which seventy thousand people then die, while the Chronicler, recording the same event, writes then Satan stood against Israel and incited David to number Israel (1 Chronicles 21:1).

The pattern from Job. As the theology above sets out, the pattern is Job’s: Satan the near agent, God the one who governs, David the one who chose. Neither account makes God the tempter (James 1:13), and neither excuses David, whose own confession in verse 10 owns the choice. The New Testament speaks the same way of the cross: Jesus was delivered up according to the definite plan and foreknowledge of God, and in the same sentence crucified by the hands of lawless men who are held responsible for it (Acts 2:23). What Scripture will not allow is either half alone.

That I may know the number of the people. Verse 9 states what is being counted: men who drew the sword. This is a military inventory, not a population survey, and it is exactly what this history has argued against from the beginning. Jonathan at Michmash said nothing can hinder the LORD from saving by many or by few (1 Samuel 14:6). David in the valley said the LORD saves not with sword and spear (1 Samuel 17:47). He hamstrung the captured chariot horses (8:4), because the law said a king must not multiply them. The man who wrote some trust in chariots and some in horses (Psalm 20:7) is counting his soldiers.

A ransom for every life. The law is precise about this. When Israel took a census, every man counted paid a half-shekel ransom for his life, that there be no plague among them when you number them (Exodus 30:12). The people belong to God, not to the king; numbering them without acknowledging that carries a stated penalty, plague, and plague is what falls in this chapter.

But Joab said to the king. Joab’s objection (v. 3) should make any reader stop. This is the man who murdered Abner at a gate, killed Absalom against a direct order, knifed Amasa in a road, and told his king to stop grieving for his own son. He does not call the census sinful; he says, shrewdly, that God can multiply the people a hundredfold anyway, so what is the point? Why does my lord the king delight in this thing? Delight gives it away: this is not administration but the pleasure of seeing a large number with his name on it.

Nobody stops him. Nathan is not mentioned, and nobody tells David it is a sin until it is done. The men best placed to stop him, the general and the commanders, tried and were overruled (v. 4).

At the end of nine months and twenty days. Bathsheba was an afternoon; this took the better part of a year, a field operation from beyond the Jordan to Dan, round by Sidon and Tyre and down to Beersheba (vv. 5–8), and on any day of it David could have sent a rider to call it off.

Valiant men who drew the sword. The total is 1,300,000 fighting men, the largest number in the book. The Chronicler gives 1,100,000 and 470,000 and notes that Joab left Levi and Benjamin out of the count, because the king’s command was abhorrent to him (1 Chronicles 21:5–6); the two tallies most plausibly count slightly different things.

The comfort of a large number. Joab’s question reaches well past ancient Israel. We count steps, followers, sales, savings and attendance, and we feel the number before we think about it: up feels like safety, down like fear. Counting is not the problem; a whole book of the Bible is named after two censuses. The problem is the delight. When a number becomes the place I rest, it has become a small god, and like every idol it promises security and delivers anxiety, because there is always a larger figure somewhere and the count can always fall. It is telling that David did this in old age, when strength was going and a big total could reassure him that he was still the man he had been. The gospel turns the census inside out. The shepherd in Jesus’ parable leaves the ninety-nine to look for one (Luke 15:4), and the good shepherd “calls his own sheep by name” (John 10:3). Someone known like that does not need a large number to feel safe.

Why do the numbers differ from Chronicles? Numbers in Hebrew manuscripts were easily miscopied, since they were often written with letters or abbreviations, and parallel accounts sometimes count different things, such as a total and a part. Neither touches what the passage teaches, and those who hold Scripture to be without error have always meant what was first written, not every later copy (see the introduction).

Where Christians differ. All agree that God is not the author of sin and that David was guilty. Arminians read verse 1 as permission: God allowed Satan to tempt David and did not prevent it. Reformed Christians hold that he ordains whatever comes to pass, sinful acts included, without doing evil, and governs the means (here Satan’s malice and David’s pride) to bring a just judgment on Israel.

This commentary’s view. The second. Samuel’s bare he incited David says more than permission, and Scripture speaks the same way of the cross (Acts 4:28). Yet God tempts no one (James 1:13): the desire was David’s own, and the malice was Satan’s. How God ordains without tempting, Scripture does not explain.

Uncertain wording. One place on the route is uncertain (v. 6). Where the ESV has Kadesh in the land of the Hittites, following the Greek Old Testament, the Hebrew reads the land of Tahtim-hodshi, a name found nowhere else and possibly a damaged phrase. The route itself is clear.
verseByVerse.note: Chronicles says Satan incited David (1 Chr 21:1); Samuel names the LORD, who rules even over Satan’s work (compare Job 1–2).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 10–17 — Let Us Fall into the Hand of the LORD
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Judgment falls, but David chooses to fall into the hands of a merciful God. Only when the total is read out does his heart strike him, and he confesses before anyone accuses him (v. 10). Through the prophet Gad the LORD offers three judgments (vv. 11–13), and David chooses the one with no human hand in it, “for his mercy is great” (v. 14). The plague runs from Dan to Beersheba, the very route of the census, and seventy thousand die, until the LORD himself says “It is enough; now stay your hand” at the threshing floor of Araunah (vv. 15–16). Seeing the angel, the king who counted soldiers pleads for his sheep and asks that the blow fall on him and his house (v. 17).
verseByVerse.theology: Verse 14 is a real theological judgment and not an evasion. Two of the three options put him in the hands of people: famine means dependence on neighbours who sell grain, and flight means enemy soldiers. He chooses the one where the only hand on him is God's, and gives the reason: his mercy is great.
verseByVerse.examples: Verse 17 is shepherd language, the word this whole history has used for the office (5:2; 7:8). He asks for the judgment to fall on himself instead, and it is the last thing he asks for in this book.

verseByVerse.quote: But David's heart struck him after he had numbered the people. And David said to the LORD, "I have sinned greatly in what I have done. But now, O LORD, please take away the iniquity of your servant, for I have done very foolishly." And when David arose in the morning, the word of the LORD came to the prophet Gad, David's seer, saying, "Go and say to David, 'Thus says the LORD, Three things I offer you. Choose one of them, that I may do it to you.'" So Gad came to David and told him, and said to him, "Shall three years of famine come to you in your land? Or will you flee three months before your foes while they pursue you? Or shall there be three days' pestilence in your land? Now consider, and decide what answer I shall return to him who sent me." Then David said to Gad, "I am in great distress. Let us fall into the hand of the LORD, for his mercy is great; but let me not fall into the hand of man." So the LORD sent a pestilence on Israel from the morning until the appointed time. And there died of the people from Dan to Beersheba 70,000 men. And when the angel stretched out his hand toward Jerusalem to destroy it, the LORD relented from the calamity and said to the angel who was working destruction among the people, "It is enough; now stay your hand." And the angel of the LORD was by the threshing floor of Araunah the Jebusite. Then David spoke to the LORD when he saw the angel who was striking the people, and said, "Behold, I have sinned, and I have done wickedly. But these sheep, what have they done? Please let your hand be against me and against my father's house."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Struck by conscience, David confesses unprompted, chooses to fall into the hand of the God whose mercy is great rather than into the hands of men, and, watching the plague, pleads for the people he had counted as soldiers as his sheep, asking that the judgment fall on him. God himself stops the plague.

David’s heart struck him. Only after nine months, a general’s warning and the total read out does his heart strike him (v. 10). The phrase has appeared once before, of the same man. In the cave at Engedi, after he cut the corner off Saul’s robe, David’s heart struck him (1 Samuel 24:5). Then a piece of cloth troubled his conscience; here it takes nine months and a number.

I have sinned greatly in what I have done. No prophet has spoken and nobody has confronted him; he works it out himself and says it to God. The last phrase stings: I have done very foolishly. Not yet wickedly: stupidly. An old man has done what a young man would have known better than to do.

The prophet Gad, David’s seer. Gad has been with him since the years in hiding, when he told David to leave the stronghold (1 Samuel 22:5), and here he is at the end of the reign, some forty years on. The choice he brings is itself part of the judgment. David is not told what will happen; he has to pick it, knowing the cost of each, and then live with having picked.

Let us fall into the hand of the LORD. Verse 14 is the best sentence in the chapter, and a real theological judgment rather than an evasion. Famine means years of buying grain from neighbouring nations: Israel at the mercy of people. Flight means being hunted by soldiers, the hand of man in its plainest form, as he knows from years of being hunted. Pestilence has no human agent at all: nobody to negotiate with, nobody to be merciful or merciless, nothing between the people and God.

For his mercy is great. That is a considerable thing to say while choosing a punishment. He is not saying God will go easy, but that he would rather be dealt with by God at his severest than by people at their kindest, because there is mercy in God and there may be none anywhere else. A man hunted by Saul, betrayed by Ahithophel, cursed by Shimei, lied to by Ziba and driven out by his own son has good reason to expect little mercy from people.

From Dan to Beersheba. Seventy thousand die (v. 15), and from Dan to Beersheba is the phrase of the census route (v. 2). The plague goes exactly where the counting went.

It is enough; now stay your hand. The judgment stops because God stops it (v. 16). And the writer marks the place with care, because it is about to become the point of the chapter: a particular threshing floor just outside Jerusalem.

I have done wickedly. In verse 17 David passes a harsher verdict on himself: foolish in verse 10, and now, looking at what it has cost, wicked. Then: these sheep, what have they done? That is shepherd language, the word this history has used for the office from the day the elders came to Hebron, you shall be shepherd of my people Israel (5:2), and in God’s own words in the covenant, I took you from the pasture, from following the sheep (7:8).

But these sheep, what have they done? He counted them as soldiers; he now calls them sheep. A census turns people into a figure on a tally; a shepherd knows them as creatures that cannot look after themselves. He wanted to know how many swords he had; now he watches them die and calls them a flock.

Against me and against my father’s house. His offer of himself is not a bargain; he has nothing to trade. He asks that the judgment fall where the guilt is, the one request he is entitled to make, with the same instinct that made him say to Abiathar decades earlier, I have occasioned the death of all the persons of your father’s house (1 Samuel 22:22).

The Shepherd who could. David’s offer is never taken up. A guilty man cannot bear the judgment of other guilty men, and the plague ends because God says it is enough, not because David pays. But a Son of David would stand over the same city and weep over it (Luke 19:41), and do what David could only ask to do: “The good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep” (John 10:11). On him the hand of God did fall, so that it need never fall on his flock.

Why did 70,000 die for David’s sin, and why was God angry with Israel? Verse 1 says the anger was already there: Israel itself had sinned, perhaps in the rebellions of Absalom and Sheba. The census was David’s pride, and the plague judged king and people together, as a nation stood or fell with its king.

Does God change his mind? His purposes never change (1 Samuel 15:29); relented (v. 16) describes his real response of mercy in human terms.

Textual note. Verse 13’s three years of famine follows 1 Chronicles 21:12 and the Greek Old Testament (the Septuagint); the Hebrew text of Samuel has seven, most likely a copying change.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The judgment ends at an altar, on ground David insists on paying for. Gad sends him to the spot where the angel stopped, and he goes at once (vv. 18–19). Araunah the Jebusite bows and offers everything as a gift: the floor, the oxen, even his threshing sledges and yokes for the fire (vv. 20–23). David refuses: “I will not offer burnt offerings to the LORD my God that cost me nothing” (v. 24). He pays fifty shekels, builds the altar, offers burnt offerings and peace offerings, and the LORD answers the plea for the land (v. 25). The ground will become the site of Solomon’s temple on Mount Moriah, and the book ends there.
verseByVerse.theology: Araunah's offer is generous and entirely sincere, and David refuses it in the last sentence he speaks in this book. Worship that costs the worshipper nothing is not worship of this God, and he will not begin a national altar with a gift somebody else paid for.
verseByVerse.examples: The ground he buys is the site of the temple. The Chronicler says so outright (2 Chron. 3:1), and Moriah is where Abraham was sent with Isaac (Gen. 22:2). The book ends on that ground, at the place where God stopped the judgment.

verseByVerse.quote: And Gad came that day to David and said to him, "Go up, raise an altar to the LORD on the threshing floor of Araunah the Jebusite." So David went up at Gad's word, as the LORD commanded. And when Araunah looked down, he saw the king and his servants coming on toward him. And Araunah went out and paid homage to the king with his face to the ground. And Araunah said, "Why has my lord the king come to his servant?" David said, "To buy the threshing floor from you, in order to build an altar to the LORD, that the plague may be averted from the people." Then Araunah said to David, "Let my lord the king take and offer up what seems good to him. Here are the oxen for the burnt offering and the threshing sledges and the yokes of the oxen for the wood. All this, O king, Araunah gives to the king." And Araunah said to the king, "May the LORD your God accept you." But the king said to Araunah, "No, but I will buy it from you for a price. I will not offer burnt offerings to the LORD my God that cost me nothing." So David bought the threshing floor and the oxen for fifty shekels of silver. And David built there an altar to the LORD and offered burnt offerings and peace offerings. So the LORD responded to the plea for the land, and the plague was averted from Israel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
At the very place where God stopped the judgment, David buys a threshing floor he could have had for nothing, because he will not offer God worship that costs him nothing, and the plague ends at the altar he builds there. That ground becomes the temple mount, and the book ends on it.

On the threshing floor of Araunah the Jebusite. He is sent to the exact spot where the angel stopped (v. 18), and a threshing floor is the right place for what follows. Grain was beaten there and tossed into the wind so that the chaff blew away: the standard biblical picture of judgment, used by John the Baptist of Christ, whose winnowing fork is in his hand (Matthew 3:12). It is also where the harvest is gathered. Judgment and provision happen on the same floor.

All this, O king, Araunah gives to the king. Araunah is a Jebusite, one of the people who held Jerusalem before David took it, still farming outside the city his people lost. His offer is complete and generous, and there is no reason to think it insincere: the land, the animals and the wood, and the wood is his threshing sledges and ox yokes. A man is offering to break up the tools of his own trade for firewood so that a sacrifice can be made. And he says may the LORD your God accept you, which from a Jebusite is remarkable.

I will not offer burnt offerings to the LORD my God that cost me nothing. David’s answer (v. 24) is his last recorded sentence in the book of Samuel. Nothing about the gift was improper, and David could have taken it with a clear conscience while the plague raged. The principle is not about ownership: a sacrifice that costs the one offering it nothing is not a sacrifice. Its whole meaning is that something of yours is given up; take the cost away and what is left is a ceremony with somebody else’s animal on it.

From counting to giving. This is the man who counted his soldiers. The census was about accumulating: a large number, held and admired. His last recorded act is to spend money on ground he could have had free.

The LORD responded to the plea for the land. The identical phrase closes the Rizpah chapter (21:14). Both times it follows an act of costly obedience rather than an act of violence.

Why the book stops here. The Chronicler says plainly that Solomon built the temple on Mount Moriah … on the threshing floor of Ornan the Jebusite (2 Chronicles 3:1). The ground David buys in the last verses of this book is where Solomon will build the house David was not allowed to build, where Israel’s sacrifices will be offered for nearly four centuries, and where the whole nation will come three times a year.

Mount Moriah. And Moriah is where God sent Abraham with his son and a knife, telling him to go to the land of Moriah, and offer him there as a burnt offering on one of the mountains of which I shall tell you (Genesis 22:2): the place where a father raised a knife over a son, a ram was found caught in a thicket, and Abraham named the place the LORD will provide.

Gilboa and Moriah. 1 Samuel ended on Mount Gilboa: a king dead on his own sword, his sons killed around him, his body fastened to a Philistine wall, and the men of Jabesh-gilead walking all night to bring the bones home. 2 Samuel ends on a different hill, with an altar, a plague stopped, and a man paying for ground he could have had for nothing. Between them is everything: a boy with a sling, a spear thrown four times, a cave, a crown, an ark, a covenant, a roof, a letter, a forest, a room over a gate, a psalm, and a list of thirty-seven names ending with Uriah the Hittite. The writer has told all of it without excusing any of it, and he ends not on a throne, a battlefield or a deathbed, but at an altar on a rock outside the city, where God stopped the judgment. That is where the whole story was always going.

What the altar was for. We tend to hear “burnt offering” as a present to win round an angry god. Israel was taught to see it the other way. The worshipper laid his hand on the animal’s head, “and it shall be accepted for him to make atonement for him” (Leviticus 1:4): the animal died in his place, and God himself had appointed it. That is atonement: guilty people brought back to God because a substitute bears what they deserved. So the plague stops at an altar, not at a promise from David to do better.

The true and better Isaac. Timothy Keller often pointed out that Jesus is the true and better Isaac. On this ridge Abraham was spared the loss of his son; in this same city, outside its wall, God gave his. David counted out fifty shekels of silver; we were ransomed “not with perishable things such as silver or gold, but with the precious blood of Christ, like that of a lamb without blemish or spot” (1 Peter 1:18–19). Forgiveness costs us nothing because it cost him everything.

Do not bargain. We keep trying to pay for sin with something cheap: a good week, a resolution, feeling bad for long enough. When old guilt comes back, do not bargain; rest your whole weight on the sacrifice already made, and thank him. David’s principle is not a price for pardon but the thanks of the forgiven, glad to give what costs them something.

Fifty shekels or six hundred? David paid fifty shekels of silver for the threshing floor and oxen; Chronicles gives six hundred shekels of gold (1 Chronicles 21:25), probably the price of the whole surrounding site, which became the temple mount. Araunah and Ornan are two spellings of one man’s name; the Hebrew spells it more than one way even within this chapter.

Uncertain wording. The Hebrew of verse 23 reads literally all this Araunah the king gives to the king. Most translations, like the ESV, take the first king as Araunah addressing David (O king). A few suggest he had once been the Jebusite king of Jerusalem, but the phrase is too slight to bear that.
verseByVerse.note: Compare 1 Chronicles 21:18-22:1, where David names this place as the site for the house of the LORD.

keyVerse.quote: But the king said to Araunah, “No, but I will buy it from you for a price. I will not offer burnt offerings to the LORD my God that cost me nothing.”
keyVerse.note: David’s last recorded words in the book turn the place where judgment stopped into a place of worship, on the ground where the temple would stand. Worship that costs nothing is not worship of this God, yet the price never buys pardon: the altar on this hill points to the sacrifice God himself would provide, which cost him his Son.

24.reflection:
David counted his fighting men, and Joab saw that he “delighted” in the number (vv. 1–9). What numbers do you find yourself resting in (savings, followers, results, attendance), and how can you tell when counting has become trusting?

Samuel says the LORD incited David, Chronicles says Satan did, and David says the sin was his own (v. 1; v. 10). How does holding all three together help when you face hard providences, or are tempted to blame God or the devil for your own choices?

David would rather fall into the hand of the LORD, “for his mercy is great”, than into the hand of man (v. 14). Why is that a wise choice for someone who knows he is guilty? How does the cross make it even more certain for us?

“I will not offer burnt offerings to the LORD my God that cost me nothing” (v. 24). What would worship that costs you something look like this month, and how do we keep such giving from turning into an attempt to pay for our own forgiveness?
